The first thing Theo felt upon waking was the dull, persistent ache across his chest—a tight, burning pull whenever he shifted. The cuts from the ring were healing, but healing was a process, not an instant reprieve. He lay still for a moment, eyes closed, measuring the extent of the damage with the same clinical detachment he used to assess everything in his body: the bandages were tight, the stitches held, and the bruising would fade in another few days. Good enough. The second thing he felt was the absence beside him. He cracked one eye open, fingers sliding across cool sheets where Jackie should have been. The impression of her body was still faintly visible in the fabric, but she was gone. He exhaled slowly, pushing himself upright with a wince as the wound on his arm protested. The room was cold—colder than Tuscany had been—and the gray Scottish morning light filtered through the curtains like something grudgingly offered. Theo sat on the edge of the bed, barefoot on the flagstones, and rolled his neck until it cracked. His hair was a disaster, dark waves falling loose over his forehead, and he didn't bother fixing it. Instead, he reached for the pack of cigarettes on the nightstand, lit one with a flick of his wand, and inhaled deeply. The smoke curled around him as he glanced toward the door. She's downstairs. He knew without checking the bond. There was a faint hum of tension radiating through it—not panic, not pain, but something sharper. Anticipation. Uncertainty. He could feel her thinking, the way her mind moved in circles when she was debating something she didn't want to admit mattered. The vial. Theo dragged another lungful of smoke and stubbed the cigarette out on the edge of the stone sill. He pulled on a pair of dark trousers, left the bandages visible across his bare chest, and padded barefoot out of the bedroom. The Manor was silent, save for the creak of old wood settling and the distant whistle of wind against the leaded glass. He moved quietly—instinct, more than intention—his footsteps soft on the stone stairs as he descended toward the kitchen. She was standing by the table when he entered, the vial in front of her like an accusation.

Theo paused in the doorway, one shoulder braced against the frame, pale blue eyes tracking the line of her body—bare feet, thin nightgown, the tension in her shoulders visible even from behind. He didn't announce himself. He just watched her for a moment, letting the silence stretch. "Couldn't sleep?" His voice was low, rough from smoke and the lingering remnants of sleep. He pushed off the doorframe and crossed the room, his movements deliberate, unhurried. He stopped beside her, close enough that his arm brushed hers, and looked down at the vial. "Or couldn't decide?"
He didn't reach for it. He didn't push. But the question hung between them, sharp and direct, because Theo had never been good at pretending things weren't what they were. His gaze shifted to her face, studying the mismatched eyes—moss-green and glacial blue—searching for the answer she wasn't saying out loud. He could feel the knot of tension in her gut through the bond, the way it twisted and pulled, and he resisted the urge to reach for her. Instead, he leaned back against the table, arms crossing loosely over his chest, ignoring the way the movement tugged at the stitches. "You're afraid of what you'll see," he said quietly. Not a question. A statement. "Fair enough. I'd be afraid too."
He tilted his head, watching her with the same intensity he always did—like she was the only thing in the room that mattered. The corner of his mouth twitched, not quite a smile, more a acknowledgment of shared danger. "But you're standing here at dawn, staring at it like it's going to bite you. So either you're going to take it, or you're going to put it away and stop torturing yourself." He paused, letting the words settle. "What's it going to be, Menace?"

Jackie was so deep in her thoughts and Theo moved so quietly, that she  flinched visibly when she heard his voice. It did something to her — as it always did in the mornings, low and rough. She could smell the cigarette smoke on him, and it wasn't an unpleasant smell. It was just… Theo's. 
She turned her head to look at him, and even despite the bandages it stole her breath for a second — the plain of his bare chest, sleep tousled hair, sharp blue eyes. She bit on her lip, before she could stop herself.
But then he reached over, stealing her cup and directed her mind back to the vial that rested innocently on the table. It was completely oblivious to her dilemma, just an inanimate object. And yet Jackie had a distinct feeling that it was mocking her.
"I'd blame it on the jet lag, but there's almost no time difference between Italy and here so…" she smiled at him faintly, taking back her cup and refilling it from the pot.
Then she fixed her eyes back on the vial.
"What's the worst thing I'm going to see if I drink it? I'll see it anyway, so you might as well tell me now."
It was one thing to accept Theo for the man and the monster he was. To accept the darkness in him in principle and not be afraid of its effects. It would be a different thing completely to experience it first-hand. Every ugly feeling, every shred of pain or guilt, but also the enjoyment he felt while he hurt her, or someone else.

The question landed, and Theo was quiet for a long moment.

Not the quiet of someone avoiding it. The quiet of someone actually considering it. He took the mug when she offered the refill, curled both hands around the ceramic, and stared at the steam.

"Rage," he said finally. "That's probably what would hit first." He set the mug down on the table, not looking at her yet. "Not the kind that looks like shouting. The kind that sits still and waits. I've had it my whole life and I've made peace with it, but you'd feel it the way I feel it—cold, very controlled, and hungry." He paused. "That'll be uncomfortable."

He picked up the vial. Turned it once between his fingers, watching the dark blood catch the pale morning light.

"You'll feel how much I want things. How much I want *you*—not just in bed, but—" He stopped himself, jaw tightening slightly. "It's a lot. It might read as suffocating from the outside."

He set it back down.

"And you'll feel the tether. What it actually is, not what I've described it as. Every time you've been in pain. Every time you've been afraid. I've felt all of it, and I've kept it—" He touched two fingers to his sternum briefly. "In here. That's going to be a lot of stored weight to walk into."

He looked at her then. Full on, unguarded in the way he only ever was in the early morning, when the performance of the day hadn't quite settled over him yet.

"You won't feel guilt the way you might expect. I've worked through most of what I did to you—not erased it, worked through it. What you'll find there is more like scar tissue than an open wound." His voice dropped. "But it's ugly scar tissue. Don't mistake that."

He reached out and tucked a curl back from her face, his thumb grazing her cheek briefly before his hand dropped.

"The worst thing isn't anything I've done." He was very still now. "The worst thing is how much I like having you. Not loved—*liked*. Like something that is mine and I would level everything around me to keep. You'll feel that too." His pale eyes held hers. "And you'll have to decide whether that frightens you or not."

The wind pressed against the windowpanes. The clock ticked somewhere deeper in the house.

Theo leaned back against the table and crossed his arms again, watching her hold the weight of that. He didn't soften it. She'd asked a direct question, and she deserved a direct answer—not a curated version, not the parts he was comfortable with. The whole thing, laid out in the gray Scottish morning light, because she'd earned that much from him.

"Still want to know what you're walking into?" he asked. "Or has that answered it well enough?"

She didn't interrupt him. She took another mug, because she really meant to drink the first one but he took it away from her as if she offered it to him. She didn't mind, it wasn't something she wanted to argue over. She filled the mug with the last of the coffee from the pot, then added milk. She never could drink it black as Theo and enjoy it. 
What he said didn't surprise Jackie. She suspected as much, or something similar. But to suspect it and to know it made a difference for her. Suddenly a thought crossed her mind and she laughed quietly.
"You know, instead of going back to do the Ministry work after your leave is finished, you should start working as a bouncer in Knocktur. Or something in that area. Much more opportunity to beat someone up and not feel sorry about it."
Jackie knew she was deflecting, stalling. Putting out the moment when she had to make a decision. And slowly the realisation of why was dawning on her. Because she had already made the decision. She just wanted a few more minutes of being just herself, before she'd become privy to the most intimate parts of someone else.

Theo laughed. Actually laughed—a short, genuine sound that broke the weight of the room. It softened his face briefly into something younger, less composed.

"The Ministry pays better." He reached over and stole a sip from her mug. The one with milk. He pulled a face immediately.

"That's terrible."

He set it back down in front of her with an expression of mild offense, as if she'd done it to him deliberately. He picked up his own abandoned mug—black, cold by now—and drank it anyway.

The silence that followed was different from the one before. Less loaded. He let it sit, watching her turn the mug in her hands, watching the way her eyes kept drifting back to the vial without her seeming to notice she was doing it.

*She's already decided.*

He'd felt it shift through the bond about thirty seconds into his answer. Not resolve exactly—more like the moment before someone steps off a ledge they've been standing on for too long. The decision made, the body just needing time to catch up.

He didn't say it. He gave her the minutes she was taking, because she was allowed to have them. He'd had years to grow accustomed to the weight of what lived inside him. She was about to inherit access to it in a single swallow. The least he could do was not rush her toward the edge.

He reached past her and turned the vial once on the table. Not offering it. Just acknowledging it was there.

"For what it's worth," he said, quieter now, "I've never wanted you to know me less." His thumb stilled against the glass. "Every version of it. Even the parts I'm not proud of." He paused. "Especially those."

He lifted his eyes to hers. The pale blue was very direct in the gray morning light, nothing hidden in it.

"Whatever you feel when you take it—whatever hits you first—I'm right here." His hand moved from the vial to rest flat on the table between them. Not reaching for her. Just present. "You don't have to explain your reaction to me. You don't have to manage it."

A beat.

"I already know what I am, Menace. I'm just waiting to find out what *you* make of it."

Jackie rolled her eyes when he stole her cup for the third time.  
"Serves you right, thief." She barked, snatching her cup back as soon as he let go of it. "First you stole my virginity, then my heart, then my hand, then my innermost feelings." She softened her voice fractionally at that. "And now my coffee? What's next? My sanity, apparently."  
She loved their banter, and a small, mischievous smirk bloomed on her lips as she downed the cup in a few long swigs. She put it on the counter beside her.   
"You know… I'm not really afraid of seeing all that. The part I'm *actually* afraid of, is how it'll make me react. That I'll react wrong, or that I'll recoil and it'll hurt you and… I will be able to *feel* that my reaction hurts you."  
Jackie snagged the vial from the table in a sudden movement. She opened the glass cork, and held it there — in front of her, close to her mouth, between her and him.  
"Okay. I'll do it. But you have to promise me something." She smiled again, that naughty, mischievous smirk. "Only good feelings today."  
And with that, she put the vial to her mouth and drank.

The blood hit the back of her throat and tasted like iron and old magic—metallic and dark, with something underneath it that wasn't quite a flavor. More like a frequency. Like biting down on a live wire.

And then the bond *cracked open*.

---

The first thing that came through wasn't a feeling. It was a *presence*—vast and deliberate and very, very still. Like standing at the edge of a forest at night and realizing the darkness had depth you hadn't accounted for. This was what Theo felt like from the inside. Not the man who stole her coffee and laughed at bad jokes. The *foundation* of him. Ancient-feeling, patient, and enormous.

Then the rage arrived.

Not hot. That was the shock of it—not hot at all. It was cold and structural, like load-bearing stone, and it had been there so long it had become architectural. It wasn't directed at anything in that moment. It simply *existed*, the way a river exists whether or not it's flooding. It was the thing underneath every controlled smile, every deliberate word, every careful choice. And it was so *ordinary* to him—so thoroughly domesticated—that the most unsettling part was how unremarkable he found it.

Then: *want*.

God, the want.

It hit like a wave breaking against the chest—not just desire, though that was there too, warm and persistent and specific. This was hunger in a broader sense. For her voice. For the particular way she bit her lip when she was thinking. For the weight of her beside him when he slept. For the knowledge, every single morning, that she was still *there*. It wasn't romantic in any clean sense. It was possessive in the way gravity was possessive—mindless and total and completely without apology.

She would feel exactly what he meant when he'd said *liked*. Not loved in the soft, careful sense. *Claimed*. Something that belonged to him in a way he would not negotiate and could not rationalize and had long since stopped trying to.

And underneath that—

The tether.

It unfolded like a filing cabinet thrown open. Every moment she'd been afraid and he'd felt it from a distance. Every spike of pain—sharp, physical, undeniable—that had ripped through the bond while he'd stood somewhere across a room or a country and swallowed it whole. The night Fenholt had her. The ritual. The months she'd spent hollow and unreachable. He'd felt all of it, every increment, and he had *kept it*. Not processed it. Kept it. Stacked it somewhere behind the cold rage and the enormous want, and simply continued functioning.

The weight of it was staggering.

And then—quieter, stranger, harder to name—

*Her*. As he experienced her. Not a mirror image but a portrait, painted from the outside in. The specific way she looked when she laughed before she'd decided to. The way he felt when she was sleeping against him—something that didn't have a clean translation but lived adjacent to peace, which was not an emotion he had much natural access to. The pride. The specific, almost painful pride of watching her win a duel, or hold her ground, or survive something that should have broken her.

He loved her the way a person loved the only solid ground they'd ever found.

And she would feel that it frightened him.

Not her. Never her. But the *fact* of it—how much of himself he'd built around her presence without entirely meaning to, and how he'd made his peace with it rather than ever trying to dismantle it.

---

Theo watched her face change.

He saw the exact moment it hit—the slight parting of her lips, the way her free hand shot out and found the edge of the table. He straightened off the counter immediately, both hands coming up to bracket her elbows without gripping, close enough that she could lean into him if she needed to.

His jaw was tight. His eyes tracked every flicker of her expression with the focused intensity of someone watching a controlled detonation and hoping the calculations held.

He didn't say anything. He'd promised her only good feelings and he was already regretting the confident delivery of that particular line.

The months she'd spent hollow and unreachable. He'd felt all of it, every increment, and he had *kept it*. Not processed it. Kept it. Stacked it somewhere behind the cold rage and the enormous want, and simply continued functioning.

The weight of it was staggering.

And then—quieter, stranger, harder to name—

*Her*. As he experienced her. Not a mirror image but a portrait, painted from the outside in. The specific way she looked when she laughed before she'd decided to. The way he felt when she was sleeping against him—something that didn't have a clean translation but lived adjacent to peace, which was not an emotion he had much natural access to. The pride. The specific, almost painful pride of watching her win a duel, or hold her ground, or survive something that should have broken her.

He loved her the way a person loved the only solid ground they'd ever found.

And she would feel that it frightened him.

Not her. Never her. But the *fact* of it—how much of himself he'd built around her presence without entirely meaning to, and how he'd made his peace with it rather than ever trying to dismantle it.

---

Theo watched her face change.

He saw the exact moment it hit—the slight parting of her lips, the way her free hand shot out and found the edge of the table. He straightened off the counter immediately, both hands coming up to bracket her elbows without gripping, close enough that she could lean into him if she needed to.

His jaw was tight. His eyes tracked every flicker of her expression with the focused intensity of someone watching a controlled detonation and hoping the calculations held.

He didn't say anything. He'd promised her only good feelings and he was already regretting the confident delivery of that particular line.

Theo went very still when she stepped back.

Not hurt. Not immediately. His hands dropped to his sides, fingers loose, and he let her have the distance because she'd taken it and he wasn't going to close it without permission. But his eyes didn't leave her face—tracking the tears, the shallow breathing, the way she was holding herself together with her own arms.

The vial shattered against the flagstones and he didn't look at it.

*Feel her. Don't fix her. Feel her.*

The bond was a riot. He could feel his own emotions refracting back through it, distorted by her panic, and it created exactly the feedback loop she was drowning in—his steadiness hitting her overwhelm hitting his concern hitting her—

He exhaled deliberately and *pulled back*. Not from her. From the bond. Consciously, the way you'd lower your voice in an echo chamber, he dampened the output of his own emotional state. Flattened it. Not gone, but quieter. He'd never tried that before. He wasn't certain it was possible until he felt the loop begin to slow.

*There.*

He stayed where he was. Three feet of cold kitchen air between them.

"I'm here," he said. Low and even. Not reaching. Just present, a fixed point she could orient toward if she needed one. "Take your time."

His hands stayed at his sides. The stitches pulled when he breathed but he ignored it.

He watched her struggle to form the sentence—*you are*—and never finish it, and he felt something in his chest that he didn't have a clean name for. Not dread. Something rawer than that. The particular vulnerability of being *seen* all the way down and then having to wait to find out what that meant.

He had told her the truth this morning. Every part of it.

Now he stood in the wreckage of that honesty and waited.

"You don't have to name it," he said quietly, when the silence had stretched long enough. "Not right now." His eyes held hers—pale blue, very direct, nothing guarded in them. "Just breathe."

Something moved through Theo's expression that he didn't manage to contain in time.

Not the compliment. He'd heard versions of that before and deflected all of them with practiced ease. It was the *God of Malice* that got him—the way she said it this time, weighted with the full understanding of what it meant. Not a title. A recognition.

His throat moved.

He crossed the three feet of kitchen between them in two steps and put one hand on her back—flat, steady, between her shoulder blades—and guided her to the nearest chair with the same careful economy he'd use handling something he didn't want to break. He pulled it out with his foot, sat her down, and crouched in front of her so he wasn't looming.

Up close, her face was still wet. She was still breathing in fours.

"Head down," he said quietly. "If you're going to be sick, head down."

He kept his hand on her back, moving in a slow circle. The bond was still quieter than its default—he was holding it deliberately, keeping his own volume low, giving her room to find her own footing inside the new connection.

He studied her face from below. The mismatched eyes, glassy from the shock of it. The tear tracks.

*Terrifyingly beautiful.*

"You're the first person who's ever been inside it and come out with words," he said. His voice was very low. "Usually it's just me in there." The corner of his mouth shifted, not quite a smile. "Must be crowded."

He was deflecting with the joke and he knew she'd feel that too, now. The deflection and the thing underneath it—the part of him that was still braced, still waiting to find out if *terrifyingly* would win over *beautiful* by morning.

His thumb traced one slow line up her spine.

"Still with me?"

Theo's hand stilled on her back for a moment.

"No," he said. "I've tried." He said it without self-pity, just fact. "I can dampen what comes *out* of me—what you feel from my side. I've had practice with that. But the intake—" He tapped two fingers briefly against his sternum. "That goes one way. Always on."

He sat back on his heels, studying her face.

"And before you follow that thought to wherever it's going—" his voice was quiet but firm— "don't."

He could feel the guilt threading through her. Fresh and specific, the kind that came with new information rather than old wounds. He recognized the shape of it.

"You didn't know," he said. "That was my choice. I kept it from you deliberately, for a long time, and badly." His jaw tightened slightly. "And when you found out, you were furious with me. Correctly." He paused. "So we've already had that accounting."

He stood up from the crouch—knees protesting, stitches pulling—and leaned against the table in front of her instead, arms crossing loosely. Looking down at her now, but not imposing. Just closer.

"The hard days were hard," he said simply. "Yes. Some of them were—" He stopped. Chose honesty over comfort. "Some of them were very bad. The night with Fenholt. The months after Draco left." His eyes didn't waver. "But I would do it again. The bond, the ritual, all of it. Because the alternative was losing you to the curse entirely and I had already decided that wasn't acceptable."

A beat of quiet.

"What you felt this morning—that mountain range you walked into—" The corner of his mouth moved. "That's just Tuesday for me, Menace. I've been living in there my whole life. I know the terrain." He reached out and tucked a knuckle briefly under her chin. "You'll learn it too. It'll get quieter. The first time is always the worst."

He dropped his hand.

"How's your stomach?"

Theo watched her pick up the second apple wedge with the same expression he'd had for the first one. He let her keep it this time. Mostly to see if she'd notice the deliberateness of the restraint.

"The rage." He considered it the way he considered most things—directly, without flinching from it. "Yes. Always."

He turned the coffee mug in a slow circle on the table.

"My father used to lock me in a room when I was small. Not as punishment specifically. Just—when I was inconvenient. When he had guests, or business, or simply didn't want to be reminded I existed." His voice carried no particular emotion. Just information. "I had a lot of time to sit with myself in there. And what I found, every time, was that." He tapped two fingers against his sternum. "That cold thing. Sitting at the bottom of everything."

He looked up at her.

"I tried to dissolve into it once. I was fourteen. Nearly killed another student in a duel." His mouth tightened fractionally. "After that I understood it was a tool or it was a catastrophe. Nothing in between." He paused. "So I learned the tool."

He finally picked up his fork and finished the last of his eggs.

"The vastness of it—" He set the fork down. "You felt it from the outside, all at once. I've been living in it incrementally my entire life. You learn to navigate your own geography." His eyes met hers. "The same way you learned to live with the wolf."

A beat of quiet settled between them.

"You're not afraid of it," he said. Not a question. He could feel the shape of what she was carrying through the bond—not fear, something more like orientation. Finding her footing in new terrain. "Good."

Theo watched her hold out the apple wedge.

"Reflex," he confirmed. "You hold food out, I take it. Don't leave things unattended near me if you want to keep them."

He leaned forward, elbows on the table now, and turned the coffee mug in a slow circle.

"The rage." He exhaled through his nose. "Yes. Always. As far back as I can remember having memories." He paused. "My father was—you've met him. Imagine him when I was seven. When I was ten. When I was twelve and said something at dinner he didn't approve of." His voice stayed even, but she'd feel the cold structural thing underneath it shift slightly. Like tectonic plates. "I learned very early that feeling things loudly got you hurt. So I put it somewhere else. Somewhere deep and still where it couldn't be seen."

He looked at his hands.

"The problem with containing something that size for that long is that it becomes load-bearing. It holds up everything else." He glanced up at her. "Remove it and the whole structure collapses. So I stopped trying to remove it and started—" He turned the mug again. "Building around it. Using it. Letting it out in controlled circumstances."

His mouth curved slightly.

"Dueling. Sex. Occasionally Theodore Nott Senior's face."

He picked up his coffee.

"You don't dissolve into it because you learn it's *yours*. Not something happening to you. Something you contain." His eyes held hers. "It took years. And Jackie—" His voice dropped fractionally. "I have dissolved into it. Twice. You were there for one of those times."

He didn't elaborate. He didn't need to.

"The difference between then and now is you." He said it without drama, just fact. "Having something worth governing myself *for* changed the calculation entirely."

He nodded at her plate.

"Eat the rest of the fruit before I do."

Theo's eyes dropped to the strawberry.

Then back to her face.

He felt the thought before it fully formed—*Good boy*—and something shifted in his expression that wasn't quite readable from the outside. Through the bond it was entirely readable. A flash of heat, sharp and immediate, followed by the very deliberate decision to file that particular discovery away for later.

He took the strawberry.

"You're going to regret giving me access to your thoughts," he said. His voice was very calm. "I have an excellent memory and absolutely no shame."

He ate the strawberry, leaned back in his chair, and looked at her with the particular quality of attention he reserved for things he was actively cataloguing.

Her words had landed. She'd felt that too, through the bond—not the sharp spike of want from earlier but something slower. Deeper. The specific place in him that had spent twenty years being told to be less, feel less, contain more, and had quietly learned to hate itself for failing. She'd looked directly at that place and called it *sexy*.

He was still processing it.

"Pathetic," he repeated, without heat. "That's what you're going with."

His mouth curved.

"You told a man who just had his tongue inside you that he was *pathetic.*" He tilted his head. "Ravenclaw, genuinely, what is wrong with you."

He stood, picking up his plate and hers, and carried them to the sink. Stood there with his back to her for a moment, running water over the dishes.

"I know you have more questions," he said. "Ask them. While I still have patience for conversation."

"So." His eyes dropped briefly to her mouth then back up. "Did you kiss Carrow. Last chance, Menace. Tell me the truth and I'll let it go."

A beat.

"Lie to me and I'll know."

He exhaled.

"It's not the kiss, Jackie."

She pivoted and marched out of the kitchen, her bare feet slapping against the cold floorboards as she retreated into the living room. The room was cavernous and draped in shadows. On the walls, ancient magical portraits shifted in their frames, their painted eyes following her with silent, judgmental interest. The massive fireplace was a cold, dark mouth, and the air smelled of old wood and the lingering dampness of the Scottish spring. She stopped in the dead center of the room, spinning around to face Theo. She didn't need the bond to know he was right behind her. "Samuel is… was... the only safe place I had where things weren't... complicated," she said, her voice echoing off the high ceiling. "Save for Anne and Caroline, but they never understood you, me, and Draco the way Samuel did. Or he seemed to."
She began to pace, her hands gesturing wildly. The logic was clear in her head, and she threw it at him like a shield. "You're imagining things that aren't there, Theo. He wrote letters to me because even someone like Carrow needs a place to vent. And I'm thick-skinned and inconsequential enough that he didn't have to worry about offending me in the process. I bought that CD player for him because… that's what friends do. And for the record, he never even thanked me for it or the CDs."
But as the words left her mouth, a cold, oily doubt began to seep into her mind. She tried to block it, but her memory was too vivid. She remembered the song—the one he’d performed at the last concert while she was lost in a dance with Draco. At the time, she’d just thought he was observant. She thought he was just singing about the messy, magnetic pull between her Malfoy and Nott. Then the lyrics hit her, echoing in the quiet of the Manor.

*‘I’ve admired you from a distance—That’s the safest place for me. You deserve something unbroken, Something I could never be.’*
The memory made her heart stutter. Was he talking to her? Was that his way of saying the things he’d never dare to say to her face? And then there was the kiss afterward. The gratitude. The way he’d looked at her. "Fuck…"
Jackie turned her back on Theo, her knees feeling weak. She sank onto the massive settee, the velvet cool against her skin, but she couldn't stay still. She stood up immediately, pacing again, her head spinning with the implications. "Im-fucking-possible."

Theo followed her into the living room at a measured pace. He didn't rush. He let her have the pacing, the gesturing, the echo of her voice off the high ceiling. The portraits watched her with painted interest and he ignored them entirely.

When she said *fuck* and her knees wobbled, he sat down on the arm of the settee. Not reaching for her. Just anchoring himself somewhere she could find him when the pacing stopped.

He waited until she said *im-fucking-possible* before he spoke.

"Between the Lines," he said quietly.

He let that land.

"Third song. The bridge." He watched her face. "'I've admired you from a distance—that's the safest place for me.'" He paused. "I know the setlist, Jackie. I was there."

He linked his hands loosely between his knees.

"I didn't say anything because you were happy. You had something uncomplicated and you needed that." His voice was even. Not unkind. "And Carrow is—" He stopped. Chose honesty over diplomacy. "He's not stupid. He knows exactly where he stands. He wrote the song and performed it in a room full of people instead of saying it to your face because that's the only way someone like him *can* say it."

He looked at her directly.

"He's not going to do anything about it. That's not what this is." A beat. "But you should know. Because you're walking into Sunday with your father carrying the bond and everything that came with it this morning, and you deserve to have the full picture of your own life before you do."

He reached out and caught her wrist lightly as she passed, stopping the pacing without forcing her still.

"Breathe," he said. "It doesn't have to be solved today."

"I don't care about the fucking Sunday with my fucking father," Jackie snapped. A small part of her cringed at the messy string of profanities, but she was too agitated to give it any room to breathe. Her heart was hammering against her ribs, and the air in the vast living room felt thin and cold.
She didn't pull her wrist away from his grip. Instead, she stepped into the narrow gap between the settee and the side table, closing the distance until she was standing directly in front of him. With Theo perched on the armrest, they were almost eye-to-eye, and the proximity made the bond hum with a sharp, jagged frequency.
"And you didn't tell me that because of my father, Theo. Don't lie to me." Her voice lost its heat, turning into something cold and full of venom. She stared into his pale eyes, hoping—gods, she actually *hoped*—that the sting of her words would land through the bond exactly the way she intended. She wanted to feel him flinch.
"You told me that because I told you I kissed him. You were jealous, and you wanted to hit back." She leaned in just a fraction closer, her mismatched eyes narrowed. "And maybe, somewhere deep down, you wanted me to know because you knew it would ruin everything. You know I won't be able to just be his friend now. I'll have to go and confront him, and it’s going to be ugly. It’s going to burn that bridge to the ground."
The realization tasted like copper in the back of her throat. She didn't look away, her gaze a silent challenge, daring him to try and hide behind his clinical tone.
"At the end of the day, it just makes me more yours, doesn't it?" she whispered. "One less person for me to turn to. One more door you get to close."
She stayed there, pinned by his touch and her own fury, waiting for the bond to tell her the truth his mouth probably wouldn't.

Theo didn't flinch.

But she felt it through the bond—the accusation landing, finding purchase, and the cold structural thing shifting in a way that wasn't quite a flinch but was adjacent to one. Something that lived underneath the rage. Something older and uglier and much less comfortable.

He held her gaze.

For a long moment he said nothing. The lighter was in his pocket. He didn't reach for it.

"Yes," he said finally.

One word. Flat and unadorned.

"I was jealous. I wanted to hit back." He didn't look away. "Both of those things are true."

He released her wrist. His hand dropped to his knee.

"And the rest of it—" His jaw tightened. She'd feel the cold working through him, the particular discomfort of a man being taken apart accurately and knowing it. "I'm not going to tell you you're wrong. Because I can feel that you're not entirely wrong and you'd know it if I lied."

The bond confirmed it before he finished the sentence. Not the whole truth—but enough of it.

He stood up from the armrest, which put him above her again, but he didn't use the height. He just stood there, close, looking at her with something stripped back in his expression.

"I didn't plan it," he said quietly. "I didn't sit at that table and think—*this is how I close the door on Carrow.*" A beat. "But I felt you thinking about him. And I said it. And somewhere underneath all of that—"

He stopped.

Started again.

"You're right," he said. The words came out harder than the others, like something pulled from somewhere that didn't release things easily. "I don't want you to have somewhere to go that isn't me or Draco. I hate that you needed it. I hate that I couldn't be that for you when you needed it most." His voice dropped. "And I hate Carrow a little for being there when I wasn't."

He held her gaze.

"That's the truth. All of it. Including the parts that make me the monster you already know I am."

The bond was a nightmare. It wasn't just a connection anymore; it was a high-definition broadcast of everything she didn’t want to know. It left no room for the comfortable lies they used to tell each other. She could feel the raw, jagged truth of his jealousy and the cold satisfaction underneath it—the part of him that was glad Carrow was gone. It made her stomach turn.
"He was my friend," she said quietly, her voice cracking on the last syllable.
She didn't say the rest out loud. She didn't have to. She gathered the thought—the sharp, bleeding sense of loss—and shoved it toward him through the tether with everything she had.
*You took it away. You destroyed it for me.*
The air in the living room felt too thick, saturated with his heavy presence and her own rising panic. She needed to breathe without feeling him in every lungful of oxygen.
"I need to be alone."
She turned and walked away, her bare feet silent on the floorboards as she headed for the library. She didn't look back. She pushed the heavy oak doors open and shut them with a dull, final thud that echoed through the house. The library was cold, smelling of old parchment and dust, but it offered no comfort today.
Jackie slumped into a deep leather armchair, pulling her knees up to her chest and curling into a ball. The tears she’d been holding back finally broke, hot and salty against her skin. 
The worst part was that she wasn't just mad at Theo. She was furious with herself. She realized now, with a clarity that made her chest ache, that she’d been lying to herself for months. She’d heard the lyrics. She’d seen the way Samuel looked at her when he thought she wasn't watching.
She had just chosen not to see it. She had desperately wanted Samuel to be the one safe, uncomplicated thing in her life, so she’d forced him into that role and ignored everything that didn't fit. Theo hadn't just given her information; he’d burned her last illusion to the ground.

Theo stood in the living room after the library doors closed.

The echo of the thud faded. The portraits went still. The cold Scottish light pressed through the windows and did nothing useful.

*You took it away. You destroyed it for me.*

He felt it land. Full force, exactly as she'd intended. He didn't try to deflect it or rationalize it into something smaller. He let it sit in his chest where she'd placed it and breathed around it.

*Yes,* he thought. *I did.*

He stood there for another minute. Then he walked to the fireplace, crouched down, and lit it. The wood caught slowly, the heat building in increments against the cold stone. He stayed crouched in front of it longer than necessary, forearms on his knees, watching the flame establish itself.

Through the bond he could feel her crying. The hot, specific grief of someone mourning something they'd already half-known was gone. He didn't dampen it. He let himself feel it because she was feeling it and that was the point of the bond, even when it was this.

*Especially* when it was this.

He stood. Went to the kitchen. Put the kettle on.

He made tea—proper tea, not the performative Malfoy kind, just strong and hot and honest. He put it on a tray with the last of the fruit she hadn't eaten and a blanket from the hall chest that was thick enough to be useful in an April library.

He carried it to the library doors.

He didn't knock. He set the tray down on the floor outside, carefully, so it wouldn't rattle. Then he straightened up and put his back against the wall beside the door and slid down until he was sitting on the floorboards, long legs stretched out, head back against the stone.

He didn't go in. She'd asked for alone and he was giving her alone.

But he stayed.

Jackie gave herself thirty minutes to unravel. She sat in the oversized leather chair, her knees tucked to her chin, and let herself re-examine every memory of Samuel Carrow through this new, jagged lens.
The letters weren't just a place for him to vent; they were a lifeline. The song wasn't just an observation; it was a surrender. Every time he’d looked at her after a duel, every sarcastic remark that felt like an inside joke—it all shifted. She felt stupid for not seeing it, and even angrier because she knew, deep down, she’d ignored the signs on purpose. She had wanted him to be the one simple thing in her life, and Theo had just set fire to that illusion.
She could feel Theo through the bond. He was a constant, heavy presence on the other side of the door. She smelled the tea before she heard him set the tray down—dark, bitter, and definitely over-steeped. Theo never did anything halfway, including ruining a cup of tea.
Through the tether, she felt the complicated mess of his emotions. He didn't regret what he’d done. She knew that with a cold, terrifying certainty. He’d destroy every bridge she had if it meant she stayed anchored to him, and he wouldn’t apologize for it. But underneath that was a different kind of ache—a dull, secondary hurt. He wasn't sorry for the truth, but he felt the weight of her grief because it was currently his, too.
Finally, Jackie stood up. Her legs felt heavy, but the silence in the library was starting to feel louder than her own thoughts. She walked to the French doors and sank onto the floor, her back pressing against the wood. Through the distorted glass panes, she could see the dark blur of Theo’s frame sitting on the other side.
She wasn't ready to open the door. She wasn't ready to look at him. But the silence needed to break.
She closed her eyes, focused on that new, buzzing connection in her mind, and pushed a single thought out toward him.
*Questions game?*

Theo felt it arrive.

Clean and small and entirely unexpected. He stared at the opposite wall of the corridor for a moment, the lighter still in his fingers, and felt something in his chest loosen by a fraction.

He turned his head toward the door. Through the distorted glass he could make out the dark shape of her on the other side, mirroring him.

He tapped the back of his head against the stone wall once. Exhaled.

*Fine.*

He pushed the thought back deliberately, the way she'd shown him—aimed, released.

Then, because he could and because the rules of the game gave him the opening, he spoke it aloud as well, his voice low enough that it wouldn't carry past the door.

"Fine."

He stretched his legs out further on the floorboards, crossed them at the ankle, and looked up at the corridor ceiling.

"I'll go first." He rolled the lighter once over his knuckles. "Did you know? About Carrow. Before today." He paused. "Actually know, not suspect, not half-see-it-and-look-away. *Know.*"

It was the question underneath all the others he hadn't asked in the living room. The one that mattered more than the kiss, more than the song, more than any of it.

He waited, his shoulder blades against the cold stone, feeling her on the other side of three inches of oak.

Theo’s voice was muffled by the heavy oak, but the words were clear. Jackie had just spent the last thirty minutes tearing her own memories apart, looking for the same answer, so when she spoke, the truth felt solid and heavy in her chest.
"No," she said. "If I had known… I wouldn't have let him get so close."
She let out a short, hollow laugh that didn't reach her eyes. She leaned her head back against the door, feeling the vibration of his presence on the other side. "Honestly, I was pretty sure I wasn't even his type. I remember the girls he used to hang out with at Hogwarts, and the ones he’d take upstairs during the Soirees. They were all the same—long legs, blonde, tiny waists. The kind of pretty that’s almost hard to look at."
She looked down at her own hands, calloused from dueling and rougher than the girls she was describing.
"I caught a few looks, sure. A few comments here and there. It crossed my mind that he might be interested, but I figured it was just the novelty of me. Or maybe he was just curious about what I had that finally managed to lock *you* down. I never allowed myself to even suspect… that."
She knew she was giving him way more than he’d asked for. She knew he was the one who should be apologizing, the one who had intentionally blown up her life this morning. And yet, she still felt this desperate need to explain herself. She hated that she loved him this much—that even when she was furious, she wanted him to understand her.
She shifted, the cold floor biting into her skin even through the fabric of her trousers, and focused on the bond. She didn't ask the biting version of the question—the one about how long he’d been sitting on this information just to use it as a weapon. She decided to count that as a win for her self-control.
"How long did you know?"

"Eight months," he said. "Give or take."

"The second Snake Soirée. March of last year." The lighter stilled in his fingers. "He watched you duel Parkinson's cousin. You won in under a minute and when you turned around he had—" Theo stopped. The implication of that sat quietly between them. He knew because he'd worn that expression himself, for years.

"I didn't say anything because you needed him." The words came out even, stripped of justification. "You were barely functional after Draco left. Carrow was writing letters, making you laugh, treating you like you were whole when you didn't feel it." He turned the lighter once. "I wasn't going to take that from you while you were still—"

He stopped.

"While you still needed it," he finished.

The floorboards creaked faintly as he shifted his weight.

"I told myself I'd tell you when the time was right." A long pause. "This morning wasn't the right time either. That was—" Another pause, longer. "That was jealousy. You were right about that."

He felt her processing it through the bond. He didn't try to manage her reaction.

"Your turn," he said quietly.

"My question," he said quietly. "Are you going to confront him?"

Eight months. The number felt like a physical weight pressing through the door and into her spine. Jackie leaned her head back against the wood, staring up at the dark, towering bookshelves. She felt small—ridiculously, stupidly small. How had she missed it? Looking back now, the memories shifted and clicked into place like a puzzle she’d been too blind to finish. It had to have been obvious to everyone but her.
She wanted to be grateful to him for keeping the secret—for letting her keep the one friend who made her feel like a person when she was falling apart. But the gratitude was soured by the reality of this morning. He’d kept the secret for her sake, but he’d weaponized it for his own.
"It's your turn, technically," she said, her voice low and raspy from the crying. "I was the last to ask. But if you're giving it away, I'll take it."
She went quiet for a moment, tracing a crack in the floorboard with her thumb. Through the bond, she could feel the steady, rhythmic pulse of his presence—the honesty that still felt like a bruise.
"I know why you didn't say anything to me," she continued, her voice gaining a bit of strength. "I don't condone it, but I do understand. I needed him, and you knew it. You let me have that."
She paused, her eyes narrowing in the dim light of the library. This was the part that didn't fit the Theodore Nott she knew—the one who was possessive down to his very marrow.
"But why haven't you confronted *him* about it? You’re not exactly the 'live and let live' type when it comes to me. Did you stay quiet because you thought he’d never actually make a move? Or was there another reason you let him keep pining in the wings?"

"I can respect that. Even when I hate it."

"And because confronting him would've meant telling you. Which I wasn't ready to do." He said it plainly, without softening it. "So I watched him be decent about something that was costing him, and I kept my mouth shut, and I told myself it was for your benefit."

He felt her processing that through the bond.

"Partly it was," he added. "Partly I just didn't want to have this conversation."

The lighter went still in his fingers.

"He's a better man than I gave him credit for," Theo said quietly. The words sounded like they cost something. "That's the part I really didn't want to tell you."

A beat.

"He deserves better than losing your friendship because I got jealous over a kiss."

Jackie's fingers traced the intricate carving of the doorframe, her skin feeling the chill of the wood. His admission hit her like a slow-moving wave—heavy and suffocating. He was finally being honest about Samuel's nobility, but it was too late for that to be helpful.
"Well, that’s something you should’ve thought about before you told me," she said, her voice flat. She leaned her forehead against the cool glass of the French door, watching his blurred silhouette through the distortion. "I can’t just go back and pretend nothing happened. Even if I wanted to, I couldn't. Samuel is too observant for that—he’d know something was wrong the second he looked at me."
She thought about the bridge she was about to burn. The safe, sarcastic, uncomplicated space Samuel had provided was gone, replaced by a weight she didn't know how to carry. Through the bond, she could feel Theo’s guilt, but it didn't fix the fact that her world had just gotten smaller.
"Thankfully he's on tour somewhere in Wales," she added, the distance offering a small, temporary relief. "So I have some time to prepare. Not that I know how you prepare to tell a friend you've been oblivious to the fact they were in love with you for months."
She shifted her weight, the library’s scent of old parchment and cold air settling around her. The anger was still there, but it was starting to feel more like exhaustion. She focused on the tether, feeling the steady, dark hum of Theo's presence on the other side of the oak.

"We're still playing."

"Because I am," he said simply. "A little."

Theo was quiet for a moment after she finished.

She felt the first answer land in him—not the part about Draco, though that registered too—but the part about the limb. About learning to be happy with the missing piece still missing. He'd felt her grief for Draco for a year through the bond and understood it intellectually, but hearing her name it like that, plainly and without apology, settled something in him he hadn't known was unsettled.

And the third wheel comment.

She felt the flicker of something that wasn't quite amusement. Darker than that. More complicated.

"You're not the third wheel," he said. "You never were. You're the only reason either of us is in the same room."

He didn't elaborate. She could feel he meant it structurally, not romantically. She was the load-bearing wall. Without her, the whole architecture collapsed.

He let the silence breathe for a moment before answering her question.

"I'm going to tell him the truth," he said. The lighter clicked once. "That we've been focusing on your recovery and your training and your Auror application. That we're not ready. That it's our decision and not his."

A pause.

"And then I'm going to look him in the eye and tell him that when we do have a child, it won't be because Cyrus Taylor wants a grandchild. It'll be because *you* want one."

Another beat. Quieter.

"And if he pushes past that—" The lighter went still. "I'll remind him very calmly that I have a signed statement from his own father-in-law detailing exactly how that marriage contract was arranged, and that the Wizengamot tends to look poorly on men who sell their daughters." His voice stayed even. "He'll stop pushing."

She felt the cold certainty underneath it. Not a threat performed for her benefit. Just fact.

"He won't like me after that conversation," Theo added. "He already doesn't. But he'll respect the boundary."

The floorboards shifted as he moved.

"Your father wants you to be small, Jackie. Manageable. Something he can point to without embarrassment." His voice was low, and completely without heat. "He's going to sit across from you on Sunday and realize that whatever he made, it didn't stay small. And that's going to be its own kind of answer."

A pause.

"My turn." She felt him decide on it through the bond—something he'd been circling. "The bond. Now that you have it—now that you've felt all of it." His voice dropped. "Do you regret drinking it?"

Theo was quiet for long enough that she heard him exhale slowly through the door.

"The third wheel." He said it like he was turning the words over. "You thought that." Not a question. Not mocking. Just the specific tone of someone filing something away permanently. "Jackie."

He stopped. She felt him decide against whatever he was going to say next.

"We'll come back to that."

Another silence. She felt the question about her father moving through him—the cold structural thing shifting, recalibrating. Not rage this time. Something more deliberate.

"I'm going to tell him the truth," Theo said finally. "That it's none of his business. That the clause is void, that his leverage died in the Wizengamot, and that the only reason I'm sitting in his parlour drinking his bitter tea is because his daughter asked me to be there."

A beat.

"And if he keeps pushing—" The lighter clicked once. "I'll tell him we've been trying and it hasn't happened yet. Which isn't entirely a lie." His voice was even. "We've certainly not been preventing it."

He paused.

"What I *won't* tell him is that you haven't decided yet. That's yours. He doesn't get access to your uncertainty."

The floorboards shifted as he moved.

"Your father wants leverage, Jackie. He's been without it since the Wizengamot ruling and it's made him small and desperate and petty." A pause. "Petty men ask about heirs because children are the one thing they can still imagine controlling. I'm not going to give him a number to calculate against."

Silence settled between them.

Then, quieter—

"Go back to what you said. About me and Draco." His voice dropped. "You genuinely believed that."

It wasn't the questions game anymore. The game had dissolved somewhere in the last few exchanges without either of them marking the moment.

"Two years, Jackie. Two years of feeling everything you feel. Every time you thought about him. Every time it hurt." He paused. "And you thought I'd choose *him* over you."

She felt something move through the bond that didn't have a clean name. Not anger. Not hurt exactly.

Something that felt like being profoundly, specifically misunderstood by the one person who was supposed to know you best.

"Tell me how that makes any sense to you," he said. "I genuinely want to understand."

She watched his expression, looking for any flicker of surprise. Through the tether, she felt a wave of her own pragmatism meeting his earlier assumption.
"We’ve never even talked about the possibility of having kids. You’ve never once indicated you’d ever want them. And with the amount of 'trying' we actually do—" She gave a small, weary shrug, her shoulders brushing the wood. "It just seemed like the only logical thing to do. I never tried to hide it, but if you really weren't aware... I’m sorry, I guess? I just assumed you knew."

He looked at his hands.

"I don't dislike the idea of children with you," he said carefully. "I dislike children in general. That's different." A pause. "Theo Nott Senior's parenting methods have a lot to answer for in terms of my feelings on the subject."

He glanced up at her.

"But I meant what I said to your father. That decision belongs to you." His pale eyes held hers. "When you're ready. If you're ready." A beat. "I'll follow your lead on that one."

He stretched his neck until it cracked.

"Now." His eyes settled on her face, steady and direct. "Draco."

Theo looked at her.

He'd felt the door open before she pushed it—the shift in her through the bond, the decision forming. He hadn't moved. He was still sitting against the wall, legs stretched out, the tray with the cold tea beside him untouched.

He held her gaze for a moment.

"I knew," he said.

Flat. Simple. No performance around it.

"You're a Ravenclaw who spent three years terrified of a curse that controlled her body. Of course you'd take every measure available to control the things you could." He turned the lighter once. "I wasn't going to bring it up until you did. It's your body, Jackie. It's your decision when and if that changes."

He looked at her directly.

"What I told your father would've been a deflection. Not a complaint."

He reached over and picked up the cold tea from the tray, handed it to her anyway, and leaned his forearms on his knees.

"Now." His pale eyes settled on her face with the particular focused weight she'd felt through the bond all morning. "Draco."

He wasn't letting it go. She'd felt that before she opened the door.

"You spent a year watching me feel everything you feel. You *know* what you are to me. And you still built an entire fear around me choosing him." His voice stayed quiet. Even. "So either you don't trust what I feel for you—" He paused. "Or you don't trust *him* not to want me to."

His head tilted fractionally.

"Which one is it?"

Jackie felt a knot in her chest loosen the second he confirmed he knew. For some reason, the idea that she had been keeping a secret from him—even an unconscious one—had been vibrating through the bond like a dissonant note. Knowing he was already aware of the potion let her relax internally, the tension bleeding out of her shoulders. She looked down at the mug of tea he’d handed her. She took a sip and immediately winced; it was freezing and so bitter it set her teeth on edge. Still, she took another swallow. He’d made it for her, and in the language of Theodore Nott, that mattered more than the temperature. "We both loved *him* way longer than we ever loved each other," she said, her voice sounding small in the quiet library. "It’s a little funny, actually. Thinking about a fourteen-year-old me and a fourteen-year-old you at Hogwarts. We had virtually nothing in common, except for the fact that we were both secretly in love with the same boy."
She shifted her back against the doorframe, looking at him properly. Through the bond, she could still feel the raw, focused weight of his attention. "And you hated me before you loved me," she added. "Or you wanted to have me, at least once I came back for that last year after the War. I knew in principle that you loved me, of course—you’ve proven that enough times for me to never doubt it. But I didn't know how deep that went. Not until today."
The air in the hallway felt still, weighted by the things they hadn't said before Tuscany. Jackie felt a heat crawl up her neck, a blush she couldn't suppress. She took another sip of the bitter tea to give her hands something to do. "Before the trip... before Tuscany, I thought it didn't matter anyway. I thought Draco was as straight as they come. And then he admitted that he’d thought about you like that before, while you..."
She stopped, the image of the three of them in the bedroom in Italy flashing through her mind— the way Theo directed their pleasure, the way Draco gave in and followed, the way Theo touched him and made him come. She looked Theo square in the eye, the blush deepening but her gaze steady.

"Was it everything you thought it would be?" she asked, her voice dropping to a whisper. "Everything you dreamt about with him, all those years? When he unraveled in your hand?"

"It was him," he said finally. "Actually him. Not the version I'd built in my head out of resentment and wanting and years of telling myself it didn't matter."

The hallway was very quiet.

"He's terrified of what it means," Theo continued, quieter still. "You felt that too. The way he goes still when it gets too real. The way he needs it to happen sideways, like if nobody names it directly it doesn't count." The corner of his mouth shifted. Not quite a smile. Something more complicated. "I'm not going to push him. I'll wait until he's ready or I'll wait forever. Either way."

He looked at her directly.

"Does it bother you?" His voice was even but she'd feel the genuine uncertainty underneath it. "Watching that. Knowing that I—" He paused. "That it's not just you I feel that way about."

He turned the lighter over once. Stopped.

The pride he had to put down to get there."

He was quiet for a moment.

"When he let go—" His jaw shifted. "I've taken things from people my whole life. That's the first time someone gave me something that size and I didn't know what to do with it."

His eyes held hers.

"So yes," he said. "It was everything. And I have no idea what to do with that either."

Jackie offered him a smile—one of those rare, soft breaks in her expression that she usually kept tucked away. He was so often the immovable force that he rarely needed her to be the gentle one, but in the thin, grey light of the library, he looked stripped back. "See?" she said, her voice barely a murmur. "This right there is why I was worried."
She didn't specify if she was talking about the words he’d just forced out or the raw, pulsing vulnerability she could feel radiating through the bond. Both were equally telling. "It’s not that I didn’t trust your love for me, Theo. I never did," she continued. She leaned her head back against the doorframe, watching a dust mote dance in the air between them. "I just knew that once the two of you got past the years of hatred and resentment—once you finally allowed yourselves to *feel*—it wouldn't matter where we were. Italy, a villa, a tiny apartment in London. You’ll inevitably gravitate toward each other. It’s just what souls meant to be together do."
Through the tether, Theo would feel a strange kind of sadness emanating from her. It lacked the sharp, jagged edge of pain; instead, it felt hollow and quiet, like a room that had finally been emptied of its furniture. It was the frequency of acceptance. She was letting him feel the version of her that understood she wasn't the only sun in their universe. She was the tether—the common ground that pulled them closer until they were close enough to reach for each other without her. "I know Draco isn't ready for that yet," she said, her fingers tracing the rim of the cold mug. "He gave up every ounce of his pride when he came back to us. He knows he has to share me with you. He knows I’ll never be his wife in name, and that there are parts of my soul that will always be yours alone. He isn’t ready for the cost of admitting he wants you, too. But he does. And eventually, he will."
She tipped the mug back, draining the last of the bitter, freezing tea in one go, as if deciding the unpleasantness was better over with than lingering. She set the cup back on the tray with a small, final *clink*. "I know what you feel now.

I know you won’t stop loving me, even when he finally lets you love him back." She looked at him, her mossy-green and glacial-blue eyes searching his. "But I hope you understand now why I was a little worried. It’s a lot of gravity for one house to hold."

Theo listened without interrupting. That alone said something—he who always had the next move already calculated, the counter already forming before the sentence finished.

He looked at the empty mug she'd set down.

"Souls meant to be together," he repeated quietly. Not mocking. Tasting the phrase, deciding what to do with it.

He leaned his head back against the wall, looking up at the corridor ceiling. Through the bond she'd feel it—the thing her words had touched that he wasn't going to dress up or deflect. The particular ache of being known this precisely by someone. Of having your own interior landscape described back to you more accurately than you'd described it to yourself.

"I understand why you were worried," he said. "I'm not going to tell you the fear was irrational." A pause. "It wasn't."

He looked at her.

"But here's what you're missing." His voice was very quiet. "You're not the tether in the mechanical sense. You're not just the common ground we cross to reach each other." His pale eyes held hers steadily. "You're the reason either of us became worth reaching for."

He let that sit.

"Draco spent a year rebuilding himself so he could come back to *you*. Not to me. To you." He turned the lighter once, slowly. "Whatever happens between him and me—whenever that is, if it is—it exists because of what you made possible. Not instead of it."

The dust mote drifted between them in the gray light.

"A lot of gravity," he repeated softly. "Yes." The corner of his mouth shifted. "Good thing the house is solid."

He reached over and picked up the empty mug from the tray, looked at it, set it back down.

"Come here," he said simply. Not a demand. Just Theo, asking.

She pulled eggs and a pack of bacon from the icebox, the familiar sounds of a pan heating up filling the room.

She landed in a silent crouch, pinned the ham with her paws, and gave Jackie one last murderous look before beginning her feast. "You’re welcome," Jackie breathed, shaking out the tension in her hands. The flat was bathed in the pale, watery light of a London April morning. Outside the floor-to-ceiling windows, the city was waking up in a haze of gray clouds and light drizzle, but inside, everything was perfectly, maddeningly neat. Draco’s kitchen was a study in black marble and polished chrome, with not a single stray teaspoon out of place. It was a sharp contrast to the sprawling, lived-in chaos of Nott Manor, and for a moment, the silence felt heavy. Draco wasn't in the main living space. The door to the bedroom was still closed, suggesting he was either still asleep or lost in a long shower. Jackie shucked off her leather jacket and hung it on the coat hanger, then took off her shoes — she wouldn't clutter his pristine surface if she could help it. She moved to the stove, her movements practiced and quiet. She filled the kettle—heavy, silver, and perfectly polished—and set it to boil. The hum of the kitchen felt grounding. She pulled eggs and a pack of bacon from the icebox, the familiar sounds of a pan heating up filling the room.

The bedroom door opened at 7:53.

Draco emerged in grey sleep trousers and nothing else, hair still disheveled in the particular way that only happened before he'd had the chance to ruin it with effort. He had the look of someone who had been awake for several minutes already but had refused to acknowledge it—his jaw set, his shoulders carrying the faint tension of a man who'd heard the Apparition crack and spent the intervening minutes deciding whether to pretend he was still asleep.

He wasn't pretending.

His eyes found her immediately. The pan on the stove. The kettle. Her jacket on his hook instead of slung over his sofa.

Something in his face shifted, almost imperceptibly. The tight line of his mouth eased by a fraction.

"You brought ham," he said. Not a question. He was watching Luna demolish it in the corner with the expression of a man who had accepted, without grace, that his cat was irredeemably corrupt.

He crossed to the kitchen, brushing past Jackie close enough that she'd feel the warmth off him, and opened a cabinet to retrieve two mugs. His movements were deliberate, unhurried—the specific economy of motion of someone who had lived alone long enough to have rituals.

"You didn't have to do that." He nodded at the pan. "I usually just—"

He stopped. Looked at what she'd laid out. Eggs, bacon, the good cast iron she'd correctly identified as the only pan worth using.

"—have tea," he finished, in a tone that admitted defeat.

He measured the tea leaves with the focus of a man performing a small, sacred act. Two measures. Temperature of the water checked by holding his palm briefly over the kettle's mouth. He didn't explain any of it.

"How was the Apparition?" His back was to her. "Highlands to London is a long pull without a relay point. You look—" He turned just enough to glance at her over his shoulder. The gray eyes did a quiet, efficient scan. Face. Hands. The set of her spine. "—intact."

*She's here.*

The thought was simple enough that he didn't bother dissecting it. He poured the water. Set her mug on the counter in front of her—close enough to reach, placed exactly where she'd want it.

Luna, having demolished the ham with the focused brutality she reserved for meaningful occasions, leapt onto the nearest barstool and fixed Jackie with a gaze that was either affectionate or territorial. With Kneazles it was difficult to distinguish.

"She's been insufferable since Sunday," Draco said, not looking at the cat. "She knocked an inkwell onto a case file. I had to rewrite four pages." He sat on the opposite barstool, wrapping both hands around his mug. "I considered having her re-homed."

Luna blinked.

"I didn't," he added, with the flatness of a man who had never seriously considered it.

He watched Jackie at the stove for a moment. Outside, the rain had thickened against the windows, dragging gray light across the polished floor. The flat was warm—he'd spelled the heating on before he'd gotten out of bed, which was information he also didn't offer.

"You've got an hour before I have to leave." His thumb moved once around the rim of his mug. "Which means you have approximately forty minutes before I become someone worth talking to."

It wasn't quite an invitation. It wasn't quite deflection either. It was Draco at 8am, which meant it was both.

Jackie didn't miss the way his eyes lingered on her—that sharp, silver gaze that always seemed to be cataloging her, checking for cracks or signs of wear. She turned back to the pan, the steady rhythm of breakfast-making acting as a buffer against the sudden, sharp awareness of being back in his space. With a practiced flick of her wrist, she cracked two eggs into the sizzling fat, then used the edge of her knife to trim a small, fatty strip of uncooked bacon.

She held it out toward the barstool. Luna’s ears twitched. The Kneazle didn't rush; she leaned forward with predatory deliberation, sniffing the offering before daintily taking it from Jackie’s fingers.

"Well, you left her for a week," Jackie said, her voice carrying a playful lilt as she nudged the cat’s velvet-soft ear with a knuckle. "I’m sure her babysitter—the florist’s cousin, Jack, if I remember correctly—was perfectly nice, but still. It’ll take her a moment to forgive you for the abandonment."

She felt a small, private victory in the fact that Luna was currently choosing snacks over bloodshed. It was a step up from their usual dynamic, which typically involved Jackie checking her ankles for puncture wounds.

Once the eggs were perfect, the yolks still wobbly and bright, Jackie plated the food and slid them onto the marble counter next to their stools. She leaned her hip against the black stone, surveying the room. The flat was beautiful, but it was *tight*. Every time she was here, she found herself mentally moving the furniture, trying to find space for a proper dining table, only to realize there simply wasn't any. It reinforced the quiet hope she’d been nursing since their trip to Rome: that by next year, this wouldn't be 'Draco’s flat' or 'Theo’s Manor,' but a home for all three of them. Somewhere with enough room for Draco's neatness, Theo's shadows, and her own chaotic light.

She picked up her mug, the warmth seeping into her palms, and watched the London drizzle streak the floor-to-ceiling windows. The city was a smudge of gray and neon, a world away from the jagged, mist-heavy peaks of the Highlands.

"The Apparition gods were kind," she murmured, taking a slow sip of the tea. It was exactly how she liked it—Draco’s attention to detail was a love language he refused to name. "No traffic, no splinching, and I’m not even nauseous. I guess after a month of hopping between here and the Manor, my body finally decided to stop protesting the physics of it. I’ve adjusted."

It was a little too close for comfort—Luna’s golden eyes were fixed on Jackie’s face with unsettling intensity—but she refused to flinch. She focused on her plate, using the side of her fork to slice into the egg yolk, watching the yellow spill across the white. A slow, knowing smirk tugged at the corner of her mouth, an unspoken challenge to his 'forty-minute' rule.

Then, it hit.

Deep in the back of her mind—somewhere behind her own heartbeat—a sudden, sharp prickle of coldness flared. It wasn't her own. It was a dark, possessive thrum, a flicker of sharp-edged jealousy that tasted like iron and Highland peat.

*Theo.*

The smirk faded just a fraction. It was the first time she’d felt him so clearly while being physically distant, and the sensation was jarring—like a ghost walking through her chest. She took another bite of her breakfast, trying to keep her expression neutral, but her hand tightened instinctively around the handle of her mug.

Draco's fork stilled.

Not dramatically—just a half-second pause before he resumed cutting his bacon into even thirds, the way he always did. But he'd caught it. The smirk fading. Her hand tightening on the mug. The infinitesimal withdrawal behind her eyes, like a door eased shut without quite latching.

He filed it. Said nothing.

Instead he ate, shoulder close enough to hers that Luna had to rearrange herself with obvious resentment, and let the comfortable weight of the flat settle back around them. Rain on glass. The soft click of silverware. The specific quiet that existed in this kitchen and nowhere else he'd ever lived.

"Jack is the florist's *nephew*," he said, reaching across her to top up his own tea without asking. "And Luna bit him on day two. He left a very formal note explaining that he would not be returning." He set the kettle down. "I paid him double anyway. Seemed the ethical thing to do."

Luna's tail flicked once. Absolved of nothing.

He ate two more bites. Then, without looking at her, he said: "The forty-minute rule is a general advisory. Not a hard restriction."

His eyes moved sideways to her face. That quiet, diagnostic scan she'd probably memorized by now—the one he deployed when he was deciding how much to say and how much to leave alone.

What he saw was: something off.

Not distress. Not anything she was showing. It was subtler than that, a quality in the way she'd pulled back into herself between one breath and the next. Like she'd heard something in a frequency he didn't have access to.

*Theo.*

The thought arrived without invitation. He dismissed it with the same efficiency, setting his fork down and resting his forearm on the counter.

"You're going to tell me it's nothing," he said. Not unkindly. "So I won't ask."

He picked up his mug. Drank. Watched the rain for a moment.

"But you did that thing." He gestured at her hand with his chin—the one still wrapped around her mug with slightly too much grip. "The knuckle thing. You do it when something lands on you sideways and you're deciding whether it's worth mentioning."

He turned to look at her directly. No pressure in it. Just attention, level and unhurried, the kind he'd learned to offer instead of demand.

"You don't have to decide right now." He reached past her again—this time to steal the last strip of her bacon, completely unrepentant. "You've got until I have to put on a shirt."

Luna chose this moment to stand fully, stretch with theatrical slowness, and place one enormous paw directly on Draco's forearm.

He looked at the paw. Looked at the cat. Something in his expression suggested a long, private war he was choosing not to re-litigate this morning.

"She does this," he said flatly, "when she thinks I'm not paying enough attention to her." He didn't move the paw. "It's manipulation. I'm aware. I find it works anyway."

He left his arm exactly where it was.

Outside, a bus hissed past on wet asphalt. The city noise was muffled here—one of the few things he'd insisted on when he'd taken the flat, that it be high enough to muffle the worst of it. London without the noise felt almost manageable. Almost his.

His eyes drifted back to her face.

*Something changed while she was gone. More than one thing.*

He could feel the edges of it the way you felt a room that had been rearranged while you weren't looking—everything technically in place, nothing quite where you'd left it.

He didn't push. He turned back to his tea and let the silence do its work.

Luna's golden eyes narrowed to slits.

For a long, dangerous moment the Kneazle held perfectly still, tail rigid, assessing whether the snow leopard behind Jackie's eyes constituted a genuine territorial claim or a bluff she could profitably call.

She decided, with the dignity of a creature that chose its battles, to step down from the barstool entirely. She landed without sound and walked toward the sofa with her tail elevated at an angle that communicated profound disdain for everyone present.

Draco watched her go.

"She'll remember that," he said. "She has an extremely detailed memory for slights."

But his arm hadn't moved. Her hand was still on his forearm and he'd done nothing about it, which for Draco at 8am was approximately the same as throwing himself at her feet.

He looked down at her hand. Then at her face. The dry comment he'd been assembling—something about the statistical insignificance of missing someone after twenty-four hours—didn't make it out.

"It's not stupid," he said.

He turned his arm over, slowly, until her hand was resting against his palm instead of his forearm. His fingers closed loosely around hers. Not tight. Just—present.

"It's eighteen hours, actually." His thumb moved once across her knuckles. "I counted. Which is considerably more stupid, so you're ahead on this one."

He looked at her for a moment with that particular expression he still hadn't learned to fully conceal—the one that sat just underneath the composure, quiet and unguarded and entirely his.

Then he looked away. Back at the window. The rain.

"The week felt different," he said. "Having you both there." A pause. His jaw shifted slightly, working through something. "Good different. Mostly." He added the qualifier like a man hedging a bet he'd already committed to. "Nott was—"

He stopped.

Tried again.

"He was less insufferable than I anticipated." The words came out deliberate, evenly spaced, like he was defusing something. "Which is its own kind of problem, as it turns out."

His thumb was still moving across her knuckles. He probably hadn't noticed.

"Don't tell him I said that."
