The flat settled into its evening rhythm.

Rain against glass. The scratch of Draco's quill. Luna's quiet movements between kitchen and windowsill.

Draco worked through the case file with the efficiency of someone who found the material genuinely beneath him but refused to do it sloppily. The Fwooper smuggling dispute involved three separate Ministry departments, two international trade agreements, and one spectacularly ill-advised attempt to pass off a muted Fwooper as a standard canary. He annotated the relevant clauses, drafted a two-paragraph summary, and closed the file in thirty-four minutes.

He reached for his tea without looking up from the desk.

It was the correct temperature. He noticed.

His eyes moved to Jackie in the armchair. She had the green book open across her knees, her chai balanced on the armrest, her brow furrowed in the particular way it did when something had caught her properly—not confused, just focused. She turned a page without looking up.

He watched her for a moment.

*She's already in it.*

He recognized the posture. He'd sat in it himself, sixth year, in the Slytherin dormitory at two in the morning with that exact book open on his lap and his hands shaking badly enough that the pages had trembled. He'd found it in the restricted section by accident, looking for something else entirely. He'd read it cover to cover in three nights and built the first version of his mental fortress before Christmas.

He'd never told anyone he owned it.

He capped his quill. Stacked the case file. Set it aside with the neat finality of a man closing one chapter and opening another.

He retrieved the chess set from the lower shelf—a black marble set, heavy and uncompromising, a gift from his father that he kept because it was excellent and spite was a complicated thing. He set it on the coffee table without ceremony, the pieces arranging themselves with soft, authoritative clicks.

Luna immediately abandoned the windowsill and positioned herself beside the board.

"You're not playing," Draco told her.

Luna sat down directly beside his queen's pawn.

He looked at Jackie over the top of the board.

"Whenever you're ready," he said. "I'm not rushing you."

He picked up his tea. Settled back. Crossed one leg over the other with the patience of a man who had been thinking about this rematch for six weeks and was content to wait another five minutes.

His white king caught the lamplight and threw a small, sharp gleam across the ceiling.

Jackie closed the green book with a heavy thud, the weight of the Architecture of the Mind still resonant in her palms. She set her empty chai mug aside, the spiced scent lingering in the air like a ghost. Across the room, the clicks of the marble chess pieces were sharp, authoritative, and impossibly familiar. She stood and stretched, her muscles complaining after the long day at St. Mungo’s. When she sat across from him at the coffee table, the atmosphere in the flat shifted. The earlier vulnerability was still there, but it was being channeled now—funneled into the sixty-four squares between them. Draco moved first. "Pawn to $e4$," he commanded. The white marble piece slid forward with a grinding sound. Jackie didn't hesitate. "Knight to $f6$." Her black knight trotted into place, the Alekhine’s Defense—a challenge right out of the gate. "Pawn to $e5$," Draco countered immediately, his eyes never leaving hers. The pawn pushed her knight. Jackie looked at the board. For a fleeting, reckless second, her mind flashed to a sacrifice at $g4$—a move that would have been loud and messy. But she felt the ghost of the soul-tether pull at her, a reminder of the need for internal stability. She recalibrated. "Knight to $d5$," she said. The knight retreated to the center, settling into its strong-point. "Running already?" Draco asked, the corner of his mouth twitching. "Just finding better ground," she shot back. "Pawn to $d4$." Draco claimed more of the center. He watched her hand hover over the board for a beat too long as she reconsidered the $g4$ line before settling on her next command. "Second-guessing yourself already?"
"Just checking the weather," Jackie muttered. "Pawn to $d6$." Her pawn struck at his chain, demanding an opening. "Knight to $f3$." Draco developed his piece, reinforcing the center with a cold, clinical precision. "Safe doesn't suit you, Jackie."
She leaned forward, her heterochromatic eyes narrowing as she felt the competitive spark catch. "Play with fire and get burned," she purred, her voice low and dangerous. "Pawn takes $e5$."
The black pawn smashed into the white one, clearing the center and opening the lanes.

"Funny," Draco said, his voice dropping an octave as his knight surged forward. "I was about to say the same thing. Knight takes $e5$."
His knight was now centralized, a looming threat in the heart of the board. Jackie felt the pressure, the way he squeezed the space. She needed her bishop. "Pawn to $g6$," she commanded, preparing the kingside fianchetto. She watched the black marble piece slide into place and added, almost mindlessly, "War requires sacrifices."
The words hung in the air, heavier than she’d intended. She saw the way the lamplight caught the hard line of Draco’s jaw. The silence that followed wasn't the comfortable quiet of earlier; it was the sudden, sharp silence that followed a blow. She realized it the moment the words left her mouth—the way they must have landed for a man who had stood on the wrong side of a real war, who had seen his home turned into a morgue and his arm turned into a ledger for a madman. "I—" Jackie backtracked, her voice losing its edge. "I meant the game, Draco. Just the game."
She looked down at the board, the black and white marble suddenly looking a lot less like a distraction and a lot more like the world they were trying so hard to rebuild.

Draco's eyes stayed on the board for a moment after she said it.

His jaw hadn't tightened. His expression hadn't closed. But there was a beat—just one—where something moved behind his eyes that wasn't about chess.

Then he looked up at her.

"I know," he said. Quiet. Even. "I know what you meant."

He didn't elaborate. He didn't reassure her further or make her feel worse about the slip. He just let it land and pass, the way he'd learned to let certain things pass—not because they didn't matter, but because making them larger wouldn't serve either of them.

His attention returned to the board.

Luna had shifted closer during the exchange, her large frame now pressed against Draco's knee. He didn't acknowledge it, but his hand dropped briefly to the back of her neck before returning to the edge of the table.

He studied the position for a long moment. The fianchetto she was building on the kingside was solid—she was learning not to overcommit early, which had cost her in March. He'd been counting on the aggressive line. She hadn't taken it.

*Better ground,* she'd said.

His mouth moved slightly.

"Bishop to $c4$," he said.

The white bishop slid diagonally across the board with a sharp, deliberate sound, pointing directly at the soft center of her position. A quiet threat. Not loud. Not rushed.

His eyes moved from the board to her face.

"Your move."

The white king had nowhere comfortable to go.

Draco looked at the board for four full seconds. The kind of silence that meant he was running lines, checking variations, finding the exits one by one and discovering each of them compromised.

"King to d2," he said.

The marble king slid reluctantly to d2, stepping into the open, exposed and graceless in the way kings never wanted to be. It was the only move. He knew it. She knew it.

He leaned back.

Looked at her across the wreckage of his position—his rook gone, his bishop gone, his king dragged into the center of the board like a man hauled into a room he hadn't chosen to enter.

Luna made a small sound from beside his knee.

"Don't," he told the cat.

He picked up his tea. It had gone cold. He drank it anyway, his eyes staying on Jackie over the rim of the mug with an expression that was doing several things simultaneously—irritation, respect, something that was almost but not quite amusement.

"When you walked into my apartment this morning," he repeated. Flat. Precise. Repeating it back the way he did when something needed to be examined properly. "You were planning this at eight in the morning."

He set the mug down.

"While making breakfast."

A beat.

"You're insufferable," he said. The corner of his mouth betrayed him entirely.

His eyes dropped back to the board. Her queen sat in his position like she owned it.

*She does own it. She's owned it since move six.*

"Well," he said quietly. "Go on then."

## **SUMMARY: MOVES 11-23**

**Moves Played:**

11. Kd2 Qg2
12. Qf3 Qxf3
13. Nxf3 Nc6
14. Ke3 Bh6+
15. Kd3 Bf1
16. Ne2 Nb4+
17. Kc4 Bxe2+
18. Kc3 Bxc1
19. Kxb4 Bxb2
20. Ka5 Bxa1
21. Kb4 a5+
22. Kc5 O-O-O
23. Nd2 ...

---

**Conversation Summary (Past Tense):**

After the queen trade, Draco acknowledged Jackie was still winning but at least not about to be checkmated in three moves anymore. Jackie smiled and promised "Maybe not in three. Give me six." Draco said he'd hold her to that deadline. As Jackie developed her pieces with clinical precision, Draco observed she wasn't playing anymore—she was executing. "I'm watching a massacre," he said quietly.

When Jackie's six-move deadline approached without delivering checkmate, her frustration became evident. She gave up on her goal, saying "Apparently you're too good at tucking your tail and running." Draco responded that survival wasn't cowardice, that she was still winning, and that he was making her work for it. After she captured his rook, Jackie's voice held self-directed frustration: "I should've been able to finish it three moves ago." Draco told her she'd won eight moves ago, had executed a flawless attack, and urged her to stop punishing herself for not being more perfect.

Jackie blinked as if suddenly aware of where she was. She apologized, explaining that her father had insisted she learn chess with perfect precision since she was five, and that perfect was the only acceptable outcome. She admitted she still got competitive about it sometimes. Draco asked her how many times she failed at something and heard her father's voice berating her for it, recognizing their shared scars.

**Final Exchange (Verbatim):**

Jackie: "I... Know that. In theory. Tell me, how many times do you fail at something that Lucius would expect you to accomplish and hear his voice in the back of your mind berating you for it?"

Jackie: "I... Know that. In theory. Tell me, how many times do you fail at something that Lucius would expect you to accomplish and hear his voice in the back of your mind berating you for it?"

The black bishop slid to d4.

Draco's king had nowhere to go. The marble piece stood in the center of the board, exposed and surrounded, and didn't move because there was nowhere to move it to.

Draco looked at the board for a moment. Then he reached out and laid his king on its side with two fingers—the formal concession—and left his hand there on the table.

He didn't say congratulations. He didn't say well played.

He looked at her.

She was staring at the board with the flat, hollow expression of someone who had just won something and felt nothing about it, and he recognized that expression with a specificity that sat uncomfortably in his chest.

"Stupid girl," he repeated. Quiet. Just the words, held up to the light.

His hand moved from the toppled king to the edge of the board. He didn't reach for her. He just shifted his weight, settling onto the floor on his side of the table, closing some of the distance between them without crossing it entirely.

"He said that to you directly." Not a question.

Luna padded around the board and inserted herself into the space between them, her large frame warm and solid. Neither of them told her to move.

"My father never used that word," Draco said. "He didn't have to. He had a look." He turned his tea mug slowly in his hands. "You knew before he opened his mouth whether you'd passed or failed. Whether you'd been useful or embarrassing." His jaw shifted. "Samaya was the benchmark. Your father used her the way mine used legacy. As a measuring stick calibrated to make sure you always came up short."

He looked at her properly.

"You won," he said. "And you're sitting there hearing his voice telling you it took too long."

It wasn't a question either.

"Ask your question," he said quietly. The wager. "You've earned it."

Draco went still.

Not the careful, controlled stillness he deployed in Ministry meetings or difficult conversations. This was different—the stillness of someone who had been handed a question they hadn't prepared for and were now taking it seriously rather than deflecting it.

He looked at the toppled king on the board.

Luna shifted, her head dropping onto his knee with the weight of a creature who had decided this moment required her presence.

"Yes," he said.

No qualification attached. No *theoretically* or *perhaps someday* or *it's complicated.* Just the word, sitting plainly in the quiet flat.

He turned the tea mug once in his hands.

"I didn't think I did," he continued. "For a long time. The Malfoy name, the legacy, the expectation attached to it—" He stopped. "My mother made it very clear that the entire point of my existence was continuation. Heirs. Bloodline. The dynasty perpetuating itself." His mouth pressed briefly flat. "It made the idea feel like a duty rather than a choice. And I don't do well with things I haven't chosen."

He was quiet for a moment.

"But I work with children twice a week," he said. "And at some point I noticed that I wasn't just tolerating it." He glanced up at her. "Thomas. Iris. The way they look at things before the world has finished telling them what to see."

He stopped himself before it became too much.

"Yes," he said again, simpler. "Someday. When it's a choice and not an obligation."

His eyes met hers.

"Your turn to answer the same question."

Draco didn't answer immediately.

He looked at her—the attempted smile, the exhaustion underneath it, the deliberate pivot away from whatever question she'd actually prepared. He noted all of it and chose not to name any of it. She'd earned the right to ask something lighter. He wouldn't make her explain the choice.

He looked back at the toppled king on the board.

"Yes," he said.

Simple. No qualification attached to the front of it.

He was quiet for a moment, turning the tea mug in his hands.

"Not now. Not—" He stopped. Reorganized. "The circumstances would need to be different. Stable. I'd want them to have something I didn't." His thumb moved along the mug's rim. "A home that wasn't a performance. A father who didn't build the inside of their head into a trap."

He glanced at her sideways.

"I think about it more than I'd admit to most people," he said. "What I'd do differently. What I'd keep." A pause. "There's very little I'd keep."

Luna had settled fully between them now, her head resting on her enormous paws.

"I'd keep the chess," he said. "Early. Properly taught." The corner of his mouth moved. "None of this 'perfect or nothing' methodology your father apparently favored."

He looked at her directly then.

"Why does it cross your mind?"

Draco went very still.

Not the stillness of composure. The other kind—the kind that happened when something landed directly on a bruise he hadn't known was visible.

He looked at the toppled king on the board.

Luna, sensing the shift, pressed her flank more firmly against his leg.

He was quiet for long enough that the rain filled the silence completely. When he finally spoke, his voice was even, but it cost him something to keep it that way.

"That's not as simple a question as it sounds," he said.

He picked up the fallen king. Turned it in his fingers once, the cold marble catching the lamplight.

"Yes," he said. "In the abstract. Someday." He set the piece back upright. "I'm good with them. I know I am. Today reminded me of that, not that I'd forgotten." His thumb stilled on the king's crown. "I like who I am in that ward. I like that there's a version of me that exists there."

He put the piece down.

"But." He exhaled. "My mother sent me a Howler three weeks ago."

He hadn't planned to say it tonight. He hadn't planned to say it at all.

"She's ill. Post-Azkaban. The Healers say it's manageable but she's—" His jaw tightened. "She's spending money I don't have on care I can't afford to supplement. And the Howler was largely about how I'll never pass on the Malfoy name. How I'm a disappointment. How fooling around with someone else's wife isn't a legacy."

He looked at her directly.

"So yes. Someday. But someday is doing a great deal of work in that sentence right now."

Jackie opened her mouth, then clicked shut. She watched his fingers tighten around the marble king, the small piece of stone looking like the only thing keeping him anchored to the present. *I had no idea.* 
The words felt like lead in her throat. But of course she hadn’t—he hadn't let her in. He was telling her now, but the timing felt like a slow-motion collision. *Why didn't you say something sooner?* Her mind raced back through the last twenty-one days. Maybe it had taken three weeks for him to find the words, or maybe he’d needed the heat of Tuscany to be sure she was actually there to stay this time—that she wasn’t just passing through his life again. "I’ve never apologized to you," she said softly, her gaze fixed on his hands. "For putting her there in the first place. I know she deserved it, but… you did not."
She knew him. He was a Malfoy, and more than that, he was an Arithmancer. He lived in the world of variables and certainties. If he was speaking about this, he had already calculated the trajectory down to the last Knut. "How long?" she asked, her voice steady despite the ache in her chest. "How long until you run out of money?"
She was already running the angles, her Ravenclaw mind cataloging his assets. Not this flat—it was Ministry-assigned, and whatever rent he paid was likely far below market value. Then there was Malfoy Manor, but Draco wasn't on the deed; he had no authority to touch it. Narcissa would sooner eat her own shoelaces than sell a single stone of the Malfoy legacy. Other than that, Jackie realized with a jolt of cold clarity, Draco didn't have much. She’d read the Daily Prophet headlines about the astronomical reparations the noble families had been forced to pay to war victims. Theo’s family had faced the same. She knew his father, Cassius, had only avoided Azkaban through a series of devilish political maneuvers, and the only reason he’d agreed to let his son marry a cursed girl was for the dowry. Up until this moment, she had assumed 'losing money' meant the Malfoys were simply no longer filthy rich. She’d thought they were still wealthy by ordinary standards.

She hadn't realized Draco was actually struggling to keep his head above water.

Draco put the chess king down.

"Don't apologize for that," he said. His voice was flat but not cold. "She arranged a kidnapping. She had it coming and I've made my peace with that." He paused. "Mostly."

He stood. Not fleeing the conversation—just needing to not be on the floor for the next part of it. He collected the chess pieces with methodical efficiency, each one clicked back into the velvet-lined box.

"Eight months," he said. "Maybe ten if I stop eating well."

He said it the way he delivered every uncomfortable truth—precise, stripped of drama, as if the facts were easier to hold when they weren't dressed up.

"The reparations took most of the liquid assets two years ago. The Manor runs at a loss—the upkeep alone is—" He stopped. Closed the chess box. "It doesn't matter. The point is Narcissa controls the Manor and whatever remains tied to it, and her medical costs are coming out of what I have, not what she has, because she spent what she had." His jaw tightened briefly. "On what, exactly, I haven't been able to determine. She's not forthcoming."

He set the box on the shelf.

Turned around.

"I don't want your money," he said. Quietly but immediately, cutting off the angle before she could take it. "Or Nott's. I want that said clearly before you start calculating."

He looked at her.

"I'm telling you because you asked a question and you deserved an honest answer. Not because I need rescuing."

So his life had a timer on it as well. Or at least, the life as he knew it.
It was a cruel, humorless kind of cosmic righting of the scales. The boy who had spent years mocking others for having less was now staring down the barrel of bankruptcy. She suspected that if Potter and his friends ever found out, they’d be delighted. In her mind, that made them no better than Draco had been—if not worse.
She had opened her mouth just before he’d cut her off, the offer of her and Theo’s money sitting right on the tip of her tongue. Between her accessible dowry and Theo’s plan to sell the Highlands Manor—a gift from Cassius specifically designed to protect the asset from Ministry seizure—they had more than enough to share. It wouldn’t just be eight months; it could be years. But Draco had refused before she could even speak, and she knew him too well to degrade him by trying to argue.
“Fuck…” she muttered, because no other word felt appropriate.
Then, the computations in her head finally clicked, landing on the one variable that solved the equation for the Malfoy legacy.
“Pansy.” Her voice was flat, sounding as if it were coming from somewhere very far away. She didn't move from her spot on the floor. “The Parkinsons... that’s why your mother wanted you to marry her. They were never connected to Voldemort; they’re absolutely filthy rich. If you married her, it would save the Manor. It would save Narcissa. And it would save you.”
It sickened her to think that this was the shape of their world. But it didn't make the realization any less true.

Draco didn't move.

He stood at the shelf with his hand still on the chess box, his back half-turned to her. The rain had eased into something quieter against the glass—a low, persistent hiss rather than the earlier assault.

"Yes," he said.

One word. Flat and final.

He turned around then. Leaned against the shelf with his arms crossing, the old armor settling back into place by reflex. His face was composed but his eyes were doing something more complicated.

"That's what the Howler was actually about," he said. "Underneath the illness and the money and the disappointment. Pansy's available. Blaise won't marry her—" He stopped. Corrected himself. "Blaise hasn't married her yet. In my mother's arithmetic that's still a door that hasn't fully closed."

He looked at the middle distance for a moment.

"She outlined it very clearly. At volume." His mouth pressed into a thin line. "The whole building heard."

He was quiet for a beat.

"I'm not going to," he said. "Marry Pansy. In case that needed saying."

He pushed off the shelf and crossed to the armchair opposite her, dropping into it. His elbows went to his knees. The composed architecture of him had loosened into something more tired.

"I'm telling you this because you'd have figured it out anyway," he said. "And I'd rather you hear it from me than spend the next week being tactful about it." His eyes found hers. "I hate when you're tactful. You're terrible at it and it wastes both our time."

Luna crossed the room and jumped into his lap without invitation.

He let her stay.

"I'll find another way," he said. "I always do."

Jackie finally stood up. She walked to the window and pressed her forehead against the cool glass, staring out at the rain-slicked London streets. She hadn't even noticed when the daylight had bled out of the sky; it was likely past eight. She tracked a double-decker bus lumbering below, then a woman hurrying somewhere, clutching a small girl's hand.
“You won’t.” It pained her to say it out loud. It would have been so much easier to lean into his assurances—to pretend they weren't both too smart not to see the math. “You want me to stop being tactful? Fine. Here’s me being honest instead. There are exactly two ways you’re getting out of this, save for the one-in-twenty-two-thousand chance you win that kind of gold betting on hippogriff races. You either take the money from me and Theo—as a loan, a gift, or the dowry I was never legally able to give you—or you marry Pansy Parkinson and take hers.”
She turned to face him at last. There was no anger in her expression, no accusation—only a heavy, tired resignation. “Let it be said loudly and with precision: the first option is my strong preference. I have no desire to give you up to her, or anyone else. Not when I just got you back.”
She wrapped her arms around her torso, as if the physical pressure was the only thing keeping her from shaking. And maybe it was.
“The kind of money we’re talking about doesn’t come from a meager, secondary job at the Ministry. And they’ll never give you an influential position, Draco. Not with your name. So, I’ll play along with the fantasy that you’re going to figure it out—just for today. Because I’m exhausted, and I thought I was asking an innocent question only to get a bucket of ice water to the face. But we both know the truth.”
She walked to the armchair opposite him and retrieved the green book she’d left there. “For what it’s worth...” She paused, her voice softening. “I think you’d be a great dad.”
With that, she disappeared behind his bedroom door. Two minutes later, the sound of the shower running in the en suite cut through the quiet of the flat.

Draco sat with it.

Luna shifted in his lap, resettling her weight, and he let her. His hand moved to her back automatically, a slow, absent stroke that had nothing to do with affection and everything to do with needing somewhere to put his hands.

The bedroom door clicked shut. The shower started.

*Two ways out.* She'd said it without cruelty, which made it worse. Jackie without tact was Jackie with a scalpel—precise, clean, leaving edges too neat to argue with. He couldn't call her wrong. He'd run the same numbers himself at three in the morning for the past three weeks, staring at the ceiling of this flat that wasn't even properly his.

He stood. Luna dropped to the floor with a reproachful sound.

He collected her empty mug from the windowsill. His own from the coffee table. Carried them to the kitchen and washed them by hand, the hot water running over his knuckles while he stared at the dark window above the sink.

*I think you'd be a great dad.*

He turned the tap off.

Stood there for a moment in the quiet kitchen, the water dripping from his hands onto the steel basin.

She'd said it softly. Almost as an afterthought. Which meant she'd meant it completely—Jackie only softened her voice for the things she was most certain about.

He dried his hands. Folded the tea towel precisely and hung it back on the rail.

He fed Luna the last of the evening portion without being asked, the tin opened and emptied with mechanical efficiency while the cat watched him with her unreadable golden eyes.

"Don't," he told her.

Luna ate.

He turned off the kitchen light and moved to the bedroom doorway. Stopped. The shower was still running on the other side—the particular sound of water against tile that meant she was standing under it rather than moving through it. Taking the long version. The decompressing version.

He leaned his shoulder against the doorframe.

*A loan, a gift, or the dowry I was never legally able to give you.*

She'd thought through the architecture of it before she'd spoken. Of course she had. She was a Ravenclaw who had been doing financial battle with Ministry contract law since she was eighteen.

His jaw shifted.

Jackie held herself together until she stepped under the spray. Only when she was certain the roar of the water would muffle the sound of her sobs did she brace her hands against the tiles and let out a jagged, soundless scream.
Across the distance, the bond hummed. She felt Theo’s distress spiking like a fever—anxiety coiling tight, followed by a flare of sudden, sharp rage that wanted to tear the world apart for making her feel this way. For a heartbeat, she half-expected the air to crack and Theo to Apparate into the center of Draco's flat, but then the realization hit her: this wasn't the first time he’d felt this. It was just the first time she was awake to it.
After a moment, his emotions shifted, turning heavy and dull. Jackie recognized the change; he must have transformed, letting the animal take over to run the Highlands until he was too exhausted to act on his instincts. She wondered how many times he’d done exactly that during those hollow months after Draco left—running until his lungs burned to keep himself from hunting Draco down, while she stayed behind and cried until her throat felt like sandpaper.
Jackie stayed there, letting the emotions hit her in waves. The frustration at the sheer impossibility of the situation. The sorrow for Draco, who hadn't chosen his last name but was still being suffocated by the weight of it. The burning anger at a fate that seemed determined to poison every scrap of peace she managed to claw back.
She used the rhythm of the water and her breathing exercises to pull the emotions down and away from her. Finally, she washed her hair and dried herself, letting the damp, red waves fall nearly to her tailbone.
She studied her reflection in the mirror. Her skin was flushed from the heat, a convenient mask for the redness in her cheeks, and her eyes weren't puffy—not yet. She wouldn’t add to Draco’s burden by letting him see exactly how much his news had shattered her.

## Summary: Tuesday Afternoon & Evening

**St. Mungo's Children's Ward (2pm–5pm)**

Jackie and Draco arrived together for their first shared volunteer shift. The ward had missed them during the Italy week; the children were difficult in their absence. Draco was already with Thomas (seven, bone-growth issues, both arms in glowing casts) when Jackie arrived, soft and patient in a way that contrasted sharply with his usual self. Jackie distributed Italian sweets and enchanted postcards, bribing the children into good behaviour with promises of stories about abraxan races and Draco nearly losing his head to a palomino—which he confirmed, with dignity, had been a misunderstanding.

Healer Abernathy flagged a new patient: Mira, eight years old, silent since Sunday, tracking no one. Jackie took her without discussion, signalled to Draco with a look, and he gave her the room. She sat on the floor beside Mira's bed, read aloud from a Muggle psychology book without addressing the girl directly, and slowly coaxed her into eating the ward snacks and taking both her potions. Mira spoke twice. Draco tracked the end bed all afternoon without approaching it.

They finished the shift sorting linens and potions in the supply room. Jackie revealed the book was for herself—for managing the soul tether—and Draco offered to help her map the theory. He referenced *The Architecture of the Mind* without fully explaining when or why he'd needed it.

---

**Back at the Flat (approx. 5:30pm onwards)**

Jackie cooked the dinner she'd prepped earlier—steaks, mash, green beans. Over the meal, she told Draco about the bidirectional bond: that she'd drunk Theo's blood on Monday, making the tether mutual. Draco processed it without anger, named it precisely—he hadn't been consulted, he'd been the last to know—and accepted her apology once. He offered to help her build the mental mechanics to regulate the bond rather than be ruled by it.

"Please, don't ask me to make that choice for you. How can I ask you to stay or tell you to leave, knowing that either will destroy one or both of us?"

She took a shuddering breath and closed her eyes.

"I know you'll say that it doesn't change anything, but it does. How am I supposed to watch you lose everything—your ancestral home, your livelihood, your dignity—and what... do nothing?"

She moved then, not exactly pulling away from him, but turning onto her other side so he was facing her back. She always found saying harsh truths to his face too difficult. She had to look away, or the words would die in her throat.

"Pansy isn't a bad person. She's vain, and she has that thing with Blaise, but... she's reasonable. She wouldn't expect you to love her."

The room went very still.

Draco's hand stopped moving on her hip.

He didn't speak for a long moment. The lamp threw its shadows across the ceiling and the rain had stopped entirely, leaving a silence that had texture.

"Don't." His voice was quiet. The specific quiet that meant something was being held very carefully in place.

He sat up. Not pulling away violently—just moving, needing to not be horizontal for this particular conversation. He reached for his shirt from the floor and held it in his hands without putting it on.

"Don't do that."

He wasn't looking at her back. He was looking at the wall.

"You're lying in my bed telling me Pansy wouldn't expect me to love her." The words came out even. Measured. Each one placed deliberately. "You're solving my problem by removing yourself from the equation. And you've dressed it up as practicality so I can't argue with it without sounding like I'm being a fool about money."

He put the shirt down.

"I know what you're doing. I recognize the arithmetic because I've done it myself." His jaw shifted. "Deciding the other person would be better off with a cleaner arrangement. Deciding that stepping back is the generous choice."

He finally looked at her.

"I left once," he said. "You know what that cost. And you're asking me to do it with paperwork."

Jackie surged up, the sudden awareness of her nakedness feeling like a vulnerability she couldn’t afford anymore. She moved to the dresser, the cotton of her nightgown feeling like a shield as she pulled it over her head. She gripped the edge of the wood, her knuckles white, anchoring herself to the physical reality of the room.
“I’m not *asking* you, you absolute idiot.” Her voice cracked, sounding more wounded than she wanted to admit. It was as if she were furious with him for being too blind to see the sacrifice she was trying to lay at his feet. “Poking my eyes out would be preferable to seeing you anywhere near Pansy, let alone seeing her in a white dress.”
She finally turned to face him, the weight of the moment pressing down on her chest.
“I’m *allowing* you. I’m letting you make the choice for yourself with the knowledge that I won’t resent you. That I won’t stop loving you. That…” The words died in her throat. She had no idea how else to express the gravity of what she was surrendering.
If that was his choice, she would accept it. She wouldn't hold it against him. That was the only thing she had left to give him—absolute, painful freedom—yet he was making her feel as though she were the one physically shoving him into Pansy’s arms.

Draco stood up.

He crossed the room in four steps and stopped directly in front of her, close enough that she'd have to look at him. His shirt was still on the bed. His hair was still wrecked. He looked like a man who had run out of composed language and was working with what remained.

"Stop."

Not loud. Absolutely final.

"Stop giving me exits." His voice was rough at the edges. "I don't want them. I haven't wanted them since March and I certainly don't want one now, lying in the wreckage of a conversation that started with chess."

His hands came up and gripped her face. Not hard—careful, the way he was always careful with her—but certain. Tilting her up to look at him.

"You love me," he said. "I know that. I'm not confused about that." His gray eyes held hers without flinching. "So stop being generous with my freedom and just—" His jaw tightened. "—just be angry that it's impossible. You're allowed. I'm angry. Be angry with me."

His thumbs moved once across her cheekbones.

"I don't want Pansy." The words came out stripped of everything except their truth. "I want you. Legally, permanently, ridiculously. And the money is a problem I will solve without selling either of us to solve it."

He pressed his forehead against hers.

"So stop allowing me things," he said quietly. "And just stay here."

Draco looked at her for a long moment.

The white knuckles on the dresser. The nightgown pulled on like armor. The crack in her voice she hadn't managed to hide.

He stood up. Crossed the room.

He didn't stop until he was directly behind her, close enough that she could feel the warmth off him. He didn't touch her. He looked at her reflection in the mirror above the dresser—her red hair loose and damp, her eyes bright with the specific brightness that preceded tears she wasn't going to let fall.

"I know you're not asking," he said quietly. "That's what makes it worse."

His hands came up then. Settled on her shoulders, light. Not holding her in place. Just there.

"You're giving me permission to leave you." His voice was low, stripped of its usual architecture. "You've wrapped it in love and called it freedom and handed it to me like it's a gift." His jaw tightened. "It's not a gift. It's you deciding in advance that you're the thing that gets sacrificed when the options run out."

His eyes stayed on her reflection.

"I'm not choosing Pansy." Flat. Final. "Not in eight months. Not in ten. Not if the Manor crumbles into the ground and my mother never speaks to me again." He paused. "She barely speaks to me now. The loss is theoretical at this point."

His thumbs moved once against her shoulders.

"I need you to stop solving for my exit," he said. "It's the one variable I'm not willing to make available."

Jackie let out a breath she hadn’t realized she was holding, the tension in her chest finally snapping under the weight of his gaze. The heat of his hands on her skin felt like a rebuke to her cold logic, a reminder that they weren't just variables in an equation.
She leaned into his touch, her eyes closing for a heartbeat as she let the reality of his presence anchor her.
"Okay," she whispered, the word small but certain. "I'll stay."
She pulled back just enough to look at him, her heterochromatic eyes searching his gray ones. The Ravenclaw in her was already resetting the board, building a new structure out of the debris of their argument. If he wanted her to be angry, she could do that. But if he wanted her to stop calculating, he was asking for the impossible.
"Eight months," she said, her voice regaining its steady, structural rhythm. "That’s the window. If you haven't found your third option by then, you take the money. My money. Theo’s money. We’re not discussing it again. Since we’ve both agreed the ‘Pansy’ route is a non-starter, that is the only variable left on the table."
She didn't wait for him to argue. She reached up, hooking her fingers into the hair at the nape of his neck and pulling him down. The kiss wasn't like the one from earlier; it wasn't a desperate attempt to forget. It was a seal on a contract—messy, honest, and absolute.
When she pulled away, she kept her hands resting against his bare chest, feeling the steady, thrumming beat of his heart under her palms. The damp waves of her hair were already starting to cool against her back, but the room felt smaller, safer.
"I love you," she said, her voice finally sounding like herself again. "Thank you for choosing me."

Draco stayed where he was for a moment after she pulled back. His hands had dropped to her waist, holding loosely, and he looked at her with an expression that had shed the last of its armor.

"I'll note that you've structured that as a deadline with a predetermined outcome," he said, "which means you've already decided how it ends."

The corner of his mouth moved.

"Ravenclaw," he said. The single word carrying the full weight of resigned, helpless affection.

"I know," he said against her hair. Not to *I love you*—he'd said that already, in the kitchen doorway months ago, in the only way he knew how. He said it now the same way. Not the words. The steadiness.

"No," Draco told her.

Luna walked in anyway and settled at the foot of the bed with the authority of a creature who had never once been successfully refused.

Draco looked at Jackie over the lamp.

"Go," Jackie murmured, her voice soft but brooking no argument as she gestured toward the en-suite. "Shower. Get changed. You smell like antiseptic and stress."
Draco obliged, though he lingered for a second, his gaze tracing the exhausted slump of her shoulders before he disappeared into the bathroom. By the time the steam had cleared and he returned, Jackie was already gone. She lay beneath the covers like a doll with her strings cut, her breathing deep and heavy, pulled under by the sheer weight of the day. Draco slid in beside her, moving with practiced quiet, and gathered her into his arms. He tucked her head beneath his chin, his heartbeat slowing to match hers, and let the darkness take them both. But the darkness wasn't empty. The cool London air, smelling of rain and lavender, began to thicken. It turned heavy and cloying, smelling of ancient dust, damp stone, and the sharp, metallic tang of Nott Manor’s shadow. Jackie was in the bedroom in the Highlands. The emerald velvet hangings of the four-poster bed felt like a shroud. Theo was over her, his weight a crushing, familiar heat. It was supposed to be the game—the consensual dance of power they had choreographed to keep the darkness at bay. But the air was wrong. The pressure of his hands on her wrists was too tight, the look in his eyes too vacant, too hungry. The play-acting had curdled into something else. "*Finite*," Jackie whispered, her voice catching in her throat. It was the word. The boundary. Theo didn’t stop. He didn’t even flinch. His movements were rhythmic and relentless, a tidal wave that ignored the shore. "*Finite\!*" she cried out, her voice rising into a jagged edge of panic. She bucked beneath him, her skin crawling, the sense of violation blossoming in her chest like a poisonous flower. The trust that anchored their lives was fraying, snapping thread by thread. "Theo, stop\! *Finite\!*"
He leaned down, his face a mask of cold, predatory beauty. He didn't look like the man who brought her tea or read her poetry. He looked like the monster he had always feared he was. He let out a low, dark laugh—the sound of a tomb door closing.

"Take your time," he said. "I'm not going anywhere."

"Go," Jackie murmured, her voice soft but brooking no argument as she gestured toward the en-suite. "Shower. Get changed. You smell like antiseptic and stress."
Draco obliged, though he lingered for a second, his gaze tracing the exhausted slump of her shoulders before he disappeared into the bathroom. By the time the steam had cleared and he returned, Jackie was already gone. She lay beneath the covers like a doll with her strings cut, her breathing deep and heavy, pulled under by the sheer weight of the day. Draco slid in beside her, moving with practiced quiet, and gathered her into his arms. He tucked her head beneath his chin, his heartbeat slowing to match hers, and let the darkness take them both. But the darkness wasn't empty. The cool London air, smelling of rain and lavender, began to thicken. It turned heavy and cloying, smelling of ancient dust, damp stone, and the sharp, metallic tang of Nott Manor’s shadow. Jackie was in the bedroom in the Highlands. The emerald velvet hangings of the four-poster bed felt like a shroud. Theo was over her, his weight a crushing, familiar heat. It was supposed to be the game—the consensual dance of power they had choreographed to keep the darkness at bay. But the air was wrong. The pressure of his hands on her wrists was too tight, the look in his eyes too vacant, too hungry. The play-acting had curdled into something else. "*Finite*," Jackie whispered, her voice catching in her throat. It was the word. The boundary. Theo didn’t stop. He didn’t even flinch. His movements were rhythmic and relentless, a tidal wave that ignored the shore. "*Finite\!*" she cried out, her voice rising into a jagged edge of panic. She bucked beneath him, her skin crawling, the sense of violation blossoming in her chest like a poisonous flower. The trust that anchored their lives was fraying, snapping thread by thread. "Theo, stop\! *Finite\!*"
He leaned down, his face a mask of cold, predatory beauty. He didn't look like the man who brought her tea or read her poetry. He looked like the monster he had always feared he was. He let out a low, dark laugh—the sound of a tomb door closing.

Draco didn't speak.

He'd been awake the instant she lurched upright—not gradually, not with the confusion of interrupted sleep, but immediately, the way he always woke when something was wrong. Old reflexes. The kind built in dark years that had never fully unwound.

His hands found her in the dark. Her shoulders first, then her face, his palms pressing against her cheeks to turn her toward him. Not forcing. Just orienting.

"Jackie." His voice was low and even. "You're in my flat. London. You're here."

She was shaking badly. The sobs were the violent kind, the ones that came from somewhere below conscious thought.

He didn't ask what happened. He didn't reach for his wand or the lamp. He pulled her in, one hand flat against her back, the other cradling the back of her head, and held on.

"I've got you," he said, against her hair. "I've got you. You're here."

Luna moved up from the foot of the bed without a sound and pressed her warm, solid weight against Jackie's other side.

Draco stayed absolutely still, letting her shake. His hand moved in slow, continuous passes down her back. Not trying to stop the trembling. Just present inside it.

*Theo.*

The thought arrived and he set it aside. Not now. Whatever it was, not now.

"Breathe," he said quietly. "Just breathe. I'm here."

It took her a long time to find the edges of reality again. The panic came in waves, receding just enough to let her catch her breath before dragging her back under. Draco remained a solid, silent anchor in the dark, but she was fighting a battle he couldn't see, and for a long while, it was a losing one.
When the sobs finally quieted, she stayed slumped against him, her fingers knotted in the fabric of his shirt like a drowning person clinging to a piece of wreckage. She felt hollowed out, her body simply giving up when it had no more adrenaline to burn.
But the bond—the blood-red link between her and Theo—wasn't quiet. Miles away, Theo was a storm of restless, combustible anger. And every time his emotions spiked, Jackie’s mind flashed back to the dream: the cruel curve of his mouth, the merciless edge of his laughter. This was the true horror. The actual violation she had endured months ago had been worn down by time, the edges of the memory smoothed like river stones. But this "dream" was fresh. It was raw. It felt as if her skin were still vibrating from the touch of it.
Suddenly, the air in the room felt too thick. Draco’s arms, which had been her only sanctuary minutes ago, now felt like leaden weights. The heat of him reminded her of the dream. The weight of his body against hers reminded her of the bed in the Highlands.
"No," she gasped, the word scratching her raw throat. She shoved at his chest with a sudden, frantic strength, her movements spurred by a suffocating need to be free. "Stop. Don't... don't touch me."
Her eyes darted through the shadows of the room, wide and wild, until they locked onto the sliver of light from the slightly ajar bathroom door. She scrambled off the bed, her legs nearly giving way beneath her as she made a blind run for it. She didn't look back to see the look on his face. She slammed the door and threw the latch, the click of the lock providing the only barrier between her and the world.
Then the nausea hit—a violent, rising tide. She barely made it to the toilet before her stomach revolted, her body purging the last remnants of the nightmare in a series of agonizing heaves.

Draco sat in the dark after the bathroom door latched.

His hands were still open from where she'd shoved them away. He looked at them for a moment, then set them on his knees.

*Don't touch me.*

He knew that tone. He'd heard it before—not from her, but he recognized the quality of it. The place it came from. He didn't take it personally and he didn't follow her, which cost him something significant.

He got up. Pulled on his trousers. Moved to the bathroom door and crouched in front of it, close enough to hear the sounds of her being sick, far enough that she had the space she'd asked for.

"I'm right here," he said, through the door. Quiet. Even. "Not going anywhere. Take whatever time you need."

He sat with his back against the wall beside the door. Drew his knees up. Waited.

---

The crack of Apparition came eleven minutes later.

Not inside the flat—Draco had wards for that—but directly outside the front door, close enough that the air pressure shifted. One knock. Three precise raps that weren't a question so much as an announcement.

Draco was on his feet before the third knock landed.

He crossed the flat in silence and opened the door.

Theo stood in the hallway. Still dressed—dark trousers, shirt with the sleeves already rolled, like he'd been awake. His hair was damp at the temples. His pale eyes moved past Draco's shoulder immediately, scanning the flat, finding the strip of light under the bathroom door.

He looked at Draco's face.

"She's in there," Draco said. Not a question.

"I felt her wake up." Theo's voice was stripped of everything except the information. "The bond—it spiked and then—" He stopped. His jaw tightened. "Is she hurt?"

"Not physically."

Something moved behind Theo's eyes. He looked at the bathroom door again, then back at Draco, and for once there was no performance in him. No calculation. Just a man standing in a hallway at—Draco checked—half past two in the morning, looking like he'd run from Scotland on foot if the Apparition hadn't worked.

"It was my nightmare," Theo said. Flat. Certain. "She was in it."

Draco went very still.

When the heaves subsided, Jackie slid to the floor in front of the toilet and pressed her face against the porcelain rim, too revulsed by the dream to care about the lack of hygiene. She stood after a minute, rinsing her face and mouth. She felt dirty. The sensation was a sickeningly familiar ghost; she’d last felt this way in January of 1999 at Hogwarts. After she’d climbed the stairs to the Ravenclaw Tower. After Theo had...
She looked at the shower. She’d spent over an hour under the spray back then, scrubbing her skin raw, crying and cursing. She wanted to do the same thing now, but she knew better. It hadn’t helped then.
She’d thought she was brave. She’d thought she could withstand Theo’s darkness because she had made certain she was powerful enough to stop him. But the dream hadn't accounted for her strength. There had been no magic, no animagus transformation, no escape, and no fight. She was powerless all over again, and that helplessness was a violation all its own.
She sank back onto the floor beside the door, leaning her head against the cold tiled wall. She could smell her own sweat and feel the slickness of her nightgown sticking to her skin. She still refused to shower. She refused to mirror that day.
Jackie sat there, eyes half-closed, until she heard Draco talking to someone. She didn’t need to hear the actual voice to know who it was. Suddenly, Theo’s emotions through the bond surged, ten times stronger, and she knew he had Apparated to find her. She could feel his distress, his guilt, and his shame—she wanted none of it, but she couldn't shut it out.
"*Menace.*"
Her stomach churned at the nickname. She loved that word on his lips. She had found her highest highs when he whispered it. And now he was using it like a lifeline during her lowest low.
*Go away.*
She shoved the thought at him through the wood of the door, her mind a jagged blade. She was too exhausted to speak.

After she’d climbed the stairs to the Ravenclaw Tower. After Theo had...
She looked at the shower. She’d spent over an hour under the spray back then, scrubbing her skin raw, crying and cursing. She wanted to do the same thing now, but she knew better. It hadn’t helped then.
She’d thought she was brave. She’d thought she could withstand Theo’s darkness because she had made certain she was powerful enough to stop him. But the dream hadn't accounted for her strength. There had been no magic, no animagus transformation, no escape, and no fight. She was powerless all over again, and that helplessness was a violation all its own.
She sank back onto the floor beside the door, leaning her head against the cold tiled wall. She could smell her own sweat and feel the slickness of her nightgown sticking to her skin. She still refused to shower. She refused to mirror that day.
Jackie sat there, eyes half-closed, until she heard Draco talking to someone. She didn’t need to hear the actual voice to know who it was. Suddenly, Theo’s emotions through the bond surged, ten times stronger, and she knew he had Apparated to find her. She could feel his distress, his guilt, and his shame—she wanted none of it, but she couldn't shut it out.
"*Menace.*"
Her stomach churned at the nickname. She loved that word on his lips. She had found her highest highs when he whispered it. And now he was using it like a lifeline during her lowest low.
*Go away.*
She shoved the thought at him through the wood of the door, her mind a jagged blade. She was too exhausted to speak.

Theo felt it hit him like a physical thing.

He stayed crouched at the door. His hand had risen halfway toward the wood and he stopped it there, suspended.

*Go away.*

His eyes closed for a second.

He'd felt the dream end. He'd woken gasping in the Highlands, sheets soaked, the specific horror of the nightmare still crawling through him—and then he'd felt her wake up, hundreds of miles away, and the quality of her terror had told him everything. She hadn't just had a bad dream. She'd been inside his.

He lowered his hand.

"Okay," he said, through the door. Quiet. No performance in it. "Okay. I'm not coming in."

He stayed crouched for another moment.

"I need you to know it wasn't—" He stopped. His jaw worked. "You know what it was. You know the difference." The words came out carefully, stripped of everything except what mattered. "I'm sorry you were in it."

He stood. Stepped back from the door.

Draco was behind him, leaning against the wall with his arms crossed. Not hostile. Just present, watching Theo with the careful attention of a man taking inventory.

Theo turned to face him.

They looked at each other in the dim light of the flat.

"She needs the room," Theo said, low.

"I know that."

"But not to be alone in it."

Draco's jaw shifted. "Also know that."

Theo moved to the sofa. Sat. His elbows went to his knees and he pressed his knuckles against his mouth, his pale eyes fixed on the bathroom door across the room.

The lighter appeared in his fingers. The familiar metallic roll across his knuckles—*clink, clink, clink*—the only sound in the flat besides the distant hiss of London after rain.

Draco stayed against the wall.

Neither of them spoke.

They waited.

She wasn’t ready to face him yet—not while the ghost of his laughter still echoed in the small of her back. Even if a part of her understood it had only been a dream, and even if she knew—thanks to the bond—that he considered that dream a nightmare of the worst kind, it didn't change the way her skin crawled.

Theo straightened up from his crouch.

He moved back from the door without being asked—two full steps, giving the space she hadn't requested but clearly needed. He turned and put his back to the bathroom entirely, facing the window. His hands were loose at his sides. He stared at the dark London skyline and didn't move.

Draco was already at the dresser.

Bottom drawer. He knew which one—he'd watched her unpack three weeks ago with the same quiet attention he gave everything. His hands found the tracksuit without fumbling, the soft grey fabric familiar in the dark. He crossed back to the bathroom door and held it through the gap without looking in, without trying to see her face or make the exchange into something it didn't need to be.

"Here," he said simply.

His fingers didn't linger when she took it.

He stepped back. Moved to the foot of the bed and sat there, elbows on his knees, facing the room rather than the door. Giving her the geometry of the space—bathroom behind her, him ahead, Theo at the window, nobody blocking anything.

The flat was very quiet.

Theo hadn't spoken since she'd opened the door. He stood at the window with his back to them both, one hand braced against the frame, his reflection barely visible in the dark glass. His jaw was set. His eyes were fixed somewhere below the street.

He was doing the only thing he could do.

Staying. And staying out of the way.

Before she closed the door again, she added, “Make tea, please. I don’t think any of us are getting sleep tonight.”

She stood in front of the door for a few moments, gathering the fragments of her composure. Finally, she unlatched it and walked through Draco’s bedroom and into the living room, where both men waited for her.

She knew he would understand what she was asking. She needed to know if the violence in his head ever escalated beyond that one specific violation. Did he hit her? Did he use a blade? Did he break her body as well as her will?

Jackie exhaled and leaned forward to pick up her cup of tea. Luna, apparently deciding her work here was done, hopped off the sofa and onto the coffee table. For a moment, the kneazle stared at Theo as if she were weighing the merits of a lunge, but she simply turned around, walked the length of the table, and jumped down to trot toward her cat tree.
Jackie watched the movement, using the distraction to translate her thoughts into words. It was one thing to have a solution mapped out in the private architecture of her mind, and another entirely to relay it in a way that made sense to anyone else.
"In principle, it’s painfully simple, really. What exactly makes those dreams nightmares?" She didn't wait for an answer; she was fully submerged in her Ravenclaw problem-solver mode—a look that suited her far better than the hollowed-out version of an hour ago. "It’s the fact that you don't stop, even when I ask. Even when I use the *safeword*. So... in theory..."
Her gaze dropped back to her cup, her voice turning hesitant.
"If I never used the safeword? They would just be like any other dream of us together. I’m sure you have dozens of those... I know I do." A faint blush touched her cheeks. "There’s no point in your subconscious dreaming them if they aren't nightmares."
It was just a theory, as fragile as everything else in their situation. There was no guarantee it would stop the cycle; it might even cause Theo’s subconscious to lash out, making the dreams more frequent or more violent. To work, it would require her to realize she was dreaming so she could consciously withhold the word. Or... she would simply have to decide that she wouldn't use it even in real life, letting that resolve translate into her sleep.

Draco set his mug down.

The sound was quiet but deliberate, and both of them looked at him.

His expression was controlled in the specific way it got when he was working through something that had multiple dimensions and not all of them were comfortable. His eyes moved from Jackie to Theo and back.

"You're describing lucid dreaming as a therapeutic intervention," he said. "Restructuring the dream's trigger mechanism by removing the specific element that converts it into a nightmare." He paused. "That's not painfully simple. That's technically sophisticated and practically very difficult."

He wasn't dismissing it. His voice had the quality it got when he was taking an idea seriously enough to stress-test it.

Theo hadn't moved from the floor.

His pale eyes were fixed on Jackie with an expression that had gone very still and very careful. He'd felt the shape of what she was proposing through the bond before the words arrived, and it had done something complicated to him that he hadn't finished processing.

"No," he said.

Quietly. Absolutely.

Jackie looked at him.

"Not the theory," he said. "The theory is sound. The *method* you're suggesting." His jaw tightened. "You're talking about removing your own safeguard. In waking life, so it carries into sleep." He held her gaze. "I built that system so you'd always have a way out. I'm not letting you dismantle it to fix my nightmares."

"There are other ways into a dream," Draco said, from the armchair.

Both of them looked at him again.

He picked up his mug. "The Architecture of the Mind. The chapter on constructed mindspace." His eyes moved to Jackie. "Shared mindspace. Collaborative. You wouldn't have to remove anything. You'd just need to learn to build a door."

Jackie looked from Draco to Theo, taking slow, measured sips of her tea as she weighed their protests.
"I thought about Dreamless Sleep," she said, her voice clinical despite the underlying tremor. "But either you or I would have to take it daily. There are studies on the side effects of such continuous use. I... I had nightmares, too, after January. I asked Madam Pomfrey for it—told her I was dreaming about the curse—but after two weeks, she told me I had to taper off. It’s not a viable long-term option."
She set the half-finished mug on the table and folded her hands in her lap, the grey fabric of her tracksuit bunching under her fingers.
"Occlumency doesn't work when you’re asleep, and you need to sleep. Besides, you're forgetting one thing." Her voice took on a sharper, more serrated note. "I’m going to be giving up that word on a weekly basis now, regardless. What point is there in using it if it doesn’t work anyway?"
She leaned back slightly, her gaze hard.
"By all means, try anything else you want. Trust me, I’ll be the first to agree to any other sound idea. But as it stands—even though it makes me sick to my stomach just saying it—withholding the safeword is the only shred of agency I’d have left in those dreams."
A dark, jagged part of her wanted him to truly feel what this was doing to her. She wanted him to drown in the same hurt and dread that was currently suffocating her. Usually, she kept that vindictive impulse safely tucked away from the world, but right now, she decided to let it breathe.

Theo closed his eyes.

Just for a moment. The kind of closing that wasn't weakness but absorption—taking something in fully before responding to it.

When he opened them, the rawness was still there. He didn't try to cover it.

"Don't forgive the future ones yet," he said quietly. "Make me earn each one."

He held her gaze for a beat longer, then looked away. His hand moved to his pocket, fingers closing around the lighter without taking it out. The familiar weight of it, the cold metal edge.

He didn't say *thank you*. It would have been the wrong shape for what she'd given him.

---

Draco stood.

He collected the mugs from the table with quiet efficiency, carried them to the kitchen, and rinsed them without being asked. The sound of the water running filled the flat briefly, then stopped.

He came back to the doorway between the kitchen and the main room and looked at both of them—Jackie hollowed out and upright on the sofa, Theo still on the floor with his back straight and his hands open.

"It's past three," Draco said. "Jackie needs to sleep."

He looked at Theo. The look wasn't hostile. It was something more complicated and more honest than that.

"The sofa pulls out," he said. "There are blankets in the bottom of the wardrobe."

He walked back through the bedroom without waiting for an answer, leaving the offer standing in the room behind him.

Jackie stood up slowly, a faint smile finally touching her lips as she looked at Theo.

"Stay," was all she said to him before following Draco into the bedroom.
She curled into Draco's side, clinging to him as if he were the only truly simple, light thing she had left in her life.

Theo felt the wave of her affection move through the bond like heat through stone.

*My God of Malice.*

His throat moved. He looked up at her from the floor, this woman who had just spent an hour being sick in a bathroom and was still standing there choosing him with her whole chest open.

"Stay," she said.

He nodded once.

She disappeared through the bedroom door, and Theo sat in the quiet of the living room for a long moment. Then he reached into his pocket and set the lighter on the coffee table—a deliberate act, leaving it outside himself for the night—and pulled the blanket from the wardrobe without unfolding the sofa. He dropped onto the cushions, pulled the blanket over his shoulder, and was asleep inside three minutes.

---

In the bedroom, Draco didn't speak when she curled into his side.

He pulled her closer, one arm settling around her shoulders, his chin dropping to the top of her head. He lay there in the dark looking at the ceiling, her breathing slowly evening out against his chest.

*Simple,* she'd implied, clinging to him.

He didn't feel simple. He felt like a man holding something extraordinarily fragile in the dark while the world continued its indifferent turning outside the rain-streaked windows.

But if she needed him to be the steady thing tonight, he could do that.

He stayed awake until her breathing deepened completely. Then he closed his eyes.

---

At eight, Draco's eyes opened.

He lay still for a moment, cataloguing. Jackie's weight against him, still deeply under—her face slack in a way it almost never was while conscious, the exhaustion having finally won. He eased his arm out with careful slowness, replacing his warmth with the duvet, and stood without the floorboards creaking.

He dressed quietly. Dark trousers, a grey shirt. He paused at the bedroom doorway and looked back at her once.

Still asleep.

He pulled the door to.

---

Theo was a heap on the sofa.

He hadn't pulled it out. He'd simply folded himself across the cushions at some point, the blanket twisted around his shoulders, one arm hanging off the edge, dark hair obscuring his face. The lighter sat on the coffee table exactly where he'd left it.

Draco looked at him for a moment.

Then he went to the kitchen and filled the kettle.

The sound of coffee grinding woke Theo four minutes later—a deliberate choice of implement, loud in the morning quiet. Draco heard the sharp intake of breath, the rustle of the blanket, the particular silence of a man surfacing from deep sleep into immediate awareness.

"You didn't pull it out," Draco said, not turning from the stove. The pan was already heating. Eggs, two rashers each. He'd made enough without deciding to.

Theo appeared in the kitchen doorway, hair wrecked, blanket still around his shoulders like a very undignified cloak. His pale eyes were sharp despite the hour.

"I was tired," he said.

"There's a mechanism on the side. Takes four seconds."

Theo looked at him. "I'll keep that in mind."

He dropped the blanket over the back of the barstool and sat down. His eyes tracked to the coffee, then to the eggs.

Neither of them spoke for a moment. The kettle began to heat. The bacon hissed.

"She slept," Draco said. Flat. Informational. "Properly, I think. She went under fast and didn't move."

Theo's jaw shifted. "I know. I'd have felt it otherwise."

Draco turned the bacon. "Right."

He poured the coffee without asking—black, no sugar, the way he'd catalogued from three weeks of observation—and set it in front of Theo. He made his own tea beside it.

They stood and sat respectively in the small kitchen, the morning light coming gray and thin through the window, London beginning its noise below.

"The lucid dreaming," Theo said eventually. "You've done it."

It wasn't quite a question.

Draco was quiet for a beat. "Sixth year. Different reasons." He plated the eggs. "I can teach you the entry technique. The rest takes practice."

Theo picked up the coffee mug. He looked at it rather than Draco. "Why are you helping me."

Draco set the plate in front of him.

"I'm helping her," he said. "You're adjacent to that."

Theo looked up at him. Something moved in his expression that wasn't quite amusement but wasn't entirely without it either.

"Fair," he said.

Draco ate standing at the counter, the way he did when he was short on time. He checked the clock at eight forty-two, finished his tea, and shrugged on his coat with the efficient movements of a man with somewhere to be.

He paused at the kitchen doorway.

"She'll sleep until nine at least," he said. "There's bread for toast. Don't reorganize anything."

He looked at Theo—directly, briefly, the full weight of last night sitting between them without either of them naming it.

"Don't let her wake up alone," he said.

Then he picked up his bag and left, the door clicking shut behind him with its usual neat, final sound.

The moment stretched. Theo felt it all pour through the bond—the hazy affection, the shock of recognition, the flinch that followed like a small wound reopening. He didn't move. He'd been waiting for this exact moment all night, had rehearsed it a dozen different ways in his head while reading about mindscapes and occlusion. None of the rehearsals had prepared him.

He set the book down on the nightstand with deliberate care. His movements were slow, giving her time to recalibrate, to rebuild the walls between them that last night had torn down. He didn't bridge the distance immediately. That was the whole point—he understood now, in a way he wasn't sure he had before, that presence didn't always mean closeness. Sometimes it meant knowing when to stay still.

"He asked me not to let you wake alone," Theo said. Simple. Direct. The truth without any of the weight that usually accompanied vulnerability. His voice was quiet, not soft—there was a difference. Soft would have been apologetic. "I took it as a request with some weight behind it."

He looked at her. Really looked at her. The sleep-rough edges hadn't worn off yet, and she was caught in that suspended moment between dreams and waking—vulnerable in a way she rarely allowed herself to be. He could feel the cascade of her emotions through the bond: confusion, recognition, loss, the complicated tangle of loving two men in different rooms.

"How are you feeling?" he asked. Not *Are you okay?*—a question designed to let people lie. He wanted the truth, whatever shape it took.

The morning light filtered through Draco's windows, all clinical and precise. The flat was exactly as they'd left it—Theo's leather jacket draped over the back of one of the kitchen chairs, coffee cups from last night still sitting on the side table. The physical evidence of all three of them occupying the same space. It would have to be enough, for now.

Theo shifted his weight slightly, waiting. He understood, in the raw space of early morning and last night's shared horror, that the three of them were learning how to exist in the same gravity well. Jackie loved them both, but her body had flinched away from him. That was information. That was honest. He could work with honest.

"Draco left about twenty minutes ago," he continued, filling the silence because he could feel her circling, looking for a way to reorient. "He made coffee. It's probably cold by now. There's also—" He paused, slight twist of his mouth. "—fresh toast in the kitchen. He left a note."

A small thing, but Theo had learned that small things mattered when you were trying to rebuild trust after nightmares and borrowed trauma. Draco's presence in this flat, Draco's request that Theo stay, Draco's routine breakfast gesture—these were the threads that held them together when the tether threatened to tear them apart.

"I know last night was—" Theo started, then stopped. His jaw tightened slightly. Not anger. Precision. "I know it's complicated. Waking up to me instead of him. Especially now."

He let that hang in the space between them. The soul tether thrummed with her emotions—all of it, the tangled mess of loving two people and waking to the wrong one and knowing, somewhere in her body, that she was glad he was here anyway.

"But I'm here. And he asked me to be. So I am."

She loved when he looked at her like that, and even more so now, because she could feel his state through the bond. He wanted her; even if his body was composed and giving her space, his mind was anything but.
"Good to hear that you're still underestimating my resilience," she said, tilting her head to the side. She wasn't angry with him; she’d always much prefer to be underestimated than not taken seriously at all.
When Theo mentioned he’d be gone by the time Draco got back, she nodded. She needed things to be easier for her to focus at first, not harder. Theo’s presence never made anything easy—not just because of the soul tether, but because he’d had that magnetic effect on her for as long as she could remember.
"I don't think it's wise for you to stay. I'll be back at the Manor Friday morning, as always," she assured him. Then, she stepped into his space, tilting her head to meet his eyes. "But he won't be back until five. And he's not here now."
She traced a slow line with her finger from his chest down his shirt. "It's just you, me, and that insatiable hunger I feel emanating from you. Honestly, I don't know how you manage to function with it," she said, her finger sliding under the hem of his shirt to touch a small strip of bare skin.
Jackie wasn't entirely sure what she was aiming for. Mostly, she wanted to stop thinking about the nightmare, but she also needed to gauge her body's reaction to him. She needed to know if it would be like always, or if reliving that trauma had changed something deeper in her brain chemistry.

Theo's breath caught. It was involuntary—that small, sharp intake of air when her finger found bare skin. She could feel it through the bond, feel the sudden sharpening of his focus, the way every nerve in his body seemed to orient toward her touch like she was the only thing that mattered.

"You're testing yourself," he said. It wasn't a question. His voice had shifted already—less teasing, more grounded. His hand came up, fingers catching her wrist gently, not stopping her. Just... acknowledging. "Checking if the nightmare broke something."

He didn't move her hand away. Instead, he held it against his skin, let her feel the warmth of him, the steady thrum of his heartbeat under her palm. His eyes were sharp on hers, reading her the way he always did—seeing past the performance to what she actually needed.

"It didn't," he said quietly. "Whatever you're worried about. You're still you."

But then his jaw tightened, and his hand slid from her wrist to her hip. The hunger she was feeling through the bond sharpened, became almost tangible. He'd been awake all night, reading about Occlumency and mindscapes, keeping watch, holding himself steady while she processed shared nightmares. The restraint was wearing thin.

"You're sure about this?" His voice had gone rougher already, lower. That was Theo when arousal started taking him—the careful control giving way to something more immediate. "Because if you need me to stop at any point, you say the word. You know how this works."

His other hand came up to her jaw, tilting her face toward his. Not demanding. Offering.

"But if you want me—if you need to know that your body still wants what it's always wanted—then I'm here for that." A slight pause. His fingers brushed her cheekbone. "I'm always here for that."

The flat around them was quiet. The morning light was clinical and cold, but Theo was warm against her, solid and present. His hunger was pouring through the bond—raw and immediate and honest. No apology. No gentleness masking possession. Just the simple truth that he wanted her, had wanted her all night while reading about mindscapes, and wanted her now in a way that made his hands shake slightly as he held her.

"Talk to me," he said. "What do you need?"

He felt it land through the bond before her face finished changing.

Five seconds of warmth — her hand under his shirt, her voice still soft with sleep, that particular quality of not-quite-awake where she touched him like it was reflex, like the night before hadn't happened — and then the crash of it. Not gradual. All at once.

Theo set the book down on the duvet. Didn't reach for her.

He watched her pull away and let her. The bond was already doing what it always did — carrying her too fast, all of it at once, the shock and the sadness and the thing underneath that she probably hadn't named yet. He felt the shape of it. Didn't comment on it.

"He asked me to stay," Theo said. Flat. Factual. "Didn't want you waking up alone."

A beat. He tilted his head slightly, looking at her the way he always did when she was processing — not pushing, just present. His lighter was on the nightstand. He didn't reach for that either.

"Before you decide how to feel about that," he added, "he made breakfast first. Left yours in the oven."

He let that sit.

The morning light was coming through the gap in Draco's curtains at a low angle, catching the edge of the Architecture of the Mind where it rested between them on the duvet. Theo had read forty pages of it while she slept. It was denser than he'd expected — not unpleasant, but Draco's kind of dense, the sort of text that assumed you'd come to it already halfway fluent in its assumptions. He'd understood most of it. He'd wanted to understand all of it.

"You don't have to sort out how you feel about last night right now," he said. "I'm not asking you to."

His eyes moved over her face. She looked tired still, even awake — the kind of tired that didn't come from one bad night but from carrying something for too long. He knew what that looked like on her. He'd seen it before.

"But I'm here," he said. "So if you want to talk, or eat, or just sit here until you figure out which one it is — I'm not going anywhere."

He picked the book back up. Turned to the page he'd left. Waited.
