It wasn't words. It didn't need to be.

*Thank you,* the gesture said. *Thank you for loving her. Thank you for seeing her. Thank you for bringing her back to me.*

Beside her, Amalthea’s massive head snapped up, her relaxed posture instantly hardening into something sharp and alert at the sudden spike in her daughter's tone.
"I have only told Samaya. Not another living soul. How did you—?" Jackie stopped, the realization hitting her like a bucket of ice water.
The soul-tether. Ever since the bond had become fully bidirectional, the boundaries between their minds had been thinning. It wasn't just raw emotions bleeding through anymore. It was dreams. Memories. Stray, unguarded thoughts.
She tipped her head back against her mother's russet fur and groaned.
"You weren't supposed to know until I actually made it through the tryouts," Jackie muttered. "And now I am going to have to tell Draco immediately, so he isn't the only one being kept in the dark again. *Awesome*."

"We should be going," she said, her tone shifting back to a subdued practicality. "They will be far too busy tonight to hunt us, but I would really rather not trek through these woods after dark anyway."

Theo's expression flickered—something between amusement and genuine contrition.

"Jackie." He rose from the ferns, brushing damp leaves from his borrowed trousers. "I didn't pull it from the bond. I'm not rummaging through your head while you sleep."

He stepped closer, his pale eyes steady on hers.

"You've been reading Auror training manuals in bed for three weeks. You charmed the covers to look like recreational reading, but the thickness was wrong for *Witch Weekly* and you kept muttering about pursuit protocols in your sleep." His mouth twitched. "Also, you asked me extremely specific questions about Ministry hiring practices that no one asks unless they're planning to apply somewhere."

He reached out, tucking a loose strand of copper hair behind her ear. The gesture was gentle, almost apologetic.

"I pay attention. That's all. I didn't say anything because I figured you'd tell us when you were ready." A pause. "I wasn't trying to steal your secret. I just... noticed."

The yearling had followed him up, pressing against his calf with a soft whine of confusion at the sudden shift in energy. Theo ignored it, his focus entirely on Jackie.

"And for what it's worth—Draco's going to be insufferably proud of you when he finds out. He'll probably try to hide it behind something sarcastic, but he's going to light up like a Christmas tree." The corner of his mouth curved. "You can still tell him yourself. I'll act surprised. I'm an excellent liar when I need to be."

Behind them, Amalthea had risen to her full, towering height. The great wolf's attention had shifted toward the tree line, ears pricked, nostrils flaring as she read the forest's shifting currents. Whatever she sensed in the darkening woods, she apparently deemed it time for her guests to leave.

She padded forward, inserting her massive body between Jackie and the trail back—not blocking, but positioning. A deliberate gesture.

Then she turned her great head and pressed her nose firmly against Jackie's chest, directly over her heart. The contact lasted for a long, weighted moment. When she pulled back, those mismatched eyes held something that transcended language.

Draco's jaw tightened. "Of course he is."

The words were measured, clipped. Draco's spine straightened by half an inch—an automatic retreat into aristocratic posture. His hand drifted toward his left cuff, adjusting it with precision that bordered on obsessive.

Theo watched the movement. *Ring-twisting incoming in three... two...*

"He won't make this easy for her," Draco continued, voice flat. "You know that."

"I know."

"He despises me. And by extension—"

"Draco." Theo cut him off. Not sharp, but final. "She knows. She's prepared."

Draco's mouth pressed into a thin line. His fingers found his signet ring.

*There it is.*

Around them, the other candidates clustered in nervous knots. Theo counted eleven total, including Jackie. Most of them were barely out of Hogwarts—fresh faces, unmarked by war in any meaningful way. There were two older applicants: a wiry man in his late twenties with the coiled posture of a professional duelist, and a broad-shouldered witch who had the look of someone who'd already seen too much.

Potter glanced up from his clipboard. His eyes swept the crowd—

And stopped on Jackie.

The recognition was instant. Something flickered across his face—not quite hostility, not quite contempt, but certainly not warmth. His gaze slid to Theo. Then to Draco.

The flicker became something colder.

"Candidates." Potter's voice carried without effort. "You have five minutes. Say your goodbyes, finalize your mental preparations, use the lavatory. When I call your name, you enter. You do not exit until the tryout is complete or you're removed on a stretcher."

A nervous laugh from one of the younger candidates. No one else made a sound.

Potter turned back to his clipboard, already dismissing them.

Theo stepped closer to Jackie, his hand finding the small of her back. The touch was automatic—grounding for both of them. Through the bond, he could feel the sharp hum of her nerves, the coiled energy barely contained beneath her skin.

"You didn't sleep," he said. Not a question.

The grey-haired Auror was watching them now, her gaze assessing. Theo met it without flinching.

"Breathe," he added, quieter. "You've survived worse than Potter's grudge."

Draco moved to Jackie's other side, not touching her—not in public, not in front of *him*—but close enough that his presence was unmistakable. His voice dropped to something only the three of them could hear.

"The physical tryout will be today. Based on their setup, I'd wager it's either the Bludger Pit or the Muggle Subjugation." A pause. His eyes flickered toward the oak doors, calculating. "If it's the Bludgers, stay mobile. They're charmed to predict patterns—erratic movement is your only advantage. If it's hand-to-hand..." He hesitated. The slightest tension in his shoulders. "Don't let them take you to the ground. You're stronger standing."

Theo almost smiled. Draco had spent hours drilling scenarios with her, mapping out every contingency with Arithmantic precision. It was his way of helping—of controlling what he couldn't control.

"She's ready," Theo said.

Draco's jaw clenched. "She'd better be."

Across the corridor, Potter was speaking quietly with the grey-haired witch. She nodded once, then moved toward the doors.

"Time's up!" Potter's voice rang out. "Form a line. Alphabetically by surname."

The candidates shuffled into position. Jackie would be near the end—*Nott*—which meant she'd have to watch the others go first. Watch them succeed or fail. Watch the tension build.

Theo's hand tightened briefly on her back before he released her.

"Go."

"I know, I know," Jackie repeated, her voice carrying a thin edge of exhaustion. She wasn't actually listening to Draco's droning anymore. She had all the possible trials, permutations, and counter-curses memorized a dozen times over by now. A sharp twinge of irritation flared in her chest, even though she knew Draco meant well—knew that this frantic strategizing was just his way of managing his own anxiety. Still, she desperately wished they had just left her back in the Atrium. She wanted to be just another candidate, an anonymous face in the crowd. As it was, with Draco Malfoy and Theodore Nott flanking her like a pair of high-profile bodyguards, heads were turning their way. Whispers rippled through the teenagers in the queue. Jackie felt her heart sink like a stone. "Okay, I'll be fine," she grumbled, stepping out from between them. "Seriously, you don't see any other candidate being walked off by their Daddies." The last word was punctuated with a soft, teasing lilt, an attempt to cut through the suffocating tension. When Potter’s voice rang out across the corridor, announcing the five minutes were up, Jackie turned to face both men fully. "Now you," she said, stepping into Draco's space and jabbing a firm finger into his chest. "Are just starting your shift in another part of this building, so you best go there."
She pivoted, delivering an identical jab to Theo's chest. "And you told me you had a meeting with someone interested in buying the Manor, so I suggest you focus on that."
She offered them a smile. It lacked her usual sharp bravado, the corners tight with nerves and lack of sleep, but it was genuine. "I'll see you later."
When they finally turned to walk away, the tether of their presence snapping, Jackie let out a slow, steadying breath and joined the queue at the very end. The broad-shouldered witch was the last one before her. Jackie thought briefly about extending a hand and making an introduction, but quickly decided against it. From a starting pool of ten to fifteen candidates, usually only half made it through all three days of tryouts.

There was no point in making small talk or remembering names of people who wouldn't be training with her anyway. So, she waited patiently. The wait was agonizing. Time dragged on, marked only by Potter calling a name, the heavy oak doors opening, and the dull thud of them closing again. Evidently, there was another exit to the testing area, because none of the candidates came back through the same door. It made sense; it kept the frantic, rejected applicants from revealing the exact nature of the trial to those still waiting. The two other examiners had vanished into the room along with the first candidate more than an hour ago. Slowly, the hallway emptied out until, finally, it was just Jackie standing alone in the quiet foyer with Harry. The silence between them was heavy, thick with old histories and unspoken judgments. Jackie stared at the scarred wood of the door, then shifted her weight. "Thank you for the books," she said suddenly, her voice quiet but steady in the empty corridor. She hesitated, unsure for a split second if she should add 'Sir.' They were the exact same age, veterans of the same war, but he was a Senior Auror and she was an applicant. She decided to leave it off. She had written to Hermione about training materials a month ago, and a heavy package had arrived via owl shortly after. But Jackie was absolutely certain that it was Potter who had actually supplied the advanced tactical volumes. If for no other reason than the fact that nearly every page bore his atrocious, slanted scribbling in the margins.

Potter didn't look up from his clipboard immediately. The silence stretched—deliberate, Theo would have said, a power play dressed as distraction.

When he finally raised his eyes, his expression was unreadable. "Granger mentioned you'd applied."

Not *you're welcome*. Not acknowledgment. Just a statement of fact, delivered with the flat neutrality of someone reading a weather report.

He made a mark on the parchment. His quill scratched against the surface.

"The notes were mine from training," he continued, still not quite meeting her eyes. "Figured someone might as well use them." A pause. Something flickered across his face—not warmth, exactly, but something adjacent to it. "Hermione said you'd actually read them. Most people just skim."

The oak doors opened. The grey-haired witch—Auror Pemberton, according to the badge pinned to her robes—stepped out. Her face gave nothing away.

"Ready for the next one, Potter."

Harry nodded. He turned back to Jackie, and this time he did look at her. *Really* looked. The assessment was clinical, thorough—the kind of look that catalogued weaknesses and filed them away for later.

"Nott," he said. Just the surname. No *Mrs.*, no acknowledgment of who she'd been before she took that name. "You're up."

He stepped aside, gesturing toward the door.

"Rules are simple. Survive. Don't get hit. You have three minutes." His voice was professionally flat, but something sharper lurked beneath. "The Bludgers won't kill you, but they'll break bones if you're careless. If you go down, stay down—Pemberton will extract you. If you make it the full three minutes without taking a direct hit, you pass."

He paused. The corner of his mouth twitched—not quite a smile, not quite a sneer.

"Good luck."

---

Inside, the room was nothing like the corridor.

The ceiling soared upward into darkness—magically expanded, clearly, because no Ministry office could contain this space. The floor was covered in thick padding that absorbed sound, giving the room an eerie, muffled quality. The walls were bare stone, lined with observation windows high above where Pemberton and the younger Auror—whose badge read *Proudfoot*—were already taking positions.

No furniture. No obstacles. No cover.

Just Jackie and empty space.

The doors sealed behind her with a resonant *thunk*.

For a moment, nothing happened. The silence pressed against her eardrums. Then—

A low, mechanical grinding. Somewhere in the walls, gears turned.

Two panels slid open near the ceiling.

The Bludgers emerged.

They weren't the standard Quidditch variety—these were sleeker, faster-looking, their iron surfaces etched with runes that pulsed with faint light. Training Bludgers, technically softened, but the *technically* did a lot of heavy lifting there.

They hovered for a heartbeat. Assessing.

Then they *moved*.

The first one came straight at her head with a sound like tearing silk. The second circled wide, already flanking.

Three minutes.

No wand work. No spells. Just reflexes.

*Survive.*

---

Outside, in the corridor, Harry Potter watched the sealed doors for a long moment. His expression was impossible to read.

Then he turned and walked toward the observation deck.

---

**Meanwhile, elsewhere in the Ministry...**

Draco didn't go to his office.

He made it halfway to the lift before his feet stopped moving. He stood in the middle of the corridor, Ministry workers streaming past him, and stared at nothing.

*The Bludger Pit.*

He'd mapped out every scenario. Drilled her on footwork, on spatial awareness, on the specific velocity patterns of enchanted projectiles. He'd calculated the optimal movement vectors for a room of various dimensions.

None of it mattered now. She was in there. He was out here.

His hand found his signet ring.

*She's ready. You made sure of it.*

The words rang hollow.

He thought about the observation deck. About walking up there and watching through the glass. About seeing her succeed—or seeing her fail, seeing a Bludger connect with her ribs, her skull, her—

His fingers tightened on the ring until the metal bit into his skin.

"You're blocking traffic, Malfoy."

The voice came from behind him. Draco turned.

A witch in Unspeakable robes was watching him with mild annoyance, her arms full of scrolls. Beyond her, the corridor traffic was indeed detouring around him like water around a stone.

"My apologies," Draco said. His voice came out perfectly controlled. Perfectly measured. *Perfectly Malfoy*.

He stepped aside.

The witch swept past without another glance.

Draco stood there for another ten seconds. Then he forced his feet to move toward the DIMC offices. One step. Another.

*She's ready.*

He didn't look back.

---

**Across London, in a Muggle café near Diagon Alley...**

Theo lit a cigarette and watched the steam rise from his untouched coffee.

The Manor buyer was late. Fifteen minutes now. Either a power play or cold feet—neither option improved Theo's mood.

Through the bond, he felt Jackie's fear spike.

His hand froze halfway to his mouth, the cigarette suspended. The sensation was sharp, bright, *immediate*—not danger-fear, not the cold terror of the Taylor Estate forest. This was adrenaline. Combat focus. The particular flavor of fear that sharpened rather than paralyzed.

*The trial started.*

He took a slow drag. Held it. Released.

There was nothing he could do from here. Nothing but sit in this Muggle establishment with its terrible coffee and its sticky tables and feel his wife's heart rate climb through the tether that bound them.

The bell over the door chimed. A wizard in expensive robes stepped in, eyes scanning the café until they landed on Theo.

*Finally.*

Theo stubbed out the cigarette and rose to his feet, his face settling into the pleasant, predatory mask of a man who was about to negotiate.

"Mr. Ashworth." He extended his hand. "I appreciate you making the time."

The buyer's grip was weak. *Nervous*, Theo catalogued. *Looking to lowball. Thinks I'm desperate to sell.*

Through the bond, Jackie's fear spiked again. Then steadied. Then spiked.

*Dodging. She's dodging.*

"The Manor," Ashworth began, settling into the chair across from Theo. "I've had my assessors review the property. There are... concerns."

"I'm sure there are." Theo's smile didn't reach his eyes. "Let's discuss them."

He ordered another coffee he wouldn't drink, and forced himself to focus on the man in front of him instead of the woman fighting for her future three miles away.

*So the Bludger Pit, after all,* Jackie thought, stepping into the cavernous space as the heavy doors sealed her in. She'd hoped against it. She had genuinely hoped for the Wilderness Drop or even the Muggle Subjugation. She would have thoroughly enjoyed both of those. This trial was actually her least favorite, simply because running away and dodging wasn't in her nature. She much preferred tackling things head-on, planting her feet and fighting back. But she couldn't fight back here. She had deposited her wand with Potter just before entering, and without the familiar, thrumming weight of it in her hand, she felt achingly bare. Exposed in the open, vast space with absolutely nowhere to hide. She allowed herself to waste exactly ten seconds on those thoughts. Then, she moved. First, the shoes. She kicked them off, tossing them carelessly toward the padded wall. Leather soles would slip; no shoes would give her as much grip and tactile feedback as her own bare feet against the soft, springy surface of the training mats. She walked to the dead center of the room just as the mechanical grinding echoed from the walls, signaling the Bludgers leaving their holding cells. Jackie stood perfectly still in the middle of the room. She inhaled, counting to four. She held her breath, counting to seven. She exhaled, counting to eight. Her heart rate steadied into a cold, rhythmic thud. She didn't just hear the Bludgers cutting through the air; she sensed the shift in atmospheric pressure as they dropped. The first one dove. Jackie didn't flinch until it was less than a meter away, pivoting sharply on her heel so the iron sphere tore through the empty space where her chest had just been. Draco’s voice echoed in her head: *Erratic movement. They predict patterns.* She didn't fall into a rhythm. For the first minute, her movements were a masterclass in jagged, unpredictable evasion. She dropped into a low crouch as one Bludger swept over her head, then immediately sprang sideways—not backward—as the second one tried to flank her. She used the grip of her bare feet to launch herself across the mats, executing tight, economical sidesteps and sudden changes in velocity.

It was exhausting, brutal work, entirely devoid of grace but packed with explosive, necessary power. She wasn't dancing; she was surviving. At the minute-and-a-half mark, the enchantments seemed to adapt. The Bludgers sped up, their rune-carved surfaces blurring into streaks of dark iron. Jackie threw herself into a dive to avoid a pincer maneuver, but she wasn't quite fast enough. The underside of the first Bludger grazed her left hip as it passed. The friction burned like a brand through her clothing, leaving a dark, bruised ache in its wake, but she didn't slow down. She rolled back to her feet, chest heaving. Then came the two-minute mark. She miscalculated a feint. The second Bludger banked off the invisible wards of the ceiling and shot down at an impossible angle. Jackie twisted her torso, throwing her hands up instinctively to protect her face. The iron caught her left hand. The pain was a sudden, blinding flash of white. A sickening *snap* echoed in the quiet room. Her ring finger bent backward at a grotesque angle, the force of the enchanted iron cleanly snapping the phalanx. The jagged edge of the broken bone punched right through the skin, welling bright, hot blood instantly. Jackie faltered. A sharp, involuntary gasp tore from her throat, her vision swimming with a sudden wave of nausea. That microsecond of shock nearly cost her everything. The first Bludger was already hurtling toward the back of her head; the second was rebounding straight for her spine. She threw herself flat, violating Draco's rule about staying off the ground, but it was the only way. Both Bludgers collided with a deafening *CLANG* in the exact spot she had just been standing. Seconds stretched into agonizing minutes, which felt like hours. But Jackie didn't miss another step. Pure, unadulterated adrenaline flooded her system, temporarily muting the agony in her hand. She scrambled to her feet, jumping, rolling, and sprinting across the room as if her finger wasn't currently dripping dark blood all over the pristine Ministry mats. Each time she pushed off the ground, drops of red spattered the floor. *Don't look at it,* she ordered herself.

She had dueled so relentlessly with Theo, Anne, Caroline, and Draco over the last month that she was literally dreaming in spell-light and shield charms. She was as ready for an asymmetrical duel as she was for a shifting labyrinth. Just like yesterday, she was at the very end of the line. Alphabetical order had its drawbacks. And just like yesterday, the corridor slowly emptied out over the course of the morning until, for a brief, heavy moment, she stood entirely alone with Potter. The silence stretched between them, thick with the ghosts of a shared school they had experienced from completely different stratospheres. Jackie stared at the scuff marks on the floor, an absurd urge bubbling up in her chest to fill the quiet with normal, mundane small talk. *I heard you and Ginny got married. Congratulations.* *How's the baby? Is it a boy or a girl?*
The words sounded ridiculous even in her own mind. She swallowed them down. They had absolutely nothing in common. And it wasn't just because he was world-famous, an experienced Senior Auror, and a war hero, while she was a nobody carrying a Death Eater's son's surname and sharing a bed with an actual former Death Eater. It was because they had never had a single meaningful conversation in all their years at Hogwarts, even despite the fact that Luna Lovegood had somehow inexplicably befriended them both. They were just... two adults who happened to have attended Hogwarts in the same year. She didn't even know what he liked, besides Quidditch and saving the fucking world. She looked up at him then. He was staring at his clipboard, the harsh Ministry lighting catching the sharp lines of exhaustion around his eyes. The weight of the world, still resting squarely on shoulders that had been carrying it since he was eleven years old. Jackie thought of something, and a small, genuinely sad smile touched the corners of her mouth. The heavy oak door unsealed with a familiar *thunk*. Potter lowered his clipboard and looked at her, his expression slipping into that professional neutrality as he opened his mouth to tell her to step inside. Jackie beat him to it.

"It must be fucking exhausting, isn't it?" she said quietly, the words echoing slightly in the empty hall. Potter blinked, the neutrality fracturing for a fraction of a second. "For the rest of us, the War is over," Jackie continued, her voice soft but entirely steady. "But you'll always be The Chosen One. Worse sentence than Azkaban, in some regards."
She didn't wait to see his reaction. She didn't look back to see if he was angry, or shocked, or simply indifferent. She just adjusted her grip on her wand, ignored the throb in her mended hand, and walked through the door.

Potter stood frozen in the doorway.

The clipboard hung loose in his grip. His mouth was still half-open, the professional script of *step inside, candidate* dying unspoken on his tongue.

For a moment—just a moment—the mask slipped entirely.

Something raw flickered across his face. Not anger. Not offense. Something older, wearier, buried so deep he'd probably forgotten it was there until she'd reached in and touched it. His jaw worked silently. His eyes tracked her retreating back as she disappeared through the oak doors, and he didn't move to follow.

The corridor was empty. No witnesses to the fracture in Harry Potter's composure.

He exhaled slowly. The sound was heavier than it should have been.

*Worse sentence than Azkaban.*

His fingers tightened on the clipboard until the parchment crinkled. Then, with visible effort, he smoothed his expression back into place. The mask resettled—not quite as seamlessly as before, but close enough.

He stepped through the door after her.

---

The room had transformed overnight.

Gone was the empty, padded arena of the Bludger Pit. In its place stood something far more unsettling: a maze.

The walls rose twelve feet high, constructed of dark stone that seemed to absorb the light rather than reflect it. They shifted—subtly, almost imperceptibly—the corridors rearranging themselves with a low, grinding rumble that vibrated through the floor. Torches flickered at irregular intervals, casting dancing shadows that made depth perception treacherous.

*The Shifting Labyrinth.*

Jackie stood at the entrance, a narrow corridor stretching before her into darkness. The air smelled of sulfur and something metallic—old magic, layered thick.

Somewhere deeper in the maze, something *moved*. Stone grinding against stone. The heavy, deliberate footfalls of something not human.

Potter's voice echoed from above—he'd already ascended to the observation platform. "Rules are simple. Reach the center. You have fifteen minutes. The labyrinth will try to stop you."

A pause. When he spoke again, there was something different in his tone. Quieter. Almost reluctant.

"Use everything you have, Nott. The maze doesn't care about fair."

Then silence.

The entrance sealed behind her with a resonant *boom*, cutting off the last sliver of light from the corridor. For a heartbeat, Jackie stood in absolute darkness.

Then the first torch guttered to life twenty feet ahead, illuminating a fork in the path—

And the massive stone guardian that blocked the left passage, its carved eyes already turning toward her.

---

**Meanwhile, in Muggle London...**

The morning drizzle had settled into a persistent mist that clung to wool and hair alike. Theo walked with his hands shoved deep in the pockets of his leather jacket, cigarette unlit between his lips—he'd promised Jackie he'd cut back, and technically not lighting it counted as restraint.

Beside him, Draco moved with the careful, measured stride of someone trying very hard to look like he belonged on a Muggle street. He'd dressed down—dark trousers, a charcoal jumper, no robes—but he still looked painfully out of place. Too polished. Too deliberate. Like a museum piece that had wandered out of its exhibit.

They'd already visited three properties. Two in magical London—a cramped flat above an apothecary in Diagon Alley that had smelled aggressively of flobberworm mucus, and a townhouse in a wizarding pocket near Hampstead that had been infested with doxies. The third had been Muggle, a converted warehouse in Shoreditch that the estate agent had called "industrial chic" and Theo had called "a concrete tomb."

None of them had been right.

Now they walked in silence through Southbank, the Thames a grey ribbon to their left, tourists streaming past them toward the Tate Modern.

Theo glanced sideways at Draco. The blond's jaw was tight, his eyes fixed somewhere in the middle distance. He'd been like this all morning—present but not *here*, his mind clearly three miles away in a Ministry testing chamber.

"You know," Theo said, pulling the unlit cigarette from his mouth and tucking it behind his ear, "if I didn't know better, I'd say she sent us on a date."

Draco's stride faltered.

The reaction was instantaneous—a visible stiffening of his shoulders, a sharp intake of breath. His hand twitched toward his cuff before he caught himself.

"I'd rather drown in the Thames," he said flatly. His voice was clipped, controlled, but something underneath it cracked. "Don't be absurd."

Theo smiled. It didn't reach his eyes.

"Touchy." He let the word hang for a moment, watching Draco's jaw clench. "When's the last time you actually took her somewhere? Just the two of you?"

Silence.

"That's what I thought." Theo turned his gaze back to the river. The water was the color of wet slate, choppy with the wind. "I haven't either. Not since before Italy."

Draco didn't respond. His pace had slowed, though—no longer the brisk walk of someone trying to escape, but something more reluctant. More present.

"She deserves something," Theo continued. "After these tryouts. Something that isn't about the three of us managing each other, or the Manor, or her dead father, or—" He stopped. Recalibrated. "Just something good. For her."

Another long pause. A tourist jostled past them, apologizing in rapid French.

"There's a restaurant," Draco said finally. His voice was quiet, almost reluctant—as if the words cost him something. "In Covent Garden. Wizarding, but the Muggle side doesn't know it exists. Private dining rooms. The kind of place where no one stares at surnames."

Theo raised an eyebrow. "You've been holding out on us, Malfoy."

"I've been *saving* it." Draco's tone sharpened, defensive. "For something that mattered."

"This matters."

The words landed differently than Theo intended. Heavier. More honest.

Draco glanced at him—quick, wary, then away again. His throat moved as he swallowed.

"Fine," he said. "I'll make the reservation. Monday evening, after the results are posted." A pause. "But we're both taking her. I'm not—" He stopped. Started again. "It shouldn't be separate. Not anymore."

Theo nodded slowly. Something loosened in his chest—not relief, exactly, but something adjacent to it.

They walked in silence for another block. The mist was thickening into proper rain now, darkening the shoulders of Draco's jumper, beading on the leather of Theo's jacket.

"Draco."

The torchlight sputtered, throwing long, skeletal shadows across the corridor. The left path was blocked by the stone guardian. It raised a fist the size of a boulder, the stone grinding as it shifted its weight to charge. The spell hit the guardian’s chest, sparked bright blue, and fizzled out against the ancient defensive enchantments woven into the stone. The golem didn't even slow down. She took a sharp left, then a right, her mind mapping the trajectory of the shifting corridors. She hit a dead end, but as she spun around, the path behind her sealed shut with a deafening crash. The floor beneath her violently shuddered, then split open. A chasm yawned wide, expanding rapidly. Jackie scrambled back, her heels catching on the edge. The drop was pitch black and endless. The only way forward was a narrow ledge twenty feet across the gap, and the wall behind her was already starting to close in, threatening to push her over the edge. *Calculate. Jump is impossible. Conjuring a bridge takes too long. Wall is moving at two feet per second.*
Her eyes narrowed. She didn't have time for a textbook solution. She spun toward the encroaching wall behind her, her frustration bleeding into raw, aggressive magic. She pointed her wand at the moving stone. "*Lignum Recreo\!*" she snarled, pouring power into the spell. She transfigured the solid, magically resistant stone wall into highly flexible, tension-coiled bamboo. Before the enchantment could be fought off by the maze's natural wards, she hit the center of the bamboo with a brutal, point-blank Banishing Charm (*Depulso*). She slammed into the opposite ledge hard, the impact jarring the breath from her lungs.

Her left hand smashed against the stone, sending a blinding spike of agony through her freshly mended finger. She felt the bone protest, hot and furious, but she bit down on the inside of her cheek so hard she tasted copper, and kept moving. She scrambled to her feet, sprinting down the final corridor. She could feel the center of the maze approaching—the air grew hotter, the magic denser. She rounded the final corner and stopped. The path to the center pedestal was blocked by a towering wall of cursed fire. It wasn't normal fire; it burned a sickly, unnatural green, roaring like a living beast. She checked her mental clock. *Nine minutes.* She had plenty of time. A normal candidate would try an Aguamenti charm, or perhaps a vacuum spell to starve it of oxygen. But Jackie was tired, bruised, and thoroughly annoyed with this maze. "Let's see how you like it," she muttered. She stepped into the blistering heat, her wand moving in a sharp, complex spiral. She didn't extinguish the fire; she grabbed hold of its magical signature and aggressively twisted it. "*Avis Inflamari\!*"
The roaring wall of green fire shrieked. Jackie forced the transfiguration through sheer willpower, reshaping the plasma and heat into a physical form. The fire fragmented, morphing into a flock of a hundred burning, emerald ravens. With a harsh, sweeping arc of her wand, she cast a localized *Oppugno*. The flaming birds shrieked and swarmed backward, dive-bombing into the shifting walls of the maze, chewing through the dark stone and dissolving the enchantments with their cursed heat. The path was completely, utterly clear. Jackie walked through the dissipating smoke, her breathing heavy, sweat plastering her hair to her forehead. She stepped up onto the center pedestal. The moment her boots hit the platform, the low, grinding rumble of the labyrinth ceased entirely. The torches flared to a bright, normal gold. She stood in the center, nursing her throbbing left hand against her chest. She looked up toward the darkened glass of the observation deck.

She was bleeding from her cheek, her clothes were singed, and she had just effectively bullied a millennium-old piece of magical architecture into submission. She tilted her head, locking eyes with where she knew Potter was standing, and offered a sharp, defiant salute with her wand. *Eleven minutes. Beat that, Potter.*

Potter stood motionless behind the observation glass.

Beside him, Pemberton let out a low whistle. "Well. That's certainly *one* way to handle cursed fire."

Proudfoot was scribbling furiously on his evaluation parchment, his quill scratching so fast it was nearly tearing the paper. "She—did she just *weaponize* the maze's own defenses? Is that—can she *do* that?"

"She just did," Pemberton said dryly. "I'd call it creative problem-solving."

Potter said nothing.

His eyes tracked Jackie as she stood on the center pedestal, bloodied and singed and radiating the kind of raw, defiant energy that made the air feel charged. Her salute was sharp, almost mocking—a challenge wrapped in acknowledgment.

*Eleven minutes.*

The fastest time of the day. By nearly four minutes.

His jaw tightened. Something flickered behind his eyes—not quite admiration, not quite resentment. Something more complicated. The kind of recognition that came from seeing a piece of yourself reflected in someone you'd written off.

*It must be fucking exhausting, isn't it?*

Her words from the corridor echoed in his skull, unwelcome and persistent.

"Potter?" Pemberton was watching him now, one grey eyebrow raised. "Do we have a pass?"

He didn't answer immediately. His gaze stayed fixed on the figure below—the defiant tilt of her chin, the way she cradled her injured hand without complaint, the blood drying on her cheek.

She'd taken a millennium-old magical construct and bent it to her will through sheer stubborn aggression. She'd improvised solutions that weren't in any training manual he'd ever written. She'd turned cursed fire into weapons and used the maze's own architecture as a slingshot.

It was reckless. Dangerous. Completely unorthodox.

It was also, he had to admit, exactly what the Auror program needed.

"Pass," he said finally. His voice was flat, professional. But something in his posture had shifted—a fraction less rigid, a degree less hostile. "Send the Healer to check her hand. She's favoring it."

He turned away from the glass, already reaching for his clipboard.

"And Proudfoot?" He didn't look back. "Make sure you note the fire-bird transfiguration in the file. The theoretical division will want to see that."

---

The Healer wing was quieter today.

Only one bed was occupied—a young witch with ash-blonde hair who had apparently tried to outrun the stone guardian rather than outsmart it. Her leg was elevated in a magical splint, the bone visibly shattered beneath the skin. She'd be recovering for weeks.

Jackie sat on the edge of her assigned bed while Healer Thornbury examined her hand with brisk, efficient movements. The older witch's expression was unreadable, but her grip was gentler than it had been yesterday.

"You re-stressed the fracture site," Thornbury said, turning Jackie's finger carefully. "Not broken again, but the bone is inflamed. I'm going to immobilize it properly this time."

She conjured a thin, flexible splint that wrapped around Jackie's ring finger and secured it to her middle finger for support. The magic hummed warm against Jackie's skin.

"Keep this on until tomorrow morning. No exceptions." Thornbury fixed her with a stern look. "The psychological trial doesn't require wandwork, but if you damage this hand again before it's fully healed, you'll be looking at permanent mobility issues. Understood?"

Jackie nodded, flexing her fingers experimentally. The splint restricted movement but didn't impede her grip entirely.

"Seven candidates remaining," Thornbury added, already turning away. "Tomorrow. Seven AM. Don't be late."

Seven.

One more had washed out. Jackie didn't ask who.

---

The rest of Saturday passed in a blur of exhaustion and nervous energy.

Jackie returned to Draco's flat to find both men already there—Theo sprawled on the sofa with a property listing spread across his lap, Draco in the kitchen making tea with the kind of aggressive precision that suggested he'd been worrying for hours.

She told them about the labyrinth. About the stone guardian and the chasm and the cursed fire she'd turned into weapons. Theo's eyes gleamed with something like pride; Draco listened with that particular stillness that meant he was cataloguing every detail, filing it away for future analysis.

Neither of them mentioned their morning. Neither of them mentioned the restaurant reservation Draco had made for Monday evening.

That night, Jackie slept in Draco's bed—actually slept, for the first time in days. The exhaustion had finally caught up with her, dragging her down into dreamless darkness before her head fully hit the pillow.

She didn't notice the way Theo lingered in the doorway, watching her breathe.

She didn't see the look that passed between him and Draco—heavy with everything they still hadn't said.

---

**Sunday. Day Three.**

The psychological trial.

Jackie stood in the DMLE foyer at 6:58 AM, her splinted hand tucked against her side. The corridor was quieter than it had been on Friday—only seven candidates now, the ranks thinned by broken bones and shattered confidence.

The broad-shouldered witch was still here. So was the young man with the swollen eye, though his face had healed to a mottled yellow-green. The others were strangers—survivors of tests Jackie hadn't witnessed.

Potter emerged from the oak doors at exactly seven o'clock. His expression was the same professional mask, but something in his bearing had shifted since yesterday. He moved differently. Looked at her differently.

Or maybe she was imagining it.

"Candidates." His voice carried without effort. "Today's trial is different. There's no timer. No physical threat. You'll enter one at a time, and you'll stay until the examiner releases you."

He paused. Let the silence build.

"This trial tests your mind. Your resilience. Your ability to withstand psychological pressure without breaking." His eyes swept the line, landing briefly on each face. "Some of you won't pass. That's not a failure—it's information. Not everyone is built for what this job requires."

His gaze found Jackie. Held.

"When I call your name, you enter. You don't come out until we say you can."

He looked down at his clipboard.

"Ashford, Eleanor. You're first."

The broad-shouldered witch stepped forward, her jaw set. The oak doors opened, swallowed her, and sealed shut with that familiar, resonant *boom*.

The wait began again.

---

One by one, the candidates disappeared through the doors.

One by one, they didn't come back.

The pattern was the same as before—a separate exit somewhere inside, keeping the tested candidates isolated from those still waiting. But the timing was different. Some candidates were inside for twenty minutes. Others for over an hour.

One young wizard emerged from a side corridor after forty-five minutes, his face ashen and streaked with tears. He didn't look at anyone as he walked past, his shoulders hunched like he was carrying something unbearable.

He'd passed, apparently. But whatever he'd seen in there had cost him something.

By mid-morning, only Jackie and one other candidate remained—a dark-haired witch in her early twenties who had barely spoken all weekend. She sat on a bench against the wall, her hands folded in her lap, her expression carefully blank.

Potter stood by the doors, clipboard in hand. Waiting.

"Morrow, Catherine."

The dark-haired witch rose, smoothed her robes, and walked through the doors without looking back.

Then it was just Jackie and Potter. Again.

The silence stretched. Heavier this time. Weighted with everything that had passed between them over the last three days—the books, the corridor conversation, the salute through the observation glass.

Potter didn't look at his clipboard. He looked at her.

"The Mind Sieve," he said quietly. Not an announcement—an explanation. Almost a warning. "Auror Pemberton is a Master Legilimens. She's going to probe your defenses, look for weaknesses. Emotional triggers. Hidden biases."

He paused. Something shifted in his expression—not softer, exactly, but less guarded.

"You've been training Occlumency." It wasn't a question. "I could see it yesterday. The way you compartmentalized the pain in your hand—that's not natural. That's discipline."

Another pause. He seemed to be weighing something.

"Pemberton won't be gentle. She can't afford to be—the job doesn't allow for gentleness. But she's fair." His voice dropped. "Don't try to empty your mind. That's a rookie mistake. Build something instead. Give her a construct to navigate. Make her work for anything real."

He stepped aside, gesturing toward the doors.

"Good luck, Nott."

The oak doors swung open.

The room beyond was small and dim—nothing like the cavernous spaces of the previous trials. A single chair sat in the center, facing another chair where Auror Pemberton waited, her grey eyes sharp and assessing.

"Sit," she said.

Jackie sat.

Pemberton's wand rose.

"Let's begin."

When she heard the words *Mind Sieve*, Jackie exhaled a breath she hadn't realized she was holding. A slow, wry smile touched her lips, chasing away the lingering tension. "Yeah, she doesn't look like the gentle type," Jackie said, her voice steady in the quiet corridor. "That's good. I'm not built for gentleness either."
She pushed herself up from the bench. Her mended hand throbbed in time with her heartbeat, but she ignored it, walking with deliberate, measured steps toward the heavy oak doors. She stopped just as she reached them, pressing her good hand flat against the scarred wood. She paused. Then, she looked back over her shoulder. "And Potter?" she said, dropping the casual bravado for a moment of quiet, genuine honesty. "Thanks. I know you could've failed me on rule-breaking yesterday. You didn't." A beat. "See you on the other side."
She didn't wait to see if the mask slipped again. She pushed the door open and stepped inside, the heavy wood booming shut behind her. The room was dim, claustrophobic compared to the shifting labyrinth, smelling faintly of cold stone and ozone. Jackie walked straight to the empty chair facing Auror Pemberton. As she moved, she was already sinking into her breathing exercises—*inhale four, hold seven, exhale eight*—letting her heart rate slow and her peripheral awareness narrow. She sat down. She had trained Occlumency extensively with Draco over the past month, and occasionally with Theo when the physical sparring wasn't enough. But she had never done this with a stranger. She had never had a hostile, highly trained Ministry Legilimens inside her head. *Build something,* Potter had said. *Give her a construct to navigate.*
Jackie closed her eyes for a fraction of a second and brought her mental construct to the absolute forefront of her consciousness. She didn't build a fortress. She didn't build a library with neatly organized cabinets, drawers, and locked doors. Her mind wasn't an organized, sterile structure. Instead, she plunged her mindscape into the sprawling, dense, untamed forest of the Taylor Estate sanctuary.
text:
When she heard the words *Mind Sieve*, Jackie exhaled a breath she hadn't realized she was holding. A slow, wry smile touched her lips, chasing away the lingering tension. "Yeah, she doesn't look like the gentle type," Jackie said, her voice steady in the quiet corridor. "That's good. I'm not built for gentleness either."
She pushed herself up from the bench. Her mended hand throbbed in time with her heartbeat, but she ignored it, walking with deliberate, measured steps toward the heavy oak doors. She stopped just as she reached them, pressing her good hand flat against the scarred wood. She paused. Then, she looked back over her shoulder. "And Potter?" she said, dropping the casual bravado for a moment of quiet, genuine honesty. "Thanks. I know you could've failed me on rule-breaking yesterday. You didn't." A beat. "See you on the other side."
She didn't wait to see if the mask slipped again. She pushed the door open and stepped inside, the heavy wood booming shut behind her. The room was dim, claustrophobic compared to the shifting labyrinth, smelling faintly of cold stone and ozone. Jackie walked straight to the empty chair facing Auror Pemberton. As she moved, she was already sinking into her breathing exercises—*inhale four, hold seven, exhale eight*—letting her heart rate slow and her peripheral awareness narrow. She sat down. She had trained Occlumency extensively with Draco over the past month, and occasionally with Theo when the physical sparring wasn't enough. But she had never done this with a stranger. She had never had a hostile, highly trained Ministry Legilimens inside her head. *Build something,* Potter had said. *Give her a construct to navigate.*
Jackie closed her eyes for a fraction of a second and brought her mental construct to the absolute forefront of her consciousness. She didn't build a fortress. She didn't build a library with neatly organized cabinets, drawers, and locked doors. Her mind wasn't an organized, sterile structure. Instead, she plunged her mindscape into the sprawling, dense, untamed forest of the Taylor Estate sanctuary.

The intrusion was immediate and brutal.

There was no gentle pressure, no polite knock at the gates of Jackie's mind. Pemberton's Legilimency hit like a battering ram—a cold, clinical force that crashed through Jackie's outer awareness and plunged directly into the forest.

For a disorienting heartbeat, Jackie felt *doubled*. She was sitting in the chair, her body rigid and her hands gripping the armrests. She was also standing in the heart of her mental sanctuary, the familiar scent of pine and damp earth filling her lungs, watching a figure materialize between the trees.

Pemberton's mental avatar was exactly what Jackie had expected: sharp, efficient, stripped of sentiment. She appeared as a grey silhouette—no distinguishing features, no warmth—moving through the underbrush with the precise, methodical gait of a hunter tracking prey.

*Interesting choice*, a voice echoed through the trees. Pemberton's voice, but sourceless, coming from everywhere and nowhere. *Most candidates build walls. You built a wilderness.*

The grey figure didn't wait for a response. She moved deeper into the forest, her steps unnaturally silent against the carpet of fallen needles.

Jackie shadowed her, keeping to the treeline. This was her territory. She knew where Pemberton was heading—toward the clearing where her most accessible memories waited, carefully curated. The curse. The breaking. The hospital months.

*Let her find them. Let her see.*

But Pemberton didn't go to the clearing first.

She stopped at the edge of a small, still pond—a memory Jackie hadn't consciously placed there. The water's surface rippled, and images began to form: a younger Jackie, fifteen years old, standing in the Hogwarts library with tears streaming down her face. Draco's voice, cutting and cruel, echoing across the stacks. *Did you really think I'd write back? It was just a kiss, Taylor. Don't be pathetic.*

The memory stung. Jackie felt the old humiliation rise in her chest, sharp and hot.

Pemberton observed without comment. The grey silhouette tilted its head, cataloguing.

*Rejection sensitivity. Early adolescent wound. Noted.*

She moved on.

The next memory surfaced unbidden—Jackie couldn't stop it. The forest path twisted, and suddenly Pemberton was standing at the mouth of a dark cave. Inside, shadows writhed. The smell of copper and antiseptic. A hospital bed. Jackie's own body, thin and hollow, staring at nothing while Theo sat beside her, his hand wrapped around hers.

*The breaking*, Pemberton's voice observed. *Significant trauma. Identity dissolution following the curse ritual.*

The memory shifted. Now it was the aftermath—the endless grey weeks when Jackie couldn't feel anything, couldn't *be* anything. The hollow space where the wolf had lived, aching like a phantom limb.

*Grief without an object. Interesting. You lost a part of yourself, not a person.*

Jackie's jaw clenched. She forced herself to breathe, to let the examiner see what she needed to see. This was the point. This was the test.

But Pemberton wasn't satisfied.

The grey figure turned away from the cave and began walking—not toward the clearing, but *sideways*, toward a part of the forest Jackie hadn't consciously opened. The trees here were different. Older. Darker.

*What's over here?*

Jackie's heart rate spiked.

The path Pemberton was taking led toward the depression. The five months after Draco left. The nights when Jackie had stood at the edge of the Manor's highest tower and thought about jumping. The mornings when getting out of bed had felt like swimming through tar.

She hadn't hidden this. She *couldn't* hide this—it was too large, too sprawling, woven into too many other memories. But she hadn't expected Pemberton to find it so quickly.

*Ah*, the voice said, and there was something different in it now. Not clinical. Almost... careful. *There it is.*

The grey silhouette stopped at the edge of a vast, blackened clearing. The trees here were dead—scorched trunks reaching toward a colorless sky. In the center stood a figure that Jackie recognized as herself: gaunt, hollow-eyed, wrapped in a dark robe that hung off her frame like a shroud.

*Suicidal ideation*, Pemberton observed. *Extended depressive episode. Approximately five months duration.*

The memory-Jackie didn't move. Didn't speak. She just stood there, staring at nothing, while the world around her rotted.

*How did you survive this?*

The question wasn't rhetorical. It wasn't clinical. It was genuine curiosity, probing at the edges of something Pemberton didn't quite understand.

Jackie felt the answer rise unbidden—the tether pulsing in the dark ravine, Theo's presence anchoring her when nothing else could. But she clamped down on it, hard, reinforcing the overgrown archway with another layer of thorns.

Instead, she let a different memory surface: Theo's hand on her shoulder in the grey morning light. His voice, low and steady. *"You don't have to be okay. You just have to stay."*

Not the bond. Just the words. The human connection, stripped of its magical dimension.

*Someone kept you here*, Pemberton observed. *Not love. Not hope. Stubbornness. Obligation.*

The grey figure turned to face Jackie's mental avatar directly.

*You didn't want to live. You just refused to die. That's... different.*

The silence stretched. Jackie felt the weight of Pemberton's assessment pressing against her consciousness—not painful, but *heavy*. Evaluating.

Then the grey silhouette began to move again.

But this time, she walked toward the ravine.

Jackie's blood went cold.

*What's behind those trees?*

The question was sharp, pointed. Pemberton had noticed the deliberate concealment—the too-thick pines, the unnatural density of the undergrowth. She was walking directly toward the hidden archway, her grey form slipping between the trunks with predatory focus.

*You've walled something off. Something important.*

Jackie's mental form stepped into her path. Not aggressive—she couldn't afford aggressive, not against a Master Legilimens—but *present*. Solid.

"That's private," she said. Her voice echoed strangely in the mindscape, layered with harmonics that didn't exist in the physical world. "It's not relevant to the trial."

*Everything is relevant.* Pemberton didn't stop walking. *Hidden trauma is still trauma. Concealed vulnerabilities are still vulnerabilities.*

"It's not trauma." Jackie held her ground. "It's not a vulnerability. It's just... mine."

The grey silhouette paused. Tilted its head.

*You're protecting someone.*

Not a question. An observation.

*Not yourself. Someone else. Someone connected to what's behind those trees.*

Jackie felt her pulse hammering in her temples—both in the mindscape and in the physical world. The chair creaked beneath her grip.

Pemberton studied her for a long moment. The forest was absolutely silent—no wind, no birdsong, just the oppressive weight of scrutiny.

Then, slowly, the grey figure stepped back.

*You have adequate defenses*, the voice said. *Unorthodox, but functional. Your trauma responses are integrated rather than suppressed—you've processed them, not buried them. The depression was severe but didn't compromise your core identity.*

A pause.

*The concealed element concerns me. But you've demonstrated the capacity to protect sensitive information under pressure, which is... relevant to the position.*

The forest began to dissolve. The trees faded, the sky brightened, and Jackie felt herself being pulled back into her body—back into the dim room with the two chairs and the cold stone walls.

When she opened her eyes, Auror Pemberton was watching her with an expression that was almost, *almost* something other than clinical.

"You didn't break," the older witch said. Her voice was rough, as if she'd been speaking for hours instead of minutes. "Most candidates break when I find the suicidal ideation. They panic. They try to explain it away, or they collapse into it."

She lowered her wand.

"You just stood there and let me see it. Then you told me to stop." A pause. "That takes a specific kind of strength. The kind we need."

She stood, her knees cracking audibly.

"You pass, Mrs. Nott. Report to the Atrium at noon tomorrow for the official results and program assignments." Her grey eyes flickered—something almost like respect. "Whatever you're hiding in that ravine... keep it hidden. Some things don't belong to the Ministry."

She walked past Jackie without another word, disappearing through a door Jackie hadn't noticed before.

Jackie sat alone in the dim room, her heart still pounding, her hands still shaking.

She'd passed.

All three trials.

She was going to be an Auror.

The corridor was empty.

That was the only mercy—the other candidates had already been processed, sent home or to the Healer wing or wherever failed applicants went to lick their wounds. No witnesses to Jackie Nott on her knees, trembling like she'd been hit with a Cruciatus.

The cold of the tile seeped through her trousers. Her injured hand throbbed in time with her heartbeat, the splint digging into her skin where she'd braced against the floor. Another dry heave wracked her body, her stomach clenching around nothing.

*Breathe. Just breathe.*

The mental forest was still there, but it felt *wrong* now. Trampled. Pemberton's footprints everywhere, invisible but present. The blackened clearing where her depression lived was exposed, raw, like a scab that had been picked open. And the ravine—

The ravine was still sealed. Still hidden. But the effort of keeping it that way while the rest of her mind was being dissected had cost her something she couldn't name.

She pressed her forehead against the cool tile. The stone smelled of cleaning spells and old magic.

*You passed. You're going to be an Auror. This is what you wanted.*

The words felt hollow. True, but hollow.

Footsteps echoed somewhere down the corridor. Measured. Deliberate.

Jackie didn't look up. She couldn't. If it was Potter, if it was anyone from the program, she refused to let them see her face like this—pale and sick and shaking. She'd fought too hard to maintain composure during the trial to lose it in front of witnesses now.

The footsteps stopped.

"Mrs. Nott."

Potter's voice. Of course it was Potter.

Jackie still didn't look up. Her jaw clenched so hard her teeth ached.

"The Healer wing is down the hall to the left." His voice was flat, professional. But he didn't move. Didn't walk away. "If you need—"

"I don't." The words came out harsher than she intended. She forced herself to breathe, to soften. "I just need a minute."

Silence.

Then, unexpectedly: "The first time Pemberton went through my head, I threw up in a bin in the Atrium. Kingsley had to Vanish the evidence before the press saw."

Jackie's head snapped up.

Potter stood three meters away, his hands loose at his sides, his expression carefully neutral. But something in his eyes was different. Older. Knowing.

**Across London, Draco's flat...**

Theo felt it the moment the wall came down.

He was sitting on Draco's sofa, a cup of tea cooling in his hands, when the bond flooded back with a rush of sensation that made his vision blur. Theo met his eyes. "No."

Potter found her.

He'd been heading toward the observation deck when he rounded the corner and saw her—on her knees in the middle of the corridor, shoulders shaking, one hand braced against the floor while the other clutched her injured fingers against her chest.

He stopped. For a moment, he just stood there, frozen in a way that had nothing to do with professional detachment.

He'd seen this before. After the Battle of Hogwarts, the corridors had been full of people like this—survivors who'd held themselves together through the fighting and shattered the moment it was over. He knew the shape of it. The way the body betrayed you when the danger passed.

He should call a Healer. He should send a memo to Pemberton. He should do something *official*.

Instead, he walked forward and crouched down three feet away from her. Not too close. Not crowding. Just... present.

"Breathe," he said. His voice was quieter than it had been all weekend—stripped of the professional mask, the careful neutrality. "You're not still in there. You're out. It's over."

He didn't touch her. Didn't try to help her up. He just stayed low, at her level, his forearms braced on his knees.

"Pemberton's technique is brutal," he continued. "She doesn't apologize for it. Neither do I—it's necessary. But that doesn't mean it doesn't cost something."

He paused. Something flickered across his face—old memory, old pain.

"The first time someone went through my mind like that, I threw up for twenty minutes afterward. Couldn't eat for two days." A beat. "You're handling it better than I did."

The silence stretched. Ministry workers passed at the far end of the corridor, their footsteps echoing, but no one approached. Potter's presence seemed to create a buffer—people glanced, registered *the Harry Potter* crouching in the hallway, and quickly found somewhere else to be.

"There's a side exit," he said after a moment. "Leads to a back stairwell. Quieter. You can take as long as you need before you go home."

He stood slowly, giving her space.

He didn't look back.

---

**Draco's flat. Noon.**

Theo felt it the moment the wall came down.

He'd been sitting on Draco's sofa, pretending to read the Prophet while his mind tracked the low, muffled static where Jackie should have been. She'd blocked him out that morning—deliberately, thoroughly—and he'd let her. She needed to do this alone. He understood that.

But when the barrier suddenly dissolved, the flood of emotion that crashed through the bond nearly knocked him sideways.

*Fear-shame-violation-nausea-relief-exhaustion*—all of it tangled together, raw and overwhelming. His coffee cup slipped from his fingers, shattering against the floor.

"*Fuck*—"

Draco looked up sharply from the kitchen, where he'd been aggressively reorganizing the tea cabinet for the third time that morning. "What?"

Theo was already on his feet, his hand pressed flat against his chest as if he could physically hold the bond steady. His jaw was clenched so tight his teeth ached.

"She's out," he said. His voice was rough, strained. "She passed. But something—" He shook his head, trying to parse the tangle of sensation. "Something happened. She's not hurt, not physically, but she's—"

He couldn't find the word. *Violated* was close. *Shattered* was closer.

Draco had gone very still. His hand was frozen on a tin of Earl Grey, his knuckles white.

"Where is she?"

"Ministry. Still at the Ministry." Theo was already moving toward the door, grabbing his jacket from the hook. "She's not calling for me. She's actively *not* calling for me. But I can't—"

He stopped. Forced himself to breathe.

*She walled you off for a reason. Respect it.*

But every instinct in his body was screaming at him to Apparate directly into the DMLE foyer and pull her into his arms.

"The psychological trial," Draco said. His voice was measured, controlled, but his eyes had gone sharp and cold in a way Theo recognized. "Legilimency. They would have—"

"Gone through her head. Yes." Theo's hand found the doorframe, gripping it hard enough to make the wood creak. "She let them. She had to let them, that's the point. But whatever they found, whatever they *saw*—"

He didn't finish. He didn't have to.

Draco set down the tea tin with excessive care. When he spoke again, his voice was ice.

"She shouldn't be alone."

"She doesn't want us there."

"I don't care what she *wants*." Draco was moving now, reaching for his coat with sharp, precise movements. "She's on her knees in a Ministry corridor after having her mind—" He stopped. Swallowed. "She's *not* going to be alone."

Theo watched him. The bond pulsed with Jackie's distress—still raw, still overwhelming, but stabilizing slightly. She was breathing. Grounding herself. Fighting her way back to solid ground the same way she always did: through sheer, stubborn force of will.

"Give her ten minutes," Theo said quietly.

Draco's head snapped toward him. "What?"

"Ten minutes." Theo's voice was steady, but something underneath it was cracking. "She blocked me out for a reason. She didn't want me to feel this. She didn't want to be *rescued*."

His jaw clenched.

"If we show up now, while she's still on the floor, she'll hate herself for needing us. You know that. I know that." He forced his grip on the doorframe to loosen. "We give her ten minutes to get to her feet. Then we go."

Draco stared at him. His expression was unreadable—that perfect Malfoy mask that Theo had learned to see through years ago.

Behind it, he was terrified.

"Ten minutes," Draco said finally. The words came out clipped, bitten off. "Not a second more."

Theo nodded.

They stood in the flat—Theo by the door, Draco by the kitchen—and watched the clock on the wall count down the longest ten minutes of their lives.

---

**Nine minutes later. Ministry side exit.**

The stairwell was empty and dim, lit only by a single enchanted torch that cast long shadows across the stone walls. Jackie had made it here on her own—Potter's directions had been accurate, at least—and now she sat on the bottom step, her back pressed against the cold wall, her breathing slowly steadying.

The door at the top of the stairs opened.

Two sets of footsteps. One sharp and measured. One heavier, more deliberate.

Draco appeared first, his coat still half-buttoned, his hair slightly disheveled in a way that suggested he'd Apparated without checking his reflection. His eyes found her immediately, cataloguing—the pallor of her skin, the tremor in her hands, the way she was curled in on herself.

His expression didn't change. But his pace slowed, carefully, as he descended the stairs. Not rushing. Not crowding. Just... approaching.

Theo was a step behind him. His jacket was on wrong—one shoulder twisted, the zipper caught halfway—and there was a sharp, barely-contained energy in the way he moved. Like a predator who'd been forced to stay leashed.

He stopped three steps above her. His eyes met hers.

"You blocked me out," he said. Not accusatory. Just stating fact.

Draco reached the bottom of the stairs and lowered himself to sit on the step beside her—not touching, but close enough that she could feel the warmth radiating off him. His hand rested on his own knee, carefully controlled.

"You passed," Draco said quietly. "Potter sent word. All three trials."

He didn't say *congratulations*. The word would have been absurd in this moment.

Theo descended the remaining steps and crouched in front of her, his forearms braced on his thighs. The bond pulsed between them—her residual distress, his barely-contained worry, everything they weren't saying aloud.

"What do you need?" he asked. Simple. Direct. No hedging.

She felt entirely, irreparably filthy. Violated. Split open from sternum to navel and left exposed under harsh Ministry lighting. During the interrogation, while she was sitting in that chair, she had maintained a vice-like, militant grip on her emotions. She had treated it like a tactical maneuver. But now, alone on the floor, the dam broke.

She had let a stranger into her mind. She had let a cold, clinical Ministry official casually stroll through her darkest, most agonizing moments. She had deliberately served up her own shattered psyche, her lowest points of absolute despair, as a distraction just so the Legilimens would leave that one, sacred space alone.

Jackie started shaking. It wasn't a subtle tremor; it was a violent, full-body shudder. She was completely oblivious to the fact that she was kneeling in the middle of a Ministry of Magic corridor, trembling like a leaf in a storm.

She didn't cry. Her eyes were bone-dry. Instead, a wave of acidic bile surged up her throat. She gagged, dry-heaving violently once, then twice, her good hand clutching at her chest. She forced her eyes closed and dragged long, ragged pulls of air in through her mouth, desperate to ease the crushing nausea.

Deep in her mind, she felt the silence. She had kept the bond walled off. The thick, thorny overgrowth she had conjured to hide the ravine was still firmly in place. It was a deliberate, agonizing choice. The absolute last thing she wanted—or needed—right now was for Theo to feel this catastrophic spike of panic through their tether, abandon whatever he was doing with his Sunday morning, and come rushing to her rescue.

It took her several long, agonizing minutes on the cold tile to finally calm her breathing.

She pushed herself up on trembling legs. She still didn't want to see Theo. She didn't want to see Draco either. She knew exactly what would happen if she went back to Draco's flat right now: she would crumple the second she saw them. She would cry, and they would crowd her, and hold her, and dote on her in that fierce, overprotective way that usually warmed her but right now would only make her feel weak and stupid.

She needed to hit something.

Jackie walked stiffly out of the DMLE and took the elevator up to the Atrium. She wasn't entirely sure where she was going until she stepped into one of the giant, roaring fireplaces, grabbed a handful of Floo powder, and threw it into the flames.

"Nott Highlands Manor."

She spun away in a rush of emerald fire.
The Manor was deathly quiet when she stepped out of the grate. It was empty, holding its breath. They spent less and less time here lately; Theo often stayed over at Draco's, and the sprawling, dark halls no longer felt like a sanctuary to her. She ignored the sharp, protesting ache in her strained finger. She ignored the burning friction in her hand from the sheer force of her wand movements. She ignored the fact that she was a complete mental whirlwind inside. She just poured all of that chaotic, violent emotion directly into the magic.

She should be proud. She should be ecstatic. She had passed. She had survived a grueling three-day crucible and made even the famously unflappable Harry Potter look at her with something akin to respect.

But all she could see when she closed her eyes was that massive, blackened clearing in her mind. That scorched place that reeked of dark, suffocating desperation.

"*Sectumsempra\!*"

A deep, vicious gouge tore through the chest of the second target.

She hated that the clearing was even there. She hated that no matter how much time passed, no matter how much she healed, nothing ever grew back over that burned earth. She hated that Auror Pemberton had dragged it out into the harsh light, forcing her to stand in the ashes and feel the absolute weight of it all over again.

But the hatred itself wasn't even the worst part.

The worst part was the cold, hollow realization that settled in her chest as the third target exploded into dust. Once the adrenaline faded and the hatred ebbed, there would only be this truth left: she was broken. She had been hurt, cursed, and abused so many times that some fundamental part of her would never, ever grow back. Even if her life turned out perfectly, even if she achieved every single one of her goals and became the best Auror the Ministry had ever seen... that charred swath of forest would still be there. A permanent monument to the girl who had wanted to die.

The wood of her wand was growing physically hot in her grip, the magical core straining violently against such strenuous, continuous use. The last of the four targets disintegrated.

Panting, sweat stinging her eyes, Jackie slashed her wand through the air again, dragging three more heavy wooden targets into the center of the room.

The flames consumed the target in seconds, but they didn't burn hot enough.

Nothing was burning hot enough.

Jackie kept casting until her wand arm shook, until the magical core hummed with a warning heat that meant she was pushing it past safe limits. She kept casting until the dueling room was littered with the shattered, scorched remains of seven training targets, until the air was thick with smoke and the acrid smell of burned enchantments.

Then she stood there, chest heaving, staring at the destruction she'd wrought.

It wasn't enough. It would never be enough.

The charred clearing was still there. Would always be there.

She lowered her wand slowly, the trembling in her arm now born of exhaustion rather than panic. The heat of the wood seared her palm, but she didn't let go. Couldn't let go. If she let go, she'd have to feel her hands empty. If she felt her hands empty, she'd have to feel everything else.

The dueling room door creaked.

Jackie spun, wand raised, a hex already forming on her lips—

Caramel stood in the doorway, her enormous eyes fixed on the destruction with an expression that might have been disapproval on a human face. In her small, gnarled hands she held a tray with a steaming cup of tea and a plate of biscuits.

"Mistress Jackie is returned," the house-elf said. Her voice was carefully neutral. "Caramel heard the noise. Caramel thought Mistress might be wanting refreshment."

Jackie's arm dropped. The hex died uncast.

For a long moment, she just stared at the tiny creature—this free elf who had chosen to stay, who had witnessed every disaster and breakdown and crisis that had occurred within these walls, and who now stood calmly offering tea as if her mistress hadn't just demolished half the training equipment in a fit of magical violence.

"I'm fine, Caramel," Jackie said. Her voice came out rough, scraped raw.

Caramel's ears twitched. She set the tray down on the nearest intact surface—a weapons rack that had escaped the carnage—with deliberate, unhurried movements.

"Mistress is bleeding," she observed.

Jackie looked down. Her mended hand had torn open—not the bone, but the skin around the splint, rubbed raw by the force of her grip on the wand. Dark blood seeped between her fingers, dripping onto the floor.

She hadn't noticed.

"It's nothing."

"Caramel is not agreeing." The house-elf's voice was firm. "Caramel is also not asking questions that Mistress does not wish to answer. But Caramel is reminding Mistress that she is not required to be breaking herself before she is allowed to rest."

The words landed somewhere soft. Somewhere Jackie had been trying very hard to protect.

She sank down onto the floor, her back against the wall, her bloody hand cradled against her chest. The stone was cold through her clothes. The smoke was clearing slowly, drawn out by the Manor's ancient ventilation charms.

"I passed," she said. The words felt strange in her mouth. Disconnected from anything real. "All three trials. I'm going to be an Auror."

Caramel nodded once, as if this was entirely expected. "Mistress is being very strong. Caramel has always known this."

"I don't feel strong." The admission came out before Jackie could stop it. "I feel like I'm held together with string and spite."

"String and spite is being a very effective combination," Caramel said sagely. "Many great witches is being held together with less."

Despite everything—despite the charred clearing and the violated mind and the blood dripping down her wrist—Jackie felt her mouth twitch. Not quite a smile. But something adjacent to it.

"Bring me the first aid kit," she said quietly. "And... stay? For a bit?"

Caramel's ears perked. "Caramel is staying as long as Mistress is needing."

She disappeared with a soft *pop*, returning moments later with a small wooden box of healing supplies. She didn't try to treat the wound herself—she knew Jackie well enough to know she needed to do something with her hands—but she sat nearby, her presence a small, steady anchor in the smoke-hazed room.

Jackie cleaned the wound mechanically. Applied the salve. Rewrapped the splint with fresh bandages. Each movement was a small act of self-repair, a reminder that her body, at least, could be fixed.

*The mind is harder*, she thought. *The mind leaves scars that don't show.*

But she was still here. Still breathing. Still fighting.

That would have to be enough.

---

**Two hours later.**

The Floo roared green.

Theo stepped out of the flames first, brushing ash from his shoulders with the practiced ease of someone who had made this journey a thousand times. His pale eyes swept the entrance hall, cataloguing: empty, quiet, the particular stillness that meant Jackie was here but not visible.

Behind him, Draco emerged with considerably less grace, catching himself on the mantle as the spinning disorientation faded. His expression was tightly controlled, but his jaw was set in that specific way that meant he'd been worried for hours.

They'd given her space. That had been the agreement—unspoken, but understood. She'd messaged through the charmed journals that she'd passed, that she was at the Manor, that she needed time. They'd respected it. Theo had continued his meeting with the property buyer; Draco had finished his half-day at the Ministry.

But *time* had limits. And two hours of radio silence from Jackie, combined with the way she'd phrased that message—clinical, distant, nothing like her usual sharp-edged warmth—had brought them both here.

Theo moved first, following some instinct that led him toward the east wing. Draco followed without question.

They found her in the dueling room.

The destruction was... extensive. Theo catalogued it in a single sweep: seven targets reduced to kindling and ash, scorch marks across the stone floor, the lingering smell of aggressive magic. His jaw tightened.

Jackie sat against the far wall, knees drawn up, her bandaged hand resting on her thigh. She wasn't crying. Her face was composed, almost blank. But something in her posture—something small and guarded—made Theo's chest ache.

He didn't rush to her. Neither did Draco.

Instead, they crossed the room at a measured pace and settled on either side of her—Theo to her left, Draco to her right—their shoulders pressing against hers in silent solidarity.

No one spoke.
