The silence stretched, but it wasn't uncomfortable. It was the particular silence of people who had learned when words helped and when they didn't.

Finally, Theo reached into his jacket and pulled out his cigarette case. He didn't light one—not indoors, not here—but he turned the case over in his fingers, the familiar weight grounding him.

"You demolished half our training equipment," he observed. His voice was even, almost casual.

Jackie didn't look at him. "I'll replace it."

"I don't care about the targets." He tucked the case away. "I care about what made you need to destroy them."

She was quiet for a long moment. Her head tipped back against the wall, eyes fixed on the vaulted ceiling.

"The psychological trial," she said finally. Her voice was rough, scraped clean of its usual edge. "They used the Mind Sieve. Master Legilimens."

Draco went very still beside her.

"She saw everything," Jackie continued. The words came slowly, like she was pulling them up from somewhere deep. "The curse. The breaking. The depression after you left." A pause. Her throat moved as she swallowed. "The clearing."

Theo's hand found her knee. Not gripping—just resting there, warm and present.

"What clearing?" Draco asked. His voice was quiet. Careful.

Jackie closed her eyes.

"In my mindscape. There's a place where nothing grows. Everything's burned, dead, black." She exhaled slowly. "It's... the months when I wanted to stop existing. When the only thing keeping me here was stubbornness and Theo telling me I just had to stay."

The silence that followed was heavy. Weighted with everything none of them had ever said aloud.

Draco's hand found hers—the uninjured one—and laced their fingers together. His grip was tight. Almost desperate.

"I didn't know," he said. His voice cracked slightly. "I knew it was bad, but I didn't—" He stopped. Started again. "I should have come back sooner."

"You couldn't have fixed it." Jackie's voice was flat, matter-of-fact. "No one could. That's the point. Some things just... scar. They don't heal. They just become part of the landscape."

Theo's thumb traced a slow circle on her knee. He didn't offer platitudes. He didn't try to argue.

Jackie stood up slowly. The chair scraped against the stone floor, the sound harsh and unnaturally loud in the empty room.

She turned and walked back out through the same heavy oak door she had entered. She knew there was another exit—Pemberton had just used it—and she knew she was the very last candidate of the day, so there was no one waiting in the corridor to see her anyway. It didn't matter. She just needed to get out.

She made it exactly three steps into the DMLE foyer before her knees simply ceased to function.

She felt sick.

She felt entirely, irreparably filthy. Violated. Split open from sternum to navel and left exposed under harsh Ministry lighting. She forced her eyes closed and dragged long, ragged pulls of air in through her mouth, desperate to ease the crushing nausea.

But now, alone on the floor, the dam broke.

She had let a stranger into her mind. She had let a cold, clinical Ministry official casually stroll through her darkest, most agonizing moments. She had deliberately served up her own shattered psyche, her lowest points of absolute despair, as a distraction just so the Legilimens would leave that one, sacred space alone.

Jackie started shaking. It wasn't a subtle tremor; it was a violent, full-body shudder. She was completely oblivious to the fact that she was kneeling in the middle of a Ministry of Magic corridor, trembling like a leaf in a storm.

She didn't cry. Her eyes were bone-dry. Instead, a wave of acidic bile surged up her throat. She gagged, dry-heaving violently once, then twice, her good hand clutching at her chest. She forced her eyes closed and dragged long, ragged pulls of air in through her mouth, desperate to ease the crushing nausea.

Deep in her mind, she felt the silence. She had kept the bond walled off. The thick, thorny overgrowth she had conjured to hide the ravine was still firmly in place. It was a deliberate, agonizing choice. The absolute last thing she wanted—or needed—right now was for Theo to feel this catastrophic spike of panic through their tether, abandon whatever he was doing with his Sunday morning, and come rushing to her rescue.

It took her several long, agonizing minutes on the cold tile to finally calm her breathing.

She pushed herself up on trembling legs. She still didn't want to see Theo. She didn't want to see Draco either. She knew exactly what would happen if she went back to Draco's flat right now: she would crumple the second she saw them. She would cry, and they would crowd her, and hold her, and dote on her in that fierce, overprotective way that usually warmed her but right now would only make her feel weak and stupid.

She needed to hit something.

Jackie walked stiffly out of the DMLE and took the elevator up to the Atrium. She wasn't entirely sure where she was going until she stepped into one of the giant, roaring fireplaces, grabbed a handful of Floo powder, and threw it into the flames.

"Nott Highlands Manor."

She spun away in a rush of emerald fire.
The Manor was deathly quiet when she stepped out of the grate. It was empty, holding its breath. They spent less and less time here lately; Theo often stayed over at Draco's, and the sprawling, dark halls no longer felt like a sanctuary to her. But right now, the Manor offered the one thing she desperately needed: isolation and a place to do violence.

Jackie stormed down the corridor toward the dueling room, her wand already drawn and humming in her hand. She kicked the doors open. With a sharp flick of her wrist, she levitated four heavy, enchanted humanoid targets from the storage racks and slammed them down into the center of the room.

She didn't hesitate. She started throwing hexes.

"*Confringo\!*"

The first target shattered into a rain of splinters.

"*Expulso\! Reducto\!*"

She ignored the sharp, protesting ache in her strained finger. She ignored the burning friction in her hand from the sheer force of her wand movements. She ignored the fact that she was a complete mental whirlwind inside. She just poured all of that chaotic, violent emotion directly into the magic.

She should be proud. She should be ecstatic. She had passed. She had survived a grueling three-day crucible and made even the famously unflappable Harry Potter look at her with something akin to respect.

But all she could see when she closed her eyes was that massive, blackened clearing in her mind. That scorched place that reeked of dark, suffocating desperation.

"*Sectumsempra\!*"

A deep, vicious gouge tore through the chest of the second target.

She hated that the clearing was even there. She hated that no matter how much time passed, no matter how much she healed, nothing ever grew back over that burned earth. She hated that Auror Pemberton had dragged it out into the harsh light, forcing her to stand in the ashes and feel the absolute weight of it all over again.

But the hatred itself wasn't even the worst part.

The worst part was the cold, hollow realization that settled in her chest as the third target exploded into dust. Once the adrenaline faded and the hatred ebbed, there would only be this truth left: she was broken. She had been hurt, cursed, and abused so many times that some fundamental part of her would never, ever grow back. Even if her life turned out perfectly, even if she achieved every single one of her goals and became the best Auror the Ministry had ever seen... that charred swath of forest would still be there. A permanent monument to the girl who had wanted to die.

The wood of her wand was growing physically hot in her grip, the magical core straining violently against such strenuous, continuous use. The last of the four targets disintegrated.

Panting, sweat stinging her eyes, Jackie slashed her wand through the air again, dragging three more heavy wooden targets into the center of the room.

The soul-tether *screamed*.

Theo was in the kitchen of Draco's flat, halfway through making coffee, when the connection went dark.

Not quiet. Not muted. *Dark*. Like someone had thrown a thick blanket over a fire—the warmth was still there, somewhere underneath, but he couldn't feel it. Couldn't reach it.

His hand froze on the kettle. The metal handle bit into his palm.

"Theo?"

Draco's voice came from the sitting room, where he'd been reviewing property listings with the kind of obsessive focus that meant he was trying not to think about the trial. The question was casual, distracted.

Theo didn't answer.

He set the kettle down. His movements were very controlled, very deliberate—the kind of stillness that preceded violence. His jaw clenched so hard his teeth ached.

*She's blocking me.*

Not unconsciously. Not the natural ebb and flow of the bond when she was focused on something else. This was *intentional*. Walls thrown up with force and precision, thorns and overgrowth choking off the connection until all he could feel was a dull, distant pulse.

*Alive. But gone.*

"Theo." Draco appeared in the kitchen doorway, the property listings forgotten. His eyes were sharp, assessing. "What's wrong?"

Theo's hand found the counter. He gripped it until his knuckles went white.

"She's shielding." His voice came out flat. Dangerous. "Hard. I can't feel anything."

Draco went still. The color drained from his face by degrees.

"The trial—"

"She passed. She would have come back if she'd failed." Theo forced himself to breathe. In. Out. "She passed, and now she's hiding from me."

The silence stretched. Draco's hand drifted toward his cufflink, adjusting it with excessive attention. His tell. His fear.

"Where is she?"

Theo closed his eyes. He pushed against the wall between them—gently at first, then harder. The thorns held. She'd woven them thick, deliberate, with the kind of focus that only came from desperation.

*She doesn't want me to find her.*

The thought landed like a blade between his ribs.

"I don't know." The admission cost him something. "The bond's blocked. I can feel that she's alive, but—" He stopped. Swallowed. "She doesn't want me to know."

Draco's jaw tightened. For a moment, he looked like he wanted to say something sharp—something defensive, something that would redirect the fear into familiar antagonism. But he didn't.

Instead, he moved to the window. Looked out at the grey London afternoon.

"She does this," he said quietly. "When it's bad. She runs."

Theo's head snapped toward him. "You've seen this before?"

"Once." Draco's voice was careful. Measured. "After the... after I found out about—" He stopped. Started again. "After I confronted her about you. What you did. She disappeared for hours. Ended up in some greenhouse on the Manor grounds, freezing, refusing to come inside."

The memory hung between them. Theo remembered that night—the cold, the fear, the desperate hours of searching before Draco had found her.

"She told me things that night," Draco continued. His back was still turned, his shoulders rigid. "Things I don't think she's told anyone else. About how close she was to—" He cut himself off. His hand found his signet ring. Twisted.

"To what?"

Draco didn't answer. But his silence said everything.

*The depression. The five months. The tower.*

Theo had known, in the abstract, that she'd been bad while he and she were separated. He'd felt echoes of it through the bond—grey, suffocating weight that had made him want to tear through the world to reach her. But he'd never seen the full scope of it. She'd never let him see.

"She's at the Manor," Theo said suddenly. The certainty hit him like a physical force. "The dueling room. She goes there when she needs to break things."

Draco turned. His expression was unreadable.

"Should we—"

"No."

The word came out harder than Theo intended. He forced himself to soften, to unclench his jaw.

"No," he repeated, quieter. "If she wanted us there, she wouldn't have blocked the bond. She needs—" He stopped. Reconsidered. "She needs to hit something without us watching her fall apart."

Draco's eyes searched his face. Looking for something. Theo didn't know if he found it.

"And we just... wait?"

"We wait."

The silence that followed was heavy. Draco moved to the counter, took over the abandoned coffee preparation with mechanical precision. Theo stayed where he was, his hand still gripping the edge of the counter, his focus turned inward.

He could feel her, distantly. The pulse of *alive, alive, alive* that never stopped, no matter how thick the walls she built. But everything else was hidden—her fear, her pain, her rage. All of it locked away behind thorns he couldn't cut through without her permission.

*She's protecting you*, he realized. *She doesn't want you to feel this.*

The thought should have been comforting. Instead, it made him want to break something himself.

---

They waited.

Draco made coffee. Neither of them drank it.

Theo paced. Three steps to the window, three steps back. His hand kept drifting to his pocket, reaching for cigarettes he'd promised not to smoke indoors.

An hour passed. Then two.

The bond stayed dark.

"This is ridiculous," Draco said finally. He was sitting on the sofa, his posture perfect, his expression carved from ice. But his hands were shaking. "We should go to her."

"She'll come back when she's ready."

"And if she doesn't?"

Theo stopped pacing. He looked at Draco—really looked, past the aristocratic mask and the defensive coldness and the fear dressed up as irritation.

"Then we go to her," he said. "But not yet. Give her another hour."

Draco's jaw worked. For a moment, Theo thought he would argue—would insist on action, on doing something, on not sitting here useless while she destroyed herself in an empty house.

But he didn't.

He just nodded, once, and went back to staring at his untouched coffee.

Theo resumed pacing.

The bond stayed dark.

---

**Three hours later.**

The wards on Draco's flat shivered. Someone was at the Floo.

Theo was on his feet before the flames had finished turning green. Draco was right behind him, abandoning the pretense of reading he'd been maintaining for the last hour.

The fire flared.

Jackie stepped through.

She looked—

Theo's chest seized.

She looked *wrecked*. Her hair was plastered to her face with sweat, her clothes singed in places, her splinted hand cradled against her chest. There was ash on her cheeks, mixing with tracks that might have been tears or might have been perspiration. Her eyes were red-rimmed and hollow.

But she was here. She'd come back.

Theo didn't move toward her. Every instinct screamed at him to close the distance, to pull her against his chest and hold her until the trembling stopped. But he knew her. Knew that crowding her right now would shatter whatever fragile composure she'd rebuilt.

So he stayed where he was. Watched. Waited.

Draco had gone very still beside him. His hand was frozen halfway to his cufflink, arrested mid-motion.

The silence stretched.

Then, slowly, the thorns in Theo's mind began to thin. The bond flickered—still muted, still guarded, but no longer *dark*. He could feel her again: exhaustion, raw and bone-deep. Shame. Anger that had burned itself out into ash.

And underneath it all, a desperate, aching need that she was trying very hard not to show.

*I'm here*, he sent through the bond. Not words, exactly—more like a pulse of presence. *I'm not going anywhere.*

He didn't know if she heard it. He didn't know if she wanted to.

But he sent it anyway.

Pemberton studied her for a long moment.

The older witch sat perfectly still, her grey eyes sharp as flint. She didn't blink. Didn't shift. The only movement was the slow, deliberate rotation of her wand between calloused fingers—a habit, Jackie suspected, born from decades of wandwork under pressure.

"Most candidates try to empty their minds," Pemberton said. Her voice was low, graveled, like stones grinding together. "They think blankness is safety. It isn't. Blankness is a beacon. It screams *I'm hiding something*."

She tilted her head, assessing.

"You're not empty. Good."

Her wand rose. The tip glowed faint silver.

"Rules," she continued, without preamble. "I'm going to enter your mind. I'm going to look for fractures—trauma, bias, emotional instability. Anything that could compromise you in the field. You can resist, but you cannot attack. If you attempt offensive Legilimency, you fail immediately. If you break down entirely, I pull out and we're done. If you endure..."

A pause. Something that might have been respect flickered in her eyes.

"Then you pass."

She didn't ask if Jackie understood. She didn't wait for confirmation.

"*Legilimens.*"

---

The intrusion was immediate and *brutal*.

It wasn't the careful, probing touch Jackie had experienced with Draco—the polite knock at the door, the respectful request for entry. This was a battering ram. Pemberton slammed into her consciousness with the full weight of forty years of experience, her presence a cold, relentless pressure that shoved against Jackie's defenses like a physical force.

The forest materialized around them.

Pemberton stood at the edge of the treeline, her silver form flickering like moonlight through leaves. She took in the sprawling wilderness with a single, sweeping glance—the towering pines, the tangled undergrowth, the animal trails that wound in illogical spirals.

"Interesting," she murmured. Her voice echoed strangely in the mental space, distorted by the rustle of phantom wind. "Not a fortress. Not a library. A *sanctuary*."

She stepped forward. The forest floor crunched beneath her feet—or the memory of feet, the impression of weight.

"Let's see what you're protecting."

She moved with predatory efficiency, following one of the winding trails deeper into the trees. Jackie felt the intrusion like cold fingers trailing across her skin, probing, searching. Pemberton wasn't gentle—she pushed through thickets that should have slowed her, ignored the disorienting loops of the pathways, cut straight toward the denser clusters of memory.

The first clearing she found was bright with summer light.

*The Highlands. The dueling hall. January 2000.*

Jackie felt the memory surface before she could stop it—the cold stone beneath her feet, the weight of her wand in her hand, Theo standing across from her with something dark and desperate in his eyes. The moment she'd commanded him to *let go*. The moment he'd obeyed.

Pemberton paused at the edge of the clearing, watching the scene play out like a Pensieve projection.

"Interesting," she said again. Her tone was clinical, detached. "You took control from someone dangerous. Deliberately. You *wanted* to see what he'd do without the leash."

The memory sharpened, details flooding in—the sound of spells colliding, the smell of singed fabric, the moment Jackie had pinned Theo to the floor and *taken back* what he'd stolen from her months before.

"Trauma processing," Pemberton observed. "Unconventional method. Effective, though." She turned away from the clearing, moving deeper. "What else are you hiding in here?"

The forest shifted around them. Jackie felt the pressure intensify as Pemberton pushed harder, following the trails toward darker, denser growth.

*The hospital. St. Mungo's. The month after the curse broke.*

The memory rose like bile—the white walls, the antiseptic smell, the crushing *emptiness* where the wolf had been. Jackie as a hollow shell, unable to speak, unable to move, staring at nothing while Theo and Draco took turns sitting vigil.

Pemberton walked through the memory without comment. Her expression didn't change.

*The basement. Eirik Fenholt. The Cruciatus.*

This one hit harder. Jackie's mental construct shuddered, the trees groaning as the memory tried to surface—the cold stone floor, the taste of blood, the *endless* screaming that she'd eventually realized was coming from her own throat—

"There it is," Pemberton murmured. She'd stopped moving, her silver form perfectly still. "The fracture point."

She didn't push into the memory. She stood at its edge, observing the way Jackie's forest warped around it—the trees twisted and blackened, the undergrowth thorny and hostile.

"You survived something that should have broken you," Pemberton said. Her voice was quiet now, almost contemplative. "Most people bury trauma like this. Lock it away, pretend it doesn't exist. You've... integrated it. Made it part of the landscape."

She turned, her grey eyes finding Jackie's presence in the mindscape.

"That's rare. That's *useful*." A pause. "But it's not what I'm looking for."

She started moving again. Faster now. More purposeful.

Jackie felt the probe shift direction—away from the obvious trauma, away from the cleared pathways. Pemberton was circling toward the edges of the forest, toward the places where the trees grew thickest and the light didn't reach.

Toward the ravine.

*No.*

Jackie's will surged. The forest *responded*—the undergrowth thickening, the paths rerouting, the thorned bushes she'd cultivated around the archway growing denser, more vicious. She felt the sharp, hollow ache intensify as she poured more energy into the barrier, burying Theo deeper.

Pemberton stopped.

For a long, terrible moment, she stood at the edge of the overgrown thicket, her silver form flickering. Her eyes narrowed.

"There's something here," she said slowly. "Something you're protecting. Something *important*."

She raised her wand.

The pressure *doubled*.

Jackie's construct shuddered. The thorns strained against the force of Pemberton's will, the ancient trees groaning as the Legilimens pushed *harder*—

And then, abruptly, she stopped.

The pressure vanished. The forest settled.

Pemberton stood motionless, her wand lowering slowly. Her expression was unreadable.

"Everyone has secrets," she said quietly. "The question isn't whether you have them. The question is whether they'll compromise you in the field."

She turned away from the overgrown thicket. Away from the ravine. Away from the archway of leaning trees that Jackie had buried so deep.

"Your trauma is processed. Your defenses are sophisticated. Your instinct to protect is..." She paused, searching for the word. "Formidable."

She began to withdraw, her silver presence fading from the forest like morning mist.

"We're done here."

---

Jackie's eyes snapped open.

She was back in the dim room, sitting in the hard wooden chair. Her chest heaved with ragged breaths, sweat beading at her temples. Her splinted hand was clenched so tight against her thigh that the joints ached.

Pemberton sat across from her, perfectly composed. Her wand rested in her lap.

"Forty-seven minutes," she said. Her voice was the same graveled monotone, but something in her eyes had shifted. "Most candidates last twenty before they break."

She rose from her chair, tucking her wand into her sleeve.

"You pass." A pause. "Barely. That barrier you built at the end—I could have broken it if I'd pushed harder. You know that."

Jackie said nothing. Her throat was too tight for words.

"Whatever you're hiding in that ravine," Pemberton continued, moving toward the door, "keep it hidden. From everyone. Some secrets are worth protecting."

She stopped at the threshold, looking back over her shoulder.

"Results post tomorrow at noon. Main atrium board." Her lips twitched—not quite a smile, but close. "Get some rest, Nott. You've earned it."

The door opened.

The corridor beyond was empty.

Jackie sat alone in the dim room, her heart still pounding, the phantom pressure of Pemberton's intrusion slowly fading from her mind.

In the ravine, buried beneath thorns and shadow, the bond with Theo pulsed—quiet, steady, *safe*.

She'd kept him hidden.

She'd passed.

Pemberton's mental avatar was exactly what Jackie had expected: sharp, efficient, stripped of sentiment. She appeared as a grey silhouette—no distinguishing features, no warmth—moving through the underbrush with the precise, methodical gait of a hunter tracking prey.

*Interesting choice*, a voice echoed through the trees. Pemberton's voice, but sourceless, coming from everywhere and nowhere. *Most candidates build walls. You built a wilderness.*

The grey figure didn't wait for a response. She moved deeper into the forest, her steps unnaturally silent against the carpet of fallen needles.

Jackie shadowed her, keeping to the treeline. This was her territory. She knew where Pemberton was heading—toward the clearing where her most accessible memories waited, carefully curated. The curse. The breaking. The hospital months.

*Let her find them. Let her see.*

But Pemberton didn't go to the clearing first.

She stopped at the edge of a small, still pond—a memory Jackie hadn't consciously placed there. The water's surface rippled, and images began to form: a younger Jackie, fifteen years old, standing in the Hogwarts library with tears streaming down her face. Draco's voice, cutting and cruel, echoing across the stacks. *Did you really think I'd write back? It was just a kiss, Taylor. Don't be pathetic.*

The memory stung. Jackie felt the old humiliation rise in her chest, sharp and hot.

Pemberton observed without comment. The grey silhouette tilted its head, cataloguing.

*Rejection sensitivity. Early adolescent wound. Noted.*

She moved on.

The next memory surfaced unbidden—Jackie couldn't stop it. The forest path twisted, and suddenly Pemberton was standing at the mouth of a dark cave. Inside, shadows writhed. The smell of copper and antiseptic. A hospital bed. Jackie's own body, thin and hollow, staring at nothing while Theo sat beside her, his hand wrapped around hers.

*The breaking*, Pemberton's voice observed. *Significant trauma. Identity dissolution following the curse ritual.*

The memory shifted. Now it was the aftermath—the endless grey weeks when Jackie couldn't feel anything, couldn't *be* anything. The hollow space where the wolf had lived, aching like a phantom limb.

*Grief without an object. Interesting. You lost a part of yourself, not a person.*

Jackie's jaw clenched. She forced herself to breathe, to let the examiner see what she needed to see. This was the point. This was the test.

But Pemberton wasn't satisfied.

The grey figure turned away from the cave and began walking—not toward the clearing, but *sideways*, toward a part of the forest Jackie hadn't consciously opened. The trees here were different. Older. Darker.

*What's over here?*

Jackie's heart rate spiked.

The path Pemberton was taking led toward the depression. The five months after Draco left. The nights when Jackie had  sat on the bathroom floor, Liquid Death in her hand, the vial uncapped, ready to be drank. The mornings when getting out of bed had felt like swimming through tar.

She hadn't hidden this. She *couldn't* hide this—it was too large, too sprawling, woven into too many other memories. But she hadn't expected Pemberton to find it so quickly.

*Ah*, the voice said, and there was something different in it now. Not clinical. Almost... careful. *There it is.*

The grey silhouette stopped at the edge of a vast, blackened clearing. The trees here were dead—scorched trunks reaching toward a colorless sky. In the center stood a figure that Jackie recognized as herself: gaunt, hollow-eyed, wrapped in a dark robe that hung off her frame like a shroud.

*Suicidal ideation*, Pemberton observed. *Extended depressive episode. Approximately five months duration.*

The memory-Jackie didn't move. Didn't speak. She just stood there, staring at nothing, while the world around her rotted.

*How did you survive this?*

The question wasn't rhetorical. It wasn't clinical. It was genuine curiosity, probing at the edges of something Pemberton didn't quite understand.

Jackie felt the answer rise unbidden—the tether pulsing in the dark ravine, Theo's presence anchoring her when nothing else could. But she clamped down on it, hard, reinforcing the overgrown archway with another layer of thorns.

Instead, she let a different memory surface: Theo's hand on her shoulder in the grey morning light. His voice, low and steady. *"You don't have to be okay. You just have to stay."*

Not the bond. Just the words. The human connection, stripped of its magical dimension.

*Someone kept you here*, Pemberton observed. *Not love. Not hope. Stubbornness. Obligation.*

The grey figure turned to face Jackie's mental avatar directly.

*You didn't want to live. You just refused to die. That's... different.*

The silence stretched. Jackie felt the weight of Pemberton's assessment pressing against her consciousness—not painful, but *heavy*. Evaluating.

Then the grey silhouette began to move again.

But this time, she walked toward the ravine.

Jackie's blood went cold.

*What's behind those trees?*

The question was sharp, pointed. Pemberton had noticed the deliberate concealment—the too-thick pines, the unnatural density of the undergrowth. She was walking directly toward the hidden archway, her grey form slipping between the trunks with predatory focus.

*You've walled something off. Something important.*

Jackie's mental form stepped into her path. Not aggressive—she couldn't afford aggressive, not against a Master Legilimens—but *present*. Solid.

"That's private," she said. Her voice echoed strangely in the mindscape, layered with harmonics that didn't exist in the physical world. "It's not relevant to the trial."

*Everything is relevant.* Pemberton didn't stop walking. *Hidden trauma is still trauma. Concealed vulnerabilities are still vulnerabilities.*

"It's not trauma." Jackie held her ground. "It's not a vulnerability. It's just... mine."

The grey silhouette paused. Tilted its head.

*You're protecting someone.*

Not a question. An observation.

*Not yourself. Someone else. Someone connected to what's behind those trees.*

Jackie felt her pulse hammering in her temples—both in the mindscape and in the physical world. The chair creaked beneath her grip.

Pemberton studied her for a long moment. The forest was absolutely silent—no wind, no birdsong, just the oppressive weight of scrutiny.

Then, slowly, the grey figure stepped back.

*You have adequate defenses*, the voice said. *Unorthodox, but functional. Your trauma responses are integrated rather than suppressed—you've processed them, not buried them. The depression was severe but didn't compromise your core identity.*

A pause.

*The concealed element concerns me. But you've demonstrated the capacity to protect sensitive information under pressure, which is... relevant to the position.*

The forest began to dissolve. The trees faded, the sky brightened, and Jackie felt herself being pulled back into her body—back into the dim room with the two chairs and the cold stone walls.

When she opened her eyes, Auror Pemberton was watching her with an expression that was almost, *almost* something other than clinical.

"You didn't break," the older witch said. Her voice was rough, as if she'd been speaking for hours instead of minutes. "Most candidates break when I find the suicidal ideation. They panic. They try to explain it away, or they collapse into it."

She lowered her wand.

"You just stood there and let me see it. Then you told me to stop." A pause. "That takes a specific kind of strength. The kind we need."

She stood, her knees cracking audibly.

"You pass, Mrs. Nott. Report to the Atrium at noon tomorrow for the official results and program assignments." Her grey eyes flickered—something almost like respect. "Whatever you're hiding in that ravine... keep it hidden. Some things don't belong to the Ministry."

She walked past Jackie without another word, disappearing through a door Jackie hadn't noticed before.

Jackie sat alone in the dim room, her heart still pounding, her hands still shaking.

She'd passed.

All three trials.

She was going to be an Auror.

Jackie stood up slowly. The chair scraped against the stone floor, the sound harsh and unnaturally loud in the empty room.

She turned and walked back out through the same heavy oak door she had entered. She knew there was another exit—Pemberton had just used it—and she knew she was the very last candidate of the day, so there was no one waiting in the corridor to see her anyway. It didn't matter. She just needed to get out.

She made it exactly three steps into the DMLE foyer before her knees simply ceased to function.

They buckled completely. Jackie fell hard, her palms slapping against the cold, polished tile to brace her descent. The jarring impact sent a fresh, blinding spike of agony through her mended ring finger, but the physical pain barely registered over the roaring in her ears.

She felt sick.

She felt entirely, irreparably filthy. Violated. Split open from sternum to navel and left exposed under harsh Ministry lighting. During the interrogation, while she was sitting in that chair, she had maintained a vice-like, militant grip on her emotions. She had treated it like a tactical maneuver. But now, alone on the floor, the dam broke.

She had let a stranger into her mind. She had let a cold, clinical Ministry official casually stroll through her darkest, most agonizing moments. She had deliberately served up her own shattered psyche, her lowest points of absolute despair, as a distraction just so the Legilimens would leave that one, sacred space alone.

Jackie started shaking. It wasn't a subtle tremor; it was a violent, full-body shudder. She was completely oblivious to the fact that she was kneeling in the middle of a Ministry of Magic corridor, trembling like a leaf in a storm.

She didn't cry. Her eyes were bone-dry. Instead, a wave of acidic bile surged up her throat. She gagged, dry-heaving violently once, then twice, her good hand clutching at her chest. She forced her eyes closed and dragged long, ragged pulls of air in through her mouth, desperate to ease the crushing nausea.

Deep in her mind, she felt the silence. She had kept the bond walled off. The thick, thorny overgrowth she had conjured to hide the ravine was still firmly in place. It was a deliberate, agonizing choice. The absolute last thing she wanted—or needed—right now was for Theo to feel this catastrophic spike of panic through their tether, abandon whatever he was doing with his Sunday morning, and come rushing to her rescue.

It took her several long, agonizing minutes on the cold tile to finally calm her breathing.

She pushed herself up on trembling legs. She still didn't want to see Theo. She didn't want to see Draco either. She knew exactly what would happen if she went back to Draco's flat right now: she would crumple the second she saw them. She would cry, and they would crowd her, and hold her, and dote on her in that fierce, overprotective way that usually warmed her but right now would only make her feel weak and stupid.

She needed to hit something.

Jackie walked stiffly out of the DMLE and took the elevator up to the Atrium. She wasn't entirely sure where she was going until she stepped into one of the giant, roaring fireplaces, grabbed a handful of Floo powder, and threw it into the flames.

"Nott Highlands Manor."

She spun away in a rush of emerald fire.

The Manor was deathly quiet when she stepped out of the grate. It was empty, holding its breath. They spent less and less time here lately; Theo often stayed over at Draco's, and the sprawling, dark halls no longer felt like a sanctuary to her. But right now, the Manor offered the one thing she desperately needed: isolation and a place to do violence.

Jackie stormed down the corridor toward the dueling room, her wand already drawn and humming in her hand. She kicked the doors open. With a sharp flick of her wrist, she levitated four heavy, enchanted humanoid targets from the storage racks and slammed them down into the center of the room.

She didn't hesitate. She started throwing hexes.

"*Confringo\!*"

The first target shattered into a rain of splinters.

"*Expulso\! Reducto\!*"

She ignored the sharp, protesting ache in her strained finger. She ignored the burning friction in her hand from the sheer force of her wand movements. She ignored the fact that she was a complete mental whirlwind inside. She just poured all of that chaotic, violent emotion directly into the magic.

She should be proud. She should be ecstatic. She had passed. She had survived a grueling three-day crucible and made even the famously unflappable Harry Potter look at her with something akin to respect.

But all she could see when she closed her eyes was that massive, blackened clearing in her mind. That scorched place that reeked of dark, suffocating desperation.

"*Sectumsempra\!*"

A deep, vicious gouge tore through the chest of the second target.

She hated that the clearing was even there. She hated that no matter how much time passed, no matter how much she healed, nothing ever grew back over that burned earth. She hated that Auror Pemberton had dragged it out into the harsh light, forcing her to stand in the ashes and feel the absolute weight of it all over again.

But the hatred itself wasn't even the worst part.

The worst part was the cold, hollow realization that settled in her chest as the third target exploded into dust. Once the adrenaline faded and the hatred ebbed, there would only be this truth left: she was broken. She had been hurt, cursed, and abused so many times that some fundamental part of her would never, ever grow back. Even if her life turned out perfectly, even if she achieved every single one of her goals and became the best Auror the Ministry had ever seen... that charred swath of forest would still be there. A permanent monument to the girl who had wanted to die.

The wood of her wand was growing physically hot in her grip, the magical core straining violently against such strenuous, continuous use. The last of the four targets disintegrated.

Panting, sweat stinging her eyes, Jackie slashed her wand through the air again, dragging three more heavy wooden targets into the center of the room.

The silence hit Theo like a physical blow.

One moment, Jackie's presence hummed in the back of his mind—distant but steady, the familiar warmth of her consciousness threading through the bond. The next, it simply... vanished. Like a door slamming shut. Like a candle being snuffed.

He froze mid-sentence, his coffee cup suspended halfway to his mouth.

Across the table, Draco was saying something about property valuations, his voice carrying that particular cadence of someone who'd been talking for several minutes without noticing his audience had stopped listening. The Muggle café around them buzzed with Sunday morning chatter—families, couples, the clatter of dishes and the hiss of the espresso machine.

Theo heard none of it.

*Jackie.*

He reached for the bond instinctively, pressing against the sudden absence. Nothing. Not emptiness—that would imply a void to be filled. This was *deliberate*. A wall. Thick and thorned and absolutely impenetrable.

She'd shut him out.

"—and if we factor in the magical zoning restrictions, the Hampstead property might actually be more viable than—" Draco stopped. His eyes narrowed. "You're not listening."

"Something's wrong."

The words came out flat. Clipped. Theo set his coffee down with exaggerated care, his knuckles whitening around the ceramic.

Draco's posture shifted immediately—the property discussion abandoned, his attention sharpening to a razor's edge. "The trial. What happened?"

"I don't know." Theo's jaw clenched. "I can't feel her."

The implication landed. Draco went very still.

"What do you mean you can't—"

"She blocked me." Theo pushed back from the table, already reaching for his jacket. "Deliberately. Completely. I've never felt her do it this... thoroughly."

Draco was on his feet before Theo finished speaking. His face had gone pale beneath the café's warm lighting, his hand already moving toward his wand before he caught himself—*Muggle establishment, don't be an idiot*.

"The Ministry," Draco said. "We go to the Ministry. If something happened during the psychological trial—"

Across the table, Draco was saying something about property valuations, his voice carrying that particular cadence of someone who'd been talking for several minutes without noticing his audience had stopped listening. The Muggle café around them buzzed with Sunday morning chatter—families, couples, the clatter of dishes and the hiss of the espresso machine.

Theo heard none of it.

*Jackie.*

He reached for the bond instinctively, pressing against the sudden absence. Nothing. Not emptiness—that would imply a void to be filled. This was *deliberate*. A wall. Thick and thorned and absolutely impenetrable.

She'd shut him out.

"—and if we factor in the magical zoning restrictions, the Hampstead property might actually be more viable than—" Draco stopped. His eyes narrowed. "You're not listening."

"Something's wrong."

The words came out flat. Clipped. Theo set his coffee down with exaggerated care, his knuckles whitening around the ceramic.

Draco's posture shifted immediately—the property discussion abandoned, his attention sharpening to a razor's edge. "The trial. What happened?"

"I don't know." Theo's jaw clenched. "I can't feel her."

The implication landed. Draco went very still.

"What do you mean you can't—"

"She blocked me." Theo pushed back from the table, already reaching for his jacket. "Deliberately. Completely. I've never felt her do it this... thoroughly."

Draco was on his feet before Theo finished speaking. His face had gone pale beneath the café's warm lighting, his hand already moving toward his wand before he caught himself—*Muggle establishment, don't be an idiot*.

"The Ministry," Draco said. "We go to the Ministry. If something happened during the psychological trial—"

"She wouldn't block me if she was in danger." Theo's voice was tight, controlled. "She'd reach *for* me, not push me away. This is different."

"Then what—"

"I don't know." The admission cost him something. Theo didn't admit ignorance easily, and certainly not when it came to Jackie. "But whatever happened in that room... she doesn't want me to feel it."

They were already moving toward the door, weaving between tables with practiced efficiency. The morning drizzle had returned, misting against the glass, but neither of them noticed.

"Where would she go?" Draco asked. His voice had dropped into that clipped, aristocratic register that meant he was barely containing his own fear. "If she didn't want to see us, if she needed—"

"Space." Theo finished the thought. "Somewhere familiar. Somewhere she could—"

He stopped.

*Somewhere she could fight.*

"The Manor."

Draco's eyes widened. "She wouldn't—"

"She would." Theo was already scanning the street for an adequate Apparition point—somewhere private, somewhere the Muggles wouldn't see them vanish. "The dueling room. She goes there when she needs to break things."

"But she passed." Draco's voice cracked slightly. "She had to have passed. The psychological trial doesn't cause physical harm, and if she'd failed, they would have—"

"This isn't about passing or failing." Theo found what he was looking for—a narrow alley between two shops, shadowed and empty. He grabbed Draco's arm without ceremony, pulling him toward it. "This is about what they made her show them."

They ducked into the alley. The smell of wet brick and old garbage. The distant rumble of London traffic.

Theo turned to face Draco. In the dim light, his expression was carved from stone—but his eyes betrayed him. Fear. Real, uncontrolled fear.

"The Mind Sieve," he said quietly. "They would have probed her defenses. Looked for trauma. Triggers." A pause. "She has plenty of both."

Draco's hand found his signet ring. Twisted it. His breathing had gone shallow, carefully controlled.

"And she blocked you because—"

"Because she didn't want me to feel what they found."

The silence stretched. Cold. Heavy.

Then Draco spoke, his voice barely above a whisper: "The depression. After I left."

Not a question. A statement of fact, delivered with the particular flatness of someone confronting something they'd spent months trying not to think about.

Theo didn't respond. He didn't need to.

They Apparated.

---

The Manor materialized around them—dark halls, heavy curtains, the familiar smell of old wood and older magic. Empty. Silent.

Except it wasn't silent.

From somewhere deep in the house, muffled but unmistakable, came the sounds of combat. The sharp *crack* of spellfire. The explosive percussion of targets being destroyed. The raw, primal energy of someone pouring violence into magic.

Theo and Draco exchanged a single look.

Then they moved.

The corridors blurred past—past the library, past the sitting room, past the empty bedrooms that hadn't been used in months. The sounds grew louder as they approached the dueling wing. Closer. More visceral.

They stopped outside the doors.

Through the heavy wood, they could hear it clearly now: the hiss of flames, the crack of splintering wood, the thrum of a wand pushed nearly to its breaking point. And beneath it all, the ragged, gasping breaths of someone fighting demons that couldn't be hit back.

Draco's hand hovered over the door handle. He didn't push it open.

"She doesn't want us here," he said quietly. His voice was strange—layered with something Theo couldn't quite identify. Guilt, maybe. Or recognition.

"I know."

"If we go in there—"

"She'll be angry."

A pause.

"She'll be furious."

Another pause, longer this time.

Inside the room, something exploded. The doors rattled in their frames.

Theo's jaw tightened. He reached past Draco and pushed the doors open.

She was so far gone into her rage and her own mind that she whirled on instinct, sending a jarring, full-force *Incendio* in the direction of the movement. Jackie stopped, her arm still raised, her chest heaving, her hair plastered to her forehead with sweat.
"Go the fuck away!" she shouted at the door.
She suddenly realized that her wand hand was stinging fiercely. She lowered it to look. The skin was blistering, and the wood of her wand had started to blacken as well; too much raw magic flowing through it was threatening its structural integrity. Jackie opened her hand, and the wand clattered to the floor. The movement pulled at the fresh welts and blisters, and she winced at the sharp sting. Then, she deliberately closed her hand into a fist and opened it again, plunging right back into the agony.
*Pain.*
"Can't you two take a fucking hint?! I want to be alone!"
She didn't. Not really. Or rather, there was a part of her that knew the truth—being alone right now would only drag her deeper under.
She took three heavy steps toward the weapons rack and grabbed five small, dulled practice daggers with her good hand. Turning back toward the charred doors, she grabbed one of the daggers by the blade with her burned, freshly injured wand hand.
Pain flared again, hot and bright.
*Good.*
She stood there, breathing hard, waiting to see if either of them would be foolish enough to step through that door.

The silence stretched.

Behind the charred door, Theo stood with his palm flat against the blackened wood, feeling the residual heat seep into his skin. His jaw was clenched so tight his teeth ached. Beside him, Draco had gone absolutely still—that particular Malfoy stillness that meant he was calculating, assessing, trying to find the angle that would let him control the situation.

There wasn't one. They both knew it.

"She's burning herself out," Theo said quietly. Not to Draco—just stating fact, the way he might observe the weather. "The wand's overheating. She'll damage her core if she keeps going."

Draco's hand found his signet ring. Twisted. "She nearly hit us with an Incendio."

"She didn't aim. It was reflex."

"That's supposed to make me feel better?"

Theo didn't answer. He pressed his palm harder against the door, feeling the grain of the wood, the places where the fire had weakened it. Through the bond—nothing. Still nothing. Just that deliberate, thorned wall, thick as castle stone.

But he didn't need the bond to know what was happening on the other side.

He'd seen Jackie like this before. Not often—she was too controlled, too disciplined to let herself shatter where anyone could witness it. But he'd seen it. The night after the Wizengamot hearing, when she'd recounted every detail of what Fenholt had done to her. The morning after the Snake Soirée, when Draco had left and she'd stood in the middle of their bedroom, perfectly still, perfectly silent, for three hours.

She didn't cry when she broke. She *burned*.

"We're coming in," Theo called through the door. His voice was steady, calm—the deliberate flatness he used when negotiating with dangerous things. "You can throw whatever you want at us. We're still coming in."

No response. Just the sound of ragged breathing.

Draco's head turned sharply. "Are you *trying* to get us killed?"

"She won't hurt us."

"She just—"

"She won't hurt us." Theo met his eyes. "She's hurting herself instead. That's what this is."

The words landed like stones dropped into still water. Draco's expression flickered—something raw and wounded surfacing before he could suppress it.

*The depression. After I left.*

He'd known. Of course he'd known. Jackie had told him about the Liquid Death—had confessed it in the greenhouse, her voice flat and distant, like she was describing something that had happened to someone else. But knowing and *understanding* were different things. Knowing was abstract. Understanding was standing outside a door, listening to the woman he loved destroy herself because a Ministry examiner had forced her to relive the worst moments of her life.

Understanding was realizing that some of those worst moments were his fault.

"Together," Draco said quietly. His voice was strange—stripped of its usual careful control. "We go in together."

Theo nodded once.

He pushed the door open.

---

The dueling room was a disaster.

Shattered wood and ash covered the floor—the remnants of at least seven or eight training targets, reduced to kindling and splinters. Scorch marks climbed the walls in jagged patterns, and the air was thick with the acrid smell of burned magic and overheated wand-core. The weapon racks along the far wall had been half-emptied, practice blades scattered across the floor.

And in the center of it all, Jackie.

Theo took her in with a single, sweeping glance—the sweat-soaked hair, the heaving chest, the blistered wand hand hanging at her side. The practice daggers clutched in her other hand. The way she was gripping one blade with her burned fingers, the metal biting into welted skin.

*Pain anchor.*

He recognized it instantly. She'd shown him the technique once, during Occlumency practice—the way she used physical sensation to maintain focus, to keep her mental shields locked tight. But this wasn't focus. This was punishment.

He stopped ten feet away. Didn't approach. Didn't crowd her.

"You passed," he said. Not a question.

Draco had stopped beside him, his posture rigid, his eyes fixed on Jackie's burned hand. His face was pale, but his voice was steady when he spoke.

"The Mind Sieve. What did Pemberton find?"

"Draco." Sharper now. "What happened during the psychological trial? What did they find?"

Draco's throat moved. A visible swallow.

"She—" He stopped. Started again. "Before we left for the trip. The night of the Snake Soirée. She told me—"

Another explosion from inside the room. The door shuddered.

"*Go away!*" Jackie's voice, raw and ragged.

Draco flinched. His hand found his signet ring, twisting it with enough force to leave marks.

"She told me she'd been close." The words came out barely above a whisper. "To ending it. After I left. She had... she had a vial. Liquid Death. She'd thought about drinking it."

The words landed like stones dropped into still water.

Theo went absolutely still.

And in the center of it all, Jackie stood with five dulled practice blades in her hands, her chest heaving, her skin sheened with sweat. Her wand lay abandoned on the floor, its wood visibly blackened. Her right hand—her wand hand—was a mess of blisters and welts, the skin angry and red.

Her eyes, when they found him, were wild. Not broken—*furious*. The kind of fury that came from being cornered.

Theo stopped just inside the doorway. He didn't raise his hands. Didn't reach for his wand. Just stood there, solid and present, and let her look at him.

"I told you to go away."

"I heard you."

"Then *leave*."

"No."

The word hung between them. Simple. Absolute. Non-negotiable.

Behind him, Draco stepped through the ruined doorway. His face was still pale, his composure barely holding, but he moved to Theo's left and stopped. Flanking. United.

Neither of them advanced further.

The silence stretched. Heavy. Charged.

Theo's eyes tracked down to her burned hand, the daggers gripped tight despite what must be excruciating pain. He catalogued the details without comment—the deliberate self-infliction, the anchor through sensation, the way she was using physical agony to keep from drowning in something worse.

He understood. Better than she probably knew.

"You blocked me," he said quietly. Not an accusation. An observation.

"I didn't want you to feel it."

"I know." A pause. "But that's not your choice to make."

Her grip tightened on the daggers. Fresh blood welled where the dulled edge pressed into her palm.

Draco made a small, involuntary sound—not quite a gasp, but close.

Theo didn't move. Didn't flinch. Just held her gaze with that steady, unwavering intensity that had anchored her through worse than this.

"Whatever they found in there," he said, his voice dropping lower. "Whatever you showed them. You don't have to carry it alone."

A muscle jumped in her jaw.

"Put down the knives, Jackie."

Not a command. A request. The softest his voice had been all day.

She was so far gone into her rage and her own mind that she whirled on instinct, sending a jarring, full-force *Incendio* in the direction of the movement. Neither of them had even a second to draw their wands, but Theo swung the heavy door shut just a fraction of a second before the flaming ball hit it, charring and splintering the wood.
Jackie stopped, her arm still raised, her chest heaving, her hair plastered to her forehead with sweat.
"Go the fuck away!" she shouted at the door.
She suddenly realized that her wand hand was stinging fiercely. She lowered it to look. The skin was blistering, and the wood of her wand had started to blacken as well; too much raw magic flowing through it was threatening its structural integrity. Jackie opened her hand, and the wand clattered to the floor. The movement pulled at the fresh welts and blisters, and she winced at the sharp sting. Then, she deliberately closed her hand into a fist and opened it again, plunging right back into the agony.
*Pain.*
"Can't you two take a fucking hint?! I want to be alone!"
She didn't. Not really. Or rather, there was a part of her that knew the truth—being alone right now would only drag her deeper under.
She took three heavy steps toward the weapons rack and grabbed five small, dulled practice daggers with her good hand. Turning back toward the charred doors, she grabbed one of the daggers by the blade with her burned, freshly injured wand hand.
Pain flared again, hot and bright.
*Good.*
She stood there, breathing hard, waiting to see if either of them would be foolish enough to step through that door.

"That's not what I'm worried about."

Inside the room, silence. No more explosions. No more spellfire.

Just the sound of someone breathing through pain.

Theo closed his eyes. He thought about the last time they'd been in this room together—January of last year, the night Jackie had commanded him to let his darkness loose. The night she'd taken back what he'd stolen from her, blow by blow, until they were both bloody and spent and somehow, impossibly, closer to whole.

This was different. This wasn't a ritual. This was raw, uncontrolled breaking.

"She blocked me," Theo said, low enough that only Draco could hear. "Completely. Whatever they made her show them in that trial... she didn't want me to feel it."

Draco's jaw tightened. His eyes were still fixed on the door.

"The depression," he said. Not a question.

"Probably."

"And the—" Draco stopped. Swallowed. Started again. "The Liquid Death. She told me about it. Before you left for the trip. I thought—" His voice cracked. "I thought it was just a passing thought. Something she'd considered and dismissed."

Theo didn't respond immediately. He remembered those five months. He remembered watching Jackie slip further away each day, watching the light drain from her eyes, watching her go through the motions of living without actually *being* alive. He'd stayed. He'd held her when she let him. But he hadn't been able to reach her—not really. Not the way she'd needed.

Because she hadn't been his to reach. Not then. She'd been Draco's, and Draco had left.

"It wasn't passing," Theo said finally. His voice was quiet. Not accusatory—just honest. "It was months. Every day. She kept the vial in her nightstand drawer. I found it once, when she was sleeping. I didn't take it. I should have, but I—" He stopped. "I didn't know how to help her without making it worse."

Draco made a sound. Small, choked—somewhere between a laugh and a sob.

"And now some Ministry Legilimens has been inside her head," he said, "forcing her to stand in the middle of it. While we were looking at *property listings*."

The guilt in his voice was sharp enough to cut.

Theo turned to look at him. Really look. Draco's composure was fracturing—the careful mask slipping, the raw shame bleeding through. His hands were shaking slightly. His breathing had gone shallow.

*This is eating him alive*, Theo realized. *He's been carrying this for eighteen months, and he's never let himself actually feel it.*

"This isn't your fault," Theo said.

Draco's laugh was bitter. "I left her. I left because I couldn't forgive you, and I told myself it was *principled*, and meanwhile she was—" He stopped. His voice dropped to barely a whisper. "She was dying, and I was too proud to come back."

"You came back eventually."

"Too late."

"She doesn't think so."

Draco's eyes snapped to his face. Something raw flickered there—not quite hope, not quite despair. Something in between.

"She walled off the bond," Draco said slowly, working through it. "She didn't want you to feel what they found. But she didn't go to your flat, or mine. She came *here*. To the dueling room." A pause. "She's not trying to hide from us. She's trying to protect us from seeing it."

Theo nodded slowly. That was Jackie—always shielding, always protecting, even when she was the one bleeding.

"She can't protect us from this," Theo said. "We were already there. We already saw it—we just didn't understand what we were seeing."

Through the door, they heard movement. The soft clatter of metal against wood. A sharp, hissing intake of breath—the sound of someone in pain.

Theo's hand found the door handle.

"She's going to be furious," Draco said quietly.

"I know."

"She might throw those daggers."

"I know."

"She might—" Draco stopped. His voice cracked again. "She might not want us to see her like this."

Theo turned to meet his eyes. In the dim corridor, Draco looked younger than his twenty years—stripped of his careful composure, his aristocratic armor. Just a man who loved someone he'd hurt, standing outside a door he was terrified to open.

"She doesn't want us to see her like this," Theo agreed. "But she needs us to anyway. That's the difference."

He pushed the door open.

Draco didn't flinch.

The dagger struck his collarbone with a dull, meaty *thud*—the kind of impact that would bloom purple and black within the hour. The pain registered immediately, sharp and spreading, but he didn't move. Didn't raise his hands. Didn't reach for his wand.

He just stood there and took it.

"I deserve that," he said quietly.

His voice was steady. Controlled. But something underneath it had cracked open—the careful Malfoy composure fracturing along fault lines that had been building for eighteen months.

Beside him, Theo had gone utterly still. Not the coiled stillness of someone preparing to act—the watchful stillness of someone choosing not to. His eyes tracked the remaining daggers in Jackie's grip, cataloguing the threat, but he made no move to disarm her.

*Let her throw them. Let her rage. She needs this.*

The dulled blade clattered to the floor at Draco's feet. He didn't look at it.

"You told us not to come in," Draco said. His hand drifted toward the impact point—stopped halfway—dropped back to his side. "You told us to go away. You blocked the bond and came here alone because you didn't want us to see."

"But I've already seen it, Jackie. I was there." His voice dropped. "I just didn't stay."

The words hung in the air. Raw. Unflinching.

"You want to throw the rest?" Theo asked. His voice was low, steady. No teasing. No charm. Just the blunt honesty he defaulted to when everything else had been stripped away. "Go ahead. We're not leaving."

Jackie stood perfectly still. She didn't throw another dagger. She let them speak. She let them advance, their boots crunching on the splintered wood, their apologies and confessions hanging heavy in the smoke-filled air. Her eyes finally locked onto Theo. He was closest, his hands open, his voice pitched in that soft, careful cadence one might use to coax a wounded animal out from a corner. Like she needed saving. Jackie slowly shook her head. A smile crawled onto her face—an expression entirely devoid of warmth, heavy and laden with poison. "You really don't get it, do you?"
With a sudden, sharp twist of her wrist, she flipped the dagger. She pressed the dulled tip directly into the center of Theo's chest, pushing forward until the fabric of his shirt dipped visibly, the metal biting hard against his sternum. "You *raped* me," she said, the words slipping out like shattered glass. "You took something from me that no one will be able to give me back. You warped me. You pulled the darkest version of me to the surface."
She uncurled her good hand, letting the two remaining spare daggers clatter uselessly to the floor. Reaching up, she hooked her fingers into the collar of her T-shirt and yanked it violently to the side. The fabric stretched taut, exposing the pale skin of her shoulder and collarbone—and the cluster of jagged, half-moon shaped scars. Bite marks. "You made it impossible for me to experience pleasure in a normal way," she continued, her voice vibrating with a brutal, clinical honesty. "You made me crave pain like an addict, because my body feels that's the only thing I deserve."
She dragged the dagger away from Theo's chest, turning her wrist to point the dulled metal straight at Draco. "And you..." Her eyes narrowed, unyielding. "You just let me wait, and hope, and lose the hope, and the will to live. Because you were too much of a stuck-up ass and a coward."
She finally lowered the dagger. Her arm dropped to her side, the physical fight draining out of her, leaving only the crushing, suffocating weight of the truth. "And I've never realized how broken that made me. How ugly and distorted I will be, *forever*," she whispered.

The pain hit Theo like a physical blow.

His knees buckled. Not a stumble—a full collapse, his body crumpling as eighteen months of agony crashed through the bond in a single, devastating wave. His palms slammed against the splintered floor, splinters biting into his skin, but he barely registered it. The physical pain was nothing compared to what was flooding through him.

*This. This is what she carried. This is what I did.*

He saw the blackened clearing through her eyes—not as a distant concept, but as a lived reality. The scorched earth where nothing would ever grow. The hollow-eyed figure standing in the ashes, wrapped in darkness, waiting for the courage to stop waiting. The vial in the nightstand drawer, uncapped, ready.

The despair was absolute. Bottomless. A weight so crushing it made breathing feel like an act of defiance against the universe.

And underneath it all, woven through every layer like poison through blood: *him*. What he'd done. What he'd taken. The way he'd warped her relationship with her own body until pain and pleasure had become inextricably tangled.

Theo's breath came in ragged gasps. His hands were shaking against the floor. He didn't try to shield himself—didn't try to push back against the flood. He let it in. All of it.

*You made this. You did this to her. This is yours.*

Somewhere far away, he heard Draco make a sound—a choked, strangled noise that might have been his name. But Theo couldn't respond. He was drowning in Jackie's truth, and he didn't have the right to come up for air.

---

Draco stood frozen.

He couldn't feel what Theo was feeling—he wasn't part of the bond, wasn't connected to that ancient magic that tied them together. But he could *see* it. He could see Theo collapse like his strings had been cut. He could see the way his whole body had gone rigid with pain that had nothing to do with physical injury.

And he could see Jackie's face.

Not rage anymore. Not even accusation. Just truth—raw, unfiltered, devastating truth delivered with the clinical precision of someone who had nothing left to lose.

*You just let me wait, and hope, and lose the hope, and the will to live.*

The words echoed in his skull. He thought of the months after he'd left. The righteous anger he'd nursed like a flame, telling himself he was *principled*, that he couldn't be party to what Theo had done. He thought of the letters he'd written and never sent. The times he'd almost gone back and convinced himself it was weakness.

He thought of Jackie in that narrow bed, alone in the dark, reaching for a vial of poison while he sat in his Ministry flat and told himself he was doing the right thing.

His hand found his signet ring. Twisted it. The metal bit into his skin.

"I know," he said.

His voice came out wrecked—barely a whisper, stripped of every layer of composure he'd spent twenty years constructing. He didn't try to rebuild it.

"I know what I did. What I *didn't* do." He swallowed hard. "I told myself I was protecting my principles. That I couldn't forgive him, so I couldn't stay with you. But that was—" His voice cracked. "That was a lie I told myself because staying was harder than leaving. Because if I stayed, I'd have to look at what he did every day and still choose to be in the same room with him. And I wasn't—I wasn't strong enough."

He took a step forward. Not toward her—toward Theo. The man was still on his knees, still shaking, still drowning in whatever Jackie had flooded through the bond. Draco stopped beside him but didn't touch him.

"I made you collateral damage," Draco continued, his eyes on Jackie's face. "I told myself I was punishing *him*, but you were the one who paid for it. And I knew. Some part of me knew what was happening to you, and I still didn't come back. Because I was afraid of what it would mean if I did."

His hand dropped from his ring. Hung at his side. Empty.

"You're right. I was a coward. I *am* a coward." The admission came out flat, final. "And I don't—I don't know how to fix that. I don't know if I can."

On the floor, Theo's breathing had steadied. Marginally. He was still on his knees, still braced against the splintered wood, but his head lifted. His pale eyes found Jackie's face.

"I know what I am."

His voice was raw. Scraped clean of every defense, every layer of charming confidence. Just the truth, ugly and unvarnished.

"I've always known. I told myself I could control it—that the darkness was a tool, something I could use and put away when I was done. But I couldn't. Not with you." He swallowed. "I wanted you so badly that I convinced myself wanting was enough. That if I wanted you, I had the right to take."

He pushed himself up slowly. His legs were unsteady, his hands still trembling, but he made it to his feet. He didn't step back. Didn't try to create distance.

"You're right. I raped you. I took something I had no right to take, and I can never give it back." The words came out steady now—the steadiness of someone who had stopped trying to soften the truth. "And everything that came after—the way your body responds, the way you crave pain—that's because of what I did. What I *made* you."

His jaw clenched. Unclenched.

"I spent months telling myself I could earn forgiveness. That if I stayed, if I protected you, if I loved you well enough... eventually the scales would balance." A pause. Something raw flickered in his eyes. "But there is no balance. There's no amount of staying that undoes what I took. The debt doesn't clear."

He didn't look away from her face.

"You showed me mercy I didn't deserve. You let me back into your life, into your bed, into your *soul*. And I've spent every day since then trying to be worthy of that mercy, knowing I never will be." His voice dropped. "But I'm not going to stop trying. Not because I think I can fix what I broke—I can't. I know that now. But because you deserve someone who keeps showing up, even when they know they'll never be enough."

Beside him, Draco stood motionless. His face was pale, his eyes wet—though no tears had fallen. Not yet.

"I can't feel what you're feeling," Draco said quietly. "I'm not part of the bond. I don't get to experience what you just showed him." A pause. "But I see what it did to him. And I know—" His voice caught. "I know that whatever he's feeling right now, I deserve to feel it too. Maybe more."

He took a breath. Let it out slowly.

She looked at the two men standing in the wreckage of her making, the two men who had ruined her and saved her in equal measure. Theo moved first.

He crossed the distance between them in three strides—not running, not hesitant, just *moving* with the kind of certainty that came from finally understanding what mattered. His hands found her shoulders, then slid down her arms, careful to avoid her injured hand. He pulled her against his chest without asking permission.

"No," he said quietly. The word vibrated through his ribcage, pressed against her cheek. "No, I shouldn't have."

He didn't apologize. Didn't explain. Just held her—firm and steady and *present*—while she shook apart in his arms.

Through the bond, he felt everything. The exhaustion. The grief. The raw, bleeding wound of being truly *seen* by a stranger who had no reason to lie. And underneath it all, threaded through the pain like gold through fractured stone: love. Stubborn, impossible, unearned love that refused to die no matter how many reasons it had been given.

*I fucking love you.*

The words echoed in his skull. He tightened his grip.

"You're not an idiot," he murmured against her hair. "You're the only person who ever looked at what I am and decided to stay anyway. That's not weakness. That's—" He stopped. Swallowed. "That's the bravest thing anyone's ever done for me."

Behind them, Draco stood motionless for a long moment. His hand was still extended, hovering in the empty air where Jackie had been standing. His expression was—

*Lost*, Theo realized. Draco looked completely, utterly lost.

Then something shifted. The paralysis broke. Draco moved forward, his steps careful over the splintered wood, until he was close enough to touch. He didn't reach for her immediately—that wasn't his way. Instead, he stood at her back, his presence a solid warmth just inches away, waiting.

"You said we should have left you alone," Draco said quietly. His voice was rough, scraped raw by everything he'd admitted in the last few minutes. "But you also said you didn't want to be alone. Both things can be true."

His hand lifted. Hovered over the curve of her shoulder—not touching yet, just *there*. An offer.

"I spent nine months convincing myself that leaving was the right thing to do. That staying away was somehow... noble." The word came out bitter, self-mocking. "But it wasn't noble. It was cowardice dressed up in principle. And you almost—"

His voice broke. He stopped. Tried again.

"You almost died," he whispered. "And I wasn't there. I will never forgive myself for that. Never."

His hand finally made contact—settling gently on her shoulder, his thumb tracing a small, careful circle against the fabric of her shirt. The touch was tentative. Almost reverent.

"But I'm here now. And I'm not leaving again." A pause. "Even when you tell me to."

Theo shifted slightly, making room without letting go. Jackie was pressed between them now—Theo's chest solid against her front, Draco's warmth a grounding presence at her back. The three of them stood in the wreckage of the dueling room, surrounded by splinters and ash and the remnants of rage that had finally burned itself out.

"You said you'll never be okay again," Theo said quietly. His lips brushed against her temple as he spoke—not quite a kiss, just contact. Connection. "Maybe that's true. Maybe the clearing never grows back."

He pulled back just enough to look at her face. Her eyes were red-rimmed, her cheeks streaked with tears and soot, her expression raw and unguarded in a way he'd rarely seen.

"But you're not standing in it alone anymore," he continued. "That has to count for something."

Draco's hand slid from her shoulder down her arm, his fingers brushing lightly over her skin until they found her uninjured hand. He laced his fingers through hers—careful, deliberate, like he was handling something precious.

"You asked why we didn't leave when you told us to," Draco said. His voice was steadier now, though still rough around the edges. "It's because we've both spent too long leaving when we should have stayed. I'm done running from the hard things. Even when the hard thing is watching you hurt."

He squeezed her hand gently.

"Especially then."

The private dining room was a velvet-lined cocoon: a curved booth built for intimacy, a single floating orb casting amber light across white linen and crystal stemware. No other tables. No witnesses. The maître d' murmured something about menus appearing at their leisure and evaporated.

Theo didn't sit immediately. He watched Jackie take in the space, the slight widening of her mismatched eyes, the way her exhale shifted her bare shoulders. The bite marks he'd left stood out against her pale skin like a signature.

"You look like you're expecting an ambush," he said. No teasing lilt—just observation. "Sit down, Menace. The only dangerous thing in this room is me."

Draco had already settled into the booth, one arm draped along the back, posture deceptively casual. But his fingers drummed once against the velvet—*ring-twist adjacent*, Theo noted—before going still.

"The private rooms here are warded against eavesdropping," Draco said, his voice carrying that measured, formal cadence he defaulted to in unfamiliar territory. "I've confirmed it. Whatever happens in this room stays in this room."

The statement hung there, weighted with more than restaurant privacy.

Theo slid into the booth on Jackie's other side, close enough that his thigh pressed against hers beneath the table. The contact was grounding—for her, for him, he didn't bother distinguishing anymore. Through the bond, he felt the low hum of her exhaustion threaded with something sharper. Anticipation, maybe. Or the residual static of a day spent surrounded by Aurors who didn't know what she carried inside her head.

"First day," Theo said, turning to face her. His pale eyes were steady, demanding. "How bad was it?"

Not *how was it*. He didn't do softening.

Across the table—across *her*—Draco's gaze had sharpened with the same question, though his delivery would have been wrapped in ten more words and twice as much caution. The difference between them, laid bare as always: Theo cut to the wound; Draco circled it first.

Theo's mouth curved at her deflection—smooth, predictable, entirely *her*. He let it land, watching the way she angled her body toward him, the deliberate pivot away from whatever soft thing Draco's gaze was doing across the table.

"Work," he repeated, drawing the word out like it tasted faintly absurd. His thumb traced a slow line along the outside of her thigh beneath the tablecloth—idle, proprietary. "You want to talk about *work*."

He reached for his wine, took a measured sip, set it down. The floating orb above them cast amber shadows across his angular features, sharpening the line of his jaw.

"Fine. First day back was exactly what you'd expect. Fourteen contract disputes waiting on my desk. Three of them involved blood-feuds older than Hogwarts. One wizard threatened to hex my assistant if I didn't prioritize his filing." A pause. The corner of his mouth twitched. "I told him I'd prioritize his filing into the incinerator."

Across the table, Draco made a sound—not quite a laugh, but close. His fingers had stilled on the stem of his wineglass, gray eyes tracking the exchange with that particular watchfulness he couldn't quite turn off.

"The Department of International Magical Cooperation sent four separate memos about the Lavigne Luminary," Draco said, his voice carefully even. "Apparently our attendance has been... noted. The French delegation is treating it as a diplomatic event."

Theo's eyes cut to him. "Since when do you read Ministry gossip about our social calendar?"

"Since it started affecting my inbox."

"Right." Theo's tone carried a edge of amusement—testing, not hostile. He held Draco's gaze a beat longer than necessary. "And here I thought you just missed us."

Draco's jaw tightened. His fingers resumed their slow rotation around the glass stem—not quite a ring-twist, but close enough. He didn't take the bait.

The menu shimmered into existence on the table between them: elegant script on cream parchment, the kind that rearranged itself based on the diner's preferences. Theo ignored it.
