But he behaved. For now.

He watched her navigate the Potter question with practiced deflection, cataloguing the tension in her shoulders that didn't quite match her dismissive tone. The bond hummed with something more complicated than annoyance—a snarl of frustration threaded with something older. Theo filed it away.

"Expelliarmus," he repeated flatly. "The man defeated the Dark Lord and his signature tactical advice is *Expelliarmus*."

Draco's wineglass paused halfway to his mouth. For a moment, his careful composure cracked—something that might have been genuine disbelief flickering across his features.

"That's..." Draco set the glass down, searching for words. "That's not even a defensive spell. It's a *disarming* charm. First-year curriculum."

"Second year, technically," Theo said. "But yes."

"He used it against the Killing Curse." Draco's voice had gone very quiet, very precise—the particular cadence he adopted when something offended his sense of magical order. "During the final battle. I was *there*. And somehow it worked, because apparently the rules of magical theory don't apply to Harry Potter."

Theo reached for his wine, took a slow sip. "You sound bitter."

"I sound *accurate*." Draco's jaw tightened. His fingers found the stem of his glass again, rotating it in slow, controlled circles. "The fact that it worked doesn't make it sound strategy. It makes it a statistical anomaly that should never be repeated."

The menu shimmered between them, patient and ignored. A server materialized at the edge of their alcove, took one look at the intensity of the conversation, and wisely retreated.

Theo turned back to Jackie, his pale eyes assessing. "So. Potter's insufferable. That's not new." His thumb resumed its slow circuit on her thigh—lighter this time, almost absent. "What else? You said 'first of all' earlier. Implies there's a list."

He waited, letting the silence do the work.

Jackie turned her attention back to the shimmering menu, settling on a garden salad and the "Phoenix-Charred" Quail. She doubted actual phoenix fire was involved, but the name appealed to the dormant, heat-seeking part of her magic. As she tapped her choices with her wand to finalize the order, she leaned into the bond, sending a sharp, provocative thought straight at Theo’s mind. *What if I tell you I forgot to put my underwear on?*
The internal thrill of his immediate, microscopic tension was better than the wine. She pulled back just enough to address their questions, closing the menu. "None of them knows about the curse. Honestly, I’m not sure Potter does either. Pemberton knows, since she poked around my head, but if she told him, he didn't let on. Keeping it under wraps was one of the only smart moves Cyrus ever made."
She ticked the trainees off on her fingers, one by one. "There are six of us. Catherine Morrow—a year younger, second time trying out. Julie Knox—Ilvermorny graduate; she moved here specifically to study under Potter. I think she has a bit of a crush. Then there’s Ridoc Ashford and Drake Lightwood, both seventeen, both former Gryffindors." She raised a fifth finger. "Sawyer Prewett. I suspect he’s a legacy placement since I didn't see him at tryouts. He’s Ravenclaw; I used to help him and his yearmates with Potions homework back at school. He was in the same year as Caroline’s brother, Callum."
She finished the list with six fingers extended before reaching for her glass, a wicked, feline grin spreading across her face. "As for the name Nott... well, it would have helped if you two hadn't walked me off before the tryouts. By the first coffee break, Drake and Ridoc cornered me to ask if the rumors were true—if Nott really lets me shag Malfoy."
She chuckled, the memory of their audacity more amusing than offensive. "I told them yes, because they’d find out eventually anyway. Then Drake had the stones to ask if that meant I was 'open' to others.

I told him he must have taken a spill off a Hippogriff as a child if he thought I’d ever trade down that far."
She took a slow, satisfied sip of wine, remembering the way the blood had drained from the boy’s face. He’d stay away, but she’d already noted the flash of wounded pride in his eyes. He was a variable she’d have to watch once they were handed live wands.

The thought hit Theo like a Stunner to the chest.

His hand on her thigh went rigid. For one perfect, suspended moment, his composure cracked—jaw tightening, breath catching almost imperceptibly. The bond flooded with a surge of heat he didn't bother to contain.

*Menace.*

The word carried a promise. A threat. Both.

He forced his hand to relax, resuming that slow, maddening circuit along her thigh—but higher now, fingers brushing the hem of her dress with deliberate intent. His expression remained neutral to anyone watching. Inside, he was already calculating exactly how long this dinner needed to last before he could verify her claim personally.

Across the table, Draco had gone very still.

He wasn't privy to the bond, couldn't hear what had passed between them—but he could *see*. The slight tension in Theo's shoulders. The particular quality of Jackie's smile. The way she'd leaned into something invisible, some private current that excluded him by nature.

His fingers tightened on his wineglass. He looked away, focusing on the menu with excessive attention, and tapped his own selections: the bone marrow appetizer, the venison with blackcurrant reduction.

"Drake Lightwood." Draco's voice was carefully even—too even. The aristocratic mask settling into place. "I know that family. His father sits on the Hogwarts Board of Governors. Minor wealth, major ambition." A pause. "The boy's an idiot if he thought that approach would work on you."

"He's seventeen," Theo said, his thumb tracing a slow line along Jackie's inner thigh. "They're all idiots at seventeen."

"*You* weren't."

"I was a different kind of idiot." Theo's pale eyes cut to Draco, something sharp flickering in their depths. "The kind that thought rivalry was the same thing as honesty."

The words landed heavier than they should have. Draco's jaw tightened—ring-twist territory, though his hands stayed visible on the table.

A server appeared with their first course: delicate amuse-bouches arranged on slate, each one a miniature work of art. She set them down with practiced silence and vanished.

Jackie rolled her eyes, letting out an audible groan that vibrated with a mix of genuine exasperation and playful defiance.
"Can we please not turn our date into a strategy session for surviving a handful of seventeen-year-old jerks?" she challenged, her voice low but sharp enough to cut through their tactical brooding. "I promise I’m a big girl and I can handle myself. But if you two feel so inclined to have a planning meeting, then by all means—go ruin your *own* date with it."
There was a deliberate bite to her words, a sharp-edged reminder of the unspoken tension simmering between the two men since Saturday. The suggestion of Theo and Draco on their own date wasn't entirely random, and she let the implication hang in the air for a heartbeat before dismissing it with a laugh.
"Besides, honestly? Drake wouldn't have the first clue what to do with me if he actually got me," she added, her gaze flickering with a predatory amusement. She looked at the boy in her mind—practically a child—and imagined him trying to keep pace with her wicked, well-honed needs. He’d be out of his depth before she even took off her coat.
She turned her attention to the slate of amuse-bouches, her eyes settling on a delicate creation shaped like a miniature Golden Snitch. Its tiny, spun-sugar wings even fluttered weakly against the stone. She didn't eat it. Instead, she shifted her weight, sliding an inch or two toward Draco—slickly escaping the heat of Theo’s hand on her thigh.
She turned to Draco, her expression melting into something open, unguarded, and dangerously seductive. The amber light caught the flecks of blue and green in her eyes as she extended her hand toward him, the tiny, fluttering orb held between her thumb and forefinger.
"Open your mouth, dear," she purred.
Her intent was clear: to place the treat on his tongue, to let him lick the shimmering golden dusting from her skin if he dared. It was an invitation, a redirection of the evening's power from the political to the carnal.
At the same time, without skipping a beat, she fired a thought through the bond, aiming it straight at the center of Theo’s simmering frustration.
*You’d have to find out for yourself, love.*

Draco's brain short-circuited.

The treat dissolved on his tongue—he couldn't have identified the flavor if his life depended on it. Every nerve ending had narrowed to the phantom pressure of her fingertips against his lips, the salt-sweet taste of her skin, the way she'd looked at him like he was something to be *consumed*.

*Good boy.*

The words hit him somewhere below conscious thought. His face flooded with heat—a visible flush climbing his pale throat, staining his cheekbones. His carefully maintained composure shattered like dropped crystal.

"I—that's not—" He stopped. Started again. Failed.

His hand found his wineglass with desperate precision, lifting it to buy time, but the slight tremor in his fingers betrayed him. He took a sip he didn't taste. Set the glass down too carefully.

His gray eyes darted to Theo—looking for what, he didn't know. Rescue. Complicity. Permission to combust.

Theo was watching him with undisguised interest, pale eyes sharp and hungry. The predator cataloguing prey. His thumb continued its slow, maddening circuit on Jackie's thigh, but his attention had shifted—locked onto Draco's visible unraveling with a satisfaction he didn't bother to mask.

"Breathe, Malfoy." The words were soft. Almost gentle. The undertone was anything but. "You're turning a very interesting color."

Draco's jaw clenched. He looked away—at the floating orb, at the menu, at anything that wasn't the two of them watching him fall apart in a private booth in the middle of Covent Garden.

"That was—" His voice came out rougher than intended. He cleared his throat, tried again. "That was unnecessary."

"Was it?" Jackie's tone carried that particular edge—the one that meant she knew exactly what she was doing and had no intention of stopping.

Theo leaned back slightly, his free hand reaching for his wine. The picture of casual ease, except for the tension visible in his shoulders and the way his grip on Jackie's thigh had tightened.

"She's testing you," he said to Draco, conversational. "You know that."

"I'm aware."

"And yet." Theo's mouth curved. "Here you are. Blushing like a fourth-year who just got his first love note."

Draco's eyes snapped to him, gray and sharp. The flush hadn't faded—if anything, it had deepened—but something harder surfaced beneath the embarrassment. "At least I didn't go rigid like someone hit me with a Petrificus."

Theo stilled.

The air between them thickened. Charged. Draco had seen it—of course he had. He'd been watching them since they sat down, cataloguing every flicker of the bond he couldn't access, every private exchange that excluded him by design.

"Interesting," Theo said slowly. His voice had dropped, lost its teasing edge. "You were paying attention."

"I'm always paying attention." Draco's composure was reassembling itself, brick by careful brick. The aristocratic mask sliding back into place. But his eyes—his eyes stayed fixed on Theo with an intensity that had nothing to do with rivalry. "You're not as subtle as you think you are."

The jazz curled around them, saxophone sliding into something slower. More intimate.

Theo's thumb stilled on Jackie's thigh. His gaze held Draco's across the table—across *her*—and something unspoken crackled in the space between them.

"No," he said finally, quietly. "I suppose I'm not."

Jackie rolled her eyes, letting out an audible groan that vibrated with a mix of genuine exasperation and playful defiance.

"Can we please not turn our date into a strategy session for surviving a handful of seventeen-year-old jerks?" she challenged, her voice low but sharp enough to cut through their tactical brooding. "I promise I’m a big girl and I can handle myself. But if you two feel so inclined to have a planning meeting, then by all means—go ruin your own date with it."

There was a deliberate bite to her words, a sharp-edged reminder of the unspoken tension simmering between the two men since Saturday. The suggestion of Theo and Draco on their own date wasn't entirely random, and she let the implication hang in the air for a heartbeat before dismissing it with a laugh.

"Besides, honestly? Drake wouldn't have the first clue what to do with me if he actually got me," she added, her gaze flickering with a predatory amusement. She looked at the boy in her mind—practically a child—and imagined him trying to keep pace with her wicked, well-honed needs. He’d be out of his depth before she even took off her coat.

She turned her attention to the slate of amuse-bouches, her eyes settling on a delicate creation shaped like a miniature Golden Snitch. Its tiny, spun-sugar wings even fluttered weakly against the stone. She didn't eat it. Instead, she shifted her weight, sliding an inch or two toward Draco—slickly escaping the heat of Theo’s hand on her thigh.

She turned to Draco, her expression melting into something open, unguarded, and dangerously seductive. The amber light caught the flecks of blue and green in her eyes as she extended her hand toward him, the tiny, fluttering orb held between her thumb and forefinger.

"Open your mouth, dear," she purred.

Her intent was clear: to place the treat on his tongue, to let him lick the shimmering golden dusting from her skin if he dared. It was an invitation, a redirection of the evening's power from the political to the carnal.

At the same time, without skipping a beat, she fired a thought through the bond, aiming it straight at the center of Theo’s simmering frustration.

You’d have to find out for yourself, love.

Theo felt the loss of her thigh beneath his palm like a minor amputation.

His eyes tracked her movement toward Draco with predatory stillness—not jealousy, not exactly. Something closer to anticipation. The bond carried her teasing reply, and his jaw tightened with the effort of not reacting visibly.

*Careful, Menace. I will.*

He leaned back against the velvet booth, one arm draped along the back, watching the scene unfold with hooded eyes. The amber light caught the sharp planes of his face, the faint curve of his mouth that wasn't quite a smile.

Draco had frozen.

The tiny Snitch hovered between Jackie's fingers, its sugar wings catching the light, and Draco stared at it like she'd just offered him a live Blast-Ended Skrewt. His composure cracked—visibly, beautifully—a flush creeping up his neck as his gray eyes darted from her fingers to her face.

"That's—" His voice came out rougher than intended. He cleared his throat. "We're in *public*."

"Private room," Theo said mildly. "Warded. You confirmed it yourself."

Draco shot him a look that could have curdled milk. His fingers had found his wineglass again, gripping it like an anchor—but he wasn't drinking. His attention kept sliding back to Jackie's outstretched hand, the golden dust shimmering on her skin.

The silence stretched. The jazz crooned.

Then Draco exhaled—a controlled, deliberate breath—and leaned forward.

His lips parted.

He took the Snitch from her fingers with careful precision, his tongue brushing the pad of her thumb as he did. The contact was brief, electric. His eyes stayed locked on hers the entire time, gray and storm-dark and *furious* at himself for wanting this.

He sat back, chewing slowly, swallowing. A faint tremor in his hand as he reached for his wine.

"There." His voice was rough, barely controlled. "Satisfied?"

Theo watched the whole thing with an expression of studied neutrality that fooled no one. Heat coiled low in his stomach. Through the bond, he felt Jackie's satisfaction—the thrill of having pushed Draco past his careful boundaries, the pleasure of watching him yield.

The words landed like a physical blow.

Draco's entire body went rigid. His breath caught—audible in the velvet quiet of the private room—and something raw flickered across his features before he could suppress it. Not anger. Not embarrassment.

*Want.*

The flush that had been creeping up his neck flooded his cheeks. His pupils dilated, gray irises shrinking to thin rings around expanding black. His mouth opened, closed. No sound came out.

His fingers had gone white-knuckled on the edge of the table.

"I—" His voice cracked. He swallowed hard, tried again. "That's not—"

Nothing. He had nothing. The careful architecture of his composure had crumbled in two words, and he sat there in the wreckage, exposed and furious about it and *aching* in a way he couldn't hide.

Theo watched with the stillness of a predator scenting blood.

*Well.* The thought slid through the bond, rich with dark satisfaction. *That's interesting.*

He'd suspected. After Italy—after the night in his bedroom, after the way Draco had yielded under his hands—he'd known there was something there. Something Draco couldn't name and wouldn't admit. But *this*. This was confirmation. This was Draco Malfoy, heir to one of the oldest pureblood families in Britain, coming undone at being called *good boy* in a restaurant booth.

Theo filed it away like a weapon.

"Breathe, Malfoy." His voice was low, almost gentle—which made it worse. "You look like you're about to pass out."

Draco's jaw clenched so hard Theo heard his teeth grind. He reached for his wineglass with a hand that trembled slightly, took a long swallow, set it down with excessive care.

"I'm fine." The words came out clipped, formal—his aristocratic mask slamming back into place through sheer force of will. But his eyes, when they cut to Jackie, still held that desperate, hungry edge. "That was... unexpected."

*Unexpected.* As if she'd merely surprised him with an unusual appetizer choice.

She hadn't made the slightest attempt to try and hide the grin that split her face in two. Internally, the heat exploded, weaving along her core, from her chest down in waves. *He's so fucking hot when he blushes.*  
The thought wasn't aimed at Theo, but she didn't try to hide it from him in any way either. Draco really *was* hot when flustered, and making him so was Jackie's prime entertainment. She knew Theo noticed — he noticed everything — and knew from the bond that it had a similar effect on him as on her. She yielded, finally taking her eyes away from Draco's blush and pouring herself more wine. "France." She said, acknowledging the change of subject. "We'll be there for a week before the Luminary. Grandmere made it clear in her invitation that she hadn't seen me for so long that she wanted more than one evening. She's a busy witch, so it's possible we won't even get a chance to talk during the event itself. Me and Samaya will also sign the documents at some point, since that's the main point of the visit. We can treat it like a vacation, another Tuscany almost."  
She smiled, picking up another Golden Snitch, looking briefly at Draco with a look that said 'Want seconds?' but then she just popped it in her mouth and chewed efficiently. "Château de la Roche-Sanglant, the family estate is… It's bigger than reasonable. We'll probably get our own wing, for sure a servant… Oh, yeah. Lavignes do not own house-elves. They have actual servants."  
For some reason she blushed. She realized, more and more, that her grandmother really was probably richer than some Queens were. "Anyways, last time I was there I was thirteen so some things might have changed. But more likely than not we'll be left to our own devices for most of the time. We can visit the ravenry, we can go horse-riding or just lounge around."  
She took another sip of wine, and refilled her glass again, noting that she should probably slow down with it a little. "Grandmere is… She's scary when she wants to be, but she's never been like that towards me. But she invited me with both of you. Not Mrs and Ms Nott and Ms Malfoy.

Jaqueline Nott, Theodore Nott and Draco Malfoy."  
She went quiet for a moment, and exactly then the server brought the food, so the quiet extended a little as they all ate for a moment in companionable silence. "Any other questions?"

"A triad," he said flatly. "She's not hiding it. She's *announcing* it."

He turned to Jackie, pale eyes sharp.

"Your grandmother. What does she *want*?"

The question cut through the wine and the warmth and the lingering charge of Draco's earlier undoing. Because old families didn't make statements like this without reason. Power moved in specific ways, and a matriarch positioning her granddaughter's unconventional marriage as something to be *displayed* rather than hidden—

Matrilineal succession. Husbands taking the family name. A grandmother who'd outlasted multiple spouses and didn't flinch at scandal.

"So we're walking into a house run by a woman who collects husbands and answers to no one," he said. His thumb resumed its slow circuit on Jackie's thigh—higher now, testing. "I'm starting to see where you get it."

The quail on his plate had gone cold. He didn't care.

"The matrilineal structure changes things," Draco said quietly. "In Britain, a triad like ours would be seen as... dilution. Two men sharing one woman, neither with a clear claim to legacy." He set down his fork, fingers finding the stem of his wineglass. "But if succession passes through the female line regardless, then we're not rivals. We're—"

"Accessories," Theo finished. His mouth curved, but there was no humor in it. "Decorative additions to the Lavigne heir."

"That's not what I—"

"It's exactly what you meant." Theo's pale eyes cut to Draco, holding him in place. "And you're not wrong. In that system, we don't threaten each other. We both belong to *her*."

The words hung in the amber light, heavier than he'd intended.

*Belong to her.* He'd said it like a fact—like something he'd already accepted, already surrendered to. And maybe he had. The bond pulsed between them, carrying Jackie's complicated tangle of arousal and affection and something deeper, and Theo let himself feel it without resistance.

He'd stopped fighting this particular war a long time ago.

The silence stretched taut as a bowstring.

"That was—" Draco's voice dropped, barely audible. "That was different."

"Was it?"

The question hung in the amber light, weighted with everything they hadn't said.

Theo stirred at the sound of Draco's voice. His hand reached out blindly, finding Draco's knee, squeezing once.

"Practice." The word came out slurred, exhausted. "Communication. Learning each other's limits." His thumb traced a lazy circle on Draco's skin. "You don't start there. You build to it. Slowly."

Draco was quiet for a long moment.

His hand lingered in the air where Jackie had been, fingers curling slowly into his palm before dropping to the sheets. He looked between them—Theo sprawled and spent, Jackie settling against his side like she belonged there, the easy intimacy of their tangled limbs and synchronized breathing.

*Trust.* The word sat heavy in his chest.

He'd spent his entire life learning that trust was a liability. That vulnerability invited pain. That the people closest to you were the ones most capable of destroying you—his father's disappointment, his mother's suffocating love turned to attempted murder, every friendship that had crumbled under the weight of war and survival.

And yet.

He looked at Theo's hand, still reaching toward his knee. At Jackie's eyes, soft and patient despite everything they'd just done.

They'd seen him come apart tonight. Seen him beg. Seen him cry. And instead of using it against him, they'd held him through it. Called him *good*. Called him *perfect*.

"I don't—" His voice came out rough. He cleared his throat. "I don't know how to trust like that. I've never—"

He stopped. Closed his eyes.

When he opened them again, something had settled in his expression. Not resolution, exactly. More like... the first step toward it.

"But I want to try." The words were quiet, deliberate. "With you. Both of you."

He shifted on the bed, moving closer, until he could lie down on Theo's other side. The mattress dipped beneath his weight, and for a moment he simply lay there, staring at the ceiling, hyperaware of the warmth radiating from both bodies beside him.

Then, slowly, his hand found Theo's.

Their fingers interlaced—palm to palm, grip firm.

"Teach me," Draco said softly. "How to let go. How to—"

His voice caught. He turned his head on the pillow, grey eyes finding Theo's pale ones.

"How to be yours."

The silence that followed was absolute. Sacred.

Theo's breath shuddered out of him. His hand tightened on Draco's, and something cracked open in his expression—vulnerability, hope, *want*—that he couldn't hide and didn't try to.

"Okay." The word came out barely audible. "Okay. We will."

His other arm curled around Jackie, pulling her closer against his side, and for a moment the three of them simply lay there—breathing together, heartbeats slowly synchronizing, the weight of everything they'd shared settling into something that felt, impossibly, like peace.

"Tomorrow," Theo murmured, exhaustion finally claiming him. "We'll talk more tomorrow. About France. About... everything."

His eyes drifted closed, his grip on both of them never loosening.

"Stay. Both of you. Just... stay."

Jackie had channeled a week’s worth of boredom into a single, crunching left hook that sent Drake’s tooth skittering across the stone floor, followed by a sweep that snapped his shin like a dry branch. He’d spent the rest of the week glaring at her from across the room, but the "brain-dead bonobo" had finally learned to keep his mouth shut. She met his stares with the cold, level gaze of a predator; she knew if she didn’t assert her dominance now, they’d be nipping at her heels for the next three years. But physical dominance was easy. Samuel Carrow was the hard part. The weight of their last few letters—the things left unsaid between the lines of music recommendations—had become a physical ache. She knew he felt it too. He was dodging her, retreating into that calculated, aggressive shell, and Jackie wasn't about to let him hide. Apparating to the edge of the Carrow estate felt like stepping back in time. The manor rose out of the landscape like a weather-beaten warning, all Gothic turrets and cold, grey stone that seemed to swallow the sunlight. As the heavy iron gates sensed her invitation and groaned open, Jackie started the long trek up the drive, her arms straining under a massive stack of Charms texts and rolled parchments. She’d traded her Ministry combat gear for something that felt more like her, even if the heat was relentless. She wore black denim shorts with intricate ribbons threaded through the side seams and a simple black tank top that showed a sliver of her midriff. Over it, she’d thrown a light, black-and-blue kimono-style shirt that caught the occasional dry breeze. A black velvet choker sat snug against her throat, the small pendant resting just above her collarbone. Most importantly, her wand was strapped firmly to her bare left thigh in a leather holster—a reminder that while she was here as a tutor, she was never truly off-guard. By the time she reached the massive, arched oak doors, a thin trail of sweat was dampening the hair at the nape of her neck. She stood there for a moment, her muscles burning from the weight of the books, looking at the heavy iron knocker.

With both hands occupied and the "monastery" silence of the house pressing in on her, Jackie realized she had a tactical problem. She couldn't exactly knock without dropping seven years worth of Charms notes into the dirt.

She paused at the base of a wide stone staircase, turning back with that particular brand of academic hunger that Jackie would recognize from their shared house.

"My room's upstairs. It's got the best light, and I've already cleared my desk. Well. Mostly cleared. There's a star chart I'm working on but I can move it—" She stopped abruptly, pushing her glasses up with one finger. A flicker of something more careful crossed her face. "Sam's here too, by the way. I told him you were coming."

Jackie had always liked Lyra. Back then, Jackie had her own crowd, but Lyra had caught her eye. She caught everyone’s eye, though usually, it was the wrong kind of attention from the more judgmental pure-blood circles. "Hi Lyra\! Morgana, you've grown like three inches since I last saw you\!" Jackie said, stepping through the threshold. It had been over two years since they’d been face-to-face, a realization that made the passage of time feel uncomfortably swift. Following Lyra through the foyer, Jackie’s moss-and-ice eyes scanned the surroundings. The manor hummed with that heavy, archaic 'old-magic' signature typical of places like Nott Manor, but there were distinct cracks in the gloom. Brightly colored knit hangings and jars of dried wildflowers peeked out from dark alcoves, softening the stern Gothic architecture. It certainly wasn't Samuel’s doing, leaving Lyra as the only suspect for this domestic rebellion. "Yes, I actually still have those rings. Well, not *just* me but..." She trailed off for a second, a fleeting thought of Draco and the Protean project crossing her mind. "They're still functional, though they require a yearly renewal of the enchantment. I tried making it permanent, but maintaining the link at extended distances while balancing Friesky's Algorithm... well, I’m sure you’ve already figured out where the runic stability starts to crumble."
When Lyra mentioned her brother, Jackie offered a dismissive shake of her head, though her pulse spiked at the mention of that east corridor. "Girl, I came here to see you. Your brooding older bro knows where to find us if he wants to trade bass for a knowledge-*base*," she said, chuckling at her own terrible joke. It wasn't the whole truth, but she did genuinely want to help Lyra; she could circle back to the looming storm of Samuel Carrow later.

She let the younger girl lead her toward the stairs, the distant, angry thrum of the guitar vibrating through the soles of her platform sandals. "So," Jackie asked casually, trying to ignore the way the music cut off so abruptly, "how’s Hogwarts post-War and sans-Potter? Is it actually possible to study in the library now that there isn't a life-or-death crisis every Tuesday?"

Lyra let out a laugh that bounced off the stone walls—bright and unguarded in a way that felt distinctly un-Carrow.

"Oh, it's *blissful*." She shifted the stack of notes in her arms, navigating the curved staircase with the ease of someone who'd memorized every uneven step. "I mean, there's still the occasional cursed artifact in the Restricted Section—Madam Pince found a book last term that tried to eat a third-year's fingers—but no Dark Lords. No Carrows running detention." Her voice didn't waver on the surname, though her jaw tightened almost imperceptibly. "The family name still gets whispers, obviously. But I've gotten rather good at pretending I can't hear them."

She paused on the landing, adjusting her grip on the parchments.

"Professor Flitwick's been brilliant about it. Gave me extra practicum hours last year after some Gryffindor sixth-years decided my star charts needed 'corrections.'" The air quotes were audible. "Corrections involving permanent ink and some very creative slurs about Death Eater spawn."

Lyra said it matter-of-factly, without self-pity—just data. Her glasses caught the light from a high, narrow window as she turned down a corridor lined with faded tapestries.

"Sam wanted to come up and—well, you know how he gets. All protective fury and questionable decision-making." A fond exasperation crept into her tone. "I told him hexing children wouldn't help my social standing. He disagreed. Loudly. For about an hour."

She stopped at a door painted a cheerful cornflower blue—completely incongruous with the rest of the manor's dour palette—and nudged it open with her hip.

Lyra's room was exactly what Jackie would have expected: an explosion of warmth in the middle of a stone fortress. Sunlight streamed through tall windows draped with gauzy blue curtains, catching dust motes and making the whole space glow. Star charts papered one entire wall, layered over each other in organized chaos, with handwritten annotations in at least three different colored inks. A massive cork board above her desk was pinned with pressed flowers, Quidditch ticket stubs, and what appeared to be a moving photograph of a younger Samuel with his arm around Lyra's shoulders—both of them laughing at something off-camera.

"Put those anywhere," Lyra said, depositing her half of the stack onto an already cluttered desk. A small house-elf appeared with a sharp *crack*, carrying a silver tea service that looked older than the manor itself.

"Tibby has brought refreshments for Miss Jackie," the elf announced primly, setting the tray on a low table between two overstuffed armchairs. "And Tibby is reminding Young Miss Lyra that Master Samuel has not eaten since yesterday evening and is refusing Tibby's attempts to deliver food."

Lyra sighed. "He's *sulking*, Tibby. He'll eat when he's hungry."

"Master Samuel is always sulking," Tibby muttered, ears flattening. "Tibby is thinking he needs fewer guitars and more vegetables." She vanished with another *crack* before anyone could respond.

The silence that followed was punctuated by a muffled *thump* from somewhere down the corridor. Then another. Then a third, rhythmic—like someone kicking a wall.

Lyra glanced toward the sound, then back at Jackie. She settled into one of the armchairs, tucking her legs beneath her, and wrapped both hands around a teacup painted with tiny moons.

"So." She took a sip, watching Jackie over the rim. "Friesky's Algorithm and runic stability. That's what you want to talk about, is it?"

The question hung in the air—light, but pointed.

"I don't need to know what happened. That's between you and him. But if you're here to help—actually help—then you should probably know that he's terrified." A small, sad smile. "He just shows it by being an arse."

The room was a sanctuary of lived-in warmth, and Jackie felt the tension in her shoulders finally begin to ebb. It was a space that felt earned; she found herself wishing she’d ever had the raw, quiet courage to reclaim her own room at the Taylor estate with such vibrant defiance. "Death-Eater spawn?" Jackie echoed, a small, cynical twist to her lips. "Merlin, that’s dreadfully uncreative. You’d think with all that Gryffindor 'valor,' they’d find a more sophisticated insult." She knew the weight of the name Carrow, even if Alecto and Amycus were only Lyra’s aunt and uncle—in the post-war world, the bloodline itself was a brand that didn't wash off easily. "And yeah, I can imagine Samuel’s wrath," she added, her mind flickering to the lethal, protective grace Samuel brought to a duel. "Probably involved a lot of dark leather and terrifying eye contact."
She went quiet as Tibby delivered the tea—and the unsolicited social commentary. Jackie deposited the heavy stack of notebooks and parchments onto the floor beside the desk with a dull *thud*, then migrated toward the other armchair, shifting a few embroidered cushions to make space for herself. Lyra’s openness made her laugh. It was refreshing, a sharp palate cleanser after months of navigating her two tight-lipped, close-hearted Slytherins. Jackie had always appreciated people who weren’t afraid to say what they were thinking; it was precisely why she’d always felt a kinship with the younger girl. "I forgot I'm speaking to a true Ravenclaw," she said, lifting her teacup. The steam carried the scent of bergamot and something faint and floral. "And here I was thinking that 'being an arse' was simply your brother’s default setting." There was no real bite to the words, though discussing Samuel with his own sister felt like walking a high-wire without a net. "Look, since you’re 'seventeen and not stupid,' I’ll give it to you straight. Yes, I need to talk to him. And yes, if I’d asked him directly, he’d have found some bullshit excuse or a last-minute gig in Albania just to avoid me. But I really *do* want to help you with your studies, Lyra.

Lyra studied her for a long moment—that sharp, analytical gaze that missed nothing—then seemed to reach some internal conclusion. Her shoulders relaxed, and she reached for a massive leather-bound tome from the stack Jackie had brought.

"Alright. Books first, emotional carnage later." She cracked the spine with the reverence of someone greeting an old friend. "But I'm holding you to that promise. He's been insufferable, and I refuse to spend the rest of summer listening to him murder the same twelve notes."

What followed was three hours of genuine academic immersion.

Lyra was *good*—better than Jackie had expected. She grasped the theoretical underpinnings of advanced charm work with an intuitive ease that reminded Jackie of herself at that age, but where Jackie had always favored elegant efficiency, Lyra approached magic like a puzzle box, delighting in the complexity for its own sake. They argued about runic stability matrices, diagrammed Friesky's Algorithm across four sheets of parchment, and got into a spirited debate about whether emotional resonance actually strengthened Protean links or merely destabilized them in interesting ways.

The afternoon light shifted from gold to amber. Tibby appeared twice more—once with sandwiches neither of them touched, once to mutter darkly about "stubborn young masters" before vanishing again. The thumping down the hall had long since stopped, replaced by an oppressive silence that pressed against the edges of their conversation like a held breath.

By the time Jackie finally set down her quill, her fingers were cramped and her mind pleasantly exhausted in that specific way only deep magical theory could achieve.

Lyra stretched, her spine cracking audibly, and glanced toward the window. The sun was lower now, casting long shadows across her star charts.

"He hasn't come out once," she said quietly. Not accusatory—just observational. "Usually he at least pretends to need something from the kitchen when we have guests. Stalks past the door a few times, makes his presence known." She pulled the quill from her bun, letting her hair tumble loose around her shoulders. "The fact that he hasn't means he knows exactly why you're here. And he's running out of places to hide."

She stood, gathering the empty teacups onto the tray with practiced efficiency.

"East corridor. End of the hall. The door with the scorch marks." A pause. "If he's awful to you—and he probably will be, because that's what he does when he's scared—just... remember that he wasn't always like this. Before the war, before our aunt and uncle made the name Carrow synonymous with torture, he was actually..." She trailed off, something soft and sad flickering across her face. "He was kind. Still is, underneath all the leather and the sneering. He just forgot how to show it without feeling like he's handing someone a weapon."

Lyra moved toward the door, then hesitated with her hand on the frame.

"For what it's worth? I've never seen him write letters he doesn't send. Not to anyone." She didn't look back. "I'll be in the library if you need me. Third door on the left, past the portrait of Great-Aunt Morgause. She'll try to insult your bloodline—just ignore her."

And then she was gone, her footsteps fading down the corridor, leaving Jackie alone with the dying light and the heavy silence of the east wing.

The walk to Samuel's door felt longer than it should have.

The east corridor was darker than the rest of the manor—fewer windows, older stone, the kind of oppressive quiet that seemed to swallow sound. Jackie's footsteps echoed despite herself. The portraits here were older too, their subjects watching her passage with cold, assessing eyes. Pure-blood ancestors with sharp cheekbones and sharper judgments.

The scorch marks were impossible to miss.

Just that thick, waiting silence.

Jackie raised her hand to knock—

The door swung open before her knuckles made contact.

Samuel Carrow stood in the threshold, and he looked like hell.

His dark hair was unwashed, hanging in lank waves around a face that hadn't seen a razor in days. The sharp lines of his jaw were shadowed with stubble, and the circles under his eyes suggested he'd been sleeping about as well as he'd been eating. He was wearing a faded black t-shirt—some Muggle band logo too cracked to read—and grey joggers that hung low on his hips. His feet were bare. No leather. No silver chains. No armor.

For a moment, something raw flickered across his face—surprise, maybe, or something closer to pain—before the mask slammed down.

"Lyra's room is back that way." His voice was rough. Unused. He jerked his chin toward the corridor behind her, already moving to close the door. "You must've gotten lost."

Samuel's jaw tightened. The flicker of something vulnerable vanished beneath a sneer that didn't quite reach his eyes.

"Charming as ever, Taylor." He leaned against the doorframe, arms crossing over his chest in a gesture that might have read as casual if his knuckles weren't white. "Did you practice that one on the walk over, or does the wit just flow naturally when you're slumming it with Death Eater spawn?"

The words were sharp, deliberate—a jab designed to create distance. But his gaze kept snagging on her face, dropping to the choker at her throat, the wand strapped to her thigh, before jerking back up like he'd been caught doing something shameful.

Behind him, the room was chaos. Silver chains draped over a chair. Crumpled parchment littering the floor—letters, maybe, covered in crossed-out lines. His guitar lay on the unmade bed, strings loose like he'd been restringing it and given up halfway through.

"Lyra doesn't need a tutor." He shifted his weight, blocking more of the doorway. "She's smarter than half the professors at that school. So whatever bullshit excuse you used to get through the wards—"

He stopped. Swallowed.

His throat worked visibly, and for a moment the mask cracked again—just a fracture, just enough to show the exhaustion beneath.

"Why are you *here*, Jackie?"

Not *Lavigne*. Not *Taylor*. Her actual name, stripped of titles and distance, and it sounded like it cost him something to say it.

The late afternoon light caught the hollows under his cheekbones, the tension in his shoulders. He looked like a man bracing for a blow he'd been expecting for months.

"Because I know you didn't Apparate out to the middle of nowhere just to talk about Friesky's fucking Algorithm." His voice dropped, rougher now. "And I know you've been dodging me since Florence. So either say what you came to say or leave me alone."

His hand moved to the door's edge. Ready to slam it shut.

But he didn't.

He stood there, vibrating with barely contained *something*—anger, fear, want, all of it tangled together—and waited for her to make the next move.

The jab hit home, a sharp sting of familiar guilt, but Jackie didn't let it show. She merely absorbed it, letting the hurt settle into the stone floor beneath her sandals. She was done being polite; civil discourse was for Ministry tea rooms and the delicate dance she performed with Draco and Theo. With Samuel, the only way through was to match his jagged edges.
"You and those Gryffindors who slurred Lyra should really look into a creative writing class together," she said, her voice dropping the pretense of warmth. "The 'Death Eater' angle is growing older by the day. It’s boring, Sam. And you’re many things, but you’ve never been boring."
She knew bringing up his sister’s struggle was a low blow—a tactical strike at the one part of him that wasn't calloused—but she took it anyway. She needed him off-balance.
"And don't act like the dodging hasn't been mutual," she continued, her gaze finally locking onto his, refusing to let him retreat behind the stubble and the lank hair. "I had to use Lyra to get through the wards because I knew it was the only way you wouldn't just vanish into the shadows of this monastery the second you saw me coming."
She took a small, deliberate step forward, encroaching on the threshold he was guarding. The smell of his room—stale smoke, metallic ozone, and the scent of a man who’d been living in his own head for too long—hit her full force.
"Look. We both know we need to talk. I’m not leaving until we do. So, I can stay here and have this conversation in the hallway, I can shout it through the wood after you slam the door, or you can move those bare feet and let me in." She tilted her head, her moss-and-ice eyes challenging him. "It’s your choice, really. Which version of this mess do you want to deal with?"

The mention of Lyra hit exactly where Jackie intended.

Samuel's expression flickered—a crack in the armor, quickly plastered over with fresh hostility. His shoulders went rigid, that protective fury Lyra had described surfacing for just a heartbeat before he strangled it back down.

"Don't." The word came out low. Dangerous. "Don't you fucking *dare* use her to—"

He stopped himself. His jaw worked, grinding something back that wanted to escape.

For a long moment he just stood there, blocking the doorway, every line of his body screaming *fight or flight*. The afternoon light caught the tension cording through his forearms, the white-knuckle grip on the door's edge. He looked like a man deciding whether to throw a punch or bolt through the nearest window.

Then something in him collapsed.

Not dramatically—just a quiet surrender, a subtle loosening of the shoulders that spoke to exhaustion deeper than missed sleep. He stepped back from the threshold, turning away from her without a word, and stalked into the chaos of his room.

"Fine." He didn't look at her. "Say what you came to say. Then leave."

The room was worse up close.

Parchment everywhere—crumpled, torn, some of it scorched at the edges. Jackie could make out fragments of handwriting on the nearest piece: *I know I have no right to—* before the words dissolved into aggressive cross-outs. His guitar lay abandoned on the tangled sheets, one string snapped and curling. Empty firewhiskey bottles lined the windowsill like a sad little army. The walls were papered with "Second Sons" posters, but several had been ripped down, leaving pale rectangles on the dark paneling.

Samuel dropped onto the edge of his bed, elbows on his knees, head hanging forward. The posture stripped away the frontman swagger entirely. He looked smaller like this. Younger.

"You want to know why I've been avoiding you?" He laughed—a harsh, brittle sound. "Because I'm not a fucking idiot, Jackie. I know what this is." He gestured vaguely between them without looking up. "You figured it out. Or Nott told you. Or Draco—*fuck*, probably both of them, right? Comparing notes about poor pathetic Carrow and his sad little crush?"

"So here's your answer, since you came all this way." He finally lifted his head. His green eyes were bloodshot, red-rimmed, but steady. Defiant. "Yes. I wanted you at my shows when you'd dance in the crowd and I couldn't look anywhere else. I want you right now, standing there in those ridiculous shorts with your wand strapped to your thigh like some kind of—"

He cut himself off. Dragged both hands down his face.

"But I'm not stupid enough to think it matters." The words came out muffled through his palms. "You've got your Slytherin princes. Your perfect little arrangement. And I'm—" Another broken laugh. "I'm the bloke who writes letters he never sends and plays the same four chords until his fingers bleed because it's easier than admitting I've already lost."

He dropped his hands. Looked at her directly, something raw and terrible in his expression.

"So there. You got your confession. Happy now?"

The silence that followed her demand stretched like a held breath.

Samuel didn't move. Didn't blink. For three long seconds, he just stood there, backlit by the dying afternoon sun, his jaw working like he was chewing on glass.

Then he laughed.

It wasn't his usual laugh—that sharp, sardonic bark he deployed like a weapon. This was something uglier, rawer, a sound scraped up from somewhere he didn't let people see.

"Tell you I don't care." He pushed off the windowsill, taking a single step toward her. "That's what you want? A nice, clean denial so you can trot back to your husband and your *boyfriend* with a clear conscience?"

The word *boyfriend* came out like a slur. His lip curled, and for a moment the Slytherin cruelty he usually kept leashed flickered across his features.

"Nott." He said the name like it burned. "Right. *Nott*. Because you're married to Theodore fucking Nott, who looks at you like you hung the moon, and you're shagging Draco bloody Malfoy, who'd probably let you carve your initials into his chest if you asked nicely." Another step closer. "And I'm supposed to—what? Pretend I don't notice? Pretend it doesn't make me want to put my fist through a wall every time I see you together?"

His hand came up, raking through his unwashed hair—that rare tell, the one only Lyra and Jackie could read. Stress. Fracture. The mask slipping.

"You want me to tell you it's fine? That we're *just friends*?" He stopped, barely two feet away, close enough that she could see the exhaustion carved into the hollows beneath his eyes. "I've been telling myself that for eight fucking months, Jackie. Eight months of watching you smile at him—at *them*—and pretending I don't feel like someone's scooped out my chest with a rusted spoon."

He stopped. His shoulders were shaking—not crying, not Samuel Carrow, but something close. Something that looked like rage and grief and terror all tangled together.

"I didn't ask for this." He turned back, and his green eyes were bright with something dangerous. "I didn't *want* this. You were supposed to be a friend, Jackie. Someone I could actually talk to without calculating the angle. Someone who didn't want anything from me except—"

His voice broke again.

"Except to be myself. And then you had to go and be *you*—brilliant and sharp and absolutely fucking untouchable—and now I can't—"

He made a sound that wasn't quite a word. Frustration. Defeat.

"I can't tell you I don't care." The admission came out quiet, stripped of all his usual venom. "I've tried. Believe me, I've *tried*. I've written it down a hundred times—" He gestured violently at the crumpled parchment littering the floor. "—and I can't make the words true."

He was close enough now that she could smell the stale smoke on his clothes, the faint metallic tang of ozone from whatever magic he'd been hurling at the walls. His hands hung at his sides, fingers curling and uncurling like he didn't know what to do with them.

"So there it is." His voice was hollow. "The thing Theo wanted you to realize. The thing I've been hiding like a coward for almost a year. I'm in love with you, Jackie. Completely, pathetically, *impossibly* in love with you."

He laughed again—that same ugly, broken sound.

"And I know it doesn't matter. I know you didn't come here for *that*. I know you're married and happy and you've got two men who'd burn the world down for you." His jaw tightened. "But you asked. So there's your answer."

He stepped back. Put distance between them. His arms crossed over his chest again, but the gesture looked less like armor now and more like he was trying to hold himself together.

"Go ahead." The words came out rough, resigned. "Tell me I'm a selfish prick. Tell me I ruined everything. I know I did."

He wouldn't look at her.

"I know I did."

Jackie didn’t cry. She didn’t even shout—not at first. She simply stood in the center of the wreckage he’d made of his life and shook, her entire body vibrating with a violent, jagged energy. She clenched her hands into fists, her nails digging into her palms, wanting—needing—the bite of **pain** to keep her grounded as she felt herself start to drown. She watched him, transfixed, unable to move even as his words tore ragged holes through her chest.
Somewhere miles away, likely in Draco’s flat, she knew Theo could feel the spill of her emotions—muffled by the distance of the soul tether, but impossible to ignore. She couldn't have stopped the bleed even if she tried.
"That’s what the song was…" she said, her voice a hollow, weak thing. "And I danced to it with Draco. I *thanked* you for it. God, I couldn’t be any more fucking blind." She exhaled a shaky breath, pressing the heel of her hand against her eyes for a second. They stung, but she refused to let the heat turn into anything more.
When she looked at him again, the grief was gone, replaced by an inferno of sudden, searing anger.
"Yes. You *are* a selfish prick. You’re a fucking arse. You’re a motherfucking entitled snob\!" She bridged the gap between them in two steps, her eyes pinning him in place, her head tilted back to meet his gaze because he was so much taller than her.
"You idiot!" She swung her fist, striking him in the chest. It wasn’t the calculated, tactical blow of an Auror-in-training; it was a desperate, pathetic push against his heart. "You absolute idiot!" Another punch landed against his collarbone. "You moron! I—should—kill you! You—destroyed—everything!"
Each word was punctuated by the impact of her knuckles against him. The blows were strong and forceful at first, born of pure rage, but they quickly began to slow as the weight of it all settled on her. Finally, she stilled completely, her breaths coming in ragged, shallow gasps. She stayed there, both fists resting against his sternum, her eyes fixed on the cracked logo of his shirt.

Samuel didn't move.

He took every blow like penance—stood there with his arms at his sides while her fists connected with his chest, his collarbone, the hollow where his heart hammered against his ribs. He didn't flinch. Didn't try to catch her wrists or deflect the strikes. Just absorbed them, his jaw tight, his breathing ragged, watching her with those desperate green eyes as she fell apart against him.

When she finally stilled, her fists pressed flat against his sternum, he stayed frozen. Like moving would shatter something. Like breathing too hard might break whatever fragile equilibrium they'd stumbled into.

The silence stretched. Dust motes drifted through the amber light. Somewhere in the manor, a clock chimed the hour—distant, irrelevant.

"Yeah." His voice came out wrecked, barely above a whisper. "I know."

His hand twitched at his side. He wanted to touch her—she could see it in the aborted movement, the way his fingers curled and then forced themselves flat again. But he didn't. He kept his arms down, kept that careful distance even with her fists still resting against his chest.

"The song was—" He stopped. Swallowed. "I wrote it the night you came back from Florence. After Theo told me you'd almost died in that fucking dueling ring. After I spent six hours thinking you might already be dead and I'd never—"

His voice cracked. He looked away, jaw working.

"I didn't mean for you to dance to it with him. I didn't mean for you to *thank* me for it." A bitter, broken laugh. "I just needed to get it out. Put it somewhere that wasn't inside my chest, eating me alive."

He finally looked back at her. This close, she could see the exhaustion carved into every line of his face, the way his eyes were red-rimmed and raw. The stubble on his jaw caught the light, making him look older, rougher, nothing like the polished predator who commanded stages in Knockturn Alley.

"I tried to make it stop." The words came out quiet, almost pleading. "I tried—I took home a different person every night for two weeks after you left for France. Trying to burn it out of me. Trying to remember what it felt like to not give a shit." His throat bobbed. "It didn't work. None of them were you."

His hand came up—finally, slowly—and hovered near her shoulder without quite touching. Like he was waiting for permission. Like he expected her to flinch away.

"I know I destroyed everything." His voice dropped even lower, rough with something that might have been grief. "I know you came here hoping I'd tell you it was all in Theo's head. That we could go back to being friends who didn't *care*." His fingers trembled, still hovering. "But I can't lie to you, Jackie. Not to you. You're the only person besides Lyra who's ever seen me without the—"

He gestured vaguely at himself. The absent leather. The missing chains. The armor he'd stripped away or simply stopped maintaining.

"—without all this. And I couldn't keep pretending. Not when you were standing right there, asking me to tell you the truth."

His hand finally dropped, falling back to his side.

"So hate me." The words came out flat, resigned. "Hex me. Walk out that door and never speak to me again. I'll deserve all of it." His green eyes held hers, steady despite the devastation in them. "But don't ask me to say I don't love you. I've spent eight months choking on that lie, and I can't—"

His voice broke completely.

"I can't do it anymore."

He stood there, chest still warm where her fists rested against him, and waited. For the hex. For the slap. For the door slamming behind her as she left.

For whatever punishment she decided he deserved.

"Yeah." His voice came out scraped raw. "The song."

*Between the Lines.* He'd played it that night in March, in the smoky basement of The Crimson Flask in Knockturn Alley. Jackie had been there with Anne and Caroline. Draco had been there too—hovering at the edges, watching her from across the room while Samuel poured four months of suppressed longing into every chord.

And she'd danced.

She'd danced with Draco while Samuel sang about loving someone he couldn't have, and he'd watched them move together, and he'd kept playing because stopping would've been admitting defeat.

"I wrote it in January." His chest rose and fell beneath her fists. "After the Snake Soirée. After you dueled me and I gave you that scar—" His eyes flickered to the faint line on her cheek. "—and I realized I wasn't angry that you'd beaten me. I was angry because you looked at *him* afterward. Not me."

His hand moved—slowly, carefully—and covered both of hers where they rested against his heart. His palm was warm, calloused from guitar strings, and his fingers trembled almost imperceptibly.

"I know I destroyed everything." The words were quiet, defeated. "I know you came here hoping I'd lie to your face so you could go back to your life and pretend this never happened. And I tried, Jackie. I *tried* to give you that. But I couldn't—"

His voice cracked.

His hand over hers sent a sudden, unwanted shot of arousal through her. She could lie about it to Samuel, or even to Draco, but she’d never be able to hide it from Theo; the bond was too honest for that. She wasn’t blind—she’d always known he was handsome. During those long months when Draco was out of the picture and she and Theo were traveling the world, she’d even entertained the fleeting thought of inviting Samuel into their bedroom. A curiosity. A bit of fun to see if she actually had a taste for a threesome. But that had been a physical itch, nothing more. Her heart was already a crowded house; between Draco and Theo, there simply wasn't room for another tenant. No need for that kind of love. She stayed still, letting him have that brief, heavy contact as she listened to the jagged pieces of his truth. The inferno of her anger finally began to ebb, leaving behind something hollow and aching in its wake. She genuinely liked him. She believed he deserved to matter to someone—to be someone’s entire world—but it was a role she simply couldn't cast herself in. Even before the question of *what now* left his lips, a plan had already solidified in her mind. It was a small, painful realization of what she *could* offer. It wasn't the love he wanted, but it was a start. Beneath the sneer and the sarcasm, she recognized the grey, heavy sludge of depression. She knew that particular flavor of despair far too well. She remembered being in that dark place, knowing that if Draco had walked through her door back then, she would have done anything he asked just to feel alive again. Jackie exhaled, her sharp features finally softening into something resembling mercy. "Now," she began, her voice gaining a firm, grounded edge, "you are going to take a shower and shave. Unless this really *is* your new stage persona, in which case... you’re still going to shower and shave, because you look uglier than a troll with a case of the runs." She managed a small, tired smile and crossed her arms over her chest. "Then, we’re going to find Lyra. We’ll eat dinner and play Exploding Snap, or chess, or fucking hide-and-seek—I don't care which.

And after that, I’m sending a Patronus to my... to Theo. I’m telling him I’m staying the night."
She looked at him, her heterochromatic eyes bright with resolve. "And then you’re going to fix that poor creature," she added, nodding toward the abandoned guitar on the bed. "We’re going to talk, and you’re going to work on that gods-awful chord progression until it actually sounds like music. But first? The shower." She pointed a commanding finger toward the door of the en-suite bathroom.

Samuel stared at her.

For a long, suspended moment, he didn't move. Didn't breathe. His expression cycled through confusion, disbelief, and something that looked almost like fear—the wariness of a man being offered something he didn't trust himself to accept.

"You're..." He blinked. Shook his head slightly, as if trying to clear water from his ears. "You're *staying*?"

The word came out fractured. Wrong. Like he'd expected her to Apparate out the moment he finished his pathetic confession, leaving him alone with the wreckage of his dignity and a half-restrung guitar.

"I just told you I'm in love with you." His voice was flat, almost accusatory. "I told you I've been pining like a lovesick fifth-year for eight months. And your response is to... insult my hygiene and demand family game night?"

But something was shifting behind his eyes. The defensive sneer he'd been wearing like armor started to slip, revealing the exhausted man beneath. His gaze dropped to her pointed finger, then tracked toward the bathroom door, then back to her face.

"You're mental." The words held no heat. "Completely, certifiably mental."

He pushed off the window frame. Took one step toward the bathroom. Stopped.

"This doesn't fix anything." His back was to her now, shoulders rigid. "You know that, right? I'm not going to wake up tomorrow magically over you just because we played Exploding Snap and you watched me butcher chord progressions."

His hand found the bathroom doorframe, fingers curling around the wood.

"And Theo's going to know." A bitter edge crept into his voice. "The second you send that Patronus, he's going to know you're spending the night in the house of a man who just confessed his undying bloody love for you. He'll probably Apparate here himself just to punch me in the face."

He turned his head—just enough to catch her in his peripheral vision. The late afternoon light caught the hollows of his cheekbones, the dark circles beneath his eyes.

"Why?" The question was barely audible. "Why would you do this? You could walk out right now and never speak to me again. That's what I expected. That's what I *deserved*. So why are you..."

He couldn't finish the sentence.

His hand tightened on the doorframe until his knuckles went white. Somewhere in the distance, Lyra's voice drifted up from the lower floors—she was talking to Tibby about dinner preparations, oblivious to the emotional carnage happening in her brother's room.

"I don't understand you." Samuel's voice was rough. "I've never understood you. You should hate me right now. You should be furious that I made everything complicated when you've finally got your life sorted. Instead you're..."

He gestured vaguely at her, at the room, at the entire impossible situation.

"You're telling me to *shower*."

A sound escaped him—not quite a laugh, not quite a sob. Something broken and bewildered that he couldn't quite suppress.

"Fine." He straightened, squaring his shoulders like a man walking toward his own execution. "Fine. I'll shower. I'll shave. I'll come downstairs and pretend I didn't just eviscerate myself in front of the only woman I've ever—"

He stopped. Swallowed hard.

"Twenty minutes." His voice was steadier now, forcibly controlled. "Don't let Lyra eat all the good biscuits. She hoards them like a dragon."

He disappeared into the bathroom without looking back.

The door clicked shut. A moment later, the sound of running water filtered through the wood—and beneath it, barely audible, something that might have been a muffled curse or a choked breath or simply the sound of a man finally letting himself fall apart in private.

The air in the room was already changing, the heavy, static-filled tension of the confrontation beginning to dissolve into something quieter, though no less complex. Jackie moved toward the bathroom door with a slow, deliberate gait, placing her palm against the cold wood. She let herself imagine him for a heartbeat—stripped of his armor, standing under the spray—before she raised her voice to cut through the white noise of the water. "One, I’m going to take the 'mental' part as a compliment. I prefer 'mental' to 'newbie' any day of the week," she called out, her voice steady. "Two, I’m not expecting to fix your life with a sleepover, Sam. But healing always starts *somewhere*, and besides, Lyra has been enduring your moping long enough to deserve an evening that doesn't involve listening to you bleed out over a guitar. Three, yes—I’ve hated you. I punched you. I got over it. Honestly, I fully expected to go no-contact and cut every string when I came here this morning. Apparently, I’m not very good at cutting; the scissors snagged on the fact that I’d loathe myself for the rest of my days if I left you like this."
She turned away from the door, the heat of the shower radiating through the wood. Stepping into the center of the disaster zone, she drew her wand. With a series of sharp, efficient flicking motions, she set to work. *Scourgify* chased away the scent of stale smoke; a silent Banishing Charm sent the empty Firewhiskey bottles clattering into a bin in the corner. She knew she might piss him off—he probably liked his chaos exactly the way it was—but she couldn't stand the smell of defeat a second longer. He could mess it up again tomorrow once she was gone. Finally, she drew a deep breath, focusing on the memory of her wedding day—the complicated, beautiful mess of it. "Expecto Patronum."
The silver mist exploded from her wand, coalescing into a ginormous, sleek Irish Wolfhound. The phantom dog circled her once, its tail wagging in a slow, ghostly arc, before sitting obediently at her feet. Jackie looked into its glowing eyes and spoke in a low, calm voice. "Theo, I'm staying for the night. Everything’s okay, but he *needs* me.

The parchment was a battlefield.

Ink blots marred the margins where his quill had pressed too hard. Entire sentences were scratched out with violent, diagonal slashes, rendering them illegible. But enough remained—fragments of thought, half-formed confessions—that Jackie could piece together the shape of what he'd been trying to say.

---

*Jackie,*

*I've started this letter fourteen times. ~~Fifteen now, apparently, because I can't even count properly when~~ I keep telling myself I'll get it right eventually, but every version sounds like either a suicide note or a sonnet, and I'm not sure which is worse.*

*~~I need you to know~~*

*~~The thing is~~*

*~~When you left for Florence with them, I~~*

*I heard you're in Italy. With Nott. With Malfoy. All three of you, playing house in some fucking Tuscan villa while I'm here restringing my guitar for the third time this week because I keep snapping the E string and I don't know why.*

*That's a lie. I know why.*

*~~I'm not jealous. That would require me to believe I had any claim on~~*

*I'm jealous. There. I wrote it down. I'm jealous of Theodore Nott, who gets to wake up next to you. I'm jealous of Draco Malfoy, who gets to touch you without it meaning anything complicated. I'm jealous of whatever waiter brings you breakfast in bed, and the shopkeeper who sells you postcards, and the ~~fucking~~ cobblestones you walk on because at least they get to be near you.*

*This is pathetic. I'm aware.*

*~~You should know that I~~*

*Lyra asked me yesterday why I've been "brooding more than usual." I told her I was working on new material. She didn't believe me. She never believes me. She's the only person who knows how to read the silences between my sentences, and lately all my sentences have been silences.*

*~~I wrote you a song. I played it at the Flask in March. You were there. You danced with him while I sang it, and I watched you, and I kept playing because~~*

*I kept playing because stopping would have meant admitting I wrote it for you.*

*~~I don't expect anything. I know you're~~*

*~~What I'm trying to say is~~*

*I don't know what I'm trying to say.*

*No. That's another lie.*

*I'm trying to say that I think about you constantly. That your letters are the only thing I look forward to anymore. That when you sent me that discman from Tokyo with the note about how "even Death Eater spawn deserve good music," I laughed for the first time in weeks and then I sat in my room and held it like a ~~complete fucking~~ idiot because your hands had touched it.*

*I'm trying to say that I've never felt this way about anyone. Not once. I've fucked half of Knockturn Alley and I've never once wanted to stay the night, never once wanted to know what someone looked like when they woke up, never once cared whether they thought about me after.*

*But you—*

*~~I think about you and I can't~~*

*~~When you smile at me, I~~*

*You make me want to be someone worth staying for.*

*And I know I'm not. I know you've already found that in them—in Nott, who would kill for you, and Malfoy, who would die for you. I'm not competing. I couldn't if I tried. They're ~~better~~ more than I'll ever be.*

*But sometimes—*

*Sometimes I let myself imagine what it would be like if you looked at me the way you look at them. Just once. Just long enough for me to memorize it.*

*~~I should burn this~~*

*~~I should send this~~*

*~~I should~~*

*I don't know how to end this letter. Every closing I write sounds like goodbye, and I'm not ready to say goodbye. I'm not sure I'll ever be ready.*

*~~Love,~~*

*~~Yours,~~*

*~~Pathetically,~~*

*S.*

The doorknob began to turn.

*And I know I'm not. I know you've already found that in them—in Nott, who would kill for you, and Malfoy, who would die for you. I'm not competing. I couldn't if I tried. They're ~~better~~ more than I'll ever be.*

*But sometimes—*

*Sometimes I let myself imagine what it would be like if you looked at me the way you look at them. Just once. Just long enough for me to memorize it.*

*~~I should burn this~~*

*~~I should send this~~*

*~~I should~~*

*I don't know how to end this letter. Every closing I write sounds like goodbye, and I'm not ready to say goodbye. I'm not sure I'll ever be ready.*

*~~Love,~~*

*~~Yours,~~*

*~~Pathetically,~~*

*S.*

---

The water shut off.

The sudden silence was deafening. Jackie had perhaps thirty seconds before Samuel emerged—thirty seconds to decide whether to shove the letter back into the bin and pretend she'd never seen it, or face him with the evidence of his own vulnerability still clutched in her hands.

Through the bathroom door, she heard the rustle of a towel. The soft thud of bare feet on tile.

The doorknob began to turn.

The heavy, dull ache in her chest only tightened as she processed those final, scratched-out lines. She *wished* she could simply give him what he so desperately wanted. Maybe it was because she was inherently good, or maybe it was just her penchant for collecting broken, stray Slytherins—one didn’t necessarily exclude the other. But even as the words sank in, the regret she felt was a different breed than the fire she felt for Theo or the steady devotion she had for Draco. It was a profound, quiet sadness for a man who deserved something so much better than the hollow echo of a one-sided heartbreak. The sound of the water cutting off acted like a starting pistol. Jackie moved quickly, crumpling the parchment back into its original shape and tossing it into the bin. He wasn’t ready for her to see those words, and she certainly wasn't ready to defend her snooping in a trash can. She turned toward the center of the room, crossing her arms as the golden afternoon light caught her wavy red hair, setting it ablaze in the cooling shadows of the east wing. A stray thought about pajamas crossed her mind—she’d likely have to borrow something oversized from Lyra—but the thought vanished the moment the bathroom door swung open. "Better—?"
The word died on her tongue. Samuel stepped out, and Jackie’s breath hitched in a way that had nothing to do with magic. He was wearing nothing but a white towel slung dangerously low on his hips, his lean, damp torso still glistening from the heat of the shower. He was vigorously rubbing his dark hair with a second towel, his movements energetic and unconscious, unaware that his audience hadn't left. *Morgana’s tits, he’s fucking hot.*
It caught her completely off guard. It shouldn't have—it was an en-suite, and he likely assumed she’d retreated to Lyra’s room after her last speech. But seeing him like this—shaved, clean, and stripped of his leather armor—was a physical blow. She stood there, gaping like a complete idiot, her brain momentarily short-circuiting as she objectified her friend with the intensity of a starving woman at a feast.

The sharp line of his V-taper, the damp hair clinging to his neck, the raw, athletic grace he usually hid under layers of rebellion—it was all right there.

Samuel froze mid-motion, the towel still tangled in his hair, water droplets sliding down his chest and catching the dying light. For one suspended heartbeat, they just stared at each other—Jackie rooted to the spot, Samuel half-obscured by terrycloth, both of them caught in a moment neither had anticipated.

Then his green eyes dropped to her face. Tracked the flush creeping up her neck. Registered the way her gaze had snagged somewhere around his hipbones before jerking back up.

Something shifted in his expression.

The vulnerability from before didn't disappear—it was still there, lurking beneath the surface—but a flicker of his old confidence sparked to life. The corner of his mouth twitched. Not quite a smirk, but close.

"See something you like, Taylor?"

The name slipped out automatically—old habit, old armor—but there was no venom in it. Just a dry, self-aware humor that acknowledged the absurdity of the situation. He lowered the towel from his hair, letting the damp strands fall loose around his freshly shaved jaw.

"I assumed you'd gone to find Lyra." He didn't move to cover himself. Didn't reach for a shirt. Just stood there, water still beading on his collarbones, watching her with an expression caught somewhere between amusement and genuine uncertainty. "Didn't realize 'stay and watch me undress' was part of your healing protocol."

But beneath the quip, something raw flickered across his face.

He'd seen the way she looked at him. For just a moment—before her brain caught up with her eyes—she'd looked at him the way she looked at *them*. Want. Appreciation. Heat.

It wasn't love. He knew that. But it was *something*, and Samuel Carrow had spent eight months starving for any scrap of *something* she might throw his way.

His jaw tightened. He turned away, moving toward the wardrobe with deliberate casualness, giving her his back. The muscles there shifted as he reached for a shirt—a clean black t-shirt, soft and faded, nothing like his stage armor.

"For the record." His voice was carefully controlled as he pulled the shirt over his head. "I'm aware of the irony. I just finished telling you I'm hopelessly in love with you, and now you're watching me get dressed like I'm some sort of..." He paused, searching for the word. "...spectacle."

He grabbed a pair of worn grey trousers from a drawer, then glanced over his shoulder. The smirk was back, but it didn't reach his eyes.

"Turn around, would you? Unless you want the full show, in which case—" A bitter laugh. "—I'm not sure what that would accomplish except making both of us feel worse."

He waited, one eyebrow raised, the towel still clinging to his hips.

The room felt smaller than it had before. The air thicker. Whatever fragile equilibrium they'd established with her demands of shower-and-game-night had been disrupted by the simple, inconvenient fact of his body—and her reaction to it.

"Lyra's probably already setting up the chess board," he added, his voice softer now. "She always does when we have guests. Says it's 'civilized entertainment.'" A pause. "Fair warning: she cheats. Uses Arithmancy to calculate probability trees six moves ahead. I've never beaten her."

He was rambling. Filling the silence with words because the alternative was acknowledging what had just passed between them.

"Go on, then." He jerked his chin toward the door. "I'll be down in five. Try not to let her convince you I was a well-behaved child. She lies about that too."
