Francine's gaze lingered on Jackie for a moment—measuring, assessing—before she inclined her head in acknowledgment.

"*Les préparatifs avancent comme prévu*," she replied, her French precise and unhurried. "*Grandmère supervise personnellement les arrangements floraux. Elle est... particulière, comme toujours.*"

A hint of dry amusement flickered across her features. Geneviève's exacting standards were, apparently, a trial even for her own daughter.

"We expect over two hundred guests," Francine continued, switching to English—a courtesy to Theo and Draco, who had taken their seats on either side of Jackie. "Several delegations from the Ministry in Paris, representatives from the old families, a few... interested parties from abroad." Her eyes moved briefly to Theo. "The Notts were once well-regarded in certain French circles. Before."

The *before* hung in the air, unqualified but understood.

Bastien reached for the wine carafe, refilling his glass and then Jackie's without asking. "What my mother means is that half of wizarding France will be watching to see whether the English contingent embarrasses itself. No pressure."

"*Bastien*." Francine's tone held warning.

"What? It's true. Vivienne's been rehearsing her condescending remarks for days." He shot his elder sister a grin that held no affection. "Haven't you, *chérie*?"

Vivienne's smile tightened. "Some of us take family obligations seriously."

"And some of us take ourselves far too seriously." Bastien raised his glass in mock salute. "But please, do continue. I'm sure our cousins are fascinated by your commitment to protocol."

Across the table, Elodie had not looked away from the triad since they'd entered. Her pale fingers traced the rim of her water glass—she alone was not drinking wine—and her voice, when she finally spoke, was soft and strange.

"You rode *Lumière* today," she said to Jackie. It was not a question. "She was happy. I could feel it from my window."

The table fell briefly silent.

"Elodie sees things," Bastien murmured to Theo, sotto voce. "We've stopped asking how."

Draco's hand had found his wine glass, though he hadn't yet drunk. His posture was careful, controlled—the aristocratic mask firmly in place. But his eyes moved between the cousins, reading the currents beneath the surface.

"The stables were impressive," he offered into the silence, his tone polished and diplomatic. "Michel clearly takes great pride in his work."

"Michel has been with us for thirty years," Francine said. "He was devoted to my sister. To Amalthea." Her gaze settled on Jackie again, something unreadable in her expression. "I'm told you helped wash the horses yourself. That's... unexpected, for a guest."

Francine's expression softened by a fraction—the barest thaw in her composed demeanor.

"*Ta mère t'a bien élevée*," she said quietly. Your mother raised you well. The words carried weight, an acknowledgment that seemed to cost her something.

Vivienne, predictably, seized the opening Jackie had left her.

"The protocols are extensive," she said, her tone crisp and faintly condescending. "The Luminary is not a *party*, cousin. It is a presentation. The family will be formally introduced to the assembled guests in order of succession. You will be expected to greet the delegation heads individually, in French, with the appropriate honorifics." Her pale eyes flickered to Theo, then to Draco. "Your... companions... will be introduced as well. Their conduct reflects on the House."

"Vivienne." Francine's voice held a note of warning.

"I am merely being thorough, Maman." Vivienne folded her hands on the table, the picture of wounded innocence. "Our cousin asked. I assumed she wished to be prepared rather than embarrassed."

Bastien snorted into his wine.

"What Vivienne means," he said, "is that you'll need to smile, curtsy to the right people, and avoid hexing anyone before dessert. The bar is astonishingly low, really. Last year, old Monsieur Beaumont got drunk and tried to duel a portrait. You'll be fine."

"*Bastien*." This time it was Vivienne who snapped.

"What? It's true. The man challenged a painting of his own grandfather. Took three servants to calm him down."

Elodie laughed—a strange, silvery sound that seemed to come from somewhere far away. "The painting won," she said dreamily. "It called him a disappointment to the family name. He cried."

Draco's composure cracked, just slightly. His lips pressed together in what might have been suppressed amusement.

"The *point*," Vivienne said, her voice tight with frustration, "is that this is a significant occasion. Grandmère has invited you specifically, Jackie, because you are Amalthea's daughter and because you have... claims... on certain aspects of the inheritance. How you present yourself will determine how the family is perceived."

She let that hang for a moment before adding, with poisonous sweetness: "I trust your *companions* understand the gravity of that responsibility."

Theo had been silent throughout, his expression unreadable. Now he leaned back in his chair, wine glass balanced loosely in his fingers.

"We understand perfectly," he said, his voice smooth and unbothered. "We'll try not to duel any portraits. Though I make no promises if they insult me first."

Bastien barked a laugh. Even Francine's mouth twitched.

Vivienne's smile could have frozen the wine in their glasses.

Bastien caught the glare and raised his hands in mock surrender, mouthing *fine, fine* before reaching for his wine again.

Vivienne's eyes narrowed slightly at Jackie's offer—suspicion and vanity warring visibly across her features. She clearly hadn't expected capitulation. For a moment, she seemed caught off-balance, recalculating.

"*Peut-être*," she allowed finally, her tone cooling from hostile to merely glacial. "If time permits after dinner, I could... review the essentials with you. The receiving line order, the proper forms of address, the dance protocols."

"Dance protocols?" Draco's voice was carefully neutral, but Jackie felt his attention sharpen.

"The Luminary concludes with a formal ball," Francine explained. "The opening dance is traditionally led by the family—Grandmère with the most distinguished male guest, then the succession pairs. Jackie, as Amalthea's heir, would be expected to participate."

"With which of her *companions*?" Vivienne's emphasis dripped with implication.

Francine silenced her with a look. "That is for Jackie to decide. The family will accommodate whatever arrangement she prefers." Her gaze moved between Theo and Draco, assessing. "I trust both gentlemen know how to waltz?"

"Adequately," Theo said dryly.

"More than adequately," Draco corrected, a hint of old pride surfacing. "I was trained by Madame Voclaire herself."

Bastien let out a low whistle. "The Voclaire? From the Vienna conservatory? She's turned down half the pureblood families in Europe."

"She owed my mother a favor." Draco's expression flickered—something complicated moving beneath the surface—before smoothing back into composure.

Elodie, who had been tracing patterns on the tablecloth with her finger, looked up suddenly. Her strange eyes fixed on Draco with unsettling intensity.

"You play music too," she said. It was not a question. "Not just dancing. Something with keys. I can hear it in your hands."

The table fell silent.

Draco's wine glass stopped halfway to his lips.

"*Les mains racontent des histoires*," she said softly. "*Les siennes parlent de touches légères. De gammes répétées jusqu'à ce que les doigts saignent. De musique jouée dans des pièces vides où personne n'écoutait.*"

Hands tell stories. His speak of light touches. Of scales repeated until the fingers bled. Of music played in empty rooms where no one listened.

The table had gone very still.

Draco's face had drained of color. His fingers curled slowly inward, as though trying to hide the evidence of whatever Elodie had seen.

"*Élodie*," Francine said quietly, a note of warning in her voice.

But the girl continued, her tone dreamy and distant, as though reciting something she was reading from very far away. "He stopped playing when the dark came. When the mark burned. The music went somewhere deep, where it couldn't be touched." Her eyes lifted to Draco's face, and there was something almost gentle in her expression. "But it's still there. Waiting. It wants to come back."

Vivienne shifted uncomfortably in her seat. Even Bastien had lost his easy grin.

"My sister has... gifts," Francine said carefully, addressing Theo and Draco. "She sees things that others do not. It is not always comfortable, but she means no harm."

Elodie smiled—a strange, sweet expression that didn't quite reach her eyes. "There's a piano in the drawing room," she said to Draco, as though the previous moment hadn't happened. "A Pleyel. Very old. Very lovely. It misses being played properly."

She picked up her water glass and drank, apparently finished with the revelation.

The silence stretched.

You hated it then." A pause. Her eyes unfocused further. "You don't hate it now. Now it's the only place where you can be... unfinished. Where mistakes are allowed."

Draco had gone very still. The color had drained from his face, leaving him pale and exposed.

"Piano," Elodie continued, as though confirming something to herself. "Not harpsichord. The keys are heavier. They require commitment." Her lips curved into something that wasn't quite a smile. "You haven't played in months. The silence hurts you, but you don't know how to go back."

"Elodie." Francine's voice was sharp. "*Ça suffit.*"

The girl blinked, and the strange intensity faded from her expression. She looked around the table as though suddenly remembering where she was.

"I'm sorry," she said, sounding genuinely confused. "Did I say something wrong?"

Bastien cleared his throat. "Just your usual party trick, *petite soeur*. Nothing to worry about."

Vivienne looked between her sister and the English guests with barely concealed irritation. "Elodie, *vraiment*—"

Theo's response came back tinged with dry amusement, though something more vulnerable flickered beneath it.

*You never asked.*

He took a measured sip of his soup, his expression betraying nothing to the table at large.

*My mother taught me. Before.* The word carried weight—a demarcation line between the childhood he rarely spoke of and everything that came after. *She said music was the only language my father couldn't corrupt. That the notes meant exactly what they meant, nothing more, nothing less.*

A pause. Through the bond, Jackie felt him weighing how much to share.

*I stopped playing after she died. The sound reminded me of her hands on the keys, her voice counting time. It felt like summoning a ghost.* His mental voice grew quieter. *I didn't think I'd ever want to play again.*

Across the table, Draco was mechanically eating his soup, his gaze fixed on the bowl. The color still hadn't fully returned to his face. Whatever Elodie had seen in him—whatever she'd dragged into the light—had shaken something loose.

Theo's attention shifted, tracking Draco's careful movements.

*He plays too. Better than me, probably—he had the formal training. But he carries the same wound. Someone made it about performance instead of joy, and now the instrument feels like a test he's already failed.*

His hand was still on Draco's knee beneath the table. Jackie could feel the faint echo of it through the bond—the warmth, the steadiness.

*Elodie sees things we bury. That's what makes her dangerous.* A flicker of something almost like respect. *And what makes her kind. She doesn't weaponize it. She just... speaks.*

He finally looked up, meeting Jackie's eyes across the table.

*If you want to hear me play, I will. Tonight, maybe. After.* A thread of vulnerability wound through the thought. *It's been years. I might be terrible.*

Jackie focused on her soup, her mental voice quiet for a long moment as she processed the weight of what they were both carrying.
*Do I have to ask about every specific thing for you to tell me?* she sent eventually, the thought carrying a faint, bruised edge.
Then, after a beat: *If you play, he’ll love it—and he’ll immediately convince himself he’s inferior. If he plays, he’ll feel every pair of eyes on him like a judge and worry he’s failing a test he never asked to take.*
A wave of bitterness washed through her toward a world that had turned even music into a source of shame for them. It was a knot she couldn't untangle—not right now. She pulled her attention back to the physical room, searching for a safer topic.
"So, Bastien," she said, looking at her cousin. "Who will you be dancing with?" She kept her gaze on him, but the question was clearly intended for Vivienne as well. She was curious if there were partners in their orbits who simply hadn't arrived at the château yet.

Bastien's grin turned wolfish.

"Whoever will have me, *cousine*. I'm not particular." He swirled his wine lazily. "Though I suspect Grandmère will pair me with one of the Beaumont daughters. She's been making pointed comments about *alliances* and *suitable matches* for months."

"The elder Beaumont girl," Francine confirmed, her tone brooking no argument. "Célestine. She's accomplished, well-bred, and her family controls significant interests in the southern vineyards."

"She's also dull as dishwater," Bastien muttered into his glass.

"*Bastien.*"

"What? It's true. The woman spent forty minutes at the last gathering telling me about her collection of enchanted thimbles. *Thimbles*, Maman."

Vivienne's lips thinned with barely concealed satisfaction. "Some of us understand that marriage is a strategic arrangement, not a romantic comedy."

"And some of us would rather die alone than discuss thimbles for the rest of our lives."

"Children." Francine's voice cut through the bickering like a blade. Both siblings fell silent.

Jackie caught Elodie watching the exchange with distant amusement, as though observing creatures in a menagerie.

"I won't be dancing," Elodie offered, unprompted. "The music is too loud inside my head when everyone is touching. It gets... tangled."

Vivienne sighed. "Elodie will be excused after the formal presentations, as always."

"And you, Vivienne?" Jackie asked, keeping her voice carefully neutral. "Is there someone waiting to sweep the future Matriarch onto the dance floor?"

The question landed precisely where Jackie had aimed it. Vivienne's composure flickered—just for an instant—before the mask reasserted itself.

"I will dance with whomever Grandmère assigns," she said coolly. "Unlike some, I understand my duty to the House."

Bastien snorted. "She's been corresponding with Henri Delacroix for six months and thinks none of us have noticed."

"*Bastien!*"

"The owl comes every Tuesday and Thursday. Like clockwork. Very romantic."

Vivienne's face had gone pink—the first genuine emotion Jackie had seen from her that wasn't disdain. Her hands gripped her soup spoon with white-knuckled intensity.

"That is *private correspondence* regarding *family business*—"

"Is that what they're calling it now?"

Theo's hand tightened on Draco's knee beneath the table. Through the bond, Jackie felt a ripple of dark amusement from him: *And here I thought our family dynamics were complicated.*

It was refreshing to see them bicker like the family they were, rather than feigning the stifling politeness of the night before. Jackie suspected the Matriarch’s absence had loosened their tongues. She took a sip of her wine as she finished her soup, letting the warmth settle.
"At the risk of seeding insurgent thoughts in that perfectly well-adjusted head of yours," Jackie began, looking at Vivienne without a trace of hostility for the first time. "You aren't married *yet*. And Henri sounds to me like a capable dancer—perhaps even charming enough to convince Grandmère to let you lead the floor with him."
Suddenly, Jackie understood why Vivienne and Samaya got along so well. They were both rigid, both the eldest daughters, and both saw life as a relentless string of political maneuvers. It had to be exhausting—living like that. She felt a sudden, unexpected pang of sympathy for Vivienne; it occurred to her then that she had yet to meet a person, or a creature, she couldn't empathize with—save for Fenholt. Perhaps that was her true talent, hidden beneath the scars and the history: finding the sliver of goodness in others, if any existed at all.
"I can speak to Grandmère on your behalf," she added, her tone sincere, "if you’d like me to."

The table went still.

Vivienne's expression cycled through shock, suspicion, and something that might have been cautious hope before settling into wary neutrality. Her fingers loosened on the spoon, though she didn't set it down.

"You would do that?" The words came out careful, stripped of their usual frost. "Why?"

It was, Jackie realized, possibly the first genuine question Vivienne had asked her since she'd arrived.

Bastien had gone quiet, watching the exchange with raised eyebrows. Even Francine seemed caught off guard, her composure flickering as she looked between her eldest daughter and her niece.

"Because life is short," Jackie said simply. "And because I know what it's like to have someone else decide who you belong to."

The words landed with weight. Vivienne's gaze dropped to her soup bowl, and for a moment, the ice queen of the Lavigne succession looked almost... young. Uncertain.

"Henri is..." She stopped. Started again, her voice lower. "He is not what Grandmère would choose. His family is respectable, but not powerful. He has no political value. He is simply—"

"Someone you want," Jackie finished quietly.

Vivienne's throat worked. She didn't confirm it aloud, but she didn't deny it either.

"Grandmère listens to you," Francine observed, her tone thoughtful rather than accusatory. "More than she listens to most. You are Amalthea's daughter—her favorite's child. If you spoke for Vivienne..."

"I make no promises," Jackie said. "But I can try."

The silence stretched. Then, slowly, Vivienne inclined her head—a gesture that cost her something.

"*Merci, cousine.*" The words came out stiff, unpracticed. But real.

Elodie smiled her strange, distant smile. "The threads are shifting," she murmured to no one in particular. "How lovely."

Theo's voice slid through the bond, warm with something like pride: *You just made an ally out of your worst critic. Impressive.*

"I..." Vivienne swallowed. "Thank you. I—that is—" She stopped, visibly struggling with words that didn't come naturally. "*Merci, cousine.*"

The French felt like a peace offering.

Bastien let out a low whistle. "Well. That's the first time I've heard Vivienne thank anyone for anything since 1994."

"*Bastien.*" But Vivienne's voice lacked its usual venom. She was still looking at Jackie, something recalibrating behind her pale eyes.

Francine observed the exchange with the careful attention of a woman revising her assumptions. Her gaze lingered on Jackie—measuring, reassessing.

"You have your mother's heart," she said finally. "I had wondered if England had... hardened you. I see now that it has not."

Elodie smiled her strange, dreamy smile. "The wolves in her blood know how to protect the pack. Even the ones who bite."

No one asked her to clarify. By now, they'd learned not to.

Through the bond, Theo's presence brushed against Jackie's consciousness—warm, approving.

*You just made an ally out of an enemy. Without a single hex.* A thread of genuine admiration wound through the thought. *Your mother would be proud.*

Draco had remained silent throughout the exchange, but Jackie felt his attention sharpening. He understood the politics of what she'd just done—the careful placement of a favor that cost nothing but could yield everything. It was the kind of move a Malfoy would make, though perhaps with less sincerity.

The servants appeared to clear the soup course, replacing it with delicate plates of herb-crusted fish and roasted vegetables. The interruption gave everyone a moment to breathe.

By offering to intervene for Vivienne, Jackie was effectively inserting herself into the center of a centuries-old power structure. She just hoped the lifeline she’d thrown her cousin wouldn’t end up being the rope that tied her hands. Without the looming presence of the Matriarch, the conversation drifted into safer, lighter territories. Bastien recounted stories of his misadventures in Paris, and even Vivienne contributed, sharing sharp, witty observations about the upcoming guests that lacked her usual venom. For a brief hour, they weren't just political rivals or distant heirs; they were simply a family sharing wine and a meal in the fading August heat. As the final plates were cleared, Elodie rose with a sudden, ethereal grace, her strange eyes bright. "I’d like to play the harp," she announced, and the suggestion was accepted without question. They migrated as a group to the drawing room, a sprawling, magnificent space that felt like the heart of the château's history. Floor-to-ceiling windows stood open to the night air, letting in the scent of damp earth and jasmine. The room was a museum of aristocratic life: several velvet settees in shades of deep moss and cream, an obsidian and ivory chess table in one corner, and an array of instruments. Beside Elodie’s gilded harp sat the silent piano Elodie had mentioned earlier—Margaux’s piano—its dark wood polished to a mirror shine, waiting for a hand that knew its secrets. They settled onto a deep, velvet settee, Jackie finding herself comfortably sandwiched between her two men.

She leaned her weight into Draco, resting her head on his shoulder as the first silvery, haunting notes of the harp began to fill the room. The music was like Elodie herself—drifting, unpredictable, and heartbreakingly beautiful. Under the cover of the melody, Jackie reached out through the bond, her mental voice a soft, careful nudge. *So, are you going to play, or should I ask him to? Theo's response came back measured, thoughtful.

*Ask him.*

He let the thought settle before continuing.

*If I play first, he'll convince himself he can't follow it. If you ask him—if you give him the choice—it becomes something he's offering, not something he's competing against.*

Through the bond, she felt him weighing Draco's stillness beside her. The careful way he held himself, the tension that hadn't fully released since Elodie had peeled back his defenses at dinner.

*He needs to be seen. Not compared. Not judged. Just... witnessed.*

Elodie's harp wove through the room like moonlight on water, each note hanging in the air before dissolving into the next. Across the room, Vivienne had settled into an armchair with a glass of wine, her expression softer than Jackie had ever seen it. Bastien sprawled on a chaise longue, eyes half-closed. Francine sat upright and attentive, but even her rigid posture had eased.

*Besides,* Theo added, a thread of dry humor surfacing, *if he plays and it's beautiful—which it will be—I'll have an excuse to kiss him senseless later. For artistic merit.*

His hand found Jackie's beneath the folds of her dress, fingers intertwining.

*Tell him the keys have been waiting for someone who understands them. Elodie's words, not mine. He won't be able to resist the poetry of it.*

The harp's melody shifted into something slower, more contemplative. Elodie's strange eyes had drifted closed, her fingers moving as though guided by something beyond conscious thought.

*And if he refuses,* Theo concluded, *I'll play. But give him the first chance. He's earned it.*

Jackie felt an immediate bloom of heat at Theo’s casual mention of kissing Draco. It was a visceral reaction, one that caught her off guard.
*Have you ever?* she sent, the question flickering through the bond with a sudden, sharp curiosity. *I mean, I know you haven't while I’ve been around. But have the two of you ever actually... kissed?*
It was a strange distinction to make, especially given the depths of intimacy they had already navigated in Italy and the cramped heat of Draco’s apartment. But wanting a body—desiring the skin and the friction—felt primal, almost biological. Wanting to *kiss*, however, felt like a bridge to something else. It implied a different kind of tenderness, a specific brand of emotional surrender that they hadn't yet fully articulated.
Outwardly, Jackie shifted her weight, pulling away from Draco just enough to lean toward his ear. She kept her voice a mere thread of sound, careful not to disrupt the silver tether of Elodie’s harp.
"Would you like to play?"
It was a simple question. She didn't frame it as a request or a performance; she offered it as a choice, a quiet invitation to reclaim something he had lost.

Draco went very still.

For a long moment, he didn't respond. His gaze moved to the fortepiano—dark wood gleaming in the candlelight, keys untouched for years—and something complicated shifted behind his eyes. Longing. Fear. The particular ache of a wound that had never properly healed.

"I haven't played since—" He stopped. Swallowed. "Not since before the war."

Through the bond, Theo's answer to Jackie's earlier question arrived soft and honest:

*Once. The night before your wedding to Draco. At the stag party. I kissed him outside the club, and he didn't pull away.* A pause, weighted with memory. *We've never spoken of it since. I told him I wouldn't initiate again unless he asked. He hasn't asked.*

The admission carried no bitterness—only patience, and something tender beneath it.

*But I think about it. More than I should.*

Elodie's harp sang on, oblivious to the quiet storms unfolding around her.

Draco's hands had curled in his lap, fingers pressing against his thighs. His voice, when it came, was barely audible.

"The last time I played, my father was in the room. He told me I was wasting time on sentiment when I should be preparing for—" A breath. "For what was coming. He said music was a weakness. That Malfoys didn't indulge in weakness."

His jaw tightened.

"I closed the lid and didn't open it again."

Across the room, Elodie's melody slowed, each note stretching longer, creating space. As though she knew. As though she was waiting.

"But here..." Draco's gaze drifted back to the fortepiano. "He's not here. He can't reach me here."

He looked at Jackie, then past her to Theo. Something fragile surfaced in his expression—a question he couldn't quite voice.

*Should I?*

It wasn't spoken aloud. But they both heard it anyway.

Jackie bit her inner cheek—hard enough to feel the coppery tang of blood. She kept her expression perfectly composed as she looked at Draco, even as a storm of disbelief raged through her mind.
*WHAT?\! You kissed him the night before our wedding? And neither of you ever—I should fucking strangle both of you\!*
As she sent the thought to Theo, her initial shock softened into a reluctant, amused recognition. Theo had bared his intentions—his desire for Draco—all the way back then. And he had waited for consent ever since. Patience and giving space were perhaps the two skills Theo was least equipped with, yet he had practiced them religiously for years, all for Draco’s sake.
"If you're asking me, I'd very much like to hear you play," she said, her voice soft and grounding. "But only if you *want* to, Draco. Not because it’s expected of you, and certainly not because you feel you have to prove anything."

Through the bond, Theo's response carried a thread of rueful amusement beneath the vulnerability.

*In my defense, I was drunk. And he looked—* A pause, weighted with old longing. *He looked like he needed someone to see him. Really see him. Not the mask, not the name. Just... him.*

Another pause.

*I've been waiting three years for him to ask for more. I can wait longer if I have to.*

Draco hadn't moved. His eyes were fixed on the fortepiano as though it were a door he'd locked years ago and only now realized he still carried the key.

Elodie's harp had fallen silent. She sat with her hands folded in her lap, watching him with that strange, knowing patience of hers. The room held its breath.

"I want to," Draco said finally. The words came out rough, scraped from somewhere deep. "I think I've wanted to for a long time. I just..."

He stood. The movement was stiff, uncertain—none of his usual aristocratic grace. He crossed the room slowly, each step deliberate, until he stood before the instrument.

His fingers brushed the fallboard. The wood was cool beneath his touch, smooth with age and care.

"Great-grandmother Margaux," he murmured, almost to himself. "Elodie said it belonged to her."

"She played every evening," Francine said quietly from her chair. "Until the day she died. She said the music kept the ghosts company."

Draco's throat worked. He lifted the fallboard, revealing keys yellowed with age but perfectly maintained. For a long moment, he simply looked at them.

Then he sat.

His hands hovered over the keyboard—trembling slightly, though he tried to hide it. He drew a breath. Released it.

And began to play.

The first notes were hesitant, searching. A simple melody, something half-remembered from childhood. But as his fingers found their place, muscle memory took over, and the music began to unfold—rich and aching, full of longing and loss and something that might have been hope.

It was Chopin. A nocturne. The kind of piece that required technical precision but rewarded emotional surrender.

Draco played with his eyes closed, his body swaying slightly with the phrases. The tension bled from his shoulders. The mask fell away.

For the first time since they'd arrived in France, he looked completely, utterly at peace.

Draco held her gaze for a long, suspended moment.

Then, slowly, he rose from the settee.

The room seemed to shift around him as he crossed to the fortepiano—conversations dying, attention gathering like moths to flame. Elodie's harp fell silent, her strange eyes opening to track his movement with knowing satisfaction.

He stood before the instrument, one hand resting on its polished surface. The wood was cool beneath his fingers, smooth with age and care. For a moment, he simply breathed.

Then he sat.

The bench creaked softly beneath his weight. His hands hovered above the keys—pale, elegant, trembling almost imperceptibly. He closed his eyes.

And began to play.

The first notes of Gnossienne No. 1 spilled into the room like water finding its level—slow, deliberate, aching with a melancholy that seemed to rise from somewhere deeper than memory. The melody moved in strange intervals, suspending itself between resolution and longing, never quite arriving where the ear expected it to go.

Draco's fingers found the keys with the certainty of muscle memory, though his technique had softened with years of disuse. The occasional hesitation only made it more beautiful—more human. This wasn't a performance. It was a confession.

Through the bond, Theo's presence pressed warm against Jackie's consciousness.

*He's magnificent.*

The words carried no competition, no jealousy. Only quiet, reverent awe.

The music wound through the drawing room like smoke, settling into the corners, seeping into the velvet and the stone. Vivienne had gone very still, her wine glass forgotten in her hand. Bastien's eyes had opened fully, his usual irreverence stripped away. Even Francine's composure had cracked—her lips parted slightly, something old and sorrowful moving behind her eyes.

Elodie smiled.

Draco played on, lost somewhere inside the music. His shoulders had dropped, the rigid tension finally releasing. His face, usually so carefully controlled, had softened into something raw and unguarded. In this moment, he wasn't a Malfoy. He wasn't a former Death Eater, or a man carrying the weight of his father's sins. He was simply a boy who had loved something beautiful and been told it made him weak.

The final notes hung in the air, suspended between breath and silence.

Then faded.

Draco's hands remained on the keys, head bowed. He didn't move. Didn't speak.

The room held its breath.

Bastien's eyes had opened fully, his usual irreverence stripped away. Even Francine's composure had cracked—her lips parted slightly, something old and sorrowful moving behind her eyes.

Elodie smiled.

Draco played on, lost somewhere inside the music. His shoulders had dropped, the rigid tension finally releasing. His face, usually so carefully controlled, had softened into something raw and unguarded. In this moment, he wasn't a Malfoy. He wasn't a former Death Eater, or a man carrying the weight of his father's sins. He was simply a boy who had loved something beautiful and been told it made him weak.

The final notes hung in the air, suspended between breath and silence.

Then faded.

Draco's hands remained on the keys, head bowed. He didn't move. Didn't speak.

The room held its breath.

Jackie had no idea when she’d started crying. She only realized it when the warmth trailed down her cheeks and dripped onto her hands, where they were clenched tightly in the silk of her lap. She sat up straight, her body inclined toward him as if drawn by an invisible tether. The music was slow and measured—not a virtuosic, showy piece that demanded flawless technique, but something far more difficult. It was as if Draco were pouring his soul directly through his fingertips.
For the first time, she truly noticed his hands: long, elegant, moving with a paradoxical blend of strength and gentleness. These were the same fingers that had gripped a wand with the intent to kill. She couldn't see the Mark from where she sat, but she felt its presence—a faded, eternal brand. A testament to the depths he had once descended. The song *was* him. It was the boy whose father had never loved him; the child who had learned far too young that to love is to destroy, and to be loved is to be the one destroyed.
*He is… perfect.*
The music faded into a heavy silence, and Jackie let out a shuddering exhale. She didn't bother wiping her tears; no one was looking at her anyway. Every eye in the room was fixed on Draco, who remained hunched over the keys as if the weight of the notes were still pressing down on his shoulders. She didn't want to shatter the stillness, but the words escaped her nonetheless—hoarse, hushed, and desperate.
"Play something else. *Please.*"
*Something for me.* She didn't say it, but she thought it.

Draco's shoulders tensed at her voice—a flinch, as though he'd forgotten anyone else existed.

Slowly, he raised his head. His eyes found hers across the room, and what she saw in them stole her breath: raw vulnerability, the particular terror of being truly seen. His gaze tracked the tears on her cheeks, and something in his expression cracked further.

He looked down at the keys again. His fingers trembled.

Then he began to play.

This piece was different. Where the Gnossienne had been melancholy and suspended, this was yearning given form—a melody that climbed and fell like breathing, like the tide, like a heart learning to beat again after forgetting how. It wasn't a song Jackie recognized. She wasn't certain it was a song at all. It felt improvised, pulled from somewhere beneath conscious thought—a conversation between his hands and the instrument, with her as the only audience that mattered.

The notes wove together in phrases that ached with wanting. Not the sharp, desperate want of possession, but something softer. Gentler. The want of a man who had spent years believing himself unworthy of tenderness, finally allowing himself to reach for it.

Through the bond, Theo's presence was a steady warmth at her side. He hadn't moved, hadn't spoken, but she felt his attention split between Draco at the piano and her tear-streaked face. His thumb traced slow circles against her palm where their hands remained intertwined.

*He's playing for you,* Theo sent quietly. *Only for you. The rest of us are just witnesses.*

The music swelled, climbed toward something that felt almost like hope—then gentled, descending into a resolution so tender it hurt to hear. The final chord hung in the air like a held breath.

Then silence.

Draco's hands lifted from the keys. He sat motionless, head bowed, breathing unsteady.

Across the room, Elodie made a soft sound—not quite a sigh, not quite a word. Her strange eyes glistened.

"That one was new," she whispered. "That one was *born* just now."

Her tears finally ceased. She had asked for the music, and he had given it to her—though she’d had no idea what the cost would be to her soul. It was as if he had distilled those long months of longing, of forced distance, and of missing one another into a single, aching cadence. It felt profound and intimate, reaching levels that even physical touch couldn't hope to graze.
Jackie listened, transfixed. Only Theo could bear witness to the raw ache, the yearning, and the utter devastation the music wrought in her. It radiated off her in waves, and she made no conscious effort to dam the flow. She wasn't even truly there anymore; she had forgotten how to think, how to move, how to breathe.
Then the piece reached its peak and faded, the final note piercing right through her heart.
She rose from the settee, untangling her fingers from Theo’s, and walked toward Draco. She didn't care that the Lavignes were watching.
*Let them watch. Let them see. Let them understand exactly why he is mine and I am his—and that I will never, **ever** apologize for it.*
She stopped beside the piano stool and took his chin gently, tilting his head up until he was forced to look at her. She made him meet her glistening eyes and bear witness to her tear-streaked cheeks.
"I love you, Draco Malfoy."
Her voice was hoarse, barely a whisper, yet in that profound silence, she was certain every person in the room heard it. Then, she leaned down and kissed him.
It wasn't a kiss of passion, nor a mere peck; it was a gentle, lingering pressure—a tender touch of her lips to his that stopped just short of deepening into something scandalous. If such a public display of affection could even be considered appropriate at all.
When she pulled back, she threaded her fingers with his and led him back to the settee. She settled him there and immediately moved toward the side table where the carafes of wine sat.
"More wine, anyone?" she asked, her voice steady as she finally broke the spell.

The room exhaled.

Bastien recovered first, raising his empty glass with a grin that held genuine warmth. "I thought you'd never ask, *cousine*."

Vivienne sat frozen, her expression caught between scandal and something that might have been envy. Francine's composure had returned, though her eyes lingered on Draco with a new assessment—not judgment, but recognition. As though she were seeing him clearly for the first time.

Elodie simply smiled, her fingers trailing absently over her harp strings. "The keys are happy now," she murmured to no one in particular. "They were so lonely before."

Draco hadn't moved from where Jackie had placed him on the settee. His face was flushed, his breathing uneven, his carefully constructed walls lying in ruins around him. When Theo's hand found the back of his neck—that familiar, grounding pressure—he leaned into it without resistance.

"Breathe," Theo said quietly, pitched for Draco's ears alone. "You're alright. You did beautifully."

Draco's laugh was shaky, wet at the edges. "I don't—I haven't—"

"I know." Theo's thumb traced a slow circle against his nape. "I know."

Through the bond, Theo reached for Jackie as she poured wine with hands that were steadier than they had any right to be.

*That was the bravest thing I've ever seen you do. Both of you.*

A pause. Then, softer:

*I meant what I said earlier. About kissing him senseless for artistic merit. Consider this your formal notice that I intend to collect. Tonight.*

Jackie felt the weight of his attention—protective, possessive, aching with something that had no clean name.

*He's ours,* Theo sent. *And after what he just gave this room, I want to give him something back. Something that's only for us.*

Bastien accepted his refilled glass with a theatrical bow. "To music," he declared, raising it high. "And to cousins who know how to make a memorable evening."

"To music," Francine echoed, her voice measured but not unkind.

Even Vivienne raised her glass, though she said nothing. Her eyes kept drifting to Jackie with an expression that suggested several of her assumptions had been permanently revised.

Jackie felt a profound sense of relief when no one reached for a barb or a cutting remark about the kiss. She would have defended it—ferociously—had they tried. There was a particular truth that those who mocked her polyamorous relationship could never seem to grasp: loving them both when they hated each other had nearly torn her soul in two. To love them now, when they finally loved each other as well, was infinitely easier. It was a shield that no amount of outside mockery or disdain could ever hope to pierce. It was good, it was *right*, and for the first time in years, it felt like home.
*Consider me warned—and turned on—by that declaration,* she sent back to Theo, her mental voice shimmering with a mix of heat and affection. *I wouldn't have it any other way.*
She returned to the settee with two flutes of wine, pressing one into Draco’s hand. Morgana knew he’d need the liquid courage to navigate the aftermath of such a raw display.
*After what we put him through today… he deserves everything,* she added privately to Theo. *So, tonight isn't about you or me. It’s about him.*
She raised her own glass in a steady toast. "To music, and to cousins," she said, before taking a long, meaningful drink. She didn't rush, but she didn't sip for show, either; she needed the vintage to ground her as much as Draco did.
As Elodie’s fingers found the harp strings once more, Jackie settled back against Draco’s side. She reached out, her free hand finding his, and interlaced her fingers with his in the quiet, golden light of the drawing room.

Theo's hand found Draco's shoulder, a quiet counterpoint to Jackie's interlaced fingers. Between them, Draco sat in a state of stunned surrender—wine glass clutched like a lifeline, color still high on his cheekbones, breathing slowly steadying.

*Agreed,* Theo sent back through the bond. *Tonight is his. Whatever he needs. Whatever he'll let us give.*

Elodie's harp wove a gentler melody now, something pastoral and unhurried, as though she understood the room needed time to recover from the intensity of what had come before. The music settled over them like a blanket, softening the edges of the evening.

Bastien had sprawled back on his chaise, wine in hand, watching the three of them with an expression of genuine curiosity rather than mockery. Whatever conclusions he was drawing, he kept them to himself.

Vivienne excused herself shortly after—something murmured about correspondence and early mornings—but she paused at the doorway, her gaze lingering on Jackie.

"*Merci*," she said quietly. "*Pour tout.*" For everything.

Then she was gone, silk rustling in her wake.

Francine remained a while longer, observing with the careful attention of a woman cataloguing information for future use. When she finally rose, she crossed to where the triad sat and stopped before Draco.

"You play beautifully, Monsieur Malfoy." Her voice was cool but sincere. "My sister would have appreciated your gift. She always said the best musicians were the ones who played as though they had something to confess."

Draco looked up at her, startled. "I—thank you, Madame."

Francine inclined her head. Then her gaze moved to Jackie, and something almost warm flickered in her expression.

"*Bonne nuit, ma nièce.* Sleep well. Tomorrow will be... eventful."

She departed with the same measured grace with which she'd arrived, leaving only Bastien and Elodie in the drawing room with them.

Bastien drained his glass and hauled himself upright with theatrical reluctance. "I know when I'm intruding on a moment," he announced, offering Jackie a wink. "Elodie, *petite soeur*, time to let the lovebirds roost."

Jackie bid her goodnights to the family, lingering a moment longer with Elodie. She caught the younger girl’s hand, a silent, warm *“Thank you for calling it back to him,”* passing between them before Elodie drifted away. When the heavy doors finally clicked shut, leaving only the three of them in the flickering candlelight, Jackie turned to speak—but Draco beat her to it. His voice was a hollow rasp, the words unspooling like old, jagged silk. *“...burned it out of me. Along with everything else.”*
Jackie’s breath hitched in her throat. Those words—*everything else*—contained a universe of unspoken horrors, of a childhood systematically dismantled by a man who mistook cruelty for discipline. A wild, primal roar of fury erupted within her. She wasn't entirely sure if it was hers or Theo’s—likely a toxic, beautiful cocktail of both—but she didn't fight it. She wanted to reach up and curse the very stars. She found herself wishing, with a terrifying sincerity, that Lucius Malfoy would somehow escape Azkaban. Not so he could be free, but so she could find him. So she could be the Auror she was training to be, hunt him into whatever dark corner he hid in, and end him. Slowly. Thoroughly. She knew the most murderous of these impulses likely belonged to Theo, but she didn’t push them away; she stoked them, letting the fire warm the cold spaces Draco's confession had left behind. "I—" Jackie started, then stopped. It was a rare thing for her to be truly at a loss for words. She reached out, her fingers grazing the fabric of his sleeve, right over the spot where the Dark Mark lay hidden. "I’m so sorry we weren't there, Draco. To pull you up. To keep you from drowning."
She looked into his eyes, her own burning with a fierce, protective light. "I know you’d tell me it wasn't our fault. That we were just children. But so were you. And it didn't stop him from forcing you to take that."
She stood up then, the movement decisive. She took the empty wine glass from Draco’s hand and set it on the side table beside her own.

She wanted to make the memory of that man inconsequential—a shriveled, pathetic thing that held no power over the man standing before her. She wanted to kill the ghost that still paced the hallways of Draco’s mind. Only now did she fully appreciate the weight of Bastien’s words from the day before. He was right. It was really fucking hard to kill a ghost. But she was more than willing to try.

Draco let himself be pulled upright.

He moved like a man surfacing from deep water—disoriented, blinking, not quite certain of the shape of the world around him. His fingers tightened around Jackie's, anchoring himself to her presence.

Theo rose beside them, a silent shadow at Draco's back. His hand found its familiar place at the nape of Draco's neck, warm and steady.

"Come on," Theo said quietly. "We've got you."

They moved through the château's corridors in silence, the candles in their wall sconces guttering as they passed. The heat of the day had finally broken, leaving the stone halls cool and still. Somewhere in the distance, a clock chimed the hour—late, later than any of them had realized.

Draco walked between them like something precious being carried home.

When they reached their chambers, Theo closed the door behind them with a soft click. The suite was dim, lit only by the moonlight streaming through the open windows and the faint glow of enchanted candles that flickered to life at their entrance.

Through the bond, Jackie felt Theo's intention crystallize—patient, deliberate, utterly focused.

*Let me.*

It wasn't a command. It was a request.

He moved around Draco, positioning himself in front of him while Jackie remained at his back. His hands came up to frame Draco's face—gentle, careful, giving him every opportunity to pull away.

"I told you once," Theo said, his voice low, "that I wouldn't initiate again unless you asked."

Draco's breath caught. His gray eyes, still raw from the evening's exposure, searched Theo's face.

"I'm not asking you to ask," Theo continued. "I'm asking you to let me. Just this once. Let me show you what I see when I look at you."

The silence stretched. Draco's hands had begun to tremble again—not with fear this time, but with something else entirely.

"I don't—" His voice cracked. "I don't know how to—"

"You don't have to know." Theo's thumb traced the line of Draco's cheekbone. "You just have to stay."

Behind Draco, Jackie pressed close, her forehead resting against his shoulder blade. Her warmth seeped through the thin fabric of his shirt, grounding him from behind while Theo held him from the front.

"Stay," she whispered against his spine. "We've got you."

Draco's eyes closed. A shudder ran through him—surrender, finally, after years of holding on until his fingers bled.

"Okay," he breathed. "Okay."

Theo leaned in and kissed him.

Draco stood frozen for one terrible, endless heartbeat.

Then something in him broke open.

His hands came up—trembling, uncertain—and fisted in the front of Theo's shirt. Not pushing away. Pulling closer. A sound escaped him, something between a gasp and a sob, muffled against Theo's mouth.

And he kissed him back.

It wasn't graceful. It wasn't polished. It was messy and raw and desperate, years of suppressed wanting finally given permission to exist. Draco kissed like a man drowning, like Theo was air, like this single point of contact was the only thing keeping him tethered to the earth.

Through the bond, Theo's relief crashed through Jackie like a wave—sharp and bright and edged with something that might have been joy. His hands slid from Draco's face to his hair, fingers tangling in the pale strands, holding him close.

*He's kissing me back.*

The thought came through fractured, disbelieving.

*He's actually kissing me back.*

Theo gentled the kiss by degrees—slowing the urgency, transforming desperation into something more deliberate. More thorough. He kissed Draco the way he did everything else: with complete, devastating attention. Every brush of lips, every careful pressure, every soft exhale was a declaration.

Draco made a sound against his mouth—half whimper, half moan—and Theo swallowed it whole.

When they finally broke apart, both were breathing hard. Draco's eyes were glassy, unfocused, his lips swollen and parted. He looked wrecked in the best possible way.

"Theo—" His voice came out ruined. "I—"

"I know." Theo pressed his forehead to Draco's, their breath mingling in the narrow space between them. "I know."

His hands were still in Draco's hair. He made no move to release him.

"I've wanted to do that for years," Theo admitted quietly. "Since before the wedding. Since before any of it. I just—I needed you to be ready."

Draco's laugh was wet, shaky. "I don't think I'll ever be ready. I think I'll always be terrified."

"That's alright." Theo's thumb traced the curve of his ear. "Terrified is fine. You just have to keep choosing anyway."

For three heartbeats, nothing happened.

Draco stood frozen beneath Theo's mouth—rigid, uncertain, caught between instinct and the weight of years spent convincing himself this wasn't something he wanted. Theo felt the tremor run through him, felt the war happening beneath the surface.

He didn't push. Didn't deepen the kiss. He simply stayed—lips pressed soft against Draco's, patient as stone, giving him all the time in the world to choose.

Then Draco's hands came up.

They fisted in the fabric of Theo's shirt, pulling him closer with a desperation that seemed to surprise Draco himself. A sound escaped him—broken, raw, something between a gasp and a sob—and suddenly he was kissing back. Not with technique or control, but with the clumsy, devastating honesty of a man who had spent years starving and only just realized he was allowed to eat.

Theo's chest cracked open.

*Finally. Finally.*

He cradled Draco's face like something precious, tilting his head to deepen the kiss. Draco tasted like wine and surrender, and Theo wanted to drown in it. His thumbs traced the sharp line of Draco's jaw, the flutter of his pulse, the dampness at the corner of his eyes where tears had gathered without falling.

"There you are," Theo murmured against his mouth. "There you are."

Draco made another broken sound—half laugh, half sob. His forehead dropped to Theo's shoulder, his breathing ragged and uneven.

"I thought—" His voice fractured. "I thought if I let myself want this, it would destroy everything. That you'd—that she'd—"

"We're not going anywhere." Theo's hand moved to the back of Draco's neck, holding him steady. "Neither of us. You're stuck with us now, Malfoy."

Draco's mouth opened. Closed. Opened again.

The request hung in the air like a blade—simple, impossible. His entire body had gone taut, the surrender of moments ago giving way to something older, deeper. The ingrained terror of wanting things out loud.

"I—" His voice caught. He looked away, jaw working. "You can't ask me to—I don't—"

Theo stepped closer, eliminating the distance Draco was trying to create. His hand found Draco's hip, steadying him.

"Yes, you do." Theo's voice was low, patient, implacable. "You know exactly what you want. You've known for months. Maybe years." His thumb traced a slow circle against Draco's hipbone. "The only thing stopping you is the voice in your head that says you don't deserve it."

Draco's breath shuddered out of him. His eyes, when they finally lifted, were wet and desperate.

"I want—" He stopped. Swallowed hard. Started again. "I want to not be in control. Just once. I want—" His voice dropped to barely a whisper. "I want both of you. At the same time. I want to feel—"

He couldn't finish. The words tangled in his throat, shame and desire warring across his features.

"I want to feel like I belong to someone," he finally managed, the confession ripped from somewhere deep. "Like I'm—like I'm *wanted*. Not tolerated. Not an addition. *Wanted.*"

His hands were shaking again. His eyes found Jackie's, then Theo's, naked with vulnerability.

"I want you to show me I'm yours."

Draco's breath stuttered.

He stood before them—undone, raw, stripped of every defense he'd spent his life constructing. The candlelight caught the tremor in his hands, the rapid flutter of his pulse at his throat, the way his chest rose and fell with shallow, uneven breaths.

"I—" He stopped. Swallowed hard. His eyes darted between them, searching for permission, for judgment, for some indication of where the boundaries lay.

He found only patience. Only waiting.

"I don't know how to ask for things." The admission came out hoarse, almost angry. "I was taught that wanting was weakness. That if you had to ask, you didn't deserve it. That—"

His voice cracked.

Theo stepped closer, but didn't touch. Not yet. "We're not your father, Draco. We're not going to punish you for wanting."

"I *know* that." Draco's hands clenched at his sides. "I know that, but knowing and *believing* are—" He made a frustrated sound, something between a growl and a sob. "I've spent twenty years learning to kill every desire before it could be used against me. You're asking me to undo all of that in a single night."

"No." Theo's voice was impossibly gentle. "We're asking you to start. One word at a time. One want at a time."

Draco's eyes closed. His breathing slowed, deliberate and measured—the rhythm of a man forcing himself toward a cliff's edge.

When he spoke again, his voice was barely audible.

"I want..." A shudder ran through him. "I want to not be in control. Just for tonight. I want to stop thinking, stop calculating, stop—" His throat worked. "Stop being afraid that every choice I make is the wrong one."

His eyes opened, finding Theo's face first, then moving to Jackie's.

"I want you to show me what you see. Both of you. Because I can't—" His voice fractured completely. "I can't see it myself. I look in the mirror and I still see the boy who took the Mark. Who let his father shape him into something monstrous. Who left when staying got hard."

Tears slipped down his cheeks now, unchecked.

"I want to believe I'm worth keeping. I want you to make me believe it."

She wanted to kiss the tears off his cheeks. She wanted to find a way to let Draco share their bond, if only for one night. It would be so much easier if he could just feel them, peer into the deepest corners of their hearts and minds and see for himself how they saw him. She decided, somewhere in the back of her mind, that she'd ask Filippo once she saw him. She knew making it permanent would be too good to be true. She exhaled. Held Draco's gaze for a few seconds, then looked away. She wanted to backtrack, to tell him she misspoke. The night had been so perfect, and she felt the ugly voice in her whisper that she was about to ruin everything again. Just like she always did. But she felt Theo's presence in her mind — he was giving her his permission, and it meant the world to her. That he was willing to let her bare him like that. 
Jackie pulled her wrist from Draco's grip and walked towards the window. She didn't care that she was still naked. She needed somewhere else to look at. Something distant and indifferent, for the memories she was going to bring up.
"Theo had loved you, since he knew he liked boys. Well, it was a crush at first, same as mine. It was actually a little funny, when you think about it. You had two different people silently pining for you all those years, and you had no idea. And we had no idea about each other. Anyway…"
She fixed her eyes somewhere in the darkness, on the faint outline of the forest.
"When he found out about the betrothal contract, he was thrilled at first. He'd wanted me for a while then, I think a year or two. But he convinced himself not to act on it. And then he found out he'd get me. Officially. Wedding and all. But then the same day me and him both found out, we came back to Hogwarts for our last year. And then the next day me and you made those Protean Rings, and we finally talked and you finally admitted that you didn't get my letters that summer in Fifth Year. And he saw that, Draco. He saw how you looked at me, and how I looked at me."
For a while she was silent. 
"Do you want me to continue?" She asked suddenly, looking at his reflection in the window. She wanted to give him an out if he chose to take it. If he'd rather be ignorant than broken.

The silence that followed was absolute.

Draco sat frozen on the bed, his face drained of all color. His hands had stilled on the mattress, knuckles bone-white, as though the slightest movement might shatter him.

In the doorway, Theo hadn't moved. His expression remained carefully blank, but through the bond, Jackie felt the storm beneath—old shame, old grief, the wound that would never fully heal no matter how many times they tended it.

"He wanted to ruin you," Draco repeated slowly. Each word landed like a stone. "For *me*."

His gaze moved to Theo's reflection, then to the man himself. Something terrible was happening behind his eyes—a recalculation, a dismantling of every assumption he'd built his hatred upon.

"All those years I convinced myself you were just—" His voice splintered. "That you were cruel because cruelty came naturally. That you hurt her because you *could*. Because you didn't care."

He rose from the bed, the sheet falling away. He didn't seem to notice his own nakedness. He took one step toward Theo, then another, until they stood face to face in the doorway.

"You cared too much," Draco whispered. "That's why you did it. You loved both of us, and we—*I*—"

His hand came up, hovering near Theo's face but not touching. Trembling.

"I never saw you. I never *once* looked past my own assumptions to see what was actually there." Tears spilled down his cheeks. "How many years did you spend wanting me while I treated you like you were nothing?"

Theo's jaw was tight, his breathing carefully controlled. But his eyes—those dark, unreadable eyes—had gone glassy.

"Draco—" His voice came out rough, cracked.

"No." Draco shook his head. "Let me say this. I need to say it."

He stepped closer still, until there was barely an inch between them.

"I'm sorry," he breathed. "For every cruel word. Every sneer. Every time I made you feel like you weren't worth my attention when the truth was—" His voice broke completely. "The truth was you were worth everything, and I was too blind and too frightened to see it."

“Jealousy is an ugly thing. It has a tendency to fester,” Jackie said, her voice sounding thin in the quiet of the room. “And Theo had been promised he’d get me, but I still only looked at you. I despised him for the contract, for the way he smiled like he’d already won.” She leaned her forehead against the cool glass of the window, the dark silhouette of the French forest stretching out like a void beyond the château. “He tried, Draco. He really did. He took me to Hogsmeade, sat with me in the library while I studied... you told me yourself once that he was taught how to make people like him from the time he was a boy. I thought it was just another performance then.”

She closed her eyes, the memory of that year at Hogwarts—the weight of the Protean rings and the stolen glances—pressing heavily against her chest. “Then he kissed me, and I felt something. But I was too stubborn, or maybe just too terrified to admit that my heart was splitting in two. I wanted to just love you. I went to your Quidditch practice and kissed you in the changing room, and when you came back to the Common Room, he *knew*. You didn’t even have to say a word. You took me away from him, and I took you away from him. We were practically building our happiness on the pyre of his yearning for each of us.”

It was only then that she caught Theo’s reflection in the window—a pale, silent ghost lingering in the doorway. Jackie trembled, and it wasn’t from the night air. Through the soul tether, she reached out, sending him a desperate wave of love, sorrow, and raw remorse.

“So that morning... when he saw me sneaking out of your bedroom,” she continued, her breath fogging the glass. “I know, and you know, that nothing happened. You just let me stay because I’d only just turned back into a human and I was exhausted. But he didn’t have the bond then. He didn't have the clarity. He only had the sight of the girl he was forced to marry coming out of the bed of his rival… and his first love.”

The silence that followed was absolute.

Draco sat frozen on the bed, his face drained of color. His hands had gone slack against the mattress, all the tension bleeding out of him as the truth settled into his bones.

In the doorway, Theo hadn't moved. His expression remained carved from stone, but through the bond, Jackie felt the tremor running through him—old pain, old shame, the wound that had never fully scarred over.

"Because of me." Draco's voice was barely a whisper. "He hurt you because of *me*."

It wasn't a question. It was a reckoning.

His eyes found Theo's—not through the window's reflection this time, but directly. The two men stared at each other across the dim room, years of history and hurt and unspoken longing suspended between them.

"You loved me," Draco said. The words came out hollow, devastated. "All that time. And I was so blind, so *stupid*—I thought you hated me. I thought I hated you. And instead we were just—"

He couldn't finish. His hand came up to press against his mouth, a visible attempt to hold himself together.

Theo moved then. Slow, deliberate steps across the room until he stood at the foot of the bed, close enough to touch but not touching. His jaw was tight, his breathing carefully controlled.

"I did hate you," Theo said quietly. "For a while. It was easier than wanting something I couldn't have." His gaze held Draco's without flinching. "And yes. What I did to Jackie—part of it was because of you. Because I watched her walk out of your room and something in me *broke*."

He didn't look away. Didn't soften it.

"That doesn't excuse it. Nothing excuses it. But you asked for the truth, and that's what it is." His voice dropped lower. "I was nineteen, and jealous, and so fucking in love with both of you that I couldn't see straight. And I made a choice that I'll regret for the rest of my life."

The muscle in his jaw worked.

"But I'm not that person anymore. Jackie knows that. She's forgiven me—not because I deserved it, but because she chose to." His eyes stayed locked on Draco's. "The question is whether you can live with knowing what I was. What I did. And why."

The silence that followed was absolute.

Draco sat frozen on the bed, his face drained of all color. His hands had stopped shaking—they'd gone completely still, pressed against the mattress like he'd forgotten how to move them. His eyes were fixed on some middle distance, seeing nothing.

In the doorway, Theo hadn't moved. His arms were still crossed, his posture deceptively casual, but through the bond Jackie felt the earthquake happening beneath the surface. Old shame, old grief, the particular agony of having his worst moment dissected and understood.

He didn't defend himself. Didn't explain. Just stood there, letting Draco see him.

"You—" Draco's voice emerged cracked, barely human. "You did that to her because of *me*?"

Theo's jaw tightened. A single nod.

"I spent two years hating you." Draco's breathing had gone shallow, rapid. "Convincing myself you were irredeemable. That what you did proved you were everything I refused to become. And the whole time—the whole *fucking* time—"

He pressed the heels of his hands against his eyes, a sound escaping him that was half laugh, half sob.

"I was the reason. I was always the reason."

"No." Theo's voice was quiet, rough. He pushed off from the doorframe, taking a single step into the room. "What I did was my choice. My failure. You didn't make me do anything."

"But I—"

"You existed. You loved her. That's not a crime, Draco." Theo's hands had curled into fists at his sides. "I'm the one who took something that didn't belong to me because I couldn't stand losing. That's on me. Only me."

Draco's hands dropped. His eyes—red, wet, devastated—found Theo's face.

"How can you love me?" The question came out broken, bewildered. "After what I cost you? After what my existence drove you to do?"

Theo crossed the remaining distance. He stopped at the edge of the bed, close enough to touch but not touching. His expression was raw in a way Draco had never seen—stripped of charm, of control, of everything he used to keep the world at arm's length.

I told you he slept with me, so I'd never be truly yours. I poked a tiger with a stick, heedless of the fact that it could bite me. And it did."
She looked at Draco then, but there wasn't any sorrow or sadness or even accusation, just a steely resolution.

She took one more step closer, feeling the heat radiating off their bodies now. 
"I know I can. I've forgiven him. Can you?"

Draco was trembling.

Not the fine shivers from before—this was something deeper, something tectonic. His whole frame shook with the force of what he was trying to process. His eyes moved between them—Jackie, standing bare and unflinching in the moonlight; Theo, raw and exposed at the edge of the bed.

"I—" His voice broke. He tried again. "For two years, I told myself I was the only one who saw him clearly. The only one who understood what he was. I used it to justify leaving. To justify every cruel thought, every moment I looked at him and saw nothing but the violence he was capable of."

His hands fisted in the sheets, knuckles white.

"But I wasn't seeing him at all, was I? I was seeing myself. The parts I couldn't accept. The darkness I was taught to bury." A wet, broken laugh escaped him. "I called him a monster because I was terrified of the monster in me. The one my father built. The one that took the Mark and followed orders and—"

He couldn't finish. His breath came in ragged gasps.

Theo hadn't moved. His hand still hovered near Draco's jaw, not quite touching. Through the bond, Jackie felt him holding himself together by threads—waiting, hoping, terrified of what came next.

"You want to know if I can love the monster?" Draco's voice was barely a whisper. His eyes found Theo's and held them. "I've been in love with him since I was fourteen years old and too afraid to name it."

He reached up—slowly, deliberately—and covered Theo's hand with his own, pressing it against his cheek.

"I don't need to forgive what you did to her," he said quietly. "That's not mine to give. She's already given it. What I need—"

His voice cracked.

"What I need is for you to forgive me. For all the years I made you wait. For every time I looked at you with hatred when I should have—when I *wanted* to—"

He couldn't say it. But he turned his head, pressing his lips to Theo's palm.

The gesture said everything.

"That's what I heard."

Draco blinked. A sound escaped him—half laugh, half sob. "I think I'm in love with a madwoman."

"Two madpeople," Theo corrected. His thumb traced a circle against Draco's chest, feeling the steady thrum of his heart. "Welcome to the arrangement."

From the bathroom, the sound of water splashing. Jackie's voice drifted out, muffled but unmistakably demanding: "Are you two going to stand there holding hands all night, or are you getting in this bath?"

Theo's mouth curved. He tugged gently at Draco's hand.

"You heard her."

Draco rose on unsteady legs, the sheet falling away. He looked wrecked—tear-streaked, exhausted, utterly undone. But there was something new in his eyes. Something that hadn't been there before.

Hope.

They walked into the bathroom together, and the steam wrapped around them like an embrace. Jackie was already submerged to her shoulders, her hair floating around her like dark seaweed, watching them approach with a satisfaction that bordered on smug.

"Took you long enough," she said. "Get in. We have approximately six hours before someone knocks on that door expecting us to be functional humans, and I intend to spend at least half of that unconscious."

They all fell asleep the moment they hit the mattress, the air still heavy with the lingering steam of the bath and the faint, herbal medicinal scent of the soap. No one bothered with clothes, or even underwear; after the raw physical and emotional intimacy of the day, fabric felt like a redundant barrier against the skin. Jackie drifted off with her back pressed into the furnace-warmth of Theo’s chest, her face buried in the clean, damp scent of Draco’s neck. She could feel their foreheads touching over her crown, creating a closed circuit of warmth. Above her, Theo was murmuring—a low, gravelly vibration against her skull. She couldn't catch the words through the haze of exhaustion, but the rhythmic, melodic cadence of it sounded less like talk and more like a whispered prayer. In the dead of night, the nightmare returned for Theo, likely dragged to the surface by the memories they had unearthed. It wasn’t the thrashing terror it once was, thanks to the techniques from Filippo’s Czech friend, but the silence was still shattered by a sharp, hitched intake of breath. They both woke with a jolt, the dry rustle of linen loud in the dark as Theo pulled her flush against him, his grip so fierce it felt as though he feared she might shatter like glass. Across the bed, the rhythm of Draco’s breathing shifted as he rolled onto his stomach, the sheets bunching with a soft *crinkle* around his legs. Jackie wasn't crying, but her own breaths came in ragged, shallow bursts. She lay still, anchored by the scent of Theo’s skin—salt and fading lavender—as he whispered a frantic, low-volume litany against her skin: *"I'm sorry. I'm so, so sorry. I love you. You're so perfect. Thank you. I'm sorry."* The words lulled her back into a heavy, dreamless sleep that felt like a mercy. Jackie woke first in the morning, greeted by the cool, earthy scent of dawn drifting through the window. The oppressive weight of yesterday’s heat had lifted; while it would surely climb back to twenty-five or twenty-seven degrees by noon, for now, the sheets felt crisp rather than clinging.

She untangled herself from Theo’s limbs—his skin now cool to the touch—and moved with a hushed step across the floorboards. She stepped into the burgundy dress, the fabric whispering against her thighs. The silence of the room was punctuated only by the soft click and hiss of her corset laces as she dressed, but left her high-heeled boots in the wardrobe for now, preferring the silent, tactile press of her bare feet against the rug. She turned back to the bed, watching them. It was a rare peace; they looked truly exhausted, the usual sharp edge of alertness smoothed away by sleep. Walking around to Draco’s side, she sat on the edge of the mattress, the frame groaning faintly under her weight. She watched the steady, rhythmic rise and fall of his shoulders, the muscles of his back looking like a landscape of pale marble in the morning light. Reaching out, she traced imagined patterns on his skin—her touch so light it was merely the ghost of a sensation, a silent promise kept in the stillness of the room.

Draco stirred beneath her touch.

Not quite awake—his breathing remained deep and even—but something in him registered her presence. He shifted, turning his face toward her on the pillow, his features slack and unguarded in a way he never allowed himself during waking hours. The sharp angles of his jaw, the pale sweep of his lashes, the faint crease between his brows that smoothed away as her fingers traced his spine.

Behind her, Theo remained motionless. The nightmare had taken something from him; she could feel the residue of it through the bond, a bruised quality to his stillness that spoke of exhaustion deeper than physical. He'd curled onto his side sometime in the night, one arm flung across the space where Jackie had been, as though even in sleep he reached for her.

The morning light crept further into the room, painting gold across the rumpled sheets.

Draco's eyes opened.

Gray irises, still hazy with sleep, found her face. For a moment he simply looked at her—no masks, no calculation, just quiet recognition. Then the corner of his mouth curved, barely perceptible.

"You're staring," he murmured, his voice rough with disuse.

He didn't move away from her touch. If anything, he pressed into it slightly, his shoulders shifting beneath her fingertips like a cat arching into a stroke.

"What time is it?"

The question was practical, but the way he asked it wasn't—lazy, unhurried, as though the answer didn't particularly matter. As though he had nowhere else he'd rather be than here, half-asleep beneath her hands, with Theo's breathing steady behind them.

Something had shifted in him overnight. The desperation of last night's surrender had settled into something quieter. He wasn't bracing for impact anymore. Wasn't waiting for the other shoe to drop.

He simply *was*.

His hand found hers on his back, fingers intertwining loosely.

"Is he all right?" A murmur, barely audible. His gaze had flickered past her to where Theo lay. "I heard him. In the night."

Jackie smiled as she watched Draco’s eyes open. She had always felt she could drown in them, even years ago when they held nothing but ice and disdain. Today, they were different—the gray was softer, like the mist of a clearing storm.
"Eight in the morning, more or less. I think Colette will bring breakfast in an hour," she informed him. Her hand stilled when he caught it, and she leaned down to press a lingering kiss to his knuckles before gently untangling her fingers from his.
"I want to do something," she murmured. Shifting her weight, she began to work his back muscles more firmly, her palms kneading the heavy tension she found lingering there.
At Draco’s question, her gaze flickered to Theo’s curled form behind her. "He had the nightmare again. I think talking through everything yesterday brought it to the surface. It wasn't as bad as it used to be, but it still shakes him every time it happens. He’ll be okay, though."
She went quiet for a moment, her focus narrowing to the rhythmic pull of muscle beneath her hands. "I might need to duel him later, just for good measure—keep his head in the present so he doesn't slip into old habits. We’ll see how he wakes up."

Draco groaned softly as her palms found the knots in his shoulders—a low, involuntary sound of relief that vibrated through his chest.

"Christ, that's—" He broke off, pressing his forehead into the pillow. "When did I become this tense?"

The question was rhetorical. They both knew the answer: years. Decades, maybe. A lifetime of holding himself rigid against a world that punished vulnerability.

He let her work in silence for a moment, his breathing deepening as she found a particularly stubborn cluster of tension near his left shoulder blade. His fingers curled loosely in the sheets, knuckles no longer white, just... resting.

"The nightmare," he said eventually, his voice muffled by the pillow. "Is it always about—" He stopped. Swallowed. "About what happened? With you?"

He didn't turn to look at her. The question hung in the morning air, fragile as spun glass.

From across the bed, Theo stirred. Not waking—not yet—but shifting, his arm reaching across the empty space where Jackie had been and finding nothing. A small furrow appeared between his brows. His hand patted the sheets twice, searching, before settling against the still-warm indent she'd left behind.

Draco watched this from the corner of his eye. Something flickered across his face—not jealousy, not anymore. Something softer. Recognition, perhaps. The understanding that Theo's need for Jackie wasn't a threat to be managed but a truth to be witnessed.

"He reaches for you even in sleep," Draco murmured. "I used to hate that. The way he needed you so completely." A pause. His voice dropped lower. "Now I think I understand it better than I want to admit."

Jackie’s hands worked his muscles with relentless precision. She was generally gentle, but whenever she found a knot, she leaned into it, using the heel of her palm and the steady pressure of her thumbs to grind the tension out. Draco’s groan of relief brought a small, satisfied smile to her lips.
"Yes. That's the only kind of nightmare he ever gets," she murmured. "In fact, I suspect it’s the only kind of dream he has at all. I’ve never seen any others through the bond—though perhaps it doesn’t reach that far, save for this one exception."
She glanced aside as Theo shifted, his hand searching the sheets on instinct. There was something heartbreakingly vulnerable in the gesture, like a child reaching for a misplaced comfort—though Jackie doubted Theo had ever been allowed a stuffed animal. She supposed neither of them had, given the fathers they were raised by.
She nodded at Draco’s admission, her hands tracing the long line of muscle flanking his spine, working from the nape of his neck down to the small of his back. For a long moment, she remained silent, letting the quiet of the room settle. Then, in a hushed tone so as not to disturb Theo’s fragile rest, she replied.
"It’s easier to understand once you’ve been on the receiving end of that need." Her smile sharpened into a slight, knowing smirk. "I bet if you moved closer right now, he’d settle against you just as easily as he does with me."
