Jackie shook the woman's hand gently but firmly. Then followed her inside and had to use most of the control she had to stop herself from looking around like a child in Weasley Wizard Wheezes. The birds were magnificent, and felt almost sentient. It was like being watched by over a hundred creatures that only knew how to obey their master and neither of them was one. 
She had never been inside the ravenry. It wasn't permitted for children or teenagers, and now Jackie understood why. The birds were as lethal as they were beautiful and she could bet that they'd gladly poke an intruder's eye out without a second thought. 
"It's much easier to control the flow of information, if we are the ones delivering it." She said, as they walked into the second chamber. Suddenly she was afraid of Genevieve Lavigne. Jackie knew that the empire was built way before her, that she inherited it, but throughout her rule, it only blossomed further. It took an absolutely ruthless person to keep an undertaking so significant and risky from falling into ruin. One open accusation of the ravens revealing their master's secrets would be enough to tarnish the Corvus Network's opinion, precisely because it was so high.
She caught the way her men glanced at each other and rolled her eyes mentally.
*Didn't know you liked mature women.* She sent through the bond to Theo, and she couldn't entirely cover the fact that she was a little jealous of that awed look in his eyes.

Theo's response came back instantly, dry as dust.

*I like competence. And anyone who's built an intelligence network that spans European wizarding society deserves a certain... appreciation.* A beat. *Besides, you're the one who married a man with a thing for power. This is entirely your fault.*

Ahead of them, Céline had paused before a smaller, more private alcove set apart from the training area. The ravens here were different—older, their plumage carrying that same iridescent sheen as the large one she'd shown them earlier.

"The bonded pairs," she explained. "These birds have already been matched to recipients. They will serve only their designated master until death."

Draco leaned closer to examine one of the ravens, which regarded him with an expression of profound disdain.

"How do you determine the matches?" he asked. "Is it a matter of temperament, or—"

The raven snapped at his finger.

Draco jerked back, dignity ruffled. "Charming."

"They choose," Céline said, something almost like amusement flickering across her severe features. "We present candidates, but the final bond is the bird's decision. They are... particular."

She turned to Jackie, her gaze sharpening with intent.

"Which brings me to why I requested this tour, Madame Nott. Your grandmother and I have discussed the matter, and we agree: it is time you were offered a raven of your own."

Theo went very still beside her.

*That's not a gift*, he sent through the bond, his tone suddenly serious. *That's an invitation. Into the inner circle.*

Céline gestured toward a separate chamber, its entrance draped in white silk.

"The unbonded juveniles are kept here. If you would follow me, we can see if any of them find you... acceptable."

The transition from the clinical, stone-hewn interior to the grand aviary was a shock of silver and light. *Yeah, well…* Jackie started to snap back with a sharp retort, but then she caught herself. He was entirely right. She had married him knowing full well how power-hungry he was; in truth, she loved that edge in him. It was the iron that met her own. *I walked right into that one, didn't I?*
She let the bond go quiet as Céline led them toward the smaller alcove. Jackie studied the bonded birds, her mind spinning with the implications. These were the messengers of the elite—the silent, winged keepers of Europe's most dangerous secrets. She thought of her father, Cyrus; he had coveted a Lavigne raven for decades, a status symbol he was never deemed worthy to possess. It was one of the many bitter seeds that had grown into his hatred for her mother's family. When Céline declared that Jackie was to be given one, her breath hitched. Her mouth parted slightly, and she had to physically clamp her jaw shut to avoid looking completely undone. Had her morning gone differently—had she still been drowning in the guilt of her "weakness"—she would have felt like a fraud. But after the raw honesty in the dueling room, she felt a strange, steadying resolve. She wasn't a Lavigne by name, and she never had been, but here, blood spoke louder than any signature. "I am honored, Madame Renoir," Jackie said, inclining her head with a crispness that mirrored Céline’s own. She offered no further gratitude. Lavignes took what was theirs with grace, never with groveling. She followed Céline through the heavy silk curtain into a transition chamber—a narrow, utilitarian space holding racks of specialized feed and various iron utensils. The air here smelled of dried grain and well-oiled leather. Céline pulled a thick, scarred leather glove from a hook and handed it to Jackie. "You should put this on," she advised, her voice dropping to a low, expectant hum. She gestured to a heavy oak door. "Go out first. We will follow. Walk to the center and wait. If one chooses you, it will come."
Céline turned a heavy silver key in the lock and pushed the door open.

Jackie stepped out and felt the sudden, sharp whistle of the wind through the structure. The aviary was a masterpiece of Victorian-inspired engineering—a massive, soaring dome that mirrored a winter garden, though the glass had been replaced by a shimmering, fine-gauge silver wire mesh. In the dead center of the rotunda stood a magnificent, ancient tree. It was entirely leafless, its gnarled branches bleached to a bone-white pallor that made it look like a skeletal sculpture against the sky. Dozens of ravens perched upon its limbs like heavy, feathered snowdrifts. As Jackie’s boots clicked against the gravel path, the silence of the dome was broken by the dry, rhythmic rustle of wings. A few of the younger birds startled, taking flight in a flurry of brilliant white before relocating to the higher cross-beams, but most simply watched her. Their pale gold eyes tracked her every movement with a chilling, sentient focus. The air was filled with the faint, metallic tang of the silver wire and the earthy scent of stone. Jackie reached the center of the dome, beneath the reach of the white tree, and stood still. She felt the heavy, watchful presence of Theo and Draco at the door behind her—a grounding weight in her mind. She waited. The ravens shifted, their beaks clacking like dice in a cup. For a long minute, nothing happened. Then, a shadow detached itself from the highest, most jagged branch of the bone-white tree. The sound of its descent was heavy—a slow, powerful *whump-whump-whump* of wings that beat against the air with more force than any post owl. The bird landed on her gloved wrist with a jolt that nearly knocked her off balance, its talons digging deep into the thick leather. It was larger than the others, its feathers a pristine, blinding white that seemed to glow from within. It didn't look at her with curiosity; it stared into her eyes with a terrifying, ancient recognition. *Mine,* the thought didn't come from the bond, but it felt just as clear.

The weight of the raven on her arm was substantial—not painful, but *present*. A declaration. Jackie held perfectly still as the bird regarded her with those ancient golden eyes, its head tilting in sharp, birdlike movements that somehow conveyed intelligence far beyond any ordinary creature.

Behind her, she heard Céline's sharp intake of breath.

"Remarkable," the woman murmured. "That one has refused every candidate for the past three years. We had begun to wonder if she would ever bond at all."

The raven's beak opened, and a low, croaking sound emerged—not quite a caw, but something more melodic. Almost like laughter.

"What's her name?" Jackie asked, her voice barely above a whisper.

"She has none yet. The bonded bird receives its name from its master." Céline moved closer, her eyes bright with something that might have been respect. "It is traditional to choose something meaningful. A quality you wish to embody, or—"

A sudden commotion from the tree cut her off.

Another raven had taken flight—smaller than Jackie's, but no less striking. Its wings beat with frantic urgency as it swooped down from the branches, circling the dome in a wide, agitated arc.

Theo's hand moved instinctively toward his wand.

"Don't," Céline commanded, her voice sharp. "Movement will only—"

But the bird wasn't attacking.

It dove past Jackie, past Céline, past Theo—and landed directly on Draco's shoulder.

The silence that followed was absolute.

Draco stood frozen in the doorway, his face a mask of shock. The raven settled against his neck with a proprietary air, its talons gripping the fabric of his shirt, its golden eyes fixed on his profile with unmistakable intent.

"That's..." Céline's composure cracked for the first time. She stared at Draco as though he'd sprouted a second head. "That's not possible. He wasn't presented. He wasn't vetted. The birds don't choose outsiders—"

The raven on Draco's shoulder made a sound that could only be described as smug.

"Apparently," Theo said dryly, "this one disagrees."

Draco hadn't moved. He barely seemed to be breathing. His eyes found Jackie's across the dome, wide with something between terror and wonder.

The transition from the clinical, stone-hewn interior to the grand aviary was a shock of silver and light. *Yeah, well…* Jackie started to snap back with a sharp retort, but then she caught herself. He was entirely right. She had married him knowing full well how power-hungry he was; in truth, she loved that edge in him. It was the iron that met her own. *I walked right into that one, didn't I?*
She let the bond go quiet as Céline led them toward the smaller alcove. Jackie studied the bonded birds, her mind spinning with the implications. These were the messengers of the elite—the silent, winged keepers of Europe's most dangerous secrets. She thought of her father, Cyrus; he had coveted a Lavigne raven for decades, a status symbol he was never deemed worthy to possess. It was one of the many bitter seeds that had grown into his hatred for her mother's family. When Céline declared that Jackie was to be given one, her breath hitched. Her mouth parted slightly, and she had to physically clamp her jaw shut to avoid looking completely undone. Had her morning gone differently—had she still been drowning in the guilt of her "weakness"—she would have felt like a fraud. But after the raw honesty in the dueling room, she felt a strange, steadying resolve. She wasn't a Lavigne by name, and she never had been, but here, blood spoke louder than any signature. "I am honored, Madame Renoir," Jackie said, inclining her head with a crispness that mirrored Céline’s own. She offered no further gratitude. Lavignes took what was theirs with grace, never with groveling. She followed Céline through the heavy silk curtain into a transition chamber—a narrow, utilitarian space holding racks of specialized feed and various iron utensils. The air here smelled of dried grain and well-oiled leather. Céline pulled a thick, scarred leather glove from a hook and handed it to Jackie. "You should put this on," she advised, her voice dropping to a low, expectant hum. She gestured to a heavy oak door. "Go out first. We will follow. Walk to the center and wait. If one chooses you, it will come."
Céline turned a heavy silver key in the lock and pushed the door open.

The minutes stretched like taffy.

Jackie stood motionless beneath the bone-white tree, acutely aware of every rustle, every shift of feathers above her. The ravens watched with that uncanny intelligence, heads tilting in unison as though conducting some silent assessment she couldn't perceive. A few of the younger birds hopped along their branches, curious but uncommitted. One opened its beak in a soft, croaking call that echoed through the dome.

None descended.

Behind her, she heard Céline's measured breathing, the faint creak of leather as Theo shifted his weight. Through the bond, she felt his attention—sharp, watchful, but carefully neutral. He wasn't worried. He was *waiting*.

Then—movement.

A raven detached from a high branch, wings spreading wide as it glided down in a lazy spiral. It was smaller than some of the others, sleek and elegant, with feathers that caught the filtered light like polished pearl. It landed on a low branch at Jackie's eye level, regarding her with solemn consideration.

Jackie extended her gloved hand slowly.

The raven hopped closer. Closer still. Its golden eyes bored into hers with an intensity that felt almost like recognition.

And then it turned away.

Jackie blinked, a flicker of surprise cutting through her composure. The raven launched itself from the branch—not toward her, but *past* her, winging toward the entrance where the others stood.

"Extraordinary," Céline breathed.

The raven landed on Draco's shoulder.

Draco went rigid, his face draining of color. The bird was *heavy*—he could feel the grip of its talons through his shirt, the warm weight of its body settling against the curve of his neck. Its beak was inches from his ear, and when it turned its head to examine him, one pale gold eye filled his entire field of vision.

"Don't move," Céline commanded, her voice sharp with something that sounded almost like alarm. "Don't—"

But the raven had already made its decision.

It pressed its head against Draco's jaw—a gesture that was unmistakably, impossibly *affectionate*—and let out a low, warbling croon. The sound vibrated through his chest, resonant and strange.

"That's not possible," Céline said. She had crossed the space without Jackie noticing, her composure cracked for the first time since they'd met. "The unbonded birds are presented only to vetted candidates. They don't choose outsiders. They *can't*—the breeding ensures—"

The raven turned to look at her.

It was, Jackie thought with a wild surge of inappropriate amusement, the most disdainful expression she had ever seen on any creature. The bird ruffled its feathers pointedly, then returned its attention to Draco, nibbling gently at a strand of his platinum hair.

"I think," Theo said slowly, his voice carefully controlled despite the laughter Jackie could feel bubbling through the bond, "that someone forgot to inform the bird of the rules."

Draco hadn't moved. He stood frozen, barely breathing, as though any sudden motion might shatter whatever strange magic was unfolding.

"What do I do?" he asked, his voice barely above a whisper.

The raven answered for him.

It spread its wings—wider than seemed possible for its frame—and let out a cry that echoed through the dome like a bell. The other ravens responded, a chorus of calls rising and falling in what sounded almost like *approval*.

Then it settled more firmly onto his shoulder, tucking its wings with an air of absolute finality.

*Mine*, the gesture said. *This one is mine.*

Céline stood in stunned silence, her careful mask stripped away to reveal something raw—not anger, Jackie realized, but *wonder*. As though she were witnessing something she'd only ever read about in the Network's oldest records.

"In four hundred years," she said finally, her voice hushed, "this has happened exactly three times. A raven choosing someone outside the bloodline. Outside the vetting." She looked at Draco with new eyes—assessing, recalculating. "The last was in 1847."

Draco swallowed hard. "What does it mean?"

"It means, Monsieur Malfoy, that you have been claimed by a creature that answers to no authority but its own." Céline's mouth curved into something that was almost a smile. "It means this bird looked at you and saw something worth bonding to for the rest of its life."

The raven settled on Jackie's wrist with the weight of inevitability.

Theo watched from the doorway, something tightening in his chest. Through the bond, he felt the echo of that ancient recognition—not his own, but Jackie's, bleeding through despite her shields. The bird had chosen her with the certainty of a predator selecting its territory.

*Mine.*

Beside him, Draco stood transfixed. His gray eyes tracked the magnificent creature, something unreadable flickering across his features—not jealousy, exactly, but a hollow sort of longing. The look of a man accustomed to standing on the outside of extraordinary things.

Céline had gone very still.

"Magnificent," she breathed, and for the first time, her composure cracked into genuine awe. "That is Éclipse. She has refused every candidate we've presented for the last seventeen years. We had begun to believe she would die unbonded."

The raven—Éclipse—mantled her wings once, a display of ownership that seemed to encompass not just Jackie but the entire dome. Her pale gold eyes swept the room with imperial disdain.

Then they landed on Draco.

The bird's head tilted. Sharp. Assessing.

Draco froze.

"Monsieur Malfoy," Céline said slowly, her voice carrying an odd note of warning, "I would advise you not to—"

But Éclipse had already launched herself from Jackie's wrist.

The movement was so sudden that Theo barely tracked it—a blur of white feathers and ancient purpose, crossing the dome in three powerful wingbeats. Draco stumbled backward, his hand flying up instinctively, and Éclipse landed on his bare forearm with a grip that made him hiss through his teeth.

Blood welled immediately. The raven's talons had pierced skin.

But Éclipse didn't attack. She *settled*. Her wings folded with deliberate precision, and she fixed Draco with that same terrifying, knowing stare.

*Mine.*

The silence in the dome was absolute.

Céline's face had drained of color. She stood rigid, her hands clenched at her sides, visibly struggling to process what she had just witnessed.

The Director seemed to be cycling through several stages of crisis simultaneously. Her jaw worked. Her hands unclenched, then clenched again. Finally, she drew a long, steadying breath.

"The bond is irrevocable," she said, her voice regaining some of its former crispness, though a tremor lurked beneath. "Once a raven chooses, it cannot be undone. The bird serves its master until death." She looked at Draco with an expression that mixed horror with reluctant respect. "It appears, Monsieur Malfoy, that you have been... claimed."

"I didn't—" Draco started.

"It does not matter what you did or did not do." Céline cut him off, though not unkindly. "The ravens see what we cannot. They choose based on qualities invisible to human perception. If Éclipse has selected you, then she has seen something in you worth serving."

She paused, her gaze sharpening.

"Though I confess, I am... curious what that might be. You are not Lavigne blood. You are not even French. And yet—"

Éclipse ruffled her feathers pointedly and fixed Céline with a glare of such withering contempt that the Director actually took a step back.

Theo bit the inside of his cheek to keep from laughing.

The transition from the clinical, stone-hewn interior to the grand aviary was a shock of silver and light. *Yeah, well…* Jackie started to snap back with a sharp retort, but then she caught herself. He was entirely right. She had married him knowing full well how power-hungry he was; in truth, she loved that edge in him. It was the iron that met her own. *I walked right into that one, didn't I?*
She let the bond go quiet as Céline led them toward the smaller alcove. Jackie studied the bonded birds, her mind spinning with the implications. These were the messengers of the elite—the silent, winged keepers of Europe's most dangerous secrets. She thought of her father, Cyrus; he had coveted a Lavigne raven for decades, a status symbol he was never deemed worthy to possess. It was one of the many bitter seeds that had grown into his hatred for her mother's family. When Céline declared that Jackie was to be given one, her breath hitched. Her mouth parted slightly, and she had to physically clamp her jaw shut to avoid looking completely undone. Had her morning gone differently—had she still been drowning in the guilt of her "weakness"—she would have felt like a fraud. But after the raw honesty in the dueling room, she felt a strange, steadying resolve. She wasn't a Lavigne by name, and she never had been, but here, blood spoke louder than any signature. "I am honored, Madame Renoir," Jackie said, inclining her head with a crispness that mirrored Céline’s own. She offered no further gratitude. Lavignes took what was theirs with grace, never with groveling. She followed Céline through the heavy silk curtain into a transition chamber—a narrow, utilitarian space holding racks of specialized feed and various iron utensils. The air here smelled of dried grain and well-oiled leather. Céline pulled a thick, scarred leather glove from a hook and handed it to Jackie. "You should put this on," she advised, her voice dropping to a low, expectant hum. She gestured to a heavy oak door. "Go out first. We will follow. Walk to the center and wait. If one chooses you, it will come."
Céline turned a heavy silver key in the lock and pushed the door open.

Jackie stepped out and felt the sudden, sharp whistle of the wind through the structure. The aviary was a masterpiece of Victorian-inspired engineering—a massive, soaring dome that mirrored a winter garden, though the glass had been replaced by a shimmering, fine-gauge silver wire mesh. In the dead center of the rotunda stood a magnificent, ancient tree. It was entirely leafless, its gnarled branches bleached to a bone-white pallor that made it look like a skeletal sculpture against the sky. Dozens of ravens perched upon its limbs like heavy, feathered snowdrifts. As Jackie’s boots clicked against the gravel path, the silence of the dome was broken by the dry, rhythmic rustle of wings. A few of the younger birds startled, taking flight in a flurry of brilliant white before relocating to the higher cross-beams, but most simply watched her. Their pale gold eyes tracked her every movement with a chilling, sentient focus. The air was filled with the faint, metallic tang of the silver wire and the earthy scent of stone. Jackie reached the center of the dome, beneath the reach of the white tree, and stood still. She felt the heavy, watchful presence of Theo and Draco at the door behind her—a grounding weight in her mind. She waited. The ravens shifted, their beaks clacking like dice in a cup. For a long minute, nothing happened. Then, a shadow detached itself from the highest, most jagged branch of the bone-white tree.

The sound of its descent was heavy—a slow, powerful *whump-whump-whump* of wings that beat against the air with more force than any post owl. The bird landed on her gloved wrist with a jolt that nearly knocked her off balance, its talons digging deep into the thick leather. It was larger than the others, its feathers a pristine, blinding white that seemed to glow from within. It didn't look at her with curiosity; it stared into her eyes with a terrifying, ancient recognition.

*Mine,* the thought didn't come from the bond, but it felt just as clear.

Theo felt the moment the raven chose her.

It resonated through the bond like a struck bell—not Jackie's emotions, but something older, stranger. A recognition that predated language. He watched the massive bird settle on her wrist, its pale gold eyes boring into hers with an intensity that made the hair on his arms stand on end.

*Magnificent*, he thought, and meant both of them.

Beside him, Draco had gone very still.

Céline stood at Theo's other shoulder, her expression betraying nothing—but Theo caught the slight widening of her eyes, the almost imperceptible intake of breath. The bird that had chosen Jackie was clearly significant, though whether by size or lineage or some other metric, he couldn't say.

"Remarkable," Céline murmured. "That one has refused every candidate for three years. We had begun to think she would never bond."

A dry rustle of feathers drew Theo's attention upward.

One of the younger ravens had descended from its perch—not the dramatic, spiraling drop of Jackie's bird, but a slow, deliberate glide. It landed on the lowest branch of the bone-white tree, barely six feet from where they stood, and cocked its head at an almost comical angle.

It was looking at Draco.

"Madame Renoir," Theo said carefully, "is that bird supposed to be doing that?"

Céline turned. Her composure cracked—just for an instant, but enough.

"No," she said, her voice sharp with surprise. "The juveniles do not approach unbidden. They certainly do not approach *unvetted visitors*."

The raven hopped down another branch. Then another. Its movements were jerky, almost puppetish, but its eyes—those same pale gold eyes—were fixed on Draco with unwavering focus.

Draco hadn't moved. He stood frozen, one hand half-raised as though uncertain whether to defend himself or reach out.

"What do I do?" he asked, his voice barely above a whisper.

"Nothing," Céline said, though she didn't sound certain. "Do not move. Do not speak. Let it—"

The raven launched itself from the branch.

It crossed the distance in a single, powerful wingbeat and landed on Draco's shoulder—not his arm, his *shoulder*—talons gripping the fabric of his shirt hard enough to dimple the skin beneath. Draco flinched but held his ground, his breath coming fast and shallow.

The bird pressed its beak against his jaw. Not pecking. *Nuzzling*.

A sound escaped Céline that might have been a laugh in a less controlled woman.

"Well," she said, her voice carrying an edge of genuine bewilderment. "This has never happened before."

Theo stared at the tableau before him: Jackie in the center of the dome, a queen crowned by her pale familiar; Draco at the threshold, claimed by a bird that had no business claiming him.

*Of course*, he thought, something warm and wondering unfurling in his chest. *Of course the ravens would want them both.*

The juvenile on Draco's shoulder gave a soft, crooning sound—almost like a purr—and settled its wings against its body with an air of profound satisfaction.

Draco's eyes found Theo's, wide and slightly panicked.

"Is this... normal?" he managed.

"Nothing about either of you is normal," Theo replied dryly. "Why should this be any different?"

Céline had recovered her composure, though a faint line remained between her brows. She studied Draco with new interest—the sharp, calculating assessment of a woman recalibrating her understanding of a situation.

"The birds choose," she said slowly, as though reminding herself. "We present candidates, but the bond is theirs to make. This one—" She gestured to the juvenile on Draco's shoulder. "—has shown no interest in anyone since it hatched. We assumed it was simply... difficult."

"Difficult," Draco repeated flatly. "Wonderful. It sounds like we're perfect for each other."

The raven made a sound that was distinctly smug.

The moment the bond solidified, the air in the aviary seemed to hum. Jackie had never felt the need for a familiar at Hogwarts; the communal owls were functional, and the Nott family post-birds were efficient tools. She had never realized she was waiting for a soul-deep recognition until this weight—this living, breathing extension of herself—settled on her arm.
*Mine,* she projected, and the raven didn't just hear the thought; it absorbed it. The bird leaned in, its beak clicking softly against her ear, a gesture of terrifying intimacy.
Then, the shift in the atmosphere at the threshold caught her attention. She turned, her own raven shifting its weight with a heavy, rhythmic rustle of feathers to maintain its balance as Jackie moved. When she saw the juvenile claimed Draco, a slow, radiant smile spread across her face.
*First he charms the Lavignes with the piano, now he’s practically stolen one of their ravens,* she sent to Theo, her mental voice bright with pride. *Watch out, or they’ll want to have me remarried to ensure he stays.*
She crossed the gravel with a measured gait, discovering that her familiar was a master of its own gravity, its talons anchoring into her shoulder through the thin fabric of her top. The pain was sharp, a stinging reminder of the bird's lethal potential, but she welcomed it. It was a grounding cord to the present.
"Well, and here I was thinking I’d have my five minutes of glory," she said as she reached them. There was no heat in her voice, only a deep, resonant appreciation for the symmetry of the moment. She looked at Draco, who looked as though he were holding his breath for fear of offending the creature on his shoulder, then turned her gaze to Céline.
"Can we name them?"

Céline's expression flickered—a momentary crack in her professional composure that revealed something almost like amusement.

"Name them?" She repeated the question as though Jackie had asked if the sky was, in fact, blue. "Madame Nott, they are *yours* now. You may do with them as you wish—within reason."

She stepped closer, studying the juvenile on Draco's shoulder with renewed interest. The bird had settled into a posture of complete contentment, its head tucked against Draco's neck, one pale gold eye watching Céline with what could only be described as territorial suspicion.

"This one is from the spring clutch," Céline said, consulting some internal catalogue. "Hatched in April. Female. We had catalogued her as... recalcitrant."

"Recalcitrant," Draco echoed, his voice strained. "Is that Corvus Network terminology for 'bites everyone who approaches'?"

"Among other behaviors, yes."

Theo made a sound that was suspiciously close to a snort.

*A recalcitrant raven*, he sent to Jackie, his mental voice rich with barely contained laughter. *For a recalcitrant aristocrat. The universe has a sense of humor.*

Céline had turned her attention to Jackie's bird—the larger, older female who had descended from the highest branch.

"And this one," she said, her voice dropping into something almost reverent, "is Argent. The matriarch of the unbonded flock. She was hatched seventeen years ago and has refused every candidate since. We assumed she would die unbonded."

The raven—Argent—turned her head to fix Céline with a look of profound disdain, as though offended by the assumption.

"Of course," Céline added dryly, "she has always been particular."

"A family trait, perhaps," Theo observed, earning himself a sharp look from both women.

Draco's juvenile chose that moment to stretch her wings, nearly clipping his ear. He ducked instinctively, and the bird gave a croaking sound that was unmistakably laughter.

"She needs a name," Jackie said, watching the interplay with visible delight. "Something dignified. Something that suits a recalcitrant creature who chose a Malfoy."

Draco shot her a look of pure exasperation.

"I didn't *ask* to be chosen," he protested. "I was standing here minding my own business—"

"You were staring at them," Theo corrected mildly. "With that expression you get when you're cataloguing something for later acquisition."

"I was *appreciating their aesthetic value*—"

The juvenile nipped his ear. Not hard—just enough to make him yelp.

"She doesn't like excuses," Céline observed, a hint of genuine warmth creeping into her voice. "A good quality in a familiar. She will keep you honest."

She turned back to Jackie, her demeanor shifting into something more formal.

"You understand what this means," she said. "Both ravens—yours by right of bond. They will carry your correspondence, guard your secrets, and die before betraying you." A pause, weighted with significance. "The Network recognizes these bonds. You are now, both of you, under the protection of the Corvus covenant."

Her gaze slid to Theo, assessing.

"And you, Monsieur Nott? No bird has stirred for you."

Theo smiled—that particular smile that never quite reached his eyes.

"I'm not surprised," he said easily. "I suspect they recognize a predator when they see one. Why bond with something that might eat you?"

Argent made a sound that was distinctly unimpressed.

Céline studied him for a long moment, her expression unreadable. Then, unexpectedly, she laughed—a short, sharp sound that echoed off the silver mesh dome.

"You would have made an excellent addition to the Network, Monsieur Nott," she said. "In another life, perhaps."

"In another life," Theo agreed, "I might have accepted."

The moment stretched between them—two predators acknowledging each other across an invisible boundary.

Then Céline turned briskly back to Jackie.

"The birds will need to acclimate to your magical signatures before they can carry messages reliably. "I didn't *ask* to be chosen," he protested. "I was standing here minding my own business—"

"You were staring at them," Theo corrected mildly. "With that expression you get when you're cataloguing something for later acquisition."

"I was *appreciating their aesthetic value*—"

The juvenile nipped his ear. Not hard—just enough to make him yelp.

"She doesn't like excuses," Céline observed, a hint of genuine warmth creeping into her voice. "A good quality in a familiar. She will keep you honest."

She turned back to Jackie, her demeanor shifting into something more formal.

"You understand what this means," she said. "Both ravens—yours by right of bond. They will carry your correspondence, guard your secrets, and die before betraying you." A pause, weighted with significance. "The Network recognizes these bonds. You are now, both of you, under the protection of the Corvus covenant."

Her gaze slid to Theo, assessing.

"And you, Monsieur Nott? No bird has stirred for you."

Theo smiled—that particular smile that never quite reached his eyes.

"I'm not surprised," he said easily. "I suspect they recognize a predator when they see one. Why bond with something that might eat you?"

Argent made a sound that was distinctly unimpressed.

"You would have made an excellent addition to the Network, Monsieur Nott," she said. "In another life, perhaps."

Jackie was prepared to fight Céline, her grandmother, and the entire hierarchy of the Corvus Network if it came to it. It wasn't just because she believed the bird’s choice superseded tradition; it was because Draco looked truly awed by the creature, and the creature looked equally captivated by him. They deserved this. She knew that if anyone tried to strip her of her own raven right now, she would meet them with teeth and magic—she could only assume a similar, fierce connection was already forging between Draco and his bird.
"Thank you, Madame Renoir. I know this is unconventional," Jackie said, her voice steady and ringing with Lavigne authority. "But perhaps the bird recognized something that human laws fail to grasp."
She caught the Director's questioning gaze and added, reaching out to touch Draco’s hand gently. "He is mine. Therefore, he is not an outsider—not by any measure that matters to that raven, anyway."
They followed Céline back inside, retracing their steps through the alcove and the main aviary. As they walked, Jackie noticed the handlers and workers turning their heads, their tasks forgotten as they stared at Draco. The whispers started the moment their strange procession passed, a low hiss of French skimming across the stone floors.
*I’m just glad he was chosen, for once,* she sent to Theo, her heart swelling with a protective heat. *He might suspect people of deceiving him, but there is no deception in this. No faking a bond like that.*
Her raven looked around with a bored, regal disinterest. Jackie reached out again through the bond, just to confirm that the bird’s mind was still there in her periphery—a cold, sharp presence she could touch at will.
"Can we let them fly?" she asked as they neared the exit. "Will they find their way back to us even before we name them?"

Céline paused at the threshold, turning to regard Jackie with something that might have been approval.

"The bond is the anchor," she explained. "Once formed, distance is irrelevant. They will always find you—across continents, through wards, regardless of magical interference. That is what makes them invaluable."

She gestured toward the open sky visible through the mesh dome behind them.

"You may release them whenever you wish. They will hunt, explore, and return when called—or when they sense you need them." A thin smile crossed her lips. "Though I would advise against releasing them indoors. They become... irritable when confined unnecessarily."

Draco's raven chose that moment to nip at his ear—not hard enough to draw blood, but enough to make him flinch.

"Noted," he said dryly.

They emerged from the aviary into the bright midday sun, the heat a sharp contrast to the climate-controlled interior. Jackie's raven spread its wings briefly, catching the light until its feathers blazed like white fire, then settled back against her shoulder with a proprietary air.

Theo squinted against the glare, one hand shading his eyes.

"Lunch should be soon," he observed. "Unless the Lavignes expect us to subsist on awe and political maneuvering alone."

*He's deflecting*, Jackie felt through the bond—not words, but impression. The morning had been heavy; Theo was reaching for lightness the way a drowning man reached for air.

Draco had fallen into step beside them, his hand occasionally rising to touch the juvenile on his shoulder as though confirming it was still there. The bird tolerated this with remarkable patience, occasionally bumping its head against his fingers.

"I need to send word to the Ministry," Draco said, his tone thoughtful. "If I'm going to be receiving official Corvus Network documentation, there are... implications. Politically speaking."

"Implications," Theo repeated, amused. "You've been claimed by a French intelligence asset and you're worried about *paperwork*."

"I'm worried about the seventeen different ways this could be interpreted by people who already think I'm a security risk." Draco's voice was light, but something sharper lurked beneath. "A Malfoy with access to the Lavigne communication network? The *Prophet* will have a field day."

"Let them," Jackie said, her voice carrying an edge of steel. "You were chosen. That's not something that can be politicized away."

The path curved toward the main château, the formal gardens spreading out before them in geometric precision. Somewhere in the distance, a groundskeeper was trimming hedges with methodical wand-strokes.

Draco's raven suddenly launched itself from his shoulder, powerful wings carrying it upward in a spiraling climb. It circled once, twice, then arrowed toward the tree line with purposeful speed.

Draco stopped walking, his hand frozen mid-reach.

"Did I—was that—"

"Hunting," Céline's voice came from behind them; she had followed to see them off. "It will return within the hour. The bond is fresh; it needs to test its range."

She inclined her head to Jackie, then to Draco.

"The formal documentation will arrive this evening, as I said. In the meantime—" Her gaze swept over all three of them with that sharp, assessing quality. "—welcome to the Network. Both of you."

She turned and disappeared back into the aviary without another word.

Theo watched her go, then glanced at Jackie.

"I feel distinctly left out," he remarked. "You've both acquired magical spy-birds and I'm just... here. Holding metaphorical coats."

The sting was a ghost—there and gone before it could take root.

Theo's hands found her waist, pulling her closer with the casual possessiveness that came as naturally to him as breathing. Through the bond, she felt the truth of it: he wasn't jealous, not really. The ravens were tools, assets, symbols of a power structure he understood intimately. What mattered to him was simpler. *Her. Draco. This.*

"Own is a strong word," he murmured, his voice dropping to that low register that vibrated against her palms. "I prefer... *have custody of*. It sounds less feudal."

His thumb traced a lazy circle against her hip.

*Before*, he sent back, the thought rough-edged with intent. *Definitely before. Lunch can wait.*

Draco, who had been watching his raven disappear into the tree line with an expression of dazed wonder, turned back to find them practically wrapped around each other in the middle of the garden path.

"We're in public," he observed, though his tone carried no real censure. If anything, there was a thread of amusement beneath the aristocratic disapproval. "The groundskeeper is staring."

Theo didn't look away from Jackie.

"Let him."

"The *groundskeeper*, Theo. Who almost certainly reports to the kitchen staff, who report to the household manager, who reports to Francine, who reports to—"

"Geneviève. Yes. I'm aware of how information flows in this family." Theo's smile was sharp, unhurried. "Perhaps I want her to know."

Draco pinched the bridge of his nose.

"You're impossible. Both of you." But he was moving closer as he said it, drawn into their orbit despite his protests. "At least take it inside before you start a diplomatic incident."

Theo's hand extended toward him—an invitation, not a demand.

"Then come inside with us."

The words hung in the warm afternoon air, laden with more than their surface meaning. Draco's gaze dropped to Theo's outstretched hand, then lifted to meet his eyes. Something flickered between them—the echo of that morning, of hands pressed against chests and truths spoken in half-lit rooms.

Draco took his hand.

"Fine," he said, as though he were agreeing to something tedious rather than stepping willingly into their gravity. "But we're eating *eventually*. I refuse to face the American cousins on an empty stomach."

"Own is a strong word," he murmured, his voice dropping to that low register that vibrated against her palms. "I prefer... *have custody of*. It sounds less feudal."

His thumb traced a lazy circle against her hip.

*Before*, he sent back, the thought rough-edged with intent. *Definitely before. Lunch can wait.*

Draco, who had been watching his raven disappear into the tree line with an expression of dazed wonder, turned back to find them practically wrapped around each other in the middle of the garden path.

"We're in public," he observed, though his tone carried no real censure. If anything, there was a thread of amusement beneath the aristocratic disapproval. "The groundskeeper is staring."

Theo didn't look away from Jackie.

"Let him."

"The *groundskeeper*, Theo. Who almost certainly reports to the kitchen staff, who report to the household manager, who reports to Francine, who reports to—"

"Geneviève. Yes. I'm aware of how information flows in this family." Theo's smile was sharp, unhurried. "Perhaps I want her to know."

Draco pinched the bridge of his nose.

"You're impossible. Both of you." But he was moving closer as he said it, drawn into their orbit despite his protests. "At least take it inside before you start a diplomatic incident."

Theo's hand extended toward him—an invitation, not a demand.

"Then come inside with us."

The words hung in the warm afternoon air, laden with more than their surface meaning. Draco's gaze dropped to Theo's outstretched hand, then lifted to meet his eyes. Something flickered between them—the echo of that morning, of hands pressed against chests and truths spoken in half-lit rooms.

Draco took his hand.

"Fine," he said, as though he were agreeing to something tedious rather than stepping willingly into their gravity. "But we're eating *eventually*. I refuse to face the American cousins on an empty stomach."

Theo watched her walk away, his pulse a steady drumbeat beneath his skin.

*No*, he sent back, the thought unhesitating. *It doesn't stop. It just... changes shape. Deepens.*

His hand was still wrapped around Draco's, their fingers intertwined with an ease that would have been unthinkable mere days ago. He felt Draco's grip tighten—not pulling away, but anchoring.

"She's doing that on purpose," Draco muttered, his eyes fixed on Jackie's retreating figure. His voice was strained in a way that had nothing to do with irritation.

"Obviously."

"And you're just going to let her?"

Theo turned his head, catching Draco's gaze with a look of pure, predatory amusement.

"I'm going to *follow* her," he corrected. "And so are you. Unless you'd prefer to stay out here and discuss horticulture with the groundskeeper."

He tugged Draco forward, falling into step behind Jackie with the unhurried confidence of a man who knew exactly where this path led.

The château's shadow fell across them as they approached the entrance, the ancient stone cool against the midday heat. Somewhere above, a window stood open; the faint sound of a harp drifted down—Elodie, perhaps, practicing in one of the upper rooms.

"The American cousins arrive before dinner," Draco said, his voice pitched low enough that only Theo could hear. "We have perhaps... three hours."

"Three hours," Theo repeated, savoring the words. "That's remarkably generous."

"It's remarkably *insufficient*, given the morning we've had."

Theo's laugh was soft, dark, genuine.

"Then we'd better not waste any of it."

They crossed the threshold together, the heavy doors swinging shut behind them with a resonant *thud*. The corridor stretched ahead—cool, shadowed, empty save for Jackie's silhouette disappearing around a distant corner.

Draco's hand remained in his.

Neither of them let go.

Jackie walked ahead, the cool of the château’s interior a stark, refreshing contrast to the sun-drenched gardens. She didn't look back, but she could feel them—a twin weight of focus on her spine that made her skin hum. She navigated the corridors with a predator’s grace, her boots silent on the runner, until she reached their suite and pushed the heavy oak doors open.
The room was flooded with the soft, golden light of high noon, and the scent of the gardens had been replaced by something savory.
Colette—or perhaps another silent servant—had already been there. A small table near the window was laid with crisp white linen and silver. Three bowls of creamy onion soup topped with golden-brown croutons sat steaming beside a large, vibrant garden salad tossed with herbs. It was a lunch designed for a summer day: light enough to sustain, but heavy enough to anchor.
Jackie stopped mid-step, her hand still lingering on the doorframe. The suggestive sway of her hips faltered as she looked from the steam rising off the soup to the two men entering behind her.
"We should eat first," she said, her voice dropping the sultry edge for something more grounded.
She waited for a beat, expecting Theo to argue, to pull her toward the bedroom with the raw hunger she’d felt through the bond just moments ago. But when her gaze shifted to Draco, she saw the subtle drop of his shoulders—a genuine, quiet relief. Whether it was the absence of an audience or the simple, domestic normalcy of a meal, the tension that had gripped him since the aviary seemed to slacken.
*Food first, then,* she sent through the bond, a soft, yielding thought. *The hunger isn't going anywhere.*
Seeing that the decision was made, Jackie didn't wait for a verbal confirmation. She crossed the room and sat, the silk of her leggings whispering against the chair’s velvet upholstery.
"Sit," she commanded, though it was softened by a smile as she picked up her spoon. "Before Draco starts lecturing us on the proper temperature of onion soup."

Theo's protest died on his lips the moment he saw the table.

The soup was a golden masterpiece—caramelized onions swimming beneath a lake of melted Gruyère, the croutons toasted to that precise shade of amber that crackled when touched. The salad glistened with a light vinaigrette, herbs scattered across its surface like confetti.

His stomach, which had apparently been waiting for permission, growled audibly.

"Traitor," he muttered to his own body, but he was already moving toward the table.

Draco settled into his chair with considerably more grace, unfolding his napkin with the practiced precision of a man who'd been trained to dine with royalty since before he could walk. He surveyed the spread with an appraising eye.

"The bread is fresh," he observed, reaching for a small basket tucked beside the salad. "Still warm. Someone's been watching the kitchens' timing."

"Or someone's been watching *us*," Theo countered, lifting his spoon. "The Lavignes seem to know where we are at all times. It's either impressive or deeply unsettling."

"Both," Draco said. "Always both, with this family."

The first spoonful of soup was transcendent—rich, deeply savory, the cheese pulling in long strings that required careful maneuvering. Theo made an involuntary sound of appreciation that he would later deny.

Draco smirked. "Eloquent."

"Shut up and eat your soup."

"I'm *savoring* it. There's a difference." Draco broke off a piece of bread, using it to soak up some of the broth. "The French understand that food is an experience, not merely fuel. It's one of their few redeeming qualities."

Theo raised an eyebrow. "Few?"

"Their bureaucracy is nightmarish, their wine snobbery is insufferable, and they've never met a pastry they couldn't overcomplicate." Draco paused, chewing thoughtfully. "But they do make excellent soup."

"High praise from the man who once sent back a steak at the Leaky Cauldron because it was 'aggressively mediocre.'"

"It *was* aggressively mediocre. The cook should have been ashamed."

Theo snorted, reaching for the salad. The greens were crisp, the herbs bright—mint, he thought, and something more delicate. Chervil, perhaps.

"The American cousins," Draco said, his tone shifting to something more contemplative. "What do we know about them?"

"Sons and daughter of Geneviève's brother. He runs the Lavigne operations in the States—New York, primarily, with satellite interests in New Orleans and San Francisco." Theo speared a tomato with his fork. "Less bound by French tradition, according to the household whispers. More direct."

"More direct," Draco repeated flatly. "Wonderful. Because what this week needed was *more* people asking pointed questions about our arrangement."

"You could always hide in the library."

"I could. But then I'd miss watching you charm them with your legendary social graces."

Theo's smile was sharp. "I don't charm. I *assess*. There's a difference."

"Ah, yes. The predator's approach to polite conversation." Draco reached for his wine—a light rosé that had been poured alongside the meal. "Remind me again why I find that attractive?"

"Because you have terrible taste."

"Clearly." But Draco's eyes were warm as he said it, lingering on Theo for a moment longer than strictly necessary.

The meal continued in easy rhythm—soup giving way to salad, bread torn and shared, wine sipped between bites of casual conversation. They debated the merits of French versus English magical education (Draco insisted Beauxbatons produced better theorists; Theo argued that Hogwarts produced better survivors). They speculated about whether Colette would ever recover from her mortification (unlikely) and whether the groundskeeper had indeed reported their garden indiscretion to the household network (almost certainly).

By the time the last crouton had been consumed, the tension of the morning had settled into something quieter. Not forgotten—never forgotten—but integrated. Metabolized alongside the soup.

Draco leaned back in his chair, his fingers wrapped loosely around the stem of his wine glass.

"The raven," he said, his voice softer now. "I still don't quite believe it happened."

Theo set down his napkin. "It happened. I watched a bird that hadn't bonded in three years practically throw itself at you. The handlers looked like they'd witnessed a minor miracle."

It was a mercy to simply be allowed the silence. After the jagged morning in the dueling room, Jackie found a profound relief in not having to manage them, not having to dance around their expectations or curate the atmosphere. She occasionally caught herself drifting into "the old days," comparing the sharp, guarded armor of their first year together to the lived-in intimacy of this table. It was a far kinder mental exercise than dwelling on her perceived weaknesses, so she leaned into it. She finished her soup and settled into the salad, her mind—usually a racing, high-alert thing—finally beginning to go still. Halfway through the greens, her bare feet found Theo’s leg under the table. She had kicked off her boots the moment they’d crossed the threshold; the midday heat was far too oppressive for heavy leather. She began a slow, rhythmic stroke against his ankle, her toes tracing the line of his calf with a single-minded focus that stood in stark contrast to the polite way she speared her cherry tomatoes. She took a slow sip of the chilled rosé, her gaze shifting to Draco. "Theo isn't wrong. The bird chose you, but we don't have to frame it as an accident of fate. If the Malfoy name is publicly tied to the Lavignes—even through a 'gift' as small as a familiar—it could work in your favor. It might crack open the doors your father slammed shut by following Voldemort. Of course, that will also make people talk. It will make them jealous."
She paused, a sharp, knowing glint in her eyes. "Power always does. They’ll spread rumors, Draco. You have to be prepared for the noise."
The thought triggered a memory, one that tasted as bitter as the arugula on her fork. "Did either of you hear the rumors about me during those five months? When I retreated from the world?" She sipped the wine again, her expression neutral but her voice carrying a dry edge. "I imagine you must have heard at least one. The one where I’d grown bored with the both of you and eloped with a faceless stranger?

Or the more popular one—that one of you had knocked me up, and since we didn't know which, you’d sent me away to hide the scandal?"
She shrugged, popping a tomato into her mouth and meeting Draco’s eyes with a steady, unblinking clarity. "Rumors are just noise. The less attention you pay them, the shorter their lifespan. Don't let a bird's choice become a burden just because the Ministry can't fathom it."

He set the fork down with deliberate care.

"I heard the pregnancy rumor," he said, his voice dry. "Blaise Zabini cornered me at a Ministry function and asked, with entirely too much sincerity, whether I needed recommendations for discreet midwives in Switzerland."

Draco choked on his wine.

"*Switzerland*?"

"Apparently it's where respectable pureblood families send their inconvenient heirs to gestate." Theo's mouth curved. "I told him we were considering the French Riviera instead. Better climate for scandal."

"You didn't."

"I absolutely did. His face was magnificent."

Draco pressed his fingers to his temples, caught somewhere between horror and reluctant amusement. "And people wonder why we have a reputation."

"We have a reputation because we're interesting." Theo reached for his wine, his ankle pressing back against Jackie's foot in silent acknowledgment. "The rumors about you, specifically, were considerably less creative. Mostly variations on 'Malfoy's finally shown his true colors' and 'the war hero's wife has come to her senses.'"

His tone was light, but something sharper lurked beneath.

"I may have... discouraged some of the more persistent gossips."

"Discouraged," Draco repeated flatly.

"Strongly discouraged. With words." A pause. "Mostly words."

Draco studied him for a moment, then sighed. "I don't want to know, do I?"

"Probably not."

The afternoon light had shifted, casting long shadows across the table. Draco set down his glass, his expression growing more contemplative.

"The bird isn't what concerns me," he admitted, his voice quieter now. "Not really. It's what it represents. Another tie to something larger than myself. Another... claim."

His gaze dropped to his left forearm—covered by his sleeve, but the Mark beneath was a constant presence, a brand that would never fully fade.

"Probably not."

The afternoon light had shifted, casting long shadows across the table. Draco set down his glass, his expression growing more contemplative.

"The bird isn't what concerns me," he admitted, his voice quieter now. "Not really. It's what it represents. Another tie to something larger than myself. Another... claim."

His gaze dropped to his left forearm—covered by his sleeve, but the Mark beneath was a constant presence, a brand that would never fully fade.

The silence that followed was deafening.

Theo, who had been drifting somewhere between sleep and wakefulness, went utterly still. His eyes opened slowly, fixing on the ceiling with the careful blankness of a man who had just heard a trap spring shut and was calculating his odds of escape.

Draco made a sound that might have been a laugh, might have been a choke, might have been his soul attempting to leave his body.

"I'm sorry," Draco said, his voice pitched slightly higher than usual. "Did you just ask us to explain the *logistics* of—"

"She knows how it works," Theo cut in, his tone flat. "She's asking something else."

He sat up slowly, swinging his legs off the armchair and planting his feet on the floor. His forearms came to rest on his knees, and he studied Jackie with the same careful intensity he might bring to a contract riddled with hidden clauses.

"You're asking about the curse," he said. It wasn't a question.

The Maledictus bloodline. The thing that had stolen Amalthea, that had haunted Jackie's childhood, that lurked in her veins like a sleeping serpent. The reason Geneviève's gaze sometimes lingered on Jackie's stomach with something that looked like dread.

Draco had gone pale.

"The curse only passes through the female line," he said slowly, his analytical mind clicking into gear despite the obvious discomfort. "Historically, it's been daughters who inherit. Sons are... carriers, potentially, but not afflicted."

"Historically," Theo repeated, the word weighted with skepticism. "Meaning the sample size is limited and the magic is poorly understood."

"Meaning we don't *know*," Draco admitted. "Not with certainty. The Maledictus curse is one of the oldest and least documented blood maledictions. Most families who carried it died out centuries ago. The Taylor line is one of the last—"

He stopped himself, his jaw tightening.

"Jackie's line," he corrected quietly. "One of the last."

Theo's gaze hadn't left Jackie's face.

"You broke the active curse," he said. "The wolf. But the bloodline remains. Any daughter—"

He didn't finish. He didn't need to.

The afternoon light felt heavier now, pressing down on the room like a physical weight. Somewhere outside, a bird called—not a raven, something smaller and more ordinary.

Draco leaned forward in his chair, his elbows on his knees, mirroring Theo's posture.

"Is this something you're... considering?" His voice was careful, stripped of its usual sardonic edge. "Or is this theoretical? Academic curiosity?"

The question hung in the warm air, fragile as glass.

Jackie didn't open her eyes as their voices washed over her, though the shift in the room's temperature was palpable. She hadn’t been thinking about the silver-white wolf or the jagged history of her grandfather's lineage when she spoke. To her, the curse was a beast they had already slain, a door they had kicked shut and locked behind them. If it was broken, it was gone. That was the logic she had used to keep herself whole.
But as their clinical, pureblood reasoning filled the silence—the talk of bloodlines, carriers, and limited sample sizes—the sturdy foundation of her certainty began to hairline-fracture. A small, wounded sound escaped the back of her throat, half-gasp and half-protest.
She finally opened her eyes, but she didn't turn to meet their heavy, searching gazes. Instead, she stared fixedly at the intricate molding of the ceiling, watching a sunbeam crawl across a painted cherub.
"Thanks," she said, her voice sounding thin and brittle in the quiet suite. "A minute ago, I was certain I wouldn't be able to pass it on if we broke it. Now? Now I’m not so sure."
The implication hung between the three of them, heavy as a funeral shroud. When she had asked the question, it hadn't been an academic inquiry into the mechanics of a blood malediction. It had been something else entirely—a stray, impulsive thought born of a full stomach and the safety of their presence.

Theo moved first.

He crossed the space between the armchair and the settee in three strides, lowering himself onto the edge of the cushion near her hip. His hand found hers—not grasping, just resting, his thumb tracing a slow, grounding circle against her palm.

"We don't know," he said quietly. "That's the truth. We don't know if breaking the active curse severed the bloodline entirely, or if it only freed *you*."

His voice was steady, but through the bond she felt the undercurrent—not fear, not quite, but a fierce, protective urgency. The same instinct that had driven him to learn healing spells at thirteen, to stitch himself back together in the dark. *Fix it. Find the answer. Protect what's mine.*

"But not knowing isn't the same as knowing the worst," he continued. "It means we have questions that need answers. Research. Experts. The Lavignes have archives older than the Ministry—Céline mentioned them. And there are scholars who specialize in blood maledictions. The woman in Prague that Filippo mentioned—"

"Věra Horáková," Draco supplied, his voice rough. He had risen from his chair and now stood at the foot of the settee, his arms crossed tightly over his chest. The posture was defensive, but his eyes were soft with something that looked like grief. "She's studied Maledictus curses for decades. If anyone would know whether breaking the active manifestation affects inheritance..."

He trailed off, his jaw working.

"I'm sorry," he said abruptly. "I shouldn't have—we shouldn't have turned this into a lecture on magical genealogy. That wasn't what you were asking."

Theo's thumb stilled against Jackie's palm.

"What *were* you asking?" he said, the question gentle. No pressure. No demand. Just an opening, if she wanted to take it.

The afternoon light continued its slow crawl across the ceiling. The painted cherub gazed down at them with serene, oblivious eyes—a relic of an era when the future was someone else's problem.

Draco moved closer, sinking onto the arm of the settee near Jackie's feet. His hand came to rest on her ankle, a warm, anchoring weight.

"Whatever it was," he said softly, "whatever you were thinking before we... complicated it. You can still say it. We're listening."

Jackie sat up slowly, the movement fluid but deliberate. She pulled her hand back from Theo’s grounding touch, her gaze finally snapping away from the ceiling to meet theirs. The sudden, intense focus of their protective instincts was a physical weight in the room, and she felt the familiar prickle of her own defenses rising to meet it.
"Okay, you both need to back off," she said, her voice regaining its sharp, characteristic edge. "You’re suffocating me like that, and I can't think straight when you’re both hovering like I’m made of glass."
She waited, her expression unyielding, until they retreated. Theo shifted back into his armchair, his posture still alert but less intrusive; Draco moved from the arm of the settee to his own seat, his hands resting on his knees. Only when they had settled into their respective spaces did she relax, though only slightly. She remained halfway reclined on the sofa, propping her elbow against a pile of velvet pillows to support her head.
"I was asking," she started, her eyes moving between them, "how it would work. Between the three of us."
She let the words hang in the air for a moment, letting the clinical talk of bloodlines dissipate.
"I’m working under the assumption that the curse *is* broken. That it’s dead. I’ve never given it much thought in the past because my life was... occupied. I was cursed, then I was broken. Then I was kidnapped, and broken again. I’ve been too consumed with just surviving to consider anything beyond the next week."
She shifted her weight, her gaze softening as she looked at them both—the two men who had become her world while she wasn't looking.
"I know I’ve asked you both separately, in the abstract, if children were something you even thought about. But those were private conversations, tucked away in the dark. With the relationship we have now... the way we actually *live*... we need to talk about it together. I think."
She exhaled, the last of the tension leaving her lungs.

The silence that followed was different from the one before.

Not heavy with dread, but weighted with something else—the particular stillness of two men recalibrating, shifting gears from crisis mode to something far more uncertain. *Hope*, perhaps. Or the terrifying possibility of it.

Draco spoke first, which surprised no one more than himself.

"I never thought I'd have children."

The admission came out rough, almost reluctant, as though the words had been pried from somewhere deep. He stared at his hands, fingers laced loosely together, not meeting anyone's eyes.

"Not because I didn't want them—though I told myself that, for a while. It was easier than admitting the truth." He swallowed. "I didn't think I deserved them. I didn't think I'd be... safe. That I wouldn't become my father, eventually. That the rot in the Malfoy line would find its way into me, and I'd pass it on like a second inheritance."

His jaw tightened.

"Then I left. And when I came back, I'd stopped thinking about the future entirely. I was focused on earning back what I'd lost. Proving I could stay." A ghost of a smile, bitter at the edges. "Children seemed like something that happened to other people. People with cleaner histories."

Theo had gone very still in his chair.

"I assumed I'd have them," he said, his voice carefully neutral. "Not because I wanted them, but because it was expected. The Nott line required an heir. That was the arrangement—marry, produce offspring, continue the legacy." His lip curled slightly. "I was raised to view children as... assets. Continuations of power. Bargaining chips for future alliances."

He looked at Jackie then, and something in his expression cracked open.

"I never thought about what it would mean to *want* one. To choose it, with someone I—" He stopped. Started again. "With people I actually love."

The word hung in the air—*love*—still rare enough on Theo's tongue that it carried weight.

"The mechanics are... complicated," he admitted. "Three people. One biological father, presumably, unless we're delving into experimental magic I'd rather not contemplate. Legally, socially, it would raise questions we'd have to answer."

And then, when I found out about the dowry clause—the idea of bringing a life into the world just to trigger a payout... it was wrong on so many levels. I was ready to spend the rest of my life in a courtroom just to spite that requirement. Then I was depressed, and then I was traveling, just trying to find the pieces of myself, and the future felt like a country I wasn't allowed to visit."
She looked up, her eyes moving to Theo before settling on Draco. She held his gaze for a long moment, her expression softening. "And then I saw you at St. Mungo’s," she said softly. "In the long-term ward, with those children. You were... different with them. The way you looked at them, the way you spoke—it changed something in me. It made me actually entertain the thought, not as a clause in a will, but as a reality."
She looked back down at the pillow, the silken strands now a tangled mess in her hand. "But you’re both right; it’s a nightmare logistically. If Draco were the father, the child would be a Malfoy bastard. In our world, I don't know if there's anything socially lower—no offense, Draco, but we know how the Wizengamot thinks. If it were Theo’s, the lineage would be 'neater' on paper, but then Cassius would likely spend his remaining breaths calling the legitimacy into question just to be spiteful, or find a way to disinherit the child entirely."

The room seemed to hold its breath.

Draco's hands had stilled on his knees, his knuckles white against the dark fabric of his trousers. He looked like a man who had just been handed something precious and fragile—something he was terrified of dropping.

"St. Mungo's," he repeated softly, almost to himself. "I didn't know you saw that."

He'd been volunteering in the long-term ward for months by then—a penance, he'd told himself at first, a way to prove he was more than the Mark on his arm. But somewhere between reading stories to children who couldn't sleep and holding the hands of parents who'd run out of hope, it had become something else entirely. Something that filled the hollow places his father's legacy had carved.

"The blood doesn't matter," he said, the words coming slowly, as though he were testing their weight. "I thought it did, once. I was raised to believe it was the *only* thing that mattered. But I've spent the last two years unlearning everything my father taught me, and this—"

He looked at Theo, then back at Jackie.

"A child raised by the three of us would be *ours*. In every way that counts. I don't need a Healer's confirmation to know that. I don't need the Wizengamot's blessing." His voice hardened slightly. "And I certainly don't need my father's ghost weighing in from Azkaban."

Theo had been silent, his expression unreadable. But something shifted in his posture—a subtle loosening, as though a knot he'd been holding had finally come undone.

"My father's opinion," he said quietly, "stopped mattering to me the night I healed my own broken hand in a bathroom and realized no one was coming to save me."

He leaned forward, his elbows on his knees, his gaze fixed on the floor between his feet.

"I don't know how to be a father. I have no model for it—at least, not one I'd ever want to replicate. The thought of holding something that small, that fragile, something that would look to me for guidance and protection..." He exhaled slowly. "It terrifies me."

He lifted his head, and his eyes—pale and sharp and utterly honest—found Jackie's.

"All three of us."

The room seemed to hold its breath.

Draco's expression had shifted the moment Jackie mentioned St. Mungo's—a flicker of something unguarded crossing his features before he could mask it. The memory was clearly still vivid: the children's ward, the small faces looking up at him with an openness he hadn't earned, the way their trust had cracked something loose in his chest.

He hadn't known she'd seen that. Hadn't known it had mattered.

"A year," he repeated softly, as though testing the weight of the word. "That's... not abstract. That's a timeline."

"It's a possibility," Theo corrected, but his voice lacked its usual precision. Through the bond, Jackie felt the tremor beneath his composure—not fear, exactly, but something close to vertigo. The ground shifting beneath assumptions he'd carried for two decades.

"The blood doesn't matter."

Draco said it quietly, but with a certainty that surprised even himself. He leaned forward in his chair, elbows on his knees, his grey eyes intent on Jackie's face.

"I spent my entire childhood being told that blood was *everything*. That it defined worth, destiny, belonging. And I believed it, because believing it was easier than questioning my father." His jaw tightened. "But blood didn't make me worthy of anything. It didn't make me kind, or brave, or good. It just made me a Malfoy—and we both know what that name is worth now."

He glanced at Theo, something unspoken passing between them.

"If we—if there's ever a child—I don't need it to be *mine* in the biological sense. I need it to be *ours*. Raised by people who chose each other. Who chose *it*." His voice cracked, just slightly. "That's more than I ever had. More than either of us had."

Theo was quiet for a long moment.

Then he rose from his chair—not to hover, not to crowd, but to cross to the window. He stood with his back to them, silhouetted against the afternoon light, his hands braced on the sill.

"My father viewed me as an extension of himself," he said, his voice low. "A vessel for the Nott legacy. Everything I was—my magic, my mind, my body—existed to serve his vision of what the family should become. I was never... *me*. I was just the next iteration."

He turned, leaning back against the window frame, his arms crossed over his chest.

A pause. Something flickered across his features—vulnerability, quickly suppressed.

"And yes. To answer the question you were actually asking." He swallowed. "The blood doesn't matter. I would raise Draco's child as my own without hesitation. I would raise *any* child we chose together as my own. Because family isn't about lineage. It's about who shows up. Who stays."

His gaze moved to Draco, holding there for a weighted moment.

"We've already proven that, haven't we? The three of us. We're not bound by blood or contract anymore. We're bound by choice. A child would just be... another choice. Made together."

The afternoon light had begun its slow descent toward gold, shadows lengthening across the Persian carpet. Somewhere in the distance, a clock chimed the half-hour—a gentle reminder that the world continued to turn outside this room, indifferent to the seismic shifts happening within.

Draco let out a breath he hadn't realized he'd been holding.

"A year," he said again, but this time the word sounded different. Less like a deadline. More like a promise.

"I don't need to know," he said quietly.

The words seemed to surprise even him. He blinked, as though testing their weight, then repeated them with more certainty.

"I don't need to know whose it is. Biologically." His hands had unclenched, resting open on his knees. "If we're doing this—if we're actually *doing* this—then it's ours. All of ours. The same way this relationship is ours. Not divided into neat portions, not weighed and measured."

He looked at Theo, something fierce and vulnerable in his gaze.

"I spent my entire childhood being told that blood was everything. That lineage determined worth. That the Malfoy name was a sacred trust I was obligated to continue." His voice hardened. "And then I watched my father use that logic to justify serving a monster. To justify *everything*."

He shook his head slowly.

"I'm done letting blood dictate what matters. If we have a child—" The word caught slightly, as though he was still adjusting to saying it aloud. "—they'll be *ours*. Not a Malfoy heir. Not a Nott continuation. Ours."

Theo had been silent throughout, his expression unreadable. But something had shifted in his posture—a loosening, a release of tension he hadn't seemed aware he was carrying.

"The paternity question is a trap," he said finally. "Not between us—I don't think any of us would let it become that—but in how we'd be forced to frame it for the world. The Ministry would want documentation. The *Prophet* would want scandal. Our families' solicitors would want clarity for inheritance purposes."

He leaned forward, forearms on his knees.

The cold water—because of course he'd followed Theo's suggestion—had done its work on the most obvious evidence of his arousal, but the tension remained in his shoulders, in the tight line of his jaw.

"The American cousins," he said, clearly grasping for distraction. "What do we actually know about them? Beyond 'less formal' and 'more direct'?"

His voice was steadier now, slipping back into the analytical register that served as his armor. But his hands remained at his sides, carefully not touching her, and his breathing was just slightly too controlled to be natural.

In the main room, Theo had settled into one of the armchairs, his own glass of wine in hand. Through the bond, Jackie could feel his quiet amusement—and beneath it, something warmer. Pride, perhaps. Satisfaction at how far they'd all come from the fractured, uncertain thing they'd been a year ago.

*Don't torment him too badly*, he sent, though the thought carried no real admonishment. *He needs to be able to form sentences at dinner.*

A pause.

*Although watching him try might be entertaining.*

Draco took the soap.

His fingers brushed hers in the exchange—a brief, electric contact that made his breath catch despite the cold water. He stared at the bar for a moment as though it might contain instructions for navigating this particular minefield.

"You're right," he said finally, beginning to work the soap between his hands. "About why I chose to wait. About—all of it, really."

His palms found her shoulder blades, moving in slow, careful circles. The touch was deliberately clinical, deliberately restrained—a man walking a tightrope over a very long drop.

"I spent years convincing myself that wanting things was dangerous. That if I didn't need anything, nothing could be taken from me." His voice was quieter now, thoughtful rather than raw. "My father taught me that. Every time I showed enthusiasm for something—a book, a friendship, a bloody *hobby*—he found a way to use it against me. Leverage, he called it. Understanding what someone wants so you can control them."

His hands moved lower, tracing the line of her spine with a gentleness that belied the clinical intent.

"So I stopped wanting. Or I told myself I did. I performed indifference until it felt almost real." A pause. "And then I met you. Both of you. And suddenly I wanted things so badly it terrified me."

He reached her lower back, his thumbs pressing into the muscle on either side of her spine.

"The cruelty isn't in the edging," he admitted. "It's in making me admit, out loud, that I want. That I deserve. That's the part that hurts." His hands stilled. "But you're right. It's also the part that heals."

He set the soap aside, letting the water rinse away the suds.

"I don't know the cousins' names either," he added, his tone shifting to something lighter. "But I suspect we're about to learn them in exhaustive detail. Americans aren't known for their restraint in conversation."
