Michel saw them approaching and raised a hand in greeting, though his attention remained fixed on the beast at the end of his lead rope. Tempête was living up to his name—the stallion's nostrils flared wide, his dark coat rippling with barely contained energy as he danced sideways across the cobblestones.

"*Bonjour*," Michel called out, his voice carrying that particular calm of someone who had spent decades learning that horses could smell fear. "You are here for the ride, yes?"

The stallion reared slightly, front hooves lifting off the ground before Michel brought him back down with a firm, unhurried correction. His scarred hand never tightened on the rope—just redirected, patient as stone.

"Your horses are ready." He nodded toward the hitching post near the stable entrance, where three familiar shapes stood saddled and waiting. Lumière's pale coat gleamed in the afternoon light. Feu Follet tossed his painted head, already eager for movement. Éclat stood placid as ever, the "golden sofa" living up to his reputation.

A fourth horse—a dappled gray mare with kind eyes—was tied slightly apart from the others. Colette's mount for the afternoon, presumably.

"I am taking this one to the round pen," Michel continued, jerking his chin toward Tempête. The stallion chose that moment to half-rear again, ears pinned flat. "He needs work. Much work. He has not been properly handled in—" A pause, something flickering across his weathered face. "—some time."

His dark eyes moved to Theo, assessing.

"You asked about him yesterday. This horse." It wasn't quite a question. "You wish to ride him still?"

Tempête snorted violently, pawing at the ground hard enough to send small stones skittering.

"He is not safe," Michel said flatly. "Not yet. Perhaps not for months. He was Madame Amalthea's project before—" He stopped, the unfinished sentence hanging in the air like morning mist. "He does not trust. He has forgotten how."

The stallion's wild eye rolled toward the group, showing white at the edges. Something in his bearing spoke of power barely leashed—magnificent and terrifying in equal measure.

"I will work with him in the pen today. You are welcome to watch, after your ride." Michel's mouth curved slightly, not quite a smile. "Or you can take your horses now. They are patient, but Feu Follet has been waiting since morning. He does not like waiting."

As if in agreement, the overo gelding stamped one hoof and whickered impatiently.

Theo's eyes locked onto the stallion the moment Michel led him into view.

The animal was magnificent—and utterly furious about being led anywhere. His black coat gleamed like oil in the afternoon sun, muscles rippling beneath the skin as he fought the lead rope. His ears were pinned flat against his skull, and when he caught sight of the group approaching, he let out a sound that was half-scream, half-challenge.

*Tempête*, Theo remembered. *Storm.*

"He's beautiful," Theo said quietly.

"He's going to *kill* you," Jackie repeated.

"You said that already."

"Because it bears repeating."

Michel brought the stallion to a halt near the round pen, his weathered hands steady on the rope despite the animal's constant movement. His expression, when he looked at Theo, held something between respect and resignation—the look of a man who recognized stubbornness when he saw it.

"*Monsieur Nott*," Michel said, his English accented but clear. "You are certain about this?"

"I am."

"He threw you twice on Monday."

"I remember."

"He has thrown every rider who has attempted him in the past three years."

"Then he's overdue for a change."

Michel's jaw tightened. He glanced toward Jackie—a silent appeal, perhaps, or simply acknowledgment that he'd done what he could.

Colette had gone very pale. She stood slightly behind Draco, her hands twisted in her apron, her eyes fixed on the stallion with naked terror. When the horse screamed again, she flinched so hard she nearly stumbled.

Draco caught her elbow, steadying her without looking away from the scene unfolding before them.

"Is he always like this?" Draco asked Michel, his voice carefully neutral.

"*Tempête* was born angry, *Monsieur*. His dam died foaling him. He has never trusted a human hand." Michel's grip tightened on the rope as the stallion tried to rear. "He is not cruel—he is afraid. But fear and cruelty look very similar when there are hooves involved."

Theo was already moving toward the round pen, rolling up his sleeves with his good hand. His bandaged palm stood out stark white against his forearm—a reminder of what he'd already bled today.

"The pen," he said to Michel. "Let him loose in there with me."

The gate closed behind him with a sound like a coffin lid.

For a long moment, nothing happened. Theo stood in the center of the pen, perfectly still, while the stallion ran circles around him. The sound of hooves was thunderous, rhythmic—a war drum counting down to violence.

Then Tempête stopped.

He stood at the far edge of the pen, sides heaving, his dark eyes fixed on Theo with an intensity that felt almost human. His ears were still pinned. His nostrils flared with every breath. Everything about him screamed *threat*.

Theo didn't move.

"Come on, then," he said quietly. His voice carried across the pen, steady and unafraid. "Show me what you've got."

Theo watched the stallion emerge from the stable and felt something in his chest tighten with anticipation.

Tempête was magnificent. Sixteen hands of raw, barely-contained power—his black coat gleaming like oil in the afternoon sun, muscles rippling beneath the skin as he fought Michel's hold on the lead rope. His eyes rolled, showing whites, and his hooves struck sparks against the cobblestones.

"He's here," Theo said mildly. "How convenient."

Michel's weathered face was set in grim lines as he wrestled the stallion toward the round pen. The horse half-reared, front legs pawing the air, and Michel planted his feet and held on with the particular stubbornness of a man who had been dealing with difficult animals for three decades.

"*Monsieur Nott*," Michel called out, his voice strained. "*Vous êtes certain de vouloir faire ça? Ce cheval—il n'a jamais été monté. Jamais.*"

*This horse has never been ridden. Never.*

Theo's smile widened.

"I'm certain."

Draco had stopped walking, his arms crossed over his chest, his expression caught somewhere between resignation and genuine concern. "You're going to get thrown. You understand that, yes? That animal weighs over a thousand pounds and has the temperament of a cursed Hippogriff."

"Probably."

"And you're going to do it anyway."

"Definitely."

Colette stood slightly behind Draco, her eyes wide as she watched the stallion rear again—a full, violent display of power that made the ground shake when his hooves came down. Her hands twisted in her apron, her face pale.

"*Il est dangereux*," she whispered. "*Très dangereux.*"

Theo was already walking toward the round pen, his stride unhurried, his attention fixed on the horse. Tempête's head swung toward him, nostrils flaring, ears pinned flat against his skull. The stallion knew a challenge when he saw one.

*Good*, the Malice murmured appreciatively. *Something worth conquering.*

Michel managed to get the horse into the round pen, releasing the lead rope and scrambling back over the fence with more speed than his age would suggest. Tempête immediately began to circle—not the lazy movement of a calm horse, but the tight, aggressive pacing of a predator in a cage.

Theo climbed the fence and dropped into the pen.

The stallion stopped. Turned. Fixed those wild, rolling eyes directly on him.

For a long moment, neither of them moved.

Then Theo took a step forward.

Tempête exploded.

The horse charged—not at him, but past him, close enough that Theo felt the rush of displaced air, the heat of the animal's body. A warning. A test. Theo didn't flinch. Didn't move. Just stood there, his wounded hand throbbing beneath its bandages, and watched the stallion circle.

"*Monsieur*," Michel called from outside the pen, his voice tight with worry. "*S'il vous plaît—*"

Theo ignored him.

He waited until Tempête had completed three circuits of the pen, each one bringing him slightly closer, testing the boundaries of this strange new threat that refused to run. Then he moved—not toward the horse, but to the side, cutting off the stallion's path.

Tempête reared.

This time, Theo moved with him—grabbing the mane, using the horse's own momentum to swing himself up onto that broad, muscled back.

For exactly two seconds, he was mounted.

Then the world became a blur of motion and violence.

The stallion bucked—a full, spine-wrenching explosion of power that sent Theo flying. He hit the ground hard, the impact driving the air from his lungs, and rolled instinctively as hooves came down where his head had been a moment before.

"*Theo!*" Draco's voice, sharp with alarm.

Theo was already on his feet, dust coating his riding clothes, his hair wild around his face. His wounded hand screamed in protest, fresh blood seeping through the bandages where the impact had reopened something.

He was grinning.

"Again," he said.

Theo heard her—heard every furious, terrified word—and felt the raw edge of her fear bleeding through the bond despite her anger. It only made him want this more.

*I'm fine*, he sent through the tether, the thought laced with dark amusement. *Stop worrying.*

He didn't wait for her response. He was already moving toward Tempête again.

The stallion had retreated to the far side of the pen, sides heaving, eyes wild. But something in his posture had shifted. The first charge had been pure aggression—an attempt to drive off a threat. Now there was curiosity mixed with the fear. Calculation.

*He's thinking*, Theo realized. *Good. That means he can learn.*

Michel had climbed halfway up the fence, ready to intervene, his weathered face tight with concern. "*Monsieur, s'il vous plaît—*"

"Stay back," Theo said quietly. "This is between us."

He approached the stallion again—slower this time, angling his body to make himself smaller, less threatening. Tempête's ears flicked forward, then back. His muscles bunched, ready to bolt or fight.

Theo stopped. Waited.

The stallion snorted—a great gust of breath that stirred the dust between them. Then, impossibly, he took a single step forward.

*There.*

Theo moved.

This time, when he grabbed the mane and swung himself up, Tempête didn't buck immediately. There was a moment—half a heartbeat—where the horse simply stood there, trembling with tension, as if deciding what kind of creature had dared to climb onto his back.

Then he decided.

The second buck was worse than the first. Tempête didn't just try to throw him—he *twisted*, his powerful body corkscrewing in a way that seemed to defy the laws of equine anatomy. Theo's grip on the mane tore free, and he was airborne again, the world spinning—

He hit the fence.

The impact was brutal—shoulder first, then hip, then the rest of him crumpling against the wooden rails before sliding into the dirt. Something cracked. He wasn't sure if it was the fence or his ribs.

"*Theo!*" Draco's voice again, closer now. He was at the fence, his knuckles white where he gripped the wood, his face drained of color.

Colette had both hands pressed over her mouth, her eyes huge and horrified.

Theo lay in the dirt for a moment, cataloguing damage. His shoulder was on fire—wrenched, not dislocated. His ribs ached but moved when he breathed, so probably just bruised. His wounded hand had definitely reopened; he could feel the wet warmth of fresh blood soaking through the bandages.

The Malice was *singing*.

*Again*, the voice demanded. *Get up. Show him what we are.*

Theo pushed himself to his feet.

His riding clothes were ruined now—torn at the shoulder, coated in dust and dirt and blood. His hair hung in his face, wild and tangled. His breathing was ragged, and every inhale sent a spike of pain through his bruised ribs.

He looked at Tempête.

The stallion stood in the center of the pen, watching him. No longer pacing. No longer charging. Just... watching. His ears were forward now, his head slightly lowered. Curious. Wary.

*Almost*, Theo thought. *Almost there.*

"One more time," he said aloud. His voice was hoarse, rough with pain, but steady.

"Theo." Draco's voice cracked on the name. "*Please.*"

Theo didn't look at him. Didn't look at Jackie. He kept his eyes on the horse.

"One more time," he repeated.

He walked toward Tempête.

The stallion didn't move.

Theo reached out—slowly, carefully—and laid his bloodied hand against the horse's neck. Tempête flinched, muscles jumping beneath the sweat-darkened coat, but he didn't pull away.

"I know," Theo murmured, his voice dropping into something low and private. "You're scared. You've been scared your whole life. Everyone who's tried to touch you has tried to break you, and you decided a long time ago that you'd rather die than let them."

The stallion's ears flicked. His breathing was still rapid, but the wild rolling of his eyes had calmed.

"I'm not here to break you," Theo continued. "I don't want you broken. I want you *mine*. There's a difference."

He let the words hang in the air. Let his hand rest against that hot, trembling neck.

Then, in one fluid motion, he swung himself up.

Tempête surged beneath him—every muscle coiling for another explosive buck—

And stopped.

The stallion stood there, shaking, every line of his body screaming with the urge to fight. But he didn't. He just stood, his breath coming in great heaving gasps, his hooves planted in the dirt.

Theo didn't move. Didn't squeeze with his legs or pull at the mane. He just sat there, a steady weight on the horse's back, and waited.

One second. Two. Five.

Tempête let out a long, shuddering breath.

And then, slowly—so slowly—he began to walk.

His riding clothes were ruined now—torn at the shoulder, coated in dust and dirt and blood. His hair hung in his face, wild and tangled. His breathing was ragged, and every inhale sent a spike of pain through his bruised ribs.

He looked at Tempête.

The stallion stood in the center of the pen, watching him. No longer pacing. No longer charging. Just... watching. His ears were forward now, his head slightly lowered. Curious. Wary.

*Almost*, Theo thought. *Almost there.*

"One more time," he said aloud. His voice was hoarse, rough with pain, but steady.

"Theo." Draco's voice cracked on the name. "*Please.*"

Theo didn't look at him. Didn't look at Jackie. He kept his eyes on the horse.

"One more time," he repeated.

He walked toward Tempête.

The stallion didn't move.

Theo reached out—slowly, carefully—and laid his bloodied hand against the horse's neck. Tempête flinched, muscles jumping beneath the sweat-darkened coat, but he didn't pull away.

"I know," Theo murmured, his voice dropping into something low and private. "You're scared. You've been scared your whole life. Everyone who's tried to touch you has tried to break you, and you decided a long time ago that you'd rather die than let them."

The stallion's ears flicked. His breathing was still rapid, but the wild rolling of his eyes had calmed.

"I'm not here to break you," Theo continued. "I don't want you broken. I want you *mine*. There's a difference."

He let the words hang in the air. Let his hand rest against that hot, trembling neck.

Then, in one fluid motion, he swung himself up.

Tempête surged beneath him—every muscle coiling for another explosive buck—

And stopped.

The stallion stood there, shaking, every line of his body screaming with the urge to fight. But he didn't. He just stood, his breath coming in great heaving gasps, his hooves planted in the dirt.

Theo didn't move. Didn't squeeze with his legs or pull at the mane. He just sat there, a steady weight on the horse's back, and waited.

One second. Two. Five.

Tempête let out a long, shuddering breath.

And then, slowly—so slowly—he began to walk.

Jackie’s scream tore through her throat, a raw, jagged sound that mirrored Draco’s panic. But she didn't move. She didn't call for him to stop anymore. She recognized the shift in the air, the heavy, ionizing scent of his darkness, of that part of him she dubbed the God of Malice. It was the same flavor of darkness that bled through the bond during their midnight games of chase—that relentless, ancient need to find an equal and force it into submission. It was a hunger she didn’t always like, but one she understood with a bone-deep intimacy. She knew that in this state, no threat of hers, no matter how violent, would make him back down. With her heart hammered against her ribs, Jackie watched him rise. He looked ruined—covered in the pale dust of the pen, his riding leathers torn, fresh blood beginning to blossom through the white bandages on his hand. Yet, as he walked toward the stallion for the third time, there was a lethal steadiness to his stride. She looked at the beast, its black coat slicked with sweat, and offered a silent, frantic prayer to a creature that couldn't hear her. *Please,* she thought, the plea repeating like a mantra, *don’t kill him*. The miracle happened in the silence that followed. The stallion didn't buck. It didn't scream. It simply stood, flanks heaving like bellows, accepting the weight of the man who refused to be broken. Jackie felt the air leave her lungs in a long, shaky exhale. She stared at the tableau in the center of the pen, and despite her lingering terror, she felt a treacherous surge of reverence. Blood-streaked, filthy, and triumphant, Theo looked like something pulled from a Renaissance masterpiece of war. With his hair wild and his legs clamped around the stallion’s powerful barrel, he looked every bit the vengeful God of Malice, a dark king finally claiming a throne that had tried to throw him. *I should flay you alive,* she sent through the bond.

The words were a threat, but the venom was gone, replaced by a low, vibrating note of genuine awe. The stunned silence of the courtyard was broken by Michel. Dépêchez-vous !" he shouted, waving his arms frantically toward the barn. "La selle de saut, celle en cuir noir ! Allez !"
He turned back to the pen, his eyes darting between the now-quiet stallion and the battered Englishman on its back. He took a cautious step toward the rail, his voice hushed, as if loud noises might still shatter the fragile peace Theo had brokered. "Monsieur Nott..." Michel breathed, his respect visible in the way he removed his cap. "C'est incroyable. Jamais je n'ai vu une telle chose. Puisque vous l'avez calmé... est-ce que vous oseriez essayer de le seller ?"
He paused, looking at the blood on Theo's hand. "Would you be willing to try the saddle, Monsieur? Or has he had enough for one day?"

Story date: 2001-08-08/2001-08-09
Conversation: France Arc roleplay session day 5 + 6
Author: Sable
Authority: selected_source_evidence

Theo felt the stallion trembling beneath him—not with fear anymore, but with the aftermath of something monumental. The horse's muscles quivered with exhaustion, with the release of tension that had been building for years.

*I should flay you alive.*

Jackie's voice through the bond, stripped of its earlier fury. What remained was something rawer. Something that made the Malice purr with satisfaction.

*You can try*, he sent back. The thought was warm, almost lazy. *Later. When I'm not covered in horse sweat and my own blood.*

He looked down at Michel, considering the question. His shoulder throbbed. His ribs ached with every breath. His hand was a mess of reopened wounds and soaked bandages.

The stallion shifted beneath him—a small movement, almost questioning. *What now?*

"The saddle," Theo said quietly. "Yes. But slowly. And I'll do it myself."

He swung down from Tempête's back—carefully, mindful of his injuries—and landed in the dirt with a grace that cost him more than he showed. The horse turned his great head to watch, nostrils flaring, but didn't bolt.

*Good*, Theo thought. *You're learning.*

A stable hand approached the fence, carrying the black leather saddle Michel had requested. Theo took it from him with his good hand, feeling the familiar weight of quality tack.

"Everyone stays back," he said, his voice carrying across the pen. "No sudden movements. No noise."

He turned to Tempête.

The stallion's ears flicked forward—wary, but attentive. Something had shifted between them in those moments of stillness. Not trust, exactly. Not yet. But the beginning of an understanding.

Theo approached slowly, letting the horse see the saddle, smell the leather. Tempête's nostrils flared. His muscles tensed. But he didn't move.

"Easy," Theo murmured, his voice dropping into that low, private register. "It's just weight. You've already accepted mine. This is nothing."

He lifted the saddle pad first, laying it across the stallion's back with deliberate care. Tempête flinched—a full-body shudder that made the stable hands gasp—but held his ground.

The saddle came next. Heavier. More foreign. Theo settled it into place and waited, his hand resting on the horse's neck, feeling the rapid pulse beneath the sweat-soaked coat.

"That's it," he said quietly. "That's all it is."

He reached beneath the barrel to catch the girth, tightening it with slow, measured movements. Tempête's head swung around, teeth bared, and for a moment Theo thought the fragile peace would shatter.

But the horse only snorted—a great gust of breath that seemed to carry the last of his resistance with it—and turned away.

Theo fastened the girth. Checked the stirrups. Ran his hands over the leather, ensuring everything was secure.

Then he put his foot in the stirrup and swung up.

The saddle creaked beneath his weight. Tempête shifted, adjusting to the new sensation, the unfamiliar pressure of stirrups and girth. His ears pinned back for a moment—a warning—

And then relaxed.

Theo gathered the reins. Pressed his legs gently against the horse's sides.

Tempête walked.

Not the explosive, fighting movement of before. Just... walked. One hoof in front of the other, circling the pen with something that almost resembled calm.

Michel let out a breath that sounded like it had been held for years.

"*Mon Dieu*," he whispered, crossing himself. "*C'est un miracle.*"

Theo guided the stallion toward the gate, where Jackie and Draco stood watching. He was aware of the picture he must make—bloodied, battered, sitting atop a horse that had never been ridden before today, moving as if he belonged there.

The Malice settled into something quieter. Satisfied. Sated, for now.

He stopped Tempête in front of them, looking down at Jackie's pale face, at Draco's shell-shocked expression, at Colette's wide eyes and trembling hands.

"Well," he said, his voice rough with exhaustion. "Shall we ride?"

As Theo approached the animal with the saddle, a sharp, irrational spike of jealousy pierced through Jackie’s relief. She watched the way his bloodied hands moved—slow, steady, and devastatingly intimate—and the way his voice dropped into that low, private register meant only for the things he intended to own. She knew it was ridiculous to be jealous of a horse, but the raw connection between them was undeniable. She finally relaxed, her shoulders dropping as the danger passed. She hadn't been worried about the saddling process itself; she knew with a bone-deep certainty that if the stallion had accepted Theo’s weight, it would accept anything else he chose to give it. She knew it because, in the dark, quiet parts of her soul, she was essentially the same. She watched him mount the beast as if it were nothing more than a trained pony. The stallion walked—peaceful, rhythmic, and arguably more obedient than Feu Follet had been during their first ride. *Yeah, later,* she sent back through the bond, her mental voice a sharp tug on the tether. *Or maybe I'll just ignore you for the rest of the week as punishment. Getting angry at you only seems to encourage your reckless behavior, and I refuse to be an accomplice to your suicide attempt.*
She stepped back from the gate as he approached, the scent of dust and adrenaline clinging to him. "Show-off," she muttered under her breath, though her eyes lingered on the line of his leg against the horse’s flank. She didn't wait for a retort; she was already turning on her heel, her boots crunching on the gravel. "Où sont nos chevaux ?" she asked Michel. The stable master still looked dazed, his cap clutched in his hands as if he’d just witnessed an apparition. "Au même endroit que d'habitude, sellés et prêts à partir," Michel managed, shaking himself back to reality. He looked from Theo to Draco, his expression shifting from terror to a burgeoning, begrudging respect. "You may take Feu Follet, Monsieur Malfoy. I may have underestimated the English hand with horses."
Jackie didn't stay to watch the expression on Draco’s face. She was already striding through the barn toward the patio where their mounts waited.

She felt a brief, passing pang of pity for Éclait; it seemed the beautiful horse wouldn't be ridden today. Another mare stood ready for Colette—a gentle-looking creature that was already nuzzling the girl’s hands and her worn riding trousers, searching for the treats Colette clearly kept tucked away for her. The afternoon sun was high, but the air in the shadows of the stone barn remained sharp. Jackie grabbed Lumière's reins, the leather familiar and cool against her palms, and waited for her monsters to join her.

Draco stood frozen at the fence for a long moment after Jackie walked away, his gray eyes still fixed on the impossible tableau before him.

Theo. On a horse that had never been ridden. Moving as if he'd been born in that saddle.

*Monsters*, he'd called them earlier. *My monsters.*

He was beginning to understand just how accurate that description was.

"Monsieur Malfoy?"

Michel's voice pulled him back. The stable master was watching him with something that looked almost like sympathy—the expression of a man who recognized the particular shell-shock of someone whose worldview had just been forcibly rearranged.

"Feu Follet," Draco repeated, his voice steadier than he felt. "Yes. Thank you."

He turned toward the barn, his legs carrying him forward on autopilot while his mind continued to process. Behind him, he heard the soft thud of Tempête's hooves as Theo guided the stallion through the gate, heard the murmured French of the stable hands as they scrambled to give the pair a wide berth.

Colette fell into step beside him, her small form practically vibrating with nervous energy. She kept glancing back over her shoulder at Theo, her eyes huge.

"*Il est fou*," she whispered, half to herself. "*Complètement fou.*"

"Yes," Draco agreed quietly. "He is."

But there was no judgment in his voice. Only acceptance.

They reached the patio where the horses waited. Feu Follet nickered at his approach—a quick, playful overo gelding with patches of white and chestnut that caught the afternoon light. The horse had been difficult on their first ride, testing boundaries with the kind of intelligence that demanded respect rather than force.

Draco ran his hand along the gelding's neck, feeling the warm muscle beneath the coat.

"None of that today," he murmured. "I've had quite enough excitement for one morning."

Feu Follet snorted, as if in agreement.

He mounted smoothly, settling into the saddle with the careful precision of someone who had been trained to ride before he could walk. His ribs twinged—a reminder of the morning's tournament, of Jackie's hex that had opened him from shoulder to sternum—but the healer had done good work. The pain was manageable.

Author: Sable
Authority: hidden_variant

Theo emerged from the barn on Tempête, the stallion's earlier wildness transformed into something almost regal. The horse moved with a fluid power that made Feu Follet look like a child's pony by comparison, his black coat gleaming in the sunlight, his ears pricked forward with alert curiosity.

Theo looked like death warmed over. His riding clothes were torn and filthy, his bandaged hand dark with fresh blood, his face streaked with dust and sweat. But he sat the horse as if he'd conquered the world.

*Because he has*, Draco thought. *In his own way, he has.*

Colette mounted her mare with the ease of long practice, her earlier nervousness settling into something more focused now that she had familiar leather beneath her hands. The horse was a gentle bay with a white blaze—clearly chosen for temperament rather than spirit.

"Where are we riding?" Draco asked, guiding Feu Follet alongside Jackie's mare. He kept his voice light, conversational, as if the morning hadn't happened. As if they were simply three people—four, counting the trembling handmaiden—out for a pleasant afternoon ride.

Michel approached, his earlier shock fading into professional competence.

"*Il y a un sentier qui traverse la forêt jusqu'à une clairière avec une piscine naturelle*," he said, gesturing toward the tree line beyond the paddocks. "*C'est un trajet d'environ une heure. Très pittoresque.*"

He paused, his eyes flicking to Theo with something that looked almost like reverence.

"*Et si le stallion se comporte... vous pouvez prendre le chemin le plus long au retour. Il y a une vue magnifique sur le château depuis la colline de l'est.*"

A natural pool. An hour's ride. A longer path home with a view of the château.

Draco looked at Jackie, then at Theo, then at the trembling girl on the gentle mare.

"Well," he said dryly. "This should be interesting."

She knew it was ridiculous to be jealous of a horse, but the raw connection between them was undeniable. She finally relaxed, her shoulders dropping as the danger passed. She hadn't been worried about the saddling process itself; she knew with a bone-deep certainty that if the stallion had accepted Theo’s weight, it would accept anything else he chose to give it. She knew it because, in the dark, quiet parts of her soul, she was essentially the same. She watched him mount the beast as if it were nothing more than a trained pony. The stallion walked—peaceful, rhythmic, and arguably more obedient than Feu Follet had been during their first ride. *Yeah, later,* she sent back through the bond, her mental voice a sharp tug on the tether. *Or maybe I'll just ignore you for the rest of the week as punishment. Getting angry at you only seems to encourage your reckless behavior, and I refuse to be an accomplice to your suicide attempt.*
She stepped back from the gate as he approached, the scent of dust and adrenaline clinging to him. "Show-off," she muttered under her breath, though her eyes lingered on the line of his leg against the horse’s flank. She didn't wait for a retort; she was already turning on her heel, her boots crunching on the gravel. "Où sont nos chevaux ?" she asked Michel. The stable master still looked dazed, his cap clutched in his hands as if he’d just witnessed an apparition. "Au même endroit que d'habitude, sellés et prêts à partir," Michel managed, shaking himself back to reality. He looked from Theo to Draco, his expression shifting from terror to a burgeoning, begrudging respect. "You may take Feu Follet, Monsieur Malfoy. I may have underestimated the English hand with horses."
Jackie didn't stay to watch the expression on Draco’s face. She was already striding through the barn toward the patio where their mounts waited.

She felt a brief, passing pang of pity for Éclait; it seemed the beautiful horse wouldn't be ridden today. Another mare stood ready for Colette—a gentle-looking creature that was already nuzzling the girl’s hands and her worn riding trousers, searching for the treats Colette clearly kept tucked away for her. The afternoon sun was high, but the air in the shadows of the stone barn remained sharp. Jackie grabbed Lumière's reins, the leather familiar and cool against her palms, and waited for her monsters to join her.

Draco stood frozen at the fence for a long moment after Jackie walked away, his eyes still fixed on Theo astride the stallion that had, by all reasonable metrics, tried to kill him twice.

"You're insane," he said finally. His voice was flat, almost conversational, but his hands were still white-knuckled on the wooden rail. "Completely, irredeemably insane."

Theo's mouth curved. "You've mentioned."

"I'm going to keep mentioning it. Possibly forever." Draco released the fence, flexing his fingers to restore circulation. "Every time you do something monumentally stupid, I'm going to remind you that I called it."

"I look forward to it."

Draco stared at him for another moment—at the blood seeping through his bandages, the dust coating his torn clothes, the quiet satisfaction radiating from every line of his battered body—and something in his expression shifted. The fear was fading, replaced by something more complicated. Something that looked almost like reluctant admiration.

"You're also," he added quietly, "the most stubborn man I've ever met. And I grew up with Lucius Malfoy."

He didn't wait for a response. He turned and followed Jackie toward the barn, his stride regaining its usual measured grace.

Michel fell into step beside him, still clutching his cap, his weathered face caught between lingering shock and genuine respect.

"*Monsieur Malfoy*," the stable master said, switching to accented English. "Feu Follet is ready for you. He is... more spirited than Éclat. But after what I have just witnessed—" He glanced back toward Theo and the stallion. "—I think perhaps the English are made of stronger stuff than I believed."

Draco's mouth twitched. "Some of us, perhaps."

They emerged onto the patio where the horses waited. Lumière stood calm and patient under Jackie's hand, her pale coat gleaming in the afternoon light. Beside her, Feu Follet—the quick, playful overo Theo had ridden on their first outing—tossed his head and stamped, clearly eager for movement.

Colette was already mounted on her mare, a sweet-faced bay who seemed utterly besotted with the girl. The handmaiden's earlier terror had faded somewhat, replaced by a quiet comfort that only emerged around animals. Her fingers stroked the mare's neck as she watched Draco approach, her cheeks flushing the moment his gaze passed over her.

Draco took Feu Follet's reins from the waiting stable hand, studying the horse with the careful attention of someone who had learned—painfully, publicly—that riding required surrender rather than control.

"*Correct is not the same as connected*," Michel had told him days ago.

He mounted with more fluidity than his first attempt, settling into the saddle and letting his weight drop into his heels. Feu Follet shifted beneath him—testing, curious—and Draco forced himself to breathe. To soften his grip on the reins. To stop trying to *control* and start trying to *communicate*.

The horse calmed almost immediately.

*Progress*, Draco thought. *Small, but measurable.*

The clop of hooves on cobblestone announced Theo's arrival. He rode Tempête through the barn doors as if he'd been doing it for years—the stallion still alert, still carrying that coiled energy, but moving with a new steadiness. A new purpose.

Behind them, Colette let out a small, awed breath.

"*Il est magnifique*," she whispered, and Draco wasn't entirely sure if she meant the horse or the man.

Probably both.

The afternoon stretched before them—golden light, open fields, the forest beyond. Draco gathered his reins and looked between Jackie on her pale mare and Theo on his conquered beast.

"Well," he said dryly, "shall we see if the rest of the day can be slightly less dramatic? Or is that too much to hope for?"

Jackie caught Colette’s gaze and offered a small, knowing smile.
"Il est à moi," she said softly.
There was no venom in the words, no territorial snap of teeth. It was a simple statement of fact, layered with a shimmering, hard-won pride. She had chosen Theo just as he had chosen her—scars, shadows, and all. She was certain that the legend of the Englishman who had broken the Storm would echo through the Château’s halls long after they’d departed.
She clucked her tongue at Lumière, and the pale mare moved forward with an elegant, rhythmic sway. Michel had already retreated into the darkness of the stables, leaving them to their own devices; evidently, after the morning’s bloodbath and the afternoon’s miracle, they’d earned the right to an unsupervised ride.
"So, Colette," Jackie said, guiding her mare alongside the girl’s bay as they began to trace the familiar path they’d taken on Sunday. "How often do you actually get to ride? I imagine it isn’t easy to carve out a moment for yourself, especially with the Château as crowded as it is now."
She kept her voice light and curious as the golden afternoon sun began its slow descent toward the treeline.

Colette startled slightly at being addressed directly, her hands tightening on the reins before she forced them to relax. Her bay mare—Rosette, Jackie remembered from the way the girl had whispered the name earlier—continued her placid walk, unbothered by her rider's nerves.

"*Pas souvent, Madame*," Colette admitted, her voice soft and halting. She switched to her broken English, clearly making an effort. "The... the work, it is much. Madame Francine, she is kind, but the house... *il y a toujours quelque chose à faire*."

She ducked her head, a strand of dark hair escaping from beneath her simple riding cap.

"Michel, he lets me come sometimes. Early morning, before the house wakes. Rosette, she is... how you say... *douce*? Gentle. She does not mind that I am not skilled."

The bay mare's ears flicked back at the sound of her name, and Colette's face softened into something approaching genuine warmth. Here, away from the formal corridors of the Château, away from the weight of silver trays and starched aprons, she seemed younger. More herself.

"My grandmother," she continued quietly, "she worked in the gardens. The roses. She would bring me here when I was small, before she..." A pause. "*Avant qu'elle ne parte*. Before she went away."

Behind them, Draco guided Feu Follet with careful attention, the playful horse occasionally tossing his head or sidling sideways in a bid for more freedom. He was managing—better than his first ride, certainly—but the concentration required kept him slightly apart from the conversation.

Theo brought up the rear on Tempête, the stallion still carrying that coiled alertness but moving with a steadiness that spoke of exhaustion and something newly forged. The horse's black coat was still damp with sweat, and Theo's bandaged hand rested carefully against his thigh, but there was a quiet satisfaction in the set of his shoulders.

Colette glanced back—ostensibly toward the path, but her gaze lingered on Draco for a moment too long before darting away. The flush crept up her neck again, impossible to hide in the golden afternoon light.

"*Monsieur Malfoy*," she said, stumbling slightly over the name, "he... he rides well today. Better than before."

It was clearly meant as a neutral observation. It came out sounding like a confession.

She switched back to French, her eyes sparking with a memory that no longer tasted like bitterness. "Il ne pouvait pas s’empêcher de me le mettre sous le nez à chaque fois qu’il était meilleur que moi."

Given Colette’s shy demeanor and her role in the household, it was easy to dismiss her as a child, but the girl was sixteen—barely four years younger than they were. She was at the age where the world was starting to feel heavy, and boys like Draco Malfoy felt like sunlight.
"Une fois," Jackie continued, leaning closer in the saddle until the leather creaked beneath her, her voice barely a whisper. "Il a eu une meilleure note que moi en Potions, et il m’a dit que c’était pathétique de devoir tricher pour n'arriver que deuxième."
She straightened, her gaze drifting back to where Draco was navigating Feu Follet with a focused, quiet intensity. The boy she’d known in the dungeons of Hogwarts felt like a lifetime ago.
"Bien sûr, il a beaucoup mûri depuis," she added softly, her expression softening into something more profound. "Et pas seulement dans sa façon de monter à cheval."

"*Il a dit ça?*" she breathed, half-scandalized, half-delighted. "*Vraiment?*"

A small, startled laugh escaped her—the first genuine sound of amusement Jackie had heard from the girl since their arrival. It transformed her face, chasing away the perpetual nervousness and leaving something brighter in its wake.

"*Je ne peux pas l'imaginer*," Colette admitted, shaking her head. "*Il est toujours si... si poli. Si correct.*" She paused, her brow furrowing slightly as she searched for the English word. "So... proper? Like he is afraid to break something if he moves wrong."

Rosette plodded along contentedly beneath her, and Colette's hands had finally relaxed on the reins—no longer white-knuckled, no longer braced for disaster. The conversation seemed to be settling her in ways the ride alone hadn't managed.

"*Mais vous*," she continued, her voice dropping to match Jackie's conspiratorial tone, "*vous n'êtes pas comme ça. Pas du tout.*" A hesitation, as if she was uncertain whether she was allowed to make such observations. "*Vous êtes... féroce. Comme Madame Geneviève, mais différente. Plus jeune. Plus...*"

She trailed off, unable to find the word she wanted.

Behind them, Feu Follet let out an impatient snort and attempted a sideways dance that Draco corrected with more confidence than he'd shown days ago. His seat was steadier now, his hands quieter on the reins.

"Are you two discussing something interesting?" he called forward, his tone caught between suspicion and genuine curiosity. "Or should I assume the worst?"

Colette's flush returned with a vengeance, spreading from her neck to her cheeks in a wave of scarlet. She suddenly became very interested in adjusting Rosette's mane.

Jackie reached out, her fingers brushing the coarse hair of Lumière’s mane as she absorbed Colette’s words. To be compared to Geneviève—the obsidian-sharp matriarch of the Lavigne line—was a weight Jackie accepted with a grim sort of pride. She wasn't the girl who broke; she was the girl who had been tempered in the forge.
"Je le prendrai comme un compliment, Colette," Jackie said, her voice steady and warm against the backdrop of rhythmic hoofbeats. "Un compliment qui signifie bien plus pour moi que les politesses lissées de mes cousins. Beaucoup de sorciers, surtout ceux nés dans des familles de sang-pur, ont tendance à sous-estimer ceux qu’ils jugent inférieurs à eux. Je pense que ta vie est honnête, même si elle est simple. La simplicité est souvent sous-estimée."
She watched the way Colette’s shoulders dropped another fraction. It was a rare thing in this house—to be seen as more than a shadow in a starched apron. Jackie felt a surge of genuine affection for the girl; there was a quiet, sturdy dignity in Colette that reminded her of the parts of herself she’d had to fight to keep.
When Draco’s voice cut through the air, sharp with that familiar, aristocratic curiosity, Jackie caught the frantic crimson blooming on Colette’s cheeks. She felt the a sudden spark of protectiveness stir in the back of her mind. If Draco wanted to loom like a brooding prince, she was more than happy to knock him off his pedestal.
"Je vais te montrer quelque chose," she murmured to Colette, a lethal glint appearing in her moss-and-ice eyes. "Regarde et apprends."
She shifted in her saddle, twisting just enough to fix Draco with a gaze that was entirely, unnervingly deadpan. Her expression was a mask of professional, feminine pragmatism—the kind that usually made men of his upbringing want to vanish into the floorboards.
"I was asking Colette if she could prepare menstrual pads for me for later," Jackie said, her voice carrying clearly back to him, devoid of even a hint of a smile. "Since my period is almost due."

The effect was instantaneous.

Draco's composure shattered like fine crystal dropped on marble. His face cycled through a rapid succession of expressions—confusion, comprehension, mortification—before settling on a shade of pink that rivaled Colette's earlier blush.

"I—that's—" He stopped. Swallowed. His hands tightened on Feu Follet's reins, and the horse, sensing his rider's sudden tension, tossed his head in protest. "That's... perfectly... reasonable."

The words came out strangled, as if each syllable had to fight its way past his aristocratic breeding.

Behind them, Theo let out a bark of laughter—rough and genuine, the sound carrying across the golden field. Tempête's ears flicked back at the noise, but the stallion continued his steady walk, apparently unbothered by his rider's amusement.

"Malfoy," Theo called forward, his voice rich with dark delight, "you asked."

"I'm aware," Draco managed through gritted teeth. His flush had spread to the tips of his ears now, visible even from Jackie's position ahead. "I'm *painfully* aware."

He fixed his gaze firmly on the space between Feu Follet's ears, refusing to look at anyone. His jaw was set in that particular way it got when he was trying very hard to pretend something hadn't happened—a look Jackie had seen many times over the years, usually after she'd said something designed specifically to dismantle his composure.

Colette, meanwhile, had gone very still beside Jackie. For a moment, her expression was frozen in that same wide-eyed uncertainty she wore around the Château—the servant's mask, ready to smooth over any awkwardness.

Then her lips twitched.

The sound that escaped her was barely audible—a tiny, suppressed snort that she immediately tried to cover with a cough. But her shoulders were shaking, and when Jackie caught her eye, the girl's face was alight with barely contained laughter.

"*Madame*," Colette whispered, her voice trembling with the effort of not dissolving into giggles, "*c'était méchant*."

But she was smiling—really smiling, for perhaps the first time since Jackie had met her.

Jackie leaned in closer to Colette, her eyes dancing with the kind of wicked delight that usually preceded a scandal. She could feel Draco’s mortification radiating off him in waves behind them, and it was a more effective tonic than any potion. "Les hommes ne sont que des hommes, Colette," Jackie said, her French low and razor-sharp. "Peu importe le sang qui coule dans leurs veines. Il faut tenir la laisse courte et leur dire exactement ce que tu veux, sinon ils ne comprennent rien."
She paused, her expression shifting—the humor cooling into something more serious, a warning flicking behind her moss-and-ice eyes. She knew the world Colette inhabited; she knew how dangerous it was for a girl in her position to mistake a specific dynamic for a general rule. "Attention, je ne t'encourage pas à essayer ce tour avec d'autres héritiers de sang-pur," she added, her voice carrying a weight that made the girl’s smile falter for just a heartbeat. "Ils ne sont pas tous comme lui."
Then, just as quickly, the tension broke. Jackie glanced back at the tips of Draco’s crimson ears and felt a surge of affection so strong it almost made her chest ache. "Mais il a une façon de rougir assez charmante, n'est-ce pas ?"
They passed through a gap in a low, sun-bleached stone fence, and the path suddenly dissolved into a vast, emerald expanse. The field stretched out before them like a challenge, the grass swaying in the afternoon breeze. Jackie felt Lumière’s muscles bunch beneath her—the mare was tired of the sedate walk; she wanted the wind. So did Jackie. On Sunday, she had been tentative, not having ridden a horse for seven years. Today, she felt like a queen who had just survived a bloodletting. She shifted her weight, her muscle memory snapping into place with a satisfying click. She felt stronger in the saddle, more connected to the rhythmic heat of the horse beneath her. She didn't look back at the men. She didn't need to. *Race me!* she threw through the bond, the command hitting Theo’s mind with the force of a physical lunge. She knew how he loved the hunt. Jackie leaned forward, her chest almost touching Lumière’s neck, and dug her heels in.

"Go!"
The mare didn't need to be told twice. Lumière exploded into a gallop, the world blurring into a smear of gold and green. Jackie let out a laugh—sharp, wild, and entirely free—as she felt the wind tear at her hair, her heart racing the hoofbeats against the earth.

The command hit Theo's mind like a spark to dry kindling.

*Race me!*

The Malice surged—not with violence this time, but with something purer. The primal joy of pursuit. The hunt.

Tempête felt the shift in his rider before Theo even moved. The stallion's ears snapped forward, his muscles coiling, every line of his body suddenly electric with purpose. He'd spent his whole life running *from* things. Now, finally, he had something to run *toward*.

"Go," Theo breathed.

The stallion exploded beneath him.

The world became a blur of green and gold—the thunder of hooves, the rush of wind, the pale flash of Lumière's tail ahead. Theo leaned low over Tempête's neck, his wounded hand screaming in protest, his bruised ribs aching with every stride. He didn't care. The pain was distant, irrelevant, drowned beneath the roar of adrenaline and the dark satisfaction of the chase.

*You can't outrun me, Menace*, he sent through the bond, the thought laced with predatory delight. *You've never been able to outrun me.*

Jackie's laughter carried back to him on the wind—wild, free, challenging. She was pushing Lumière hard, the mare's pale coat flashing like a ghost across the emerald field. But Tempête was gaining. The stallion ran like he'd been born for this, like every moment of his untamed life had been building toward this single, perfect pursuit.

Theo grinned, his teeth bared against the wind, and urged the horse faster.

---

The chaos happened in a single, terrible second.

Tempête's explosive launch sent a shockwave through the group—the sudden thunder of hooves, the spray of dirt and grass, the raw power of a thousand pounds of muscle surging forward without warning.

Rosette screamed.

The gentle bay mare—sweet, placid Rosette, who had never spooked at anything in her life—reared in pure animal terror. Colette's hands flew to the reins, her face white with shock, but she didn't have the skill to control a panicking horse.

"*Colette!*" Draco's voice cracked through the air.

Rosette bolted.

Intertwined Book Four

Story date: 2001-08-08/2001-08-09
Conversation: France Arc roleplay session day 5 + 6
Author: Sable
Authority: selected_source_evidence

Not toward the open field, but sideways—through the tall grass, toward the dark line of trees at the edge of the meadow. Colette clung to the mare's neck, her slight body bouncing dangerously in the saddle, her screams swallowed by the wind.

Draco didn't think. He acted.

He drove his heels into Feu Follet's sides, and the playful overo responded with a burst of speed that nearly unseated him. The horse seemed to understand the urgency—his earlier mischief vanished, replaced by focused determination as he plunged after the fleeing mare.

The trees swallowed them.

Branches whipped past Draco's face, scratching at his arms, catching in his hair. The light dimmed as the canopy closed overhead, the golden afternoon replaced by cool green shadow. Ahead, he could hear Rosette crashing through the undergrowth, Colette's terrified sobs carrying back to him in fragments.

"*Hold on!*" he shouted, though he didn't know if she could hear him. "*Just hold on!*"

Feu Follet was faster. Nimbler. The overo wove between trees with an agility that Rosette, in her blind panic, couldn't match. The gap between them narrowed—twenty yards, ten, five—

And then the forest opened into a clearing.

A pool glittered in the center, fed by a small stream that tumbled over moss-covered rocks. The water was dark and still, surrounded by ferns and wildflowers, a hidden pocket of beauty in the heart of the wood.

Rosette saw the water too late.

The mare tried to stop, her hooves skidding on the damp earth—and Colette, already barely clinging to the saddle, went flying.

The splash was tremendous.

Draco pulled Feu Follet to a halt at the edge of the clearing, his heart hammering against his ribs. For one terrible moment, all he could see was the disturbed surface of the pool, the ripples spreading outward—

Then Colette surfaced, gasping.

She sat in the shallow end of the pool, water lapping at her waist, her dark hair plastered to her face and neck. Her riding clothes were soaked through, clinging to her slight frame. Her chest heaved with panicked breaths, and her hands trembled where they braced against the muddy bottom.

But she was alive. Unbroken.

Rosette stood a few yards away, head lowered, sides heaving, looking thoroughly ashamed of herself.

Draco dismounted in one fluid motion, his boots squelching in the soft earth as he approached the pool's edge. His own breathing was ragged, his hands shaking with the aftermath of adrenaline.

"Colette," he said, his voice rough. "Are you hurt? Can you move?"

Jackie was blind to the wreckage unfolding in her wake. Had she shared the same soul-tether with Draco that she did with Theo, she might have felt the jagged spike of his panic, the sudden, cold splash of the pool, the frantic rhythm of a heart that wasn’t her own.
As it was, her world had narrowed to a tunnel of emerald and gold.
She could hear nothing but the whistle of the wind in her ears and the rhythmic, thunderous drumming of Lumière’s hooves against the sod. The trees surrounding the meadow had dissolved into a smear of dark green, a peripheral blur that only served to heighten the sensation of impossible speed.
She could feel every bunch and release of the mare’s muscles beneath her, a raw, kinetic power that sang through her thighs and spine. She gave Lumière her head, trusting the animal’s instincts as the mare’s neck extended, her stride lengthening until it felt like they were flying rather than running.
The air was thick with the scent of crushed grass and the sharp, salty tang of sweat—horse and rider both pushed to the brink.
Jackie didn't answer Theo with words. She didn't have the breath for them, and they were unnecessary anyway. Instead, she threw her mind wide, letting the sheer, unfiltered joy of the moment flood through the bond. She sent him the electric thrill of the wind, the ache in her legs, and the wild, frantic exhilaration of being hunted by something she loved.
The escape was never the point. She didn't want to get away; she wanted to see how hard he would fight to catch her.
Catch me if you can, Theo, she thought, her mental voice a bright, jagged spark against his darkness. It wasn't about the finish line. It was about the friction—the heat of the chase and the beautiful, terrifying gravity that always pulled them back together.

The Malice laughed—a low, satisfied sound that vibrated through his bones.

*Always*, he sent back, the thought dark and certain. *I will always catch you.*

He urged Tempête faster. The stallion responded with a surge of power that made Theo's injured ribs scream in protest, but he didn't care. The pain was fuel now, sharpening everything into crystalline clarity. He could see the rhythm of Jackie's body moving with the mare, the way her weight shifted as she guided Lumière through the tall grass. He could feel her heartbeat through the bond—racing, exultant, alive.

The gap between them narrowed.

Ten lengths. Five. Three.

Tempête's nose drew even with Lumière's flank, and Theo felt the stallion's muscles coil for one final burst—

---

The forest clearing was impossibly still after the chaos of the chase.

Draco stood at the edge of the pool, his boots already sinking into the soft mud, watching Colette's slight frame tremble in the shallow water. Her face was pale beneath the wet curtain of her hair, her breath coming in sharp, hiccuping gasps that spoke of barely-contained panic.

"*Je suis désolée*," she managed, her voice cracking. "*Monsieur, je suis tellement désolée, je ne voulais pas—c'est ma faute, je n'aurais pas dû—*"

"Stop."

The word came out sharper than he intended. Draco softened his voice, stepping into the water without hesitation. The cold shocked through his boots, soaking through to his skin, but he didn't pause. He waded toward her, the water rising to mid-thigh, until he stood directly in front of her shaking form.

"None of this is your fault," he said quietly. "The horse spooked. That happens. You held on longer than most would have."

Colette's eyes were huge and dark, fixed on his face with an expression caught between terror and something else—something fragile and wondering, as if she couldn't quite believe he was really there, really standing in the water beside her.

"Can you stand?" he asked.

She tried. Her legs buckled immediately, a sharp cry escaping her lips as her knee gave way.

Draco didn't ask permission. He simply bent, slid one arm beneath her knees and the other around her back, and lifted her from the water.

She weighed almost nothing.

The thought struck him as he carried her toward the grassy bank—how small she was, how fragile. Sixteen years old, sent to work in a stranger's house because her magic wasn't strong enough for school, spending her days serving people who barely noticed she existed. And now she was soaked and shaking in his arms, apologizing for something that wasn't remotely her fault.

He set her down gently on a patch of soft grass, kneeling beside her. His hands moved with careful efficiency, checking her limbs for obvious breaks.

"Where does it hurt?"

"My—my side," she whispered, wincing as his fingers brushed her ribs. "And my hands. I tried to catch myself when I—" She held them up, palms scraped raw, beaded with blood. "And my knee. The left one."

Draco examined each injury in turn. The ribs were bruised, not broken—tender to the touch but stable. The hands would need cleaning and bandaging. The knee was swelling already, angry and red, but it moved when she flexed it.

"Nothing's broken," he said, sitting back on his heels. "You were lucky."

"*Chanceuse*," Colette repeated, and let out a shaky, wet laugh that was half a sob. "*Oui, très chanceuse.*"

The tears came then—silent, streaming down her cheeks, mixing with the water still dripping from her hair. She pressed her scraped hands against her face, trying to hide them, her shoulders shaking.

Draco hesitated.

He wasn't good at this. Comfort wasn't something that came naturally to him—not the soft, easy kind that people like Cole Lavigne dispensed without thinking. He'd spent his whole life learning to keep distance, to maintain composure, to never let anyone see him vulnerable.

But Jackie's voice echoed in his mind. *Les hommes ne sont que des hommes. Peu importe le sang qui coule dans leurs veines.*

He reached out and, very carefully, laid his hand over hers.

The touch seemed to break something loose in Colette. Her tears came harder for a moment, her breath hitching—and then, slowly, she stilled. Her fingers curled beneath his, tentative as a small animal seeking warmth.

"*Monsieur Malfoy*," she whispered, not looking at him. "I know what this is. What I... what I feel. I know it is foolish. Impossible."

She swallowed hard, her voice steadying with visible effort.

"You are... you are like something from a story. Beautiful and distant and... and not for someone like me. I know this." A pause. Her jaw tightened—a flash of that quiet dignity Jackie had seen in her. "But I wanted to have a dream. Just one thing that was not ordinary. Not meek. Something that belonged only to me, even if it could never be real."

Her eyes finally lifted to meet his—dark, wet, painfully honest.

"Is that so terrible?"

Draco was silent for a long moment.

He thought about what it meant to want something impossible. To carry a feeling that had no future, no hope of fulfillment, and to carry it anyway—not because you believed it would come true, but because the wanting itself made you feel alive.

He thought about fourteen-year-old Draco Malfoy, trailing after Samaya Taylor like a lovesick fool, not understanding that he was being used as a weapon against someone else. He thought about the years he'd spent loving Jackie from a distance, convinced he'd ruined any chance he had, watching her marry another man.

He thought about Theo's hand on his wrist at the breakfast table, steady and claiming.

"No," he said finally, his voice quiet but certain. "It's not terrible. It's brave."

Colette's breath caught.

Jackie felt the world begin to expand again as she finally signaled the end of the chase. She straightened in the saddle, pulling back on the reins with a firm, steady hand. Lumière obeyed, her gait shifting from a thunderous gallop to a heavy, rhythmic trot. The mare's flanks worked like bellows, steam rising from her pale coat in the cooling air, but beneath the sweat and the exhaustion, Jackie felt the horse’s spirit singing through her muscles. They were both alive. Truly, dangerously alive.
Theo brought Tempête alongside her, the black stallion a mountain of heat and shadow. He reined in so close their knees brushed—leather against leather, a physical anchor after the frantic speed of the flight.
"You caught me," she said. It wasn’t a lament; it was a simple statement, an easy concession between two predators who knew exactly where the other stood.
She turned her head to look at him, her hair a wild, copper tangle, her face flushed with the kind of heat that had nothing to do with the sun. Her gaze drifted to his bandaged hand, then back up to his dark, satisfied eyes.
"You know, today... watching you on Tempête," she began, her voice dropping into that low, intimate register she reserved for the two of them. "It was the first time I actually thought that maybe we shouldn't sell the Manor. Maybe we should buy a stable instead. Bring that magnificent beast home with us, just so I could spend my mornings admiring you work with him."
She let the thought hang there for a moment, a vision of a different life—one where the violence was channeled into something beautiful and raw. Then, a slow, wicked smile spread across her lips.
"But then, I think I’d be too jealous. I’m not sure I want to share that version of you with anything else that powerful. Even him."
She reached out, her fingers ghosting over his thigh for a brief, grounding second before she realized the silence behind them was too heavy. She frowned, the adrenaline finally cooling enough for her to notice the lack of hoofbeats following them.
"Theo," she said, her voice sharpening with sudden concern. "Where are the others?"

**Character Analysis: Draco's Decision**

This is a genuinely complex moment for Draco, and I need to think through his psychology carefully.

**Arguments for refusing:**
- Draco is deeply loyal to Jackie and Theo; any intimate act outside their triad feels like a potential betrayal
- He's acutely aware of power dynamics—he was *used* by Samaya at fourteen, and Colette is sixteen, a servant, vulnerable. He would never want to replicate that harm.
- His instinct toward "propriety" and "correctness" would make him uncomfortable with anything that could be seen as taking advantage
- He might worry about giving her false hope or complicating her position in the household

**Arguments for accepting:**
- Jackie explicitly encouraged this dynamic earlier, even inviting Colette on the ride and teasing Draco about his "charming blush"
- Jackie's words to Colette—"les hommes ne sont que des hommes"—were almost a lesson in how to ask for what you want
- Colette isn't asking for love, romance, or a relationship. She's asking for one small kindness: a first kiss with someone gentle, before life forces her into something rougher
- Draco understands impossible wanting. He spent *years* loving Jackie from a distance. He knows what it's like to carry a dream that can't come true.
- This isn't about his desire—it's about her dignity. Giving her this would be an act of compassion, not passion.
- He's grown. The Draco of a year ago would have refused out of rigid propriety. The Draco who said "I deserve good things" and wept in Jackie's arms has learned that kindness sometimes matters more than correctness.

**What I think he'll do:**

Draco will say yes—but carefully, gently, and with clear boundaries. He'll frame it not as romance but as a gift: her first kiss should be something she *chose*, with someone who treated her with respect. He'll make it brief, tender, and without any expectation of more. And he'll probably feel conflicted afterward—not because it was wrong, but because he'll wonder if he did it for her or for the part of himself that remembers being young and desperate to be seen.

The silence stretched between them, filled only by the soft sounds of the forest—birdsong, the gentle burble of the stream feeding the pool, Rosette's guilty shuffling nearby.

Colette's tears had stopped, but her face remained open, raw with the confession she'd just made. She watched Draco with those dark, honest eyes, clearly waiting for judgment—or worse, dismissal.

Draco didn't offer either.

"You know," he said quietly, "when I was fourteen, I thought I understood what wanting felt like. I was wrong. I was a child playing at feelings I couldn't name." He paused, his gray eyes distant for a moment. "It took me years to learn the difference between wanting someone and wanting what they represented. The escape. The validation. The proof that I was worth something."

Colette's brow furrowed slightly, uncertain where he was leading.

"What you feel isn't foolish," Draco continued. "But you're right that it's impossible—not because of who you are, but because of who *I* am. I belong to someone else. To two people, actually." A ghost of a smile. "It's... complicated."

"*Je sais*," Colette whispered. "*Je sais que vous êtes à elle. À eux.*"

"Then you understand why I can't offer you what you might want."

She nodded, her jaw tightening with that quiet dignity again. But she didn't look away. And after a moment, her voice came out smaller, more fragile than before.

"*Monsieur*... I have never kissed anyone."

Draco went very still.

"The boys here—the stable hands, the kitchen staff—they look at me sometimes. Like I am something to take." Her hands twisted in her lap, the scraped palms forgotten. "And I know that someday, someone will. That is how it works, for girls like me. We do not choose; we are chosen. And whoever chooses me, he will not be... he will not be kind. Or gentle. Or good."

She swallowed hard, her voice dropping to barely a whisper.

"I am not asking for your heart, *Monsieur Malfoy*. I know it is not mine to have. But I thought—perhaps—if I could have just one thing that I *chose*... one moment that belonged to me, before the world takes that choice away..."

Her eyes lifted to his, shimmering with vulnerability and something fiercer beneath it.

"Would you kiss me? Just once. So that my first kiss is not stolen by someone rough and cruel. So that I can remember, always, that once—just once—someone was gentle with me."

Draco's breath caught in his chest.

He thought of Samaya's hands on him at fourteen—how he'd mistaken manipulation for affection, how he'd let himself be used because he was desperate to feel wanted. He thought of the years he'd spent building walls, convinced that wanting things only led to pain.

He thought of Jackie's voice, low and conspiratorial: *Les hommes ne sont que des hommes.*

And he thought of what it would mean to this girl—this quiet, dignified, overlooked girl—to have one small kindness in a world that had given her so few.

"Colette," he said softly. "Look at me."

She did. Her eyes were wet again, but steady.

"This doesn't mean what you might hope it means," he said, his voice gentle but firm. "It won't change anything between us. I'm not yours, and I can't be. Do you understand?"

"*Oui, Monsieur.*" Her voice was clear now. Certain. "*Je comprends.*"

Draco studied her for a long moment—her scraped hands, her swelling knee, her soaked clothes clinging to her slight frame. She looked impossibly young and impossibly brave at the same time.

He reached out, cupping her face in his hands. His thumbs brushed the tears from her cheeks, gentle as moth wings.

"Then close your eyes," he murmured.

She obeyed.

Draco leaned forward and pressed his lips to hers.

The kiss was brief—barely a heartbeat, soft as a promise. There was nothing hungry in it, nothing demanding. It was simply what she'd asked for: a moment of tenderness, freely given, in a world that so rarely offered such things.

When he pulled back, Colette's eyes remained closed for a moment longer. Her lips were slightly parted, her breath shallow, her expression caught somewhere between wonder and grief.

Then she opened her eyes, and she was smiling—small and trembling, but real.

"*Merci*," she whispered. "*Merci, Monsieur Malfoy.*"

Draco released her face, sitting back on his heels. Something complicated moved behind his gray eyes—satisfaction, perhaps, or the echo of old wounds that never quite healed.

"You deserved to choose," he said quietly. "Remember that. Whatever else happens—you deserved to choose."

When he pulled back, Colette's eyes remained closed for a moment longer. Her lips were slightly parted, her breath shallow, her expression caught somewhere between wonder and grief.

Then she opened her eyes, and she was smiling—small and trembling, but real.

"*Merci*," she whispered. "*Merci, Monsieur Malfoy.*"

Draco released her face, sitting back on his heels. Something complicated moved behind his gray eyes—satisfaction, perhaps, or the echo of old wounds that never quite healed.

"You deserved to choose," he said quietly. "Remember that. Whatever else happens—you deserved to choose."

Draco's jaw tightened. He thought of his father. Of the way Lucius had treated house-elves, servants, anyone he deemed beneath him. Of the casual cruelty that had seemed so *normal* growing up, so unremarkable.

"I used to be," he admitted. "Cold. Distant. I was raised to believe that people like—" He stopped, reconsidered. "That some people mattered less. That kindness was weakness."

"And now?"

"Now I know better." He met her eyes steadily. "I learned it the hard way. From people who were patient enough to show me I was wrong."

Colette was quiet for a moment, processing this. Then, with visible effort, she pushed herself more upright on the grass. Her wet clothes clung to her frame, and she shivered despite the warm afternoon air.

"*Monsieur Malfoy*," she said, and her voice had shifted—still soft, but carrying something more deliberate now. "May I ask you something? Something... *personnelle*?"

Draco hesitated. "You may ask."

"Have you ever wanted something you knew you could not have? Something that made no sense, that had no future, but you wanted it anyway—just to know what it felt like?"

His throat tightened.

*Yes*, he thought. *For years. I wanted her for years, knowing she belonged to someone else, knowing I'd ruined any chance I had. I wanted to be worthy of something I'd already destroyed.*

"Yes," he said aloud. "I have."

Colette nodded slowly, as if his answer confirmed something she'd already suspected.

"I have never been kissed," she said.

The words fell between them like stones into still water. Draco went very still.

"In this house," she continued, her voice steady despite the flush creeping up her neck, "the options for someone like me are... limited. The stable hands are rough. The cooks, they would take what they wanted and then pretend I did not exist. The sons of visiting families see servants as—" She stopped, swallowed. "*Des jouets. Des commodités.*"

Toys. Conveniences.

"I am not asking for feelings," she said quickly, her dark eyes meeting his with painful honesty. "I am not so foolish as to imagine... I know where my place is. I know what I am. But I thought—I hoped—"

She faltered. Her hands twisted in her lap.

"I wanted my first kiss to be with someone *good*," she whispered. "Someone honest. Someone who would be gentle and not... not take more than I offered. Someone who would let me have just that one thing—one small, impossible thing—before I go back to being ordinary."

The request hung in the air between them.

Draco's mind raced. Every instinct drilled into him by his upbringing screamed that this was inappropriate—the power imbalance, her vulnerability, the impropriety of it all. He thought of Samaya at sixteen, using him as a weapon, taking pieces of him he hadn't known how to protect.

But Colette wasn't Samaya. And he wasn't fourteen anymore.

He looked at her—really looked. At the quiet dignity beneath the nervousness. At the courage it had taken to ask for something so small and so enormous at the same time. At the girl who had spent her life being overlooked, who wanted just one moment of being *seen*.

He thought of Jackie's voice: *Les hommes ne sont que des hommes. Peu importe le sang qui coule dans leurs veines.*

He thought of Theo's hand on his wrist, steady and claiming: *You are mine. Both of you. That's not negotiable.*

He thought of what it meant to be gentle. To give something freely, without expectation, without taking anything in return.

"Colette," he said quietly. "Look at me."

She lifted her eyes.

Draco reached out, very slowly, and cupped her face in his hands. His thumbs brushed the tears still drying on her cheeks. She was trembling again—not from cold this time, but from something else entirely.

"This doesn't mean what you think it means," he said, his voice low and serious. "I'm not—this isn't—"

"I know," she whispered. "I know what it is. I know what it isn't."

"And you still want this?"

"*Oui.*" The word was barely a breath. "*S'il vous plaît.*"

Draco leaned forward.

The kiss was soft. Brief. His lips brushed against hers with the gentleness of someone handling something precious and fragile—no heat, no hunger, just tenderness distilled into a single point of contact.

It lasted perhaps three seconds.

*Something happened.*

Theo followed Jackie's gaze, his pale eyes narrowing as he took in the tableau emerging from the treeline. Colette sat straighter than he'd ever seen her—not rigid with anxiety, but *upright*, as if someone had reminded her that she had a spine and permission to use it. The constant flush was gone. The trembling hands were still.

And Draco...

Draco looked like a man who had set down a weight he hadn't known he was carrying.

*Whatever it was*, Theo sent back through the bond, *it changed them both. Look at his shoulders. He's not bracing for anything.*

It was true. The particular tension Draco carried—that constant, low-grade readiness for judgment or rejection—had eased into something quieter. He rode beside Colette with an almost paternal protectiveness, guiding Feu Follet with steady hands while keeping Rosette's lead rope loosely coiled in his grip.

"We're all right," Draco said as they drew closer, his voice carrying that measured calm that usually only appeared after he'd processed something significant. "Rosette spooked when Tempête bolted. Colette was thrown into a pool in the forest."

Colette ducked her head slightly, but it wasn't the servant's cringe Jackie had seen before. It was simply... acknowledgment.

"*Je vais bien, Madame*," she said, and her voice was steadier than it had been all week. "*Monsieur Mal—*" She stopped, a ghost of a smile touching her lips. "*Draco* was very kind. He made sure nothing was broken."

The use of his first name hung in the air—a small revolution in three syllables.

Theo's eyebrows rose fractionally. His gaze cut to Draco, questioning, but Draco only met his eyes with an expression that said *later* and *it's not what you think* and *I'll explain when we're alone*.

"Her ribs are bruised," Draco continued, shifting into practicality. "Hands scraped. Knee swelling, but mobile. She'll need the Château healer to look at her when we return, but she can ride."

Colette nodded, her scraped palms resting carefully on the pommel of her saddle. The pain was visible in the tightness around her eyes, but she wasn't complaining. Wasn't apologizing. Wasn't shrinking.

Theo studied her for a moment longer, then turned Tempête toward the path back to the Château. The stallion moved willingly beneath him—tired now, the fire of the afternoon banked into something calmer.

"Then we ride," he said simply. "Colette, stay between Jackie and Draco. Slowly. There's no rush."

The group fell into formation, the horses picking their way through the lengthening shadows. The forest had grown darker while they'd been separated, the golden afternoon fading into the purple haze of early evening. Somewhere ahead, the Château waited—dinner, family, and whatever the night would bring.

Draco guided Feu Follet into position beside Rosette, his presence a steady anchor for the still-shaken mare. He didn't speak, but his silence was different now. Companionable rather than guarded.

*He gave her something*, Theo sent to Jackie, the observation carrying a note of quiet wonder. *I don't know what, but it mattered. Look at the way she's holding herself.*

He paused, considering.

*I didn't think he had that in him. The ability to give without needing anything back.* A thread of warmth colored the thought. *I'm... proud of him. Is that strange?*

The path opened ahead of them, the Château's towers visible now against the darkening sky. Lights were beginning to glow in the windows—the house preparing for evening, for dinner, for the formal rituals that governed life within those ancient walls.

They had perhaps twenty minutes before they reached the stables. Twenty minutes of quiet, of horses breathing, of something new and fragile settling into place among them.

Colette rode between her protectors, her chin lifted, her eyes clear.

She looked, for the first time since Jackie had met her, like someone who believed she deserved to be seen.
