She didn't match his entirely unguarded posture—the instinct to stay coiled, ready to fight or flee, was too deeply ingrained in her muscles now. But after a moment, the quiet safety of the garden won out. She let her knees drop, extending her legs forward across the wild lawn. The grass was still heavy with morning dew, the cool dampness soaking pleasantly into her bare calves and the hem of her baby-blue dress. It was a grounding, physical reminder that she was here, outside, and breathing. She took the offered half of the croissant, studying him for a second before she spoke. "I'm sorry," she said, her tone laced with a mild, genuine skepticism, "but I have a very hard time believing you were bad at Defense."
She pulled off a flaky piece of the pastry, her mismatched eyes narrowing slightly in assessment. "Not after watching you almost beat Theo yesterday. I was actually certain I was going to have to fight you in the final. I spent half your match looking for openings and tells in your form, and I found almost none. So, if you were 'bad' at Defense at Ilvermorny, it was only because you chose not to show them how good you really were."
She fell silent for a moment, letting the observation hang in the air. She chewed the buttery pastry and took another slow sip of her coffee, watching a dragonfly hover over the surface of the pond. "As for me," she finally continued, her voice softening into a reflective hum. "I was mediocre on a broom, so I never made the Ravenclaw Quidditch team. I wasn't a Prefect, either. Honestly, other than being cursed, I had a pretty unassuming six years of school." A dry, dark amusement flickered across her face. "I mean, you know. Not counting Voldemort and the War."
She leaned her weight back on one hand, pressing her palm into the cool, damp earth. "My favorite subject was Ancient Runes. Charms was a close second. I got *Exceeds Expectations* on almost all my N.E.W.T.s—just on principle. I was kind of a massive nerd, really. If you'd seen me back then, I couldn't have even won a basic schoolyard duel against Samaya."
A laugh slipped out of her, self-deprecating and real, shaking loose some of the lingering shadows from the Solar.

"You wouldn't believe it looking at me now," she said, shaking her head at the memory of the girl she used to be. "When the Death Eaters breached the castle during my sixth year, I didn't fight. I hid up in the dormitory with the first and second years. I was a terrified little miss pissy pants back then."

I was actually certain I was going to have to fight you in the final. I spent half your match looking for openings and tells in your form, and I found almost none. So, if you were 'bad' at Defense at Ilvermorny, it was only because you chose not to show them how good you really were."
She fell silent for a moment, letting the observation hang in the air. She chewed the buttery pastry and took another slow sip of her coffee, watching a dragonfly hover over the surface of the pond. "As for me," she finally continued, her voice softening into a reflective hum. "I was mediocre on a broom, so I never made the Ravenclaw Quidditch team. I wasn't a Prefect, either. Honestly, other than being cursed, I had a pretty unassuming six years of school." A dry, dark amusement flickered across her face. "I mean, you know. Not counting Voldemort and the War."
She leaned her weight back on one hand, pressing her palm into the cool, damp earth. "My favorite subject was Ancient Runes. Charms was a close second. I got *Exceeds Expectations* on almost all my N.E.W.T.s—just on principle. I was kind of a massive nerd, really. If you'd seen me back then, I couldn't have even won a basic schoolyard duel against Samaya."
A laugh slipped out of her, self-deprecating and real, shaking loose some of the lingering shadows from the Solar.

"You wouldn't believe it looking at me now," she said, shaking her head at the memory of the girl she used to be. "When the Death Eaters breached the castle during my sixth year, I didn't fight. I hid up in the dormitory with the first and second years. I was a terrified little miss pissy pants back then."

Eli's eyebrows rose at her assessment of his dueling, a flicker of something—surprise, perhaps, or recognition—passing through his dark eyes before he schooled his expression back to neutral.

"You were watching that closely," he said. It wasn't a question. "Most people don't bother analyzing a match they're not in yet."

He didn't deny her observation. Didn't deflect with false modesty or a self-deprecating joke. He simply let it sit there, acknowledged, the way one predator might acknowledge another's assessment of their capabilities.

"Cole was the obvious one," he said after a moment, his voice quieter now. "The loud talent. The natural. People watched him and saw exactly what he was—big, fast, dangerous. They knew to be careful." He picked at a blade of grass, twisting it between his fingers. "I learned early that there were advantages to being underestimated. To letting people see the second son, the quiet one, the one who reads too much and thinks too hard."

He glanced at her sidelong.

"You don't survive being... *different*... in certain spaces without learning how to be invisible when you need to be. How to make people look past you. And then, when they've decided you're not a threat—" A faint, sharp smile. "—you have options they didn't anticipate."

He let that hang for a moment before deliberately lightening his tone.

"But yes. Madame Vautour saw through it immediately. First day of class, she hit me with a Stinging Hex and said, 'You're not fooling anyone who matters, Lavigne. Stop wasting my time.' I think I respected her more than any professor I ever had."

When she spoke about herself—the Ancient Runes, the N.E.W.T.s, the self-described "massive nerd"—Eli listened with genuine interest. But it was her final admission that made him go still.

*I didn't fight. I hid.*

He watched her face as she said it, the self-deprecating laugh that didn't quite reach her eyes, the way she framed it as weakness. *Terrified little miss pissy pants.*

"You were sixteen," he said quietly. "And there was a war."

He sat up slightly, his posture shifting to something more intent.

She let his words wash over her, sliding down like cool water over a burn. She didn't entirely believe him—she knew exactly who that terrified sixteen-year-old girl had been, trembling in the dormitory while the castle shook with spellfire. But he wasn't wrong about the rest of it. Between that night and this morning, so many things had tried to break her. Curses. Death Eaters. Basements. Betrayals. They had all failed. She had dragged herself out of the wreckage every single time, forging herself into someone who wouldn't just survive, but fight back. She picked up her third croissant, the warm, buttery pastry melting on her tongue. For a few fragile minutes, listening to Eli's steady voice under the swaying willows, she felt something terrifyingly close to peace. And then he mentioned Grandmère. The peace vanished, instantly vaporized by a flash of pure, venomous anger. Her face contorted, a visceral snarl threatening to break through before she ruthlessly caught it, smoothing her features back into a tight mask. "No, thank you," she said, her voice clipped. She paused, taking a slow breath and forcing her shoulders to drop. Eli hadn't pushed. He had sat with her on the cold marble while she couldn't breathe, offered her a distraction, and asked for absolutely nothing in return. He had earned *something*. "Grandmère summoned us to her Solar this morning," Jackie continued, her tone softening, though the underlying brittleness remained. "To sign my father's inheritance documents. I'm not sure if you heard, but he died late in April of this year."
She stared out at the pond, watching a dragonfly dart across the reeds. "But that was just the preamble. She also offered to buy a property we've been trying to sell for a few months now. Unsuccessfully. But in exchange, she extorted information from my husband." The words tasted like ash, but she made herself say them. "She didn't know what secret he'd give her, exactly. But she knew it would be monumental. She knew it would be devastating. And she demanded it anyway.

Eli was silent for a long moment.

The shift in her had been instant—the peace he'd watched settle over her features evaporating like morning mist the moment Geneviève's name crossed his lips. He'd seen the snarl rise and get suppressed, the mask slide back into place, the careful control reasserting itself over something raw and wounded.

He didn't interrupt. Didn't offer platitudes or try to soften the edges of what she was telling him. He simply listened, his dark eyes steady on the pond, giving her space to speak without the pressure of being watched.

When she finished, he let the silence breathe for a few heartbeats longer.

"I've watched her do it," he said finally, his voice quiet. "Not to me—not yet—but to others. The way she takes people apart to see what they're made of. The way she frames it as *business*, as *necessity*, as simply how things are done."

He picked up a small stone from the grass beside him, turning it over in his fingers.

"My father—her youngest son—he left. Moved to New Orleans, married American money, and never looked back. I used to think it was cowardice. Running from the weight of being a Lavigne, from the expectations, from *her*." He tossed the stone lightly, catching it again. "Now I think he was the smartest one of all of us. He saw what staying cost, and he decided the price was too high."

He glanced at her profile—the defensive curl of her body, the steel beneath the softness.

"You're not wrong about the chess," he said. "She sees the board. She sees the pieces. She knows exactly how much pressure each one can take before it breaks, and she applies *precisely* that amount." A pause. "The cruelty isn't incidental. It's the point. She believes that's how you forge strong people—by burning away everything weak until only the iron remains."

He threw the stone toward the pond. It skipped twice across the glassy surface before sinking with a soft *plop*.

"The problem with that philosophy," he continued, "is that it assumes the breaking is necessary. That there's no other way to build strength. That love and ruthlessness can't coexist." His jaw tightened briefly. "I don't believe that. I've seen people forged by kindness as much as by cruelty. But Grandmère has lived too long and seen too much to believe in gentleness anymore. She's forgotten that some things, once shattered, don't come back stronger. They just... stay broken."

He turned to look at her directly, his dark eyes serious.

"Whatever happened in that Solar—whatever secret your husband gave her—that's between you and him now. She extracted what she wanted and moved on. That's how she operates. But *you* don't have to let her define what comes next."

A beat.

"And for what it's worth... you're right to be angry. What she did this morning wasn't love, and it wasn't protection. It was acquisition. She got what she wanted, and the cost was yours to pay." His voice softened slightly. "That's not something you have to forgive. Not ever, if you don't want to."

He leaned back on his hands, tilting his face toward the sun.

"The pieces don't owe the player anything," he said quietly. "Especially not the ones who learned to walk off the board."

Jackie sat with him for a long while after that, letting the quiet morning stretch between them. She turned his words over in her mind, testing their weight. *The pieces don't owe the player anything.* It was a dangerous thought, but an incredibly liberating one.
Eventually, the sun climbed higher, burning the last of the dew from the willows. It had to be approaching ten o'clock by now. Breakfast was officially over. The sanctuary of the garden had served its purpose, but she couldn't hide out here forever. She had to go back to the suite. She had to look at Theo, and she had to look at Draco.
The thought still made her chest tighten, but her hands were no longer shaking. Eli had grounded her, pulling her back from the edge of the abyss, and she finally felt steady enough to stand. It was better to rip the bandage off all at once than to pull at it in agonizingly small increments.
She got up, her bare feet pressing into the cool earth, and began brushing the stray blades of damp grass from her baby-blue dress.
"Thank you again, Eli," she said, looking down at him with profound, quiet sincerity. "You saved me a little today. I won't ever forget it."
She offered a small, wry smile, the shadows in her eyes receding just a fraction.
"If you ever need to vent about the family, I'm told I'm very good at reading letters, even when I don't respond. Supposedly, it's almost like writing in a diary."
She smoothed out the silk of her skirt, letting out a steadying breath.
"And if you ever find yourself in London, do come visit. I have friends who know the right sort of underground clubs in Soho—the ones where gentlemen prefer the company of other gentlemen. I promise you, not all Brits are as aggressively uptight as my men."
After he replied, with a final, respectful inclination of her head, Jackie turned her back on the pond and began the long walk back toward the towering stone of the Château, ready to face the wreckage waiting for her in the suite.

Eli looked up at her, squinting slightly against the morning sun. Something in his expression shifted—a quiet respect settling into the lines of his face.

"You don't owe me thanks," he said simply. "I was in the right corridor at the right time. Anyone would have done the same."

But they both knew that wasn't entirely true. Not everyone would have stayed. Not everyone would have known what to do with a woman falling apart in their arms.

At her offer about letters, a genuine smile tugged at the corner of his mouth.

"I may take you up on that. Fair warning—my handwriting is atrocious and my complaints about the family are extensive. You might regret the invitation."

When she mentioned London, the underground clubs, the gentlemen who preferred other gentlemen—Eli's eyebrows rose. A surprised laugh escaped him, warm and real.

"Jackie Nott," he said, shaking his head slowly. "You are full of surprises."

He pushed himself up to sitting, brushing grass from his trousers, and met her eyes with something that looked almost like affection.

"I'll hold you to that. London. Soho. Aggressively *un*-uptight company." His smile softened. "And if you ever need another uncomfortable bench and a ruined cup of coffee—you know where to find me."

He watched her go, her bare feet leaving faint impressions in the damp grass, the blue silk of her dress catching the light as she disappeared through the stone archway.

Then he leaned back on his hands, tilted his face toward the sun, and let out a long, slow breath.

*What a morning.*

The door clicked shut behind them, and the silence of the suite pressed in like a physical weight.

Theo stood in the center of the sitting room, exactly where he'd stopped when they'd entered. He hadn't moved to the window, hadn't reached for the sideboard, hadn't done any of the small, restless things that usually marked his processing. He simply stood there, his bandaged hand hanging at his side, his pale eyes fixed on nothing.

Jackie's absence was a void in the room. In the bond. In him.

Colette did not accompany it—her injuries from yesterday still keeping her confined—and the young servant who wheeled it in took one look at the tension in the room and fled without a word. The silver covers remained untouched. The coffee grew cold in its pot.

At half past eight, Draco finally broke.

"We should look for her."

"No." Theo's voice was flat. Hollow. "She doesn't want to be found. Not by me."

"Then I'll go. Alone."

Theo turned his head, meeting Draco's eyes for the first time since the Solar.

"And what will you say to her?" he asked quietly. "What words do you have that will make any of this better?"

Draco's jaw tightened. His ring turned faster.

"I don't know," he admitted. "But sitting here doing *nothing*—"

"Is exactly what she needs from us right now." Theo's voice cracked on the words, just slightly. "She needs space. She needs to process without my guilt bleeding through the bond, without having to manage my reactions while she's drowning in her own."

He turned away, moving finally—to the cold hearth, where he braced one hand against the mantle and stared into the empty grate.

"I did this," he said. "I broke this. And I don't get to fix it by chasing her down and demanding absolution."

Draco stopped pacing. He stood in the middle of the room, his chest heaving with the effort of containing everything he was feeling, and looked at the man he'd just admitted to loving three days ago.

"You should have told us," he said. His voice was quieter now, the fury banked into something colder. "Years ago. You should have told *her*."

"I know."

"She might have—I don't know—she might have understood. If you'd given her the chance—"

Every moment I chose silence instead of truth because I couldn't bear to see her look at me the way she looked at me this morning."

He pushed off from the mantle, turning to face Draco fully.

"I was a coward. I am *still* a coward. And now she knows it too."

The words hung in the air between them—brutal, honest, offering nothing.

Draco's ring had stopped turning. His hands hung at his sides, his expression caught somewhere between devastation and exhaustion.

"What do we do?" he asked. The question came out small. Lost.

Theo was quiet for a long moment.

"We wait," he said finally. "We give her the space she needs. And when she's ready to come back—if she's ready—we let her decide what happens next."

"And if she doesn't come back?"

Theo's jaw tightened. Something flickered behind his eyes—fear, grief, the Malice stirring in the depths.

"Then we learn to live with what I've done."

---

The hours crawled.

Draco eventually forced himself to eat something—a croissant, half a piece of fruit, the mechanical motions of someone who knew he needed fuel even if he couldn't taste it. Theo didn't touch the food. He sat in the armchair by the cold hearth, his bandaged hand resting on his knee, his eyes fixed on the door that Jackie hadn't walked through.

At nine, Draco tried again.

"Theo—"

"Don't."

"I'm not—" Draco stopped. Started again. "I'm not trying to make excuses for you. What you did—what you *didn't* do—I can't..." He shook his head, frustration bleeding through. "I can't understand it. I don't know if I ever will."

Theo said nothing.

"But I also can't—" Draco's voice cracked. "I can't pretend the last three days didn't happen. I can't pretend I don't—"

He stopped. The word he couldn't say hung in the air between them.

*Love.*

Theo finally looked at him. His pale eyes were red-rimmed, his face carved into lines of exhaustion and grief.

"You don't have to choose," he said quietly. "Between being angry at me and... the rest of it. You can hold both."

Jackie stepped into the corridor leading to their suite just as Theo emerged, walking toward the stairs. Toward her.
Her steps faltered for a fraction of a second when she saw him. The brief, sharp flicker in her mismatched eyes was the only outward gauge of her emotional state; her mental shields remained slammed completely shut, an impenetrable wall of static. She had never intentionally kept him locked out for this long before.
It took only a heartbeat for her to recover. Her gaze slid off his face as if he were nothing more than empty space, rendering him entirely invisible. She kept her pace steady, walking right past him and giving him a wide, deliberate berth to ensure not even a fraction of their clothing would brush. Then, she continued toward the suite without looking back.
She saw Draco the moment she pushed the door open. She could see he was hurting, the exhaustion etched into his posture, but she ruthlessly forced her own emotions in check. She reached for the memory of the wild grass, the swaying willows, and the quiet pond, clinging to the image as a desperate anchor.
"Before you say anything," she said, her voice raspy but steady. "I know it's not your fault. I'm sorry I left you alone with him, but I couldn't… I had to get away. I'm not angry at you, Draco, and if you want, we can talk. But I don't want…" She swallowed, her throat tight. "I don't want to be touched, or held, or pitied. Is that okay with you?"
She was still completely barefoot, the hem of her baby-blue dress slightly damp from the garden dew, but she didn't move any farther into the room. She just stood by the closed door, her spine rigid, and waited for his answer.

Theo felt her before he saw her.

Not through the bond—that was locked tight, a wall of static where there should have been warmth—but through something older. Instinct. The particular awareness of a predator recognizing another's presence.

He looked up, and there she was.

For one fractured heartbeat, he allowed himself to hope. That she would stop. That she would look at him—really look at him—and he could say something, anything, that might begin to bridge the chasm he'd torn open this morning.

But her eyes slid past him like water around a stone.

She walked by without a word, without a touch, without so much as acknowledging his existence. The deliberate distance she kept—the careful berth to ensure not even their clothing would brush—was worse than any blow she could have landed.

He stood frozen in the corridor, listening to her footsteps recede, listening to the door of the suite open and close.

Then he made himself move.

The stairs. The stables. Tempête.

He didn't look back.

---

Draco had been standing by the window when the door opened, his reflection a pale ghost in the glass. He turned at the sound, his gray eyes finding Jackie immediately—cataloguing everything in an instant. The bare feet. The damp hem of her dress. The rigid line of her spine.

The way she was holding herself together through sheer force of will.

He didn't move toward her. Didn't reach for her. He simply stood where he was, giving her the space she'd claimed by not crossing the threshold.

*I don't want to be touched, or held, or pitied. Is that okay with you?*

The question landed somewhere in the hollow of his chest.

"Yes," he said quietly. "That's okay."

He let a beat of silence pass, letting his words settle before he continued.

"I'm not going to touch you. I'm not going to hold you." His voice was steady—careful, deliberate, stripped of the aristocratic formality he wore like armor. "And I'm not going to pity you. You don't need pity. You never have."

He took a slow breath.

His gray eyes met hers, steady and serious.

"But whatever you need, Jackie—whatever helps you get through the next hour, and the one after that—I'm here for it. No expectations. No demands. Just... here."

His ring was still on his finger, but it wasn't turning. His hands lay flat on the arms of the chair, deliberately visible, deliberately still.

He waited.

The coiled tension bled out of her shoulders, and she let out a long, ragged sigh. She hadn't even realized she'd been holding her breath while waiting for his reply.
"Thank you," she said simply.
She turned and disappeared into the bathroom to wash the dirt and dew from her bare feet, then moved to the bedroom to strip off the blue silk dress. She swapped it for practical armor: black leggings and a tight black crop top. When she emerged back into the main room, she was pulling her copper hair back, tying it off into a severe ponytail.
"No, you're right," she said, picking up the thread of the conversation. "You weren't in that basement. Though I did show you and Theodore some of it in the Pensieve that one time. So I think you should have a pretty good idea of what it was like."
She approached the breakfast trolley, noticing that the food had barely been touched. Moving with deliberate, mechanical precision, she took a croissant, sliced it open, and spread the inside with butter and a drizzle of honey. She set it on a plate along with a few apple wedges—the flesh still impossibly fresh and crisp, likely the result of preserving charms or some magical trait the Lavignes had bred into the fruit. She poured some tea into a mug, continuing to talk to him through the motions to keep herself anchored.
"I don't know what to think, what to do, or how to move forward. And you're the second person today who has suggested that I should just get through another hour." She set the tea pot down. "So that's what I intend to do."
She didn't mention who the other person was. At this point, she didn't believe she owed him—or anyone—any explanations.
Finally, she carried the plate and the mug over to the coffee table, setting them down directly in front of the armchair Draco was sitting in.
"I assume you haven't eaten breakfast," she said, her tone softening just a fraction, echoing the steady care he had once shown her. "Eat. Starving yourself won't fix anything. You were the one who made sure I always ate, even when it felt pointless. Even after… when I could barely stomach anything." She met his gray eyes, her mismatched gaze resolute. "So listen to your own wisdom."

Draco looked down at the plate she'd set before him—the sliced croissant glistening with butter and honey, the crisp apple wedges arranged with the same precise care she brought to everything—and felt something in his chest crack.

She was taking care of him.

After everything that had happened this morning. After learning the truth that had been hidden from her for two years. After walking past Theo in the corridor like he was a ghost. She had come back to this room, washed her feet, changed her clothes, and made him breakfast.

His throat tightened.

"Jackie—"

He stopped. She'd asked him not to touch her, not to hold her, not to pity her. She hadn't said anything about not being allowed to feel the weight of what she was doing.

"All right," he said quietly. "I'll eat."

He reached for the croissant, tearing off a piece and putting it in his mouth. The butter and honey melted on his tongue, rich and sweet, and he made himself chew. Swallow. Take another bite.

She was right. He hadn't eaten. He'd pushed food around the plate this morning, too sick with the knowledge of what had been revealed to stomach anything. But she was standing there, watching him, and he would not let her care for him go unanswered.

He took a sip of the tea. It was perfectly steeped—she'd remembered how he liked it, even now, even in the middle of her own devastation.

"You're right," he said after a moment, setting the mug down. "I did tell you that. Over and over, in the hospital, when you couldn't see the point of anything." His gray eyes found hers. "I didn't know if it would work. If any of it would get through. But I kept saying it anyway, because I didn't know what else to do."

He picked up an apple wedge, turning it over in his fingers.

"I still don't know what else to do," he admitted. "This morning—in the Solar—I just stood there. I didn't move, didn't speak, didn't do anything except listen while he—" His jaw tightened. "While he said things I didn't know. Things I should have known. Things he should have told us *years* ago."

He bit into the apple, the crisp snap loud in the quiet room.

Interlacing her fingers behind her head, she stared blankly into the cold, empty hearth. "The second worst part is the hypocrisy," she continued, her voice hardening. "He hid it for two years. All while preaching about not having secrets. All while looking down on me from his high horse of righteousness for keeping things from you—things of a much smaller caliber."
She paused, glancing over at Draco to ensure he was actually still eating, before returning her gaze to the cold ashes in the fireplace. "And I know I'm supposed to forgive him. Because we don't know what would've happened even if he *had* looked into Fenholt. Maybe I wouldn't have been taken, maybe I still would have been. But I can't look at him right now and not see that basement. I can't look at him and not feel my body being torn apart."
She couldn't sit still anymore. She stood up, walking over to the balcony doors and pushing one open, stopping right at the threshold. The cool morning breeze drifted in. She could see the sprawling gardens and the distant roof of the stables. The faint neigh of a horse carried on the wind. "You say you're furious with him. I'm not," she admitted, the confession sounding hollow, devoid of the fire she usually carried.

But the problem is…" She leaned her shoulder against the doorframe, her mismatched eyes fixed on the distant stables. "I don't know if I can ever trust him again."

Draco set down the croissant.

*I don't know if I can ever trust him again.*

He didn't respond immediately. He let the silence hold, watching her silhouette against the balcony door, the morning light catching the copper of her hair, the rigid line of her shoulders.

"You're not supposed to do anything," he said finally. His voice was quiet, stripped of its usual careful cadence. "There's no *supposed to* here, Jackie. No timeline. No obligation to forgive, or to trust, or to feel anything other than what you actually feel."

He pushed himself out of the armchair, but he didn't move toward her. Instead, he walked to the cold hearth, standing where Theo had stood hours earlier, his back to the empty grate.

"I watched him pace those hospital corridors for three weeks," Draco said. "I watched him refuse to eat, refuse to sleep, refuse to leave your side for more than an hour at a time. I thought—" He stopped. Swallowed. "I thought he was destroying himself because he loved you so much he couldn't bear what had happened. Because he blamed himself for not finding you faster, for not being there when Fenholt took you."

His jaw tightened.

"Now I know it was more than that. He wasn't just blaming himself for not being fast enough. He was carrying the knowledge that he *could* have prevented it. That he had a name, and a warning, and he chose to do nothing because you'd hurt his feelings."

The words came out bitter. Raw.

"And you're right—that's worse than malice. Malice is at least *honest*. It doesn't pretend to be anything other than what it is. But this?" He shook his head. "This was negligence dressed up as justified hurt. And you paid the price for it."

He turned to face her, his gray eyes finding hers across the room.

She shook her head. Once. Twice.
And then, to her absolute shock, the edges of her vision began to blur. She blinked, the sudden, hot prickle of moisture in her eyes catching her completely off guard.
Theo's devastating betrayal hadn't made her cry. The suffocating terror of her panic attack in the gallery hadn't done it. Walking past the man she married, freezing him out in the corridor as if he were nothing more than empty air, hadn't drawn a single tear. For hours, her body had been locked in a state of rigid, survivalist numbness.
But hearing Draco—Draco, who had only just confessed his profound love for Theodore three days ago; Draco, who finally had the family and the acceptance he so desperately craved—offer to throw it all away and walk out that door just for her... it shattered the dam.
The boundary she had set just ten minutes ago evaporated. She crossed the distance between them in three desperate strides and collided with his chest, falling into his arms.
The impact was solid, undeniably real. She slid her arms tight around his midsection, burying her face against him, clinging to him as if he were the only fixed point in a world that had suddenly lost its gravity. The shaking started all over again, tremors wracking her spine, but this wasn't the cold, hyperventilating terror of the basement memories. This was the violent, overwhelming release of her grief.
A single tear slipped free, hot and heavy, soaking into the fine fabric of his shirt. Then another.
"You'd do it," she whispered, her voice fractured, muffled against his chest. Her grip tightened, her fingers curling desperately into the fabric at his back. "For me… You'd leave him…"
She pulled back just a fraction—not enough to let go, just enough to look up at him. Her mismatched eyes—one moss-green, one glacial blue—shone with unshed tears and absolute, staggering disbelief.
"I don't…" She swallowed hard, the words catching in her tight throat as she struggled to comprehend the sheer magnitude of what he was offering. "Why, Draco?"

Draco caught her.

His arms came around her instinctively, pulling her close, anchoring her against the storm that was finally breaking loose. He felt the tremors run through her frame, felt the hot press of tears soaking through his shirt, and something in his chest cracked wide open.

*You'd do it. For me. You'd leave him.*

He didn't answer immediately. He simply held her—one hand pressed flat against her back, the other cradling the base of her skull, his fingers tangled in the copper strands that had come loose from her ponytail. He held her the way he'd wanted to hold her for hours, the way he'd been terrified he'd never be allowed to hold her again.

When she pulled back to look at him, her eyes swimming with tears and disbelief, he met her gaze without flinching.

*Why, Draco?*

The question hung between them—raw, honest, demanding an answer that went deeper than words.

"Because you were first," he said quietly. His voice was rough, stripped of every defense he'd ever built. "Before any of this. Before the triad, before Theo, before I understood what any of it meant. You were the girl in the gazebo when I was fifteen, and I've loved you ever since."

His thumb brushed across her cheekbone, catching a tear before it could fall.

"I spent nine months away from you, trying to convince myself I could live without this. Without *you*. I told myself it was the right thing to do—that I was too broken, too complicated, too much of a liability." His jaw tightened. "And every single day of those nine months, I woke up with your name on my lips and went to sleep with the memory of your face."

He let out a slow breath.

"I love Theo. I do. What I said three days ago—about loving the monster—I meant it. But Jackie..." His gray eyes held hers, fierce and certain. "He's not the foundation. *You* are. You've always been. Everything else—the triad, the arrangement, whatever this is that we've built—it exists because you made space for it. Because you chose to love both of us, even when it would have been easier to choose one."

His hand slid from her cheek to her jaw, tilting her face up toward his.

One moment he was holding her, forehead pressed to forehead, the weight of his confession still hanging in the air between them. The next, her lips were on his, and the entire world contracted to the point where they touched.

She kissed him slowly at first—tentative, reverent, a question wrapped in the softest pressure against his lower lip. He felt the hesitation in it, the careful testing of ground that might give way beneath her feet. And something in him broke open at the tenderness of it, at the trust she was placing in his hands after everything this morning had taken from her.

He leaned into her.

His hand tightened at the base of her skull, fingers threading deeper into her copper hair, and he answered her question with his body. *Yes. I'm here. I'm not going anywhere.*

When she deepened the kiss—when her lips parted and her tongue brushed against his—a sound escaped him. Low, involuntary, pulled from somewhere beneath his ribs. He tasted salt from her tears and black tea and honey, and underneath it all, something that was simply *her*. Something he had been chasing since he was fifteen years old and too stupid to know what wanting meant.

Her hands slid up his sides, tracing paths of heat through the fabric of his shirt, pressing flat against his chest where his heart was hammering against his ribs. He felt her palms settle over the frantic rhythm, felt her fingers curl around the sides of his neck, anchoring him to her like she was afraid he might drift away.

*I'm not going anywhere*, he wanted to say. *I would burn down the world before I let you stand alone.*

But his mouth was otherwise occupied.

His free hand found the curve of her waist, pulling her closer, eliminating the last whisper of space between them. Her body was warm against his, solid and real, and he could feel the tremors still running through her—not panic anymore, but something else. Something that felt like *relief*.

This was different.

They had kissed before—in the Astronomy Tower, on the Italian coast, in the quiet dark of hotel rooms and borrowed beds. But Theo had always been there, a presence at the edge of their awareness, a third point in the constellation they'd built. Even when he wasn't physically present, the knowledge of him had shaped the space between them.

Now that space was empty.

And Draco found, with a clarity that startled him, that he didn't miss it. Not in this moment. Not when Jackie was kissing him like he was the only fixed point in a world that had lost its gravity.

He broke the kiss—not pulling away, just creating enough distance to breathe, his forehead still pressed to hers. His chest was heaving. His hands were shaking.

"Jackie," he whispered. Her name came out ragged, stripped of every polished edge. Just two syllables, carrying everything he didn't have words for.

His thumb traced the line of her jaw, tilting her face up so he could see her eyes. Mismatched. Tear-bright. Looking at him like he was something worth keeping.

"I meant it," he said quietly. "Every word. I would choose you. I *do* choose you. Whatever comes next—whatever you decide—that doesn't change."

He kissed her again—softer this time, a gentle press of lips against the corner of her mouth, her cheekbone, the space between her brows where tension still lingered.

"One hour at a time," he murmured against her skin. "And I'll be here for all of them."

Intertwined Book Four

Story date: 2001-08-08/2001-08-09
Conversation: France Arc roleplay session day 5 + 6
Author: Sable
Authority: hidden_variant

Draco let her go.

It cost him something—releasing her from his arms, watching her cross the room to the settee—but he understood. They had shared something raw and consuming, and now she needed to breathe. They both did.

He followed her, settling onto the cushions beside her with a careful distance that respected her earlier boundaries while still remaining close enough to touch if she wanted. The morning light had shifted, streaming through the balcony doors in warm golden shafts, and for a moment the suite felt almost peaceful.

Her question about the gazebo—about what happened after—pulled a surprised sound from him. Half laugh, half breath.

"Your father punished you for your *hair*?" He shook his head slowly, something between disbelief and dark amusement flickering across his features. "I spent the entire carriage ride home convinced I'd ruined everything. That you'd never speak to me again. That I'd made an absolute fool of myself in front of the one person whose opinion actually mattered."

He leaned back against the settee, his shoulder almost brushing hers.

"My mother noticed something was different," he admitted. "She didn't say anything directly—that wasn't her way—but she kept looking at me during dinner with this particular expression. Like she was cataloguing evidence." A ghost of a smile. "The next morning, there was a book on my bedside table. Poetry. Romantic poetry, of all things. She never mentioned it, and neither did I, but I read every page."

Jackie's laugh was soft, genuine—a sound he wanted to bottle and keep.

"Poetry," she repeated. "Narcissa Malfoy left you *poetry*."

"She had depths," Draco said dryly. "Terrifying, manipulative depths, but depths nonetheless."

---

The hour unwound slowly, filled with fragments of memory neither of them had ever shared.

Authority: hidden_variant

Jackie told him about the summer she'd spent learning to ride at the Taylor Estate—how her mother had been patient and gentle, how her father had been absent, how Samaya had teased her mercilessly for falling off three times in one afternoon. She described the way Amalthea used to paint in the early mornings, canvases propped against the windows to catch the light, her copper hair loose and wild around her shoulders.

Draco, in turn, offered pieces of his own childhood. The peacocks his father had kept on the Manor grounds, which Draco had secretly named despite Lucius's insistence that they were ornamental, not pets. The hidden alcove in the Malfoy library where he'd spent hours reading Muggle novels he'd smuggled in from a secondhand shop in London—a secret that would have earned him weeks of punishment if discovered. The way his mother used to hum under her breath while arranging flowers, the only time she ever seemed truly at peace.

"She taught me piano," he said quietly, the admission surfacing unexpectedly. "When I was seven. Father didn't approve—he thought it was frivolous, unsuitable for a Malfoy heir—but she insisted. Said every cultured wizard should know how to play."

He was quiet for a moment, turning his ring slowly on his finger.

"I stopped playing after sixth year. After everything. It felt... tainted, somehow. Like I didn't deserve to touch something beautiful anymore." He glanced at Jackie. "You gave that back to me. That night with the fortepiano. I don't think I ever thanked you properly."

---

The conversation meandered through lighter territory after that—favorite sweets from Honeydukes, the most ridiculous rumors they'd heard about each other at Hogwarts, the time Cole had accidentally set his own robes on fire at dinner the night before and blamed it on a faulty candle.

When the lunch trolley arrived at noon, they ate together on the settee, sharing plates of cold cuts and fresh bread and summer fruits. The food was simple but excellent, and Jackie's appetite had returned—a small victory that Draco noted with quiet relief.

They didn't talk about Theo. They didn't talk about the Solar, or Geneviève, or the wreckage still waiting to be addressed. They simply *existed* together, carving out a pocket of peace in the midst of chaos.

---

The knock came just past one o'clock.

Draco set down his tea cup, his posture stiffening slightly at the interruption. Jackie rose from the settee, crossing to the door with the particular wariness of someone who had learned to expect bad news.

The servant on the other side was young—one of the junior footmen, perhaps, dressed in the Lavigne household livery. He bowed his head respectfully.

"*Madame Nott*," he said, his accent crisp. "*Monsieur de'Medici* has asked me to extend an invitation. He would be honored if you would join him for a tour of the Château this afternoon. He has arranged for *Monsieur Bastien* to escort you to the lower levels, where he will be waiting."

The words hung in the air.

*Filippo.*

Draco had risen from the settee, his gray eyes fixed on Jackie's back. His ring was turning again—slow, methodical, the only outward sign of the tension coiling through his frame.

The servant waited, patient and impassive, for her response.

They ate together on the settee, plates balanced on their knees, trading bites of food and fragments of conversation. The name landed in the room like a stone dropped into still water.

Draco's hand stilled completely. His gray eyes flicked to Jackie, searching her face, but he said nothing. This wasn't his decision to make.

The servant waited, patient and expressionless, for her response.

Draco looked up from where he'd been absently tracing patterns on the arm of the settee, his fingers stilling as the door swung open.

It wasn't Colette. A young man stood in the doorway—one of the junior servants, dark-haired and impeccably dressed, his posture carrying the particular rigidity of someone delivering a formal message.

"*Madame Nott*," he said, inclining his head respectfully toward Jackie. "*Monsieur de' Medici* requests the pleasure of your company for a tour of the Château this afternoon. He has asked that I escort you to the rendezvous point at your earliest convenience."

The name landed in the room like a stone dropped into still water.

Draco's hand stilled completely. His gray eyes flicked to Jackie, searching her face, but he said nothing. This wasn't his decision to make.

The servant waited, patient and expressionless, for her response.

*Filippo de' Medici.*

The name sat heavy in his chest. He remembered Florence—the crimson eyes, the supernatural stillness, the way the vampire had looked at Jackie like she was something worth collecting. He remembered the two hours she'd spent alone with him while Theo fought for his life in the ring below.

He remembered that she'd offered herself to free Theo, and that Filippo had refused.

*Tell him I'm fine. I just need time to process.*

Draco exhaled slowly. He would tell Theo, if Theo came back before dinner. He would relay the message exactly as she'd given it, and he would not elaborate, and he would not soften it.

She needed time.

That was all any of them could give her right now.

---

The servant led Jackie through the Château's winding corridors, descending stairs she hadn't taken before. The light changed as they moved deeper—the golden morning glow giving way to the cooler illumination of enchanted sconces, the air carrying a faint mineral scent she recognized from the wine cellars.

They were going underground.

The servant stopped at a heavy oak door reinforced with iron bands, its surface carved with symbols that predated the Lavigne acquisition of the estate.

"*Monsieur de' Medici* awaits you in the antechamber beyond, Madame," the young man said, inclining his head. "I am instructed to leave you here. He will escort you from this point forward."

He opened the door and stepped aside.

Beyond lay a small, elegant room—more sitting chamber than foyer, furnished with deep burgundy velvet and dark wood that seemed to drink the light from the enchanted candelabras on the walls. The ceiling was low, vaulted, the stonework ancient and impeccably maintained.

And there, standing by a writing desk with a leather-bound volume open in his hands, was Filippo de' Medici.

He looked up as she entered.

As she stepped into the antechamber, Jackie had to fight the sudden, irrational urge to cross the room and hug him. She knew a embrace would be uncomfortable for them both, and she knew neither of them actually needed it. Still, the instinct was there—perhaps a lingering side effect of the vampire's ambient allure, or perhaps just the simple, grounding relief of standing in the presence of a friend.
When he spoke, a genuine smile finally broke through her armor. She remembered his voice perfectly; she heard its exact cadence in her head every time she read one of his letters. But hearing it in person—the dark, velvety resonance of it—was a thousand times better.
"Of course I came," she said, arching a copper brow slightly. "Did you expect me not to?"
But then his crimson eyes locked onto hers, and he saw right through the pretense. He saw right past the smile, the careful composure, and the surface-level joy of seeing him.
Her smile faltered just a fraction before she let out a slow, tired breath.
"Well. My Grandmère happened," she admitted, her voice losing its forced lightness. "I'm not inclined to delve into the specifics, but she did what she is evidently best at. She used secrets as a weapon and a currency, and she drove a wedge between my husband and me."
She cut the topic off there. It wasn't that she didn't trust Filippo—she did. But she absolutely refused to let Geneviève Lavigne or Theodore Nott consume this hour, too. She didn't want to spend her afternoon dissecting her trauma when she had finally found an escape from it.
"How was your journey?" she asked, pivoting the conversation with deliberate force. "I missed you at dinner yesterday."
Not entirely sure how long they had before Filippo whisked her away on this promised tour, she didn't sit. She just stood in the center of the low-vaulted room, feeling a little awkward in her practical leggings and crop top amidst all the antique wood and deep burgundy velvet. Her mismatched eyes darted around to catalog the space, but like a compass needle finding north, they continually snapped back to him.

Filippo did not move toward her.

He remained where he was—still in that particular way of his, the kind of stillness that made the air around him feel heavier, more intentional. His crimson eyes tracked her as she spoke, absorbing every word, every inflection, every fractional shift in her expression.

*She used secrets as a weapon and a currency, and she drove a wedge between my husband and me.*

He let the silence hold for a moment after she finished. Not pressing. Simply acknowledging that she had offered something real, even if she had chosen not to elaborate.

"Your grandmother," he said quietly, "has been trading in secrets since before I was turned. It is the currency she understands best—and the one she wields with the least mercy."

He did not offer comfort. He did not minimize. He simply stated it as fact, the observation of someone who had watched powerful families operate for nearly two centuries.

Then, honoring her pivot, he allowed the subject to close.

"The journey was uneventful," he said. "I traveled by night, as is my preference. The French countryside is rather beautiful when one is not burdened by the obligation to admire it in daylight."

The corner of his mouth shifted—not quite a smile, but the ghost of one. The particular dryness that surfaced in his letters, present now in person.

"As for dinner—" He tilted his head slightly, a gesture that carried centuries of aristocratic breeding. "I thought it best to allow the household to acclimate to my presence before subjecting them to my company at table. Vampires at formal dinners tend to make the soup course rather tense. One can never quite tell if the guests are nervous about the seating arrangements or the proximity of their jugulars."

He moved then—finally—crossing to a sideboard where a crystal decanter and two glasses waited. The liquid inside was not wine. It was darker, richer, and carried a faint shimmer that suggested magical preservation.

"I am your guest, *Signor de' Medici*," she said, her smile returning. "*Facciamo come vuoi tu.*"

The snort caught him off guard.

Not visibly—Filippo had long since mastered the art of concealing surprise—but something shifted behind his crimson eyes. A fractional warmth that hadn't been there a moment before. The corner of his mouth curved, just slightly, in that particular way that meant genuine amusement rather than performance.

*I think the trick is to simply accept that your jugular is never entirely safe.*

"A wise policy," he said, his voice carrying that dry, unhurried cadence. "I find it saves a great deal of unnecessary anxiety."

He watched her close the distance between them. Two steps. Close enough that a human would feel the warmth of another body, the subtle rhythm of breath and pulse. Close enough that she would feel the *absence* of those things from him—the wrongness that most people flinched from without understanding why.

She didn't flinch.

When their fingers brushed over the glass, he felt it—the brief contact, the warmth of her skin against his cold marble smoothness. He noted the way her heart rate spiked for a single beat, the ancient prey-instinct surfacing and then being deliberately, consciously suppressed.

He had felt that response a thousand times. From servants, from duelists, from the rare brave soul who thought themselves immune to fear.

He had never felt someone push through it quite like this.

Her cough at the first sip pulled another ghost of a smile from him.

"The vintage was laid down during the reign of Louis-Philippe," he said, watching her eyes water with something that might have been satisfaction. "The winemaker believed that anything worth drinking should leave a mark. I have always found his philosophy... *simpatico*."

When she spoke Italian—*Facciamo come vuoi tu*—something in his stillness changed. Not movement, precisely. A shift in the quality of his attention. His crimson gaze found hers, held for a moment, and then slid away to the velvet settee against the far wall.

"Your accent has improved since Florence," he observed quietly. "You have been practicing."

It was not a question. It was an acknowledgment—of effort, of intention, of the particular care she had taken with something that mattered to him.

He moved toward the settee, his steps soundless on the ancient stone. He did not sit immediately; instead, he waited, allowing her to choose her position first. A courtesy so ingrained it had become reflex—185 years of aristocratic breeding layered over the manners of his human life.

"I confess," he said, his voice softer now, "I was uncertain whether you would come. Not because I doubted your word—" He paused, choosing his next words with the precision of someone who understood that language could wound. "But because I am aware that my presence here complicates things. For you. For your husband. For the... arrangement you have built."

He looked at her then—direct, unhurried, offering her the rare gift of his full attention without the weight of assessment behind it.

"I did not come to France to cause you difficulty, *cara*. If my being here makes things harder, I would rather know it now than discover it through careful silences and avoided subjects."

The words hung in the air. An opening. An invitation to honesty, offered without demand.

He waited, patient as only the immortal could be, for whatever she chose to give him.

Filippo listened.

He did not interrupt. He did not shift or fidget or fill the silence with unnecessary sounds. He simply sat—still as carved marble, his crimson eyes resting on her face with that quality of attention that made most people feel seen in ways they hadn't asked to be.

When she spoke about language—about respect, about the honesty that came with native words—something flickered behind his gaze. A recognition. An old, quiet appreciation for a sentiment he had not heard spoken aloud in a very long time.

*"La gente tende ad esprimersi più liberamente nella lingua con cui è cresciuta,"* he repeated softly, translating her observation back into the Italian she had been practicing. *"È vero."* A pause. *"It is also increasingly rare. Most people assume the world will bend to accommodate them. You have chosen to bend toward it instead."*

He let that observation settle without elaborating. A compliment, but not one that demanded acknowledgment.

When she mentioned keeping his invitation secret—when she named Draco *the pale one* with that particular edge of dark humor—the corner of his mouth shifted. Not quite a smile. Something more complicated.

"Territorial," he repeated, tasting the word. "Yes. I observed as much in Florence. Your husband looked at me as though he were calculating precisely how long it would take to remove my head from my shoulders. The pale one simply looked as though he wished I would stop existing in his general vicinity."

A beat.

"I found both responses rather flattering, in truth."

But then her voice dropped. Her eyes fell to the glass in her hands. And Filippo went very still—stiller than his usual stillness, which was already considerable.

*I am really not interested in what my husband thinks or feels at present.*

He did not ask. He had already offered her the opening once; she had declined to elaborate, and he would not press. But he heard the exhaustion beneath the words. The cold edge of something wounded.

He filed it away. Not to use—never to use—but to understand.

When she looked back up, when she offered him the afternoon and her company and the quiet observation about French high society, something shifted in his expression. Subtle. Almost imperceptible. The quality of his attention changed from *listening* to something closer to *seen*.

He was quiet for a moment. His hand moved—unconsciously, perhaps—to the pocket where his watch rested. He did not take it out. Simply touched the outline of it through the fabric.

"You are—" He stopped. Started again, his voice quieter than before. "You are one of very few people who has ever considered what my days might look like. The shape of them. The hours that must be filled when the sun is a boundary rather than a companion."

His crimson eyes found hers. Held for a moment. Then slid away—to the wall, to the doorway, to the ancient stonework that predated them both by centuries.

"Emanuele fusses," he said. "He ensures I eat. He leaves books in places where I will find them. He pretends not to notice when I have read the same passage seventeen times because I was not truly seeing the words." A pause. "But he does not ask to spend time with me. He serves. It is not the same."

He turned the watch over in his pocket. The only fidget he permitted himself.

"I have not had a friend in—" He stopped. The sentence hung unfinished, its weight heavier for its incompleteness.

When he spoke again, his voice had regained some of its characteristic cadence—that unhurried, period-specific precision. But something underneath it had changed. Cracked open, just slightly.

"The Oracle's Vaults," he said. "I think you will find them interesting. The Archive of Echoes, in particular—centuries of magical impressions retained in crystal formations. Memory made physical. The Lavignes have been collecting them since before the Revolution."

He rose from the settee in a single fluid motion—that too-perfect grace she had noted earlier.

"Your company does not bore me, *cara*," he said quietly, extending his hand to help her rise. "I suspect it never could."

Jackie looked at his extended hand. Instead of taking it immediately, she finished her drink in two quick swallows, letting the heavy, burning liquid pool in her stomach and flush her cheeks, before setting the crystal glass on the side table.
Then, she placed her hand in his. It was the most substantial physical contact she had ever shared with him, and she found, surprisingly, that the unnatural coldness didn't bother her anymore. His skin was impossibly smooth, but it felt much harder than a human's should—it didn't yield under the pressure of her fingers. It felt like holding the hand of a marble statue.
Or a body after rigor mortis had set in.
"Don't be so sure," she murmured, a wry smile touching her lips. "We can revisit that hypothesis once I reach my Grandmère's age. We'll see if there's still anything remotely interesting about me then."
She allowed him to lead her toward the heavy oak door, shifting her grip to place her hand lightly in the crook of his extended arm.
"As for my interest in your days..." She paused, the rhythm of their footsteps echoing softly against the ancient stone. "I was recently told that I have a unique ability to find the broken pieces in people and show them how they fit back together. I used to think I was just trying to be someone my mother would be proud of. But... yes. There is something in me that reacts to the pain, or sorrow, or loneliness in others, and instinctively wants to fix it. It's probably that savior complex we discussed in our letters." She let out a soft, self-deprecating laugh. "Or just profound daddy issues."
They walked a few more paces before she smoothly pivoted the topic away from herself.
"So," she asked, glancing up at his aristocratic profile. "Would you be inclined to share what your… sustenance arrangements look like for the duration of your stay here?"
She deflected again, finding that dissecting her own psyche in person was significantly harder than admitting to ugly truths in the safety of ink and parchment.

Filippo felt her hand settle into his.

The contact registered with the particular clarity of someone who had learned to catalog every sensation—the warmth of her skin, the steady pulse beneath it, the way her fingers didn't flinch against the marble-cold hardness of his own. Most people pulled away, consciously or not. A subtle recoil, a fractional withdrawal, the body's ancient wisdom asserting itself against the mind's polite intentions.

She didn't.

He helped her rise, releasing her hand the moment she was steady—and then she shifted, placing her palm in the crook of his arm instead. A deliberate choice. The kind of casual intimacy that spoke of trust, or at least the willingness to extend it.

Something in his chest—long dormant, half-forgotten—stirred.

He led her toward the heavy oak door, his stride adjusting automatically to match hers. He had not walked arm-in-arm with anyone in... he did not finish the thought.

"Your grandmother's age," he repeated, that ghost of amusement returning to his voice. "You speak as though sixty-eight years is a long time. I assure you, *cara*, from my vantage point, it is barely a blink. I have wines older than your grandmother."

The door swung open at his touch—no visible mechanism, simply old magic responding to older blood—and the corridor beyond stretched into darkness. Not true darkness; the walls themselves seemed to emanate a faint, reddish luminescence, the raw quartz of the earth bleeding its ancient light into the space.

Her words about broken pieces landed quietly, settling into the silence between their footsteps.

*I was recently told that I have a unique ability to find the broken pieces in people and show them how they fit back together.*

He did not respond immediately. He let the observation exist, turning it over in his mind the way he turned over the pocket watch when something required consideration.

"Savior complex," he said finally, his tone thoughtful rather than dismissive. "That is one way to name it. Another might be... recognition. The broken recognize each other. It is not always about fixing. Sometimes it is simply about seeing—and allowing oneself to be seen in return."

"I will not press. But I notice, *cara*. I notice what you choose not to say as clearly as what you do."

She let the silence stretch for a few steps before offering him the honesty he had gently maneuvered her toward. "I will tell you why I do not like discussing my life," she said, her voice quiet but steady. "I find it to be a topic that is either remarkably dull, entirely pathetic, or outright dreadful, depending solely on which part of my past we happen to be dissecting."
A small, misty puff of her breath became visible in the chilled air. "For that reason, most of the time, I prefer not to focus on myself. I would rather be there for others.

Filippo felt her bristle—the fractional tension in her fingers, the instinct to withdraw that she consciously overrode. He noted it the way he noted everything: without comment, without judgment, simply cataloging the data for later consideration.

When she laughed, something in him eased.

"Befriending a vampire," he repeated, that ghost of amusement flickering at the corner of his mouth. "Yes. I imagine it does come with certain... occupational hazards. Chief among them: we are rather difficult to lie to, and we have a regrettable tendency to outlive the boundaries most people rely upon to keep conversations comfortable."

He matched her slowed pace without conscious thought, his stride adjusting to hers with the fluid ease of someone who had learned to move through the world without displacing it.

*Remarkably dull, entirely pathetic, or outright dreadful.*

He let her words settle into the silence between them. The reddish glow of the quartz painted shifting shadows across the tunnel walls, and somewhere ahead, the faint sound of water dripping into stone echoed like a distant heartbeat.

"I understand," he said quietly. "More than you might expect."

He did not elaborate. He did not need to. 185 years of accumulated history—brothers lost, lovers buried, friends turned to dust—spoke for themselves.

"There is a particular exhaustion," he continued, his voice thoughtful, unhurried, "in being the subject of one's own story. Especially when the story contains chapters one would rather not revisit. It is easier to turn outward. To make oneself useful to others. To find purpose in their mending rather than one's own."

A pause. His crimson eyes remained fixed on the corridor ahead.

"The danger, of course, is that it becomes a form of hiding. A way to avoid the chapters entirely." His tone carried no accusation—only observation. "But you know this already. You are too intelligent not to."

When she asked about others joining them, he heard the shift in her voice—the pureblood practicality surfacing, the awareness of optics and observation reasserting itself.

"Bastien Lavigne was to escort us into the Vaults," he said. "He manages the extraction operations—the quartz mining, the prophecy orb forging. He is... knowledgeable, and largely uninterested in gossip." A beat. "However, I arranged for him to be called away on business approximately ten minutes after our arrival. He will rejoin us briefly at the Archive of Echoes to explain the preservation mechanisms, and then be called away again."

He glanced at her—sidelong, brief, his expression unreadable.

"I am aware of how this looks, *cara*. A young married woman, alone in the dark with a vampire, while her husband is elsewhere nursing wounds of his own making." His voice remained level, unhurried. "I did not arrange this to compromise you. I arranged it because I wished to speak with you without an audience. The distinction matters to me, even if it will not matter to the people watching from above."

The tunnel opened ahead of them into a vast underground chamber, the ceiling lost in shadow, the walls glittering with veins of raw red quartz that pulsed with their own faint, internal light. The air here was colder still, carrying the weight of centuries.

"If you would prefer Bastien to remain for the duration," Filippo said quietly, "I will send word. Your reputation is not a thing I would damage carelessly."

He stopped at the threshold of the chamber, turning to face her fully. His crimson eyes met hers—held for a moment—and then, in that particular way he had with her, slid away.

"But I confess I was hoping for the afternoon you offered. The one without lines of French high society. The one where we might simply... talk."

She felt a profound, quiet relief wash over her as he acknowledged her words. This was precisely the quality that made being around Filippo so incredibly easy. He never asked her for more than she was willing or able to offer. But even more than that, she never felt as though he was *restraining* himself from asking. Draco would never push her either, but only out of love; if she offered the words, Draco would drink them in desperately, eager to understand every fractured piece of her. Filippo, however, recognized the inherent *why* behind her privacy. He understood the particular, exhausting flavor of having lived through things so devastating that merely revisiting the memories extracted a physical toll. "Thank you," she said simply, the single phrase carrying the weight of her gratitude. "And yes, I know it can be a form of hiding. Still, sometimes that is exactly what we need. To forget about the past for a moment, and just enjoy what the present can give us."
She nodded when he mentioned Bastien. Out of all her French cousins, she was genuinely glad he was the one overseeing the Vaults. He wasn't one to indulge in the petty, venomous gossip that fueled the rest of the family, and he still carried a thread of lingering sympathy for her from their childhood days. He would likely view their subterranean excursion differently than Vivienne or Francine would. Jackie opened her mouth to assure Filippo that Bastien's planned absence was perfectly fine, but the sheer magnitude and breathtaking beauty of the chamber they had just stepped into completely stole the words from her tongue. She stopped walking, her breath catching in her throat as she stared out into the vast, cavernous space. The vaulted ceiling disappeared into deep, velvet shadows, but the walls were alive. Massive, jagged formations of raw quartz jutted from the stone, glowing with a slow, pulsing, bioluminescent red light. The haunting illumination cast long, shifting shadows across the floor and reflected off the scattered subterranean pools, making the entire chamber look like the exposed, beating heart of the earth itself. It was mesmerizing.

Something shifted in Filippo's stillness.

It was not movement—he remained exactly where he was, poised at the threshold of the vast chamber—but the quality of his presence changed. The careful, measured distance he maintained with the world contracted by some imperceptible degree.

*I am not entirely sure how to interpret the fact that you would care so much about my reputation.*

He was quiet for a moment. The red glow of the quartz pulsed slowly around them, painting shifting shadows across his aristocratic features, catching in his crimson eyes until it was impossible to tell where the light ended and his gaze began.

"I care," he said finally, his voice softer than before, "because you are one of very few people whose good opinion I find myself unwilling to lose."

The words came out with that particular cadence—unhurried, precise, each syllable chosen—but something underneath them had cracked open. A truth offered without performance.

"Reputation is currency among families like yours. Like the one I was born into, before—" He stopped. The sentence hung unfinished. "I have watched what happens when that currency is spent carelessly. The doors that close. The alliances that sour. The slow, quiet exile that follows."

He turned his head slightly, his gaze moving across the vast chamber—the glittering quartz, the shadowed ceiling, the subterranean pools reflecting their own faint, pulsing light.

"I have also watched what happens when someone decides the currency is not worth the cost of carrying it." A pause. "That is a rarer thing. And considerably more interesting."

When she told him to send Bastien away, something flickered at the corner of his mouth. Not quite a smile. Something closer to recognition.

"*Bene*," he said quietly. "*Allora siamo d'accordo.*"

He stepped forward into the chamber, guiding her with him, their footsteps echoing softly against the ancient stone. The air here was cold enough that her breath misted visibly, and he noted—without commenting—the goosebumps rising along her bare arms.

"You are cold," he observed. A statement, not a question.

What surprised Jackie wasn't that he offered her his jacket. He had been an Italian nobleman long before he was turned, and she fully believed he had spent a considerable portion of his immortal life perfecting those impeccable, courtly manners. What genuinely surprised her was that he had *noticed* she was cold in the first place. She hadn't mentioned it. She hadn't even thought much of it, and she certainly hadn't shivered. The only physical sign had been the sudden bloom of goosebumps across her bare arms. It would have been so incredibly easy for a creature like him—so far removed from the frailties of human temperature—to completely overlook such a minute biological reflex. And yet, he hadn't. She looked from the heavy charcoal wool in his outstretched hands up to his face. For the first time, she truly registered the subtle shift in his demeanor. He didn't hold her gaze for more than a few seconds, his crimson eyes purposefully sliding away. It was a deliberate tell—a quiet, conscious effort to make himself appear less imposing, less threatening. Less like the lethal apex predator he actually was. When he quietly admitted that he liked the image of her wearing his clothes, she arched a copper brow. Now *that* was positively scandalous. *"Grazie, è molto gentile da parte tua,"* she said, a wide, genuine grin breaking across her face. She turned her back to him slightly, sliding one bare arm into the silk-lined sleeve, then the other, allowing him to settle the heavy wool over her shoulders. It was far too large on her, and undeniably... cold. Slipping into it felt exactly like taking a garment straight off a wooden hanger in an unlit closet; there was absolutely no residual body heat clinging to the lining. But it smelled incredibly rich— warm leather and expensive tobacco first,  underneath that, something darker: aged wood, a faint mineral coolness like stone in a very old building. No sweetness. Nothing fresh or bright. Jackie couldn't stop herself from angling her chin down just a fraction, inhaling the scent clinging to the lapel as she began to fold back the oversized cuffs to free her hands.

Once the sleeves were adjusted, she looked back over her shoulder at Filippo, the teasing grin still bright on her face despite the haunting shadows of the cavern. "How scandalous, *Signor de' Medici*," she threw back lightly. "I'd almost say you don't care about my reputation that much after all."
She didn't give him the chance to answer. With a playful pivot, she turned and marched deeper into the glowing, subterranean chamber, the heavy charcoal wool already beginning to trap and reflect her own human heat.

His dark hair was pushed back from his face, and his sharp features carried that particular Lavigne bone structure—the aristocratic angles, the watchful eyes.

When he saw them approach, something flickered across his expression. A brief, assessing glance that took in Jackie's bare feet, her practical leggings, and the oversized charcoal jacket draped across her shoulders.

His eyebrows rose fractionally.

"*Cousine*," he said, inclining his head toward Jackie. His voice was warm but measured—the tone of someone who had learned to navigate family politics by remaining carefully neutral. "*Monsieur de' Medici.*"

"Bastien." Filippo's greeting carried that particular courtesy—formal, unhurried, the cadence of someone who had been exchanging pleasantries with aristocrats since before Bastien's great-grandfather was born. "Thank you for accommodating this visit on such short notice."

"The Vaults are always available to honored guests." Bastien's gaze moved between them—not prying, but curious. The jacket had not escaped his notice. Nor had the way Jackie's hand had rested so comfortably in the crook of Filippo's arm.

He said nothing about either.

"I trust your journey was uneventful, *Monsieur*?" Bastien asked, gesturing for them to follow as he began walking toward a narrow passage carved into the far wall. "The wards can be... temperamental with visitors who carry certain... biological distinctions."

"The wards and I have reached an understanding," Filippo said smoothly. "I promised not to drain the house-elves, and they agreed not to incinerate me on sight. A reasonable compromise."

Bastien's mouth twitched. "Grandmère mentioned you had a particular sense of humor."

"Your grandmother is too kind."

"My grandmother has never been kind a day in her life." Bastien glanced back at them, a flicker of genuine amusement breaking through his neutral facade. "But she does appreciate wit. I suspect that's why she tolerates you."

The passage narrowed as they descended, the red glow intensifying until the walls themselves seemed to breathe with light. Bastien walked ahead, pointing out features with the ease of someone who had spent years learning the Vaults' secrets—the veins of quartz that ran deeper than any mining operation had ever reached, the natural caverns that had existed long before the Lavignes claimed the land above, the places where the stone still hummed with residual prophecy.

"The extraction operations focus primarily on the upper chambers," he explained, his voice echoing slightly in the confined space. "The deeper formations are too saturated with accumulated magic to harvest safely. We learned that lesson rather dramatically in 1847."

"What happened in 1847?" Jackie asked.

Bastien paused, glancing back at her with something that might have been appreciation for the question.

"A mining team attempted to extract a crystal from the Archive of Echoes," he said. "The formation contained three centuries of accumulated memory—impressions from everyone who had ever touched it. When they broke the seal, the memories... released. All at once."

He resumed walking.

"The team experienced every death, every birth, every moment of profound emotion that had been stored in that crystal. Simultaneously." A beat. "Two of them never recovered. The third spent forty years in a monastery, refusing to speak. Grandmère's grandmother sealed the deeper chambers after that. We observe now. We do not extract."

The passage opened into another chamber—smaller than the first, but no less breathtaking. Here, the quartz formations were different: delicate, crystalline structures that rose from the floor like frozen fountains, their surfaces etched with patterns that seemed almost deliberate.

"The Prophecy Forges," Bastien said. "This is where the orbs are created. The raw quartz is shaped here, imbued with the particular resonance that allows it to capture and contain prophetic utterances."

He turned to face them, his expression shifting into something more businesslike.

"I can show you the forging process, if you're interested, or we can proceed directly to the Archive of Echoes. The Archive is—"

A soft chime interrupted him. He reached into his pocket, withdrawing a small, flat stone that pulsed with a faint blue light.

"Ah." He frowned at the stone, then looked up at them apologetically. "Forgive me. There's a situation with the northern extraction team that requires my attention." He glanced at Filippo. "I trust you can navigate from here, *Monsieur*? The Archive is through the eastern passage—follow the red veins in the wall until they turn violet. The preservation mechanisms are self-explanatory; the crystals will respond to proximity."

He reached into his jacket and produced a small square of folded parchment, pressing it into Jackie's hand.
