"But the inaction wasn't even the worst part," she said, her voice dropping, growing hoarse in the dim room. "It was the silence. He watched me bleed, he watched me break, he watched me try to put myself back together for two years... and he kept that secret to himself the entire time."
She gripped the glass tighter, the restrictive corset forcing her posture perfectly, agonizingly straight. She listed every other jagged piece of forgiveness she had already surrendered to Theodore Nott over the years. The rape that was the first connection between them. The months he had secretly monitored her emotions through the soul tether without her consent. The hidden dowry clause that had financially and legally trapped her. The dark, twisted part of his soul that genuinely liked hurting her, that thrived on the cruelty. Thirty minutes later, the words finally ran out. The silence rushed back into the room, thick and suffocating. Jackie walked back to the sideboard. Her hand was perfectly steady as she poured a second glass of wine. This time, she didn't drain it. She took one small, measured swallow, letting the dry vintage coat her throat. She turned to face Filippo. He hadn't moved from where he stood near the hearth, entirely consumed by that absolute, terrifying stillness. "So, I don't have any more forgiveness left to give," she said quietly, her mismatched eyes meeting his crimson ones. "I told him to either use *Obliviate* to erase the memory of yesterday morning from my mind, or I leave. He chose the latter."

Filippo had not moved.

For the entire thirty minutes of her recitation, he had stood near the cold hearth with that absolute, predatory stillness — not the stillness of patience, but the stillness of something very old listening with every sense it possessed. His crimson eyes had tracked her movements as she poured, drank, poured again. He had not interrupted. Had not offered comfort or condemnation. He had simply *received* what she gave him, letting it accumulate in the silence between them.

When she finally stopped speaking, the quiet that followed was not empty. It was full of everything she had just laid bare.

His hand moved. Slowly — deliberately — he reached into the pocket of his trousers and withdrew the pocket watch. The one from 1870. The one that had long since stopped ticking. He held it loosely, not looking at it, just holding it. A tell she had learned to read from his letters: something had touched an old wound.

"You have given me a great deal to hold, Jacqueline." His voice was quiet. The archaic cadence had softened, as it did when he was not performing. "I find I am uncertain where to begin."

He moved then — finally — crossing the room toward her with that particular grace that made distance seem irrelevant. He stopped three feet away. Close enough to be felt. Not close enough to crowd.

"I will not offer you comfort you did not ask for," he said. "And I will not pretend that anything I say can alter what you have endured. But I would ask you something, if you will permit it."

A pause. His crimson eyes held hers, and for once he did not look away at the meaningful moment. This was not the avoidance he usually practiced with her. This was something more direct.

"You came here. Not to weep. Not to be held. You came here dressed in armor, having told them you are leaving, and you walked directly to my door." His head tilted — that fractional movement that somehow carried more than most people's entire expressions. "I do not believe you came only to inform me of your departure."

The pocket watch turned over in his hand. Once. Twice.

"What is it you want from me, *cara*? I will give you whatever honesty I am capable of. But I find I cannot give it until I understand what you are asking."

The act of expelling it all—every jagged, poisoned piece of the last two years—had actually done something. It didn't heal the crater in her chest, but it made her feel marginally lighter. More clear-headed. The suffocating pressure had lessened just enough for her to actually draw a full breath. Hearing him ask the question, her mind instantly snapped back to the violet-lit corridors of the Archive just yesterday. *What do you want from me?* She had challenged him with the exact same words. "I'm not entirely sure what I want," she admitted, her voice losing some of its earlier, rigid detachment. "The afternoon I spent with you yesterday... it was the only time I've felt *good* in the last twenty-four hours. I think I just want that."
She traced the rim of the crystal glass with her thumb, the dark wine staining the bottom. "To feel good," she continued softly. "To talk with someone who actually knows me. Someone to whom I matter. Someone with whom I don't have to aggressively guard every single one of my feelings, and with whom I don't feel the absolute, suffocating pain and anguish that I feel when I look at Theo."
She paused. Her mismatched eyes dropped to the cold stone floor before rising to meet his crimson gaze again, stripping away the last of her defenses. "Maybe I also want you to tell me I'm not a monster for deciding to leave," she whispered. "Because a very large part of me feels like I am. Like I am being entirely selfish and cruel for breaking us apart."
A small, hollow, self-deprecating laugh escaped her throat. "*Mi dispiace,*" she murmured, the Italian slipping out as a quiet, desperate apology. "*Vengo qui senza invito e ti carico con la mia storia di traumi.*"
She sighed, translating for the sheer exhaustion of it. "I'm sorry. I come here without an invitation and burden you with my trauma history."
She set the wine glass down on the sideboard with a soft *clink* and turned to fully face him, the heavy navy fabric of her dress rustling in the quiet room. "I guess I just... yesterday, down in the dark, you told me you wanted to know me," she said, gesturing vaguely to herself with a tragic, exhausted sweep of her hand. "So... that is me.

The real me. The messy, traumatized, terrified, cowardly me."

Filippo was quiet for a long moment.

The pocket watch turned over in his hand — once, twice — and then stilled. He did not look at it. His crimson eyes remained on her face, reading something there that she had not said aloud.

"You speak Italian," he said finally. His voice was soft, stripped of its usual performative precision. "You did not mention that in your letters."

A beat. Then, quieter still:

"*Non sei un mostro, cara. Sei una donna che ha raggiunto il limite di ciò che può perdonare.*" *You are not a monster. You are a woman who has reached the limit of what she can forgive.*

He moved closer. Not crowding — never crowding — but the distance between them contracted by half. His bare feet made no sound on the cold stone.

"I have lived for one hundred and eighty-five years," he said. "I have watched people destroy themselves by staying. I have watched them destroy themselves by leaving. There is no version of this choice that does not cost you something. But the cost of leaving is not cruelty, Jacqueline. It is survival. And I will not permit you to name it otherwise."

His hand rose — hesitated — and then settled, very lightly, on her shoulder. The touch was cool, careful, asking permission even as it landed.

"You came here without invitation," he echoed, something shifting in his expression. Almost amused, but not quite. "And you apologized for burdening me. As though I have not spent the last four months writing letters to you precisely because I wished to carry some portion of what you hold."

A pause. His thumb moved once against the fabric of her dress — a small, involuntary motion.

"You are not cowardly. You are not selfish. You are a woman standing in the wreckage of something she loved, trying to find a way to continue breathing." His voice dropped lower. "That is not weakness. That is the hardest kind of strength there is."

He released her shoulder and stepped back, creating space again. His crimson eyes held hers with an intensity that had nothing to do with the allure he was still consciously suppressing.

"You wished to feel good," he said quietly. "To speak with someone who knows you. To be seen without the weight of what you feel when you look at him." A fractional tilt of his head. "I can offer you that. This afternoon, this evening, as long as you require it. We will sit, and we will talk, and I will remind you as many times as necessary that you are not a monster."

He paused. Something flickered behind his eyes — a decision being made, or unmade.

"There is also the matter of tonight," he said carefully. "We had discussed — before all of this — a private dinner. A walk through the gardens after dark." His voice was measured, each word chosen. "I do not know if that is still something you want. But if it is, the offer stands. And if it is not, then we will simply remain here, and I will pour you better wine than what you have been drinking, and you will tell me about the gown they fitted you for this morning."

The corner of his mouth lifted — just barely. The faintest ghost of warmth.

"I am told the Luminary gowns this year are particularly excessive. I confess to a certain curiosity about what the Lavigne tailors have done with you."

Filippo’s words sank into the hollowest, most terrified parts of her chest, settling there with a profound, anchoring weight. *You are a woman who has reached the limit of what she can forgive.*
She closed her eyes for a brief, shuddering second, letting the truth of it wash over her. She wasn't a monster for refusing to let herself be destroyed again. She was allowed to leave. She was allowed to survive. And according to the man standing in front of her, that survival wasn't weakness—it was strength. When his cool, careful hand settled lightly on her shoulder, Jackie didn't flinch. She didn't pull back or recoil the way she had from Draco’s touch upstairs. Instead, a physical wave of tension seemed to instantly drain out of her spine. A sudden, surprising sense of ease bloomed in her chest, the frantic, panicked rhythm of her heart finally slowing down. For a fleeting second, she genuinely wondered if he was subconsciously using the allure on her to force her to calm down. But she quickly dismissed the thought. He had explicitly told her he was suppressing it, and despite her catastrophic inability to trust the men in her life right now, she trusted him. She simply felt safe here. "Yes," she said, her voice finally losing its cold, mechanical edge as she opened her eyes. "There is absolutely no reason not to have dinner."
The faintest, wicked spark of her usual dark humor broke through the devastation, and a small, genuine smile touched her lips. "I mean, obviously *you* don't have to have it, but I will need to eat actual food at some point."
She turned away from the sideboard and walked over to the sitting area, gracefully lowering herself onto a plush velvet settee near the cold hearth. She arranged the heavy navy fabric of her dress around her and looked back up at him, noting again the unbuttoned silk shirt and disheveled hair. "I do hope I didn't interrupt anything important?" she asked, the question light but sincere. She gestured toward the sideboard where she had unceremoniously downed her first drink. "And yes, a better wine would be deeply appreciated. I just grabbed the very first thing I saw when I walked in.

I needed the liquid courage." She let out a quiet, shaky breath. "Some of the wounds I just told you about are old, but they still hurt to be spoken aloud."

The wicked spark — small as it was — landed.

Filippo's expression shifted. Not a smile, exactly, but something in the architecture of his face softened. The crimson eyes warmed by a single degree.

"I was reading," he said, moving toward the sideboard with that particular unhurried grace. "A rather tedious treatise on thirteenth-century binding rituals that I have been avoiding for approximately six decades. You have, in fact, done me a considerable favor by interrupting."

He selected a bottle from the back of the collection — darker, dustier, clearly not the one she'd grabbed — and examined the label with the particular attention of someone who had opinions about such things.

"This is a 1947 Bordeaux," he said, uncorking it with a practiced twist. "The Lavignes keep an exceptional cellar, though they tend to hide the better vintages behind the merely acceptable ones. A test, I suspect, for guests who do not know to look." He poured a generous measure into a fresh crystal glass and crossed to the settee, offering it to her. "You passed, incidentally. The wine you selected was mediocre. The fact that you drank it anyway tells me you were not here for the vintage."

He settled into the chair across from her — close enough for conversation, far enough for breathing room. His bare feet tucked beneath him with an informality that seemed deliberate, a choice to be less than perfect in her presence.

"The wounds," he said quietly, after a moment. "Yes. I imagine they do."

He was silent for a beat, watching her with that particular stillness that meant he was deciding something.

"I will tell you something I have not told many people," he said finally. "When Elisabetta was dying — the last months, when we both knew what was coming — she asked me to promise that I would not spend the century after her death refusing to feel things." His hand moved to his pocket, found the watch, held it loosely. "I told her that was an absurd request and that I would feel whatever I wished to feel. She said, *'Filippo, tu menti malissimo.'* You lie terribly. She was correct. I did spend approximately thirty years refusing to feel things. It was, I can report, an exceptionally poor strategy."

He turned the watch over once.

"The point being — you have just ripped open wounds that you have spent considerable effort keeping closed. That is not weakness. That is the opposite of what I did, which was to seal everything shut and pretend the sealing was wisdom." A pause. "You came here and you *spoke*. For thirty minutes, you spoke. That is — *cara* — that is the braver path. Even if it does not feel brave. Even if it feels like bleeding."

He set the watch on the arm of his chair, letting it rest there.

"Now. The gown. I believe I was promised excessive celestial imagery and a description that would make me regret being unable to attend the daylight fittings."

Jackie accepted the crystal glass, her fingers lingering briefly in the cool space near his. She drank the dark, heavy Bordeaux as he spoke of Elisabetta. It was infinitely better than her first choice, but she barely tasted the vintage, her attention entirely anchored to the quiet, honest cadence of his voice.
As he described the woman who had died over a century ago, a profound, melancholic poetry struck Jackie. Elisabetta had been dead considerably longer than Jackie had even been alive, yet she was still vividly present in this subterranean room, kept alive simply by surviving in his memories. It granted the mortal woman a beautiful, tragic semblance of immortality by proxy. It made the cold, terrifying reality of death feel just a little less absolute.
When Filippo deliberately pivoted, asking for the excessive details of her Luminary gown, Jackie let out a soft, teasing tsk.
"It is exceptional," she promised, a genuine, albeit fragile, smirk touching her lips. "It will completely steal your breath away. It will steal everyone's. Honestly, I will likely be fending off marriage proposals for the next two years after that performance."
Her smile faltered for a fraction of a second, the reality of her shattered life creeping back in. "I mean... once Theo and I... once it is official."
She quickly raised a single finger, pointing it at him to regain the light, teasing momentum. "But, I am absolutely not going to divulge any specifics to you. It would entirely ruin the effect for tomorrow night, and I want you to be appropriately stunned."
She shifted her weight on the plush velvet, sliding further along the settee until she was leaning heavily against the armrest nearest to his chair. The movement closed the distance between them, leaving only a small, intimate pocket of space separating her from the vampire. She took another slow sip of the exceptional wine, letting the quiet of the room settle into something comfortable rather than suffocating.
"So," she said softly, her mismatched eyes seeking his crimson ones. "Could you tell me a little more about Elisabetta? What was she like? What did she like? What did she look like?"

Filippo went very still.

Not the performative stillness he used when he was being observed, or the predatory stillness that preceded a strike. This was something else — something inward. The pocket watch sat on the arm of his chair, untouched, but his eyes flickered toward it briefly before returning to her face.

"You are asking me to remember her aloud," he said quietly. "That is not a small thing."

A beat. Then, something in his expression shifted — not quite softening, but opening. A door he did not open often.

"She was — " He stopped. Started again. "She had dark hair. Nearly black, though it caught red in certain light. She wore it pinned up, always, because she said loose hair was for girls who had not yet learned to be taken seriously. I saw it down perhaps a dozen times in thirty years. Each one felt like a secret."

His voice had dropped into a lower register, the archaic cadence fading into something plainer. More honest.

"She was not beautiful in the way that word is usually meant. Her face was too sharp, her nose too strong, her mouth too quick to say things that made people uncomfortable. But she had — " He paused, searching for the word. "Presence. When she entered a room, you knew it. Not because she demanded attention, but because she *occupied* space in a way that most people do not. She took up exactly the amount of room she required and not a centimeter less."

He picked up the pocket watch. Turned it over in his hand. The gesture was unconscious — a reflex, not a performance.

"She liked cats, though she pretended not to. She kept three of them at various points and insisted they were merely tolerated. She liked mathematics — genuinely liked it, not as a performance of intellect but because she found the patterns beautiful. She liked red wine and hated white. She liked thunderstorms and would sit at the window watching them for hours. She liked — " His voice caught, barely. " — she liked being read to. In the last year, when her eyes had grown too weak for the page, I read to her every night. Dante. Petrarch. Boccaccio. She would fall asleep to the sound of the Italian and I would keep reading anyway, because the alternative was silence."

He was quiet for a moment. The pocket watch turned over once more.

"She was practical in a way that I am not. She looked at the world and saw what it was, not what it could be or should be. She told me once that my greatest flaw was that I believed in the possibility of things. She meant it as criticism. I took it as a compliment. We argued about it for approximately two decades."

A ghost of something — not quite a smile, but adjacent to one — touched his mouth.

"She asked me to turn her. Three times, over eleven years. I refused each time. Not because I did not want her forever — I did — but because I could not bear to be the one who took her humanity. She called me a coward. She was correct." He looked at Jackie directly, the crimson eyes steady. "She died on a Tuesday in November of 1923. I have not spoken of her at this length since."

The silence that followed was not empty. It was full — full of the woman who had died nearly eighty years ago and somehow still lived in the way he turned the watch, in the particular quality of his stillness, in the door he had just opened for the girl sitting across from him.

"*Grazie*," he said quietly. "For asking. Most people do not."

To sit here now, in the smoldering ruins of her own marriage, and realize that her love had been too flawed, too poisoned by lies to survive... it was devastating. But it was also profoundly comforting to know that a love like Elisabetta and Filippo's actually existed in the world. It meant the magic of it was real, even if it wasn't meant for her.

Something passed across Filippo's face.

It was not an expression she had seen before — not the careful amusement, not the predatory stillness, not even the quiet grief of a moment ago. This was something rawer. Something that looked, for a fraction of a second, like he had been struck.

He did not speak immediately. The pocket watch had gone still in his hand.

When he finally found words, his voice was very quiet. The archaic register had dropped away entirely, leaving something bare underneath.

"You are — " He stopped. Swallowed. Tried again. "I had not intended to become this affected."

A beat. His crimson eyes were fixed on her face with an intensity that had nothing to do with hunger.

"No one has offered to carry a message for me," he said slowly, as though testing the weight of the words. "In eighty years. No one has — " Another pause. The pocket watch turned over once, reflexively. "You speak of crossing the veil as though it were simply an errand you might run. As though finding her were a matter of course."

He rose from his chair — a fluid, unconscious movement — and crossed to the cold hearth. He stood there with his back to her for a moment, one hand braced against the mantle.

"I do not believe in anything after death," he said quietly. "I told her that, at the end. She asked me, and I said I did not know. It was the most honest thing I could give her." A pause. "But you — you say it with such certainty. As though the veil were merely a door, and she were waiting on the other side of it."

He turned back to face her. The crimson eyes were bright — not with tears, because his kind did not produce them, but with something that lived in the same territory.

"*Cara.*" Just the word. Just her name, in his language for her. "If there is anything after this — if there is any place where she still exists in some form — " His voice caught. " — tell her I kept the watch. Tell her I still sit with the wisteria in spring. Tell her she was right about the cowardice, and I have regretted it every day since, and I would make the same choice again because I could not bear to be the one who changed her."

"*Cara.*" Just the word. Just her name, in his language for her. "If there is anything after this — if there is any place where she still exists in some form — " His voice caught. " — tell her I kept the watch. Tell her I still sit with the wisteria in spring. "You asked what she was like," he said finally, his voice steadier now. "She was like you. Not in the particulars — she was older, sharper, less inclined toward forgiveness. But in the — " He searched for the word. " — in the *quality* of attention. The way she looked at things. The way she looked at me."

A pause. Something flickered at the corner of his mouth — not quite a smile, but adjacent to one.

"She would have liked you, I think. She would have called you *troppo gentile* — too kind — and meant it as both compliment and warning. And she would have told you, in no uncertain terms, that leaving is not the same as failing."

He reached for his own glass — untouched until now — and raised it slightly.

"To Elisabetta," he said quietly. "Who taught me that love does not require forever to be worth having. And to you, Jacqueline Nott, who reminded me of that tonight when I had nearly forgotten."

They talked.

The conversation drifted through the afternoon hours like smoke — formless, unhurried, settling into the quiet spaces between them. Filippo told her about Florence in the spring, the way the wisteria along his *loggia* had come in heavy and purple this year. She told him about Auror training, about the particular satisfaction of outmaneuvering Drake Lightwood in the dueling ring, about the complicated détente she had reached with Harry Potter. He asked precise questions — not idle, never idle — and she found herself answering with a candor she had not expected.

At some point, the wine bottle emptied. Filippo replaced it with another without comment.

She told him about the gown — not the details, she kept that promise, but the *feeling* of it. Standing on the pedestal while enchanted fabric wrapped itself around her, watching her own reflection and not recognizing the creature looking back. He listened with that particular quality of attention she had come to associate with him — absolute, unhurried, as though she were the only thing in the world worth observing.

When the light beyond the heavy curtains shifted — though she could not see it, he could feel it, some ancient calibration in his blood — Filippo rose.

"It is dark," he said simply. "Dinner."

He led her through corridors she did not recognize, deeper into the subterranean maze of the Château and then, unexpectedly, *up* — through a servants' passage, through a door hidden behind a tapestry, and finally out into the cool evening air of an enclosed garden she had not known existed.

The table was small. Two chairs. Candles that flickered in glass globes, protected from the night breeze. The sky above was vast and dark, scattered with the first stars of evening, and the garden around them was wild in a way the formal grounds were not — roses climbing unrestrained, jasmine heavy on the air, the distant sound of water from somewhere she could not see.

A servant appeared, silent and efficient, and placed a covered dish before Jackie. The smell was exquisite — roasted duck, something with figs and honey, the particular richness of French country cooking elevated to art.

Filippo's place setting remained empty.

"You do not need to pretend," Jackie said quietly, before the servant could offer him the pretense of a plate. "Not with me."

Filippo paused. His crimson eyes found hers across the small table, and something in his expression shifted — surprise, perhaps, or something adjacent to it.

"Most people prefer the performance," he said carefully. "The appearance of normalcy."

"I am not most people." She gestured to his empty place setting. "And I would rather have you as you actually are than a version of you arranged for my comfort."

A beat of silence. Then, very slowly, Filippo inclined his head to the servant. The empty plate was removed. The pretense dissolved.

He watched her eat — not with hunger, not with the predatory attention she might have expected, but with something quieter. Something that looked almost like gratitude.

"You continue to surprise me," he said, after a while. "I had thought, after one hundred and eighty-five years, that I had exhausted the category."

Jackie smiled around a bite of the exceptional duck. "I try."

The meal continued. She ate; he talked. He told her about the garden — how it had been here when the Lavignes first acquired the Château, how it had been allowed to grow wild because some long-dead matriarch had declared it sacred to something older than the family. He told her about the roses, planted by a grandmother whose name was now forgotten, tended by generations of staff who kept the tradition without knowing its origin.

When her plate was empty and the candles had burned low, Filippo rose.

"Walk with me," he said quietly. "The roseraie is at its best in the dark. The blooms hold their scent longer when the sun is not burning it away."

He offered her his hand — cool, steady, an invitation rather than an assumption.

"I find I am not yet ready for this evening to end."

Jackie felt *good*. It was a fragile, insulated kind of good, held together by the dark edges of the wild garden and the heavy Bordeaux, but it was exactly what she had asked him for. Hours of unbroken, honest conversation. A dinner entirely free from the suffocating, choreographed pretense of the Lavigne household. She could still taste the rich honey and the savory, crisp duck skin lingering on her tongue—a grounding, physical reminder that she was still alive, still breathing. When Filippo offered his arm, she took it without a single second of hesitation. She didn't just hold him politely, the way she had carefully navigated the quartz corridors of the Vaults yesterday. This time, she stepped fully into his space and leaned against him, deliberately settling a portion of her physical weight into his side. He was cold, and his body was as unyielding as marble, but he was undeniably solid. Right now, she desperately needed something that wouldn't break when she leaned on it. They walked the gravel paths of the *roseraie* for a long while, the rhythmic crunch of their footsteps the only sound beneath the heavy, intoxicating scent of the night-blooming roses. "Some part of me would like it to last forever," Jackie said quietly into the dark. It was a terrifying thought. In exactly twenty-four hours, she would be standing under the blinding chandeliers of the ballroom, trapped in her celestial gown, playing the perfect, unbroken pureblood wife for the Luminary. And twenty-four hours after that... nothing. Just the vast, terrifying emptiness of the life she had chosen to walk away from. Eventually, the winding path deposited them in a familiar pocket of space. Jackie's steps slowed as they approached the ornate stone fountain—the exact spot where Bastien had unceremoniously pushed her into the water what felt like a lifetime ago. She stopped walking, letting her hand slip from Filippo's arm to stand at the edge of the basin. She stared down at the rippling water, watching the pale, fragmented reflection of the moonlight dancing across the dark surface.

"Remember how we talked about your... feeding arrangements yesterday?" she asked softly, the sound of the trickling fountain filling the space between her words. "And how you asked me who I had in mind when I touched my neck, and I deflected?"
She didn't turn to look at him. She kept her mismatched eyes fixed firmly on the glowing, shattered reflection of the moon in the water, her heart suddenly kicking up a frantic, heavy rhythm against the tight lacing of her corset. "I had you in mind, Filippo."

Filippo went absolutely still.

Not the performative stillness of a predator assessing prey, nor the controlled stillness of a man who had mastered himself over nearly two centuries. This was something else entirely — the stillness of something ancient being caught genuinely, completely off-guard.

The fountain trickled between them. The roses breathed their heavy perfume into the dark. And for a long, suspended moment, he did not speak.

When he finally moved, it was to step closer. Not touching her — not yet — but close enough that she could feel the particular coolness that radiated from him, the absence of warmth where a human body would have offered it.

"Jacqueline."

Just her name. No endearment. No archaic flourish. The single word landed with the weight of a deliberate choice.

"Look at me."

She turned from the fountain. His crimson eyes were fixed on her face with an intensity that bordered on unbearable — not predatory, not hungry, but *searching*. Reading her the way he read everything, with that particular quality of attention that missed nothing.

"I need to tell you something before you say anything else," he said quietly. "And I need you to hear it fully before you respond."

He took a breath — unnecessary, a human reflex he had never quite shed — and his voice dropped lower.

"When I feed from someone, there is a biological effect I cannot suppress. The bite introduces venom. It is — " He paused, choosing his words with visible care. " — an aphrodisiac. Warmth. Heightened sensitivity. Lowered inhibitions. It lasts one to three hours depending on the individual. You would remain conscious. You would remember everything. But your physical state would be significantly altered in ways that are not entirely under your control."

He held her gaze, unflinching.

"I tell you this because I will not take anything from you that you have not chosen with full knowledge. Not tonight. Not ever." A pause. "You have had a great deal of wine. You have had a devastating day. You are standing in the ruins of your marriage, and you have come to me because I am safe, because I do not demand things of you, because I am outside the wreckage."

"Tell me why," he said quietly. "Not that you want it. *Why* you want it. And if the answer is honest — if it is something more than escape — then I will give you whatever you ask."

Not the creature who runs an illegal dueling ring and binds people to contracts they do not fully comprehend." His eyes searched her face. "You are saying that underneath all of that, there is something that requires — that *deserves* — tenderness. And you are offering to provide it."

His hand slid from her jaw to the side of her neck. The touch was still feather-light, still impossibly gentle, but it rested now over her pulse point. She could feel her own heartbeat against his cool fingers.

"I should refuse," he said softly. "You have had wine. You have had a devastating day. You are not in a state to—"

He stopped. Closed his eyes briefly. When he opened them again, something had shifted in their crimson depths.

"Sì," Jackie answered simply.

She lifted her hands, letting her palms come to rest flat against the center of his chest. The silk of his unbuttoned shirt was smooth beneath her fingertips, the skin beneath it as cold and unyielding as marble. She pressed into him slightly, a deliberate, grounding pressure, as if she were trying to force her own living, beating heat to seep directly through his skin and thaw the century of ice inside him through touch alone.

"I am sure," she said, her voice perfectly steady in the quiet of the garden. "I offer you my blood. However much you want to take."

She knew he needed the words to be explicit. She knew how profoundly her agency and her uncoerced consent mattered to him—especially tonight, after the devastating violations of trust she had just laid bare upstairs. His rigorous, unwavering demand for her permission was the exact reason she felt so entirely safe giving it.

Slowly, Jackie inclined her head to the side, exposing the long, pale line of her throat. Her gaze dropped from his crimson eyes to the fine weave of his charcoal shirt.

She could feel the cool weight of his hands cradling her face, his thumb resting directly over the frantic, heavy rhythm of her pulse. He could feel every surge of life rushing just beneath the surface of her skin. She was in quiet awe of his self-control. To be an apex predator, holding a willing, beating heart so close and still waiting for the final word—the restraint it required after nearly two centuries had to be staggering.

She didn't close her eyes. She didn't tense her shoulders or brace herself for the pain. She already knew exactly what it felt like to have teeth sink into her flesh until she bled; Theo had marked her like that often enough, his bites laced with dark, possessive cruelty. This wouldn't be worse than that. This was a choice. This was a gift.

Wrapped in the heavy scent of night-blooming roses and the cool anchor of his hands, Jackie simply waited in the dark.

For a single, suspended heartbeat, Filippo did not move.

His hands remained cradling her face, his thumbs resting against the curve of her jaw. His crimson eyes traced the line of her exposed throat — the pale column of skin, the visible flutter of her pulse, the absolute stillness of her surrender. She could feel the faint tremor that ran through his fingers, there and gone in an instant. The only sign of what this was costing him.

"*Grazie, cara mia,*" he murmured. The words were barely audible, spoken against the shell of her ear as he lowered his head. "*Per la fiducia. Per il dono. Per tutto.*"

*Thank you. For the trust. For the gift. For everything.*

His lips brushed her throat first — a ghost of contact, cool and impossibly soft. Not a kiss. Something closer to reverence. He lingered there for a moment, his breath unnecessary but present, a human habit he had never shed. She felt him inhale slowly, deliberately, taking in the scent of her skin beneath the lingering notes of expensive perfume.

Then his mouth opened against her pulse point, and she felt the sharp, precise pressure of his fangs breaking the skin.

The pain was brief. A bright, clean sting that flared and then dissolved almost immediately, replaced by something else entirely. Warmth bloomed outward from the point of contact — spreading down her throat, across her collarbones, pooling in her chest like honey poured into water. Her skin flushed. Her heartbeat, already elevated, kicked into something faster, heavier, a rhythm she could feel in her temples and her wrists and the hollow of her throat.

The venom.

It moved through her bloodstream with a languid, inexorable heat. Not overwhelming — not yet — but present. Insistent. She became acutely aware of every point of contact between them: his hands on her face, his chest beneath her palms, his mouth against her throat. The cool marble of his body was no longer cold. It was *contrast* — something to press into, something that made her own heat feel more vivid by comparison.

After what felt like an eternity and no time at all, Filippo pulled back.

His tongue traced the wound — a single, careful stroke — and the bleeding stopped. The punctures would heal within the hour; she would carry no visible mark by morning. "*Cara.*" His voice was rough. Lower than usual, stripped of its careful precision. "How do you feel?"

Jackie’s breath hitched, coming in shallow, heavy pants as her entire body went pliant, melting into the cool, solid lines of his frame.
She hadn't even flinched at the initial prickle of his fangs. She had survived pain a hundred times worse than that without so much as a shudder. But this—this thick, golden haze of warmth and sudden, clawing *need*—was entirely different. It wasn't just pleasant; it was intoxicating. A desperate, irrational part of her just wanted him to sink his teeth back in, to keep drinking, to press his cool hands everywhere against her fevered skin.
When the smooth glide of his tongue traced the puncture wounds to seal them, a raw, unguarded moan tore from her throat, the sound startlingly loud in the quiet isolation of the garden.
Blood roared in her ears, rushing heavily to every nerve ending. The crushing devastation of the day, the suffocating grief waiting for her upstairs—it was all drowned out by how absolutely, undeniably *good* everything suddenly felt. He was right in front of her, an anchoring weight of cool marble against the sudden inferno of her own body.
Her hands fisted convulsively in the charcoal silk of his shirt. She tried to drag in a steady breath, attempting to pull oxygen through the thick, heavy fog in her head, but the haze refused to subside. Instead, with every frantic beat of her heart, it bloomed hotter, circulating the venom deeper into her veins until the night air against her skin felt electric.
"Ffuuck," the curse escaped her as a strangled, breathless sound.
Unable to hold herself upright, she let her heavy head drop forward, burying her flushed face directly against the cool silk covering his chest.
"It feels..." She swallowed hard, her voice thick, hazy, and entirely stripped of her usual  control. "...amazing."

Filippo's arms tightened around her.

Not restraining — *supporting*. One hand remained at the small of her back, steadying her against him; the other cradled the back of her skull, fingers threaded through her hair. He held her with the particular care of someone acutely aware of his own strength, every point of contact deliberate and controlled.

"Easy," he murmured against the crown of her head. His voice was still rough, still carrying the edge of what he had just taken from her. "The first few minutes are the most intense. It will settle."

He did not move away. Did not create distance. He simply held her, letting her press her flushed face against the cool silk of his chest, letting her fist her hands in his shirt, letting her ride the crest of the venom's initial wave.

The garden breathed around them. Roses and jasmine and the distant trickle of the fountain. The stars wheeled overhead, indifferent and eternal.

"You gave me something tonight," he said quietly, his lips brushing her hair as he spoke. "Not just the blood — though that was —" He paused. Swallowed. "That was exceptional. Your magic. I can taste it still."

His hand moved in slow, careful strokes down her spine. Grounding. Anchoring.

"But you gave me something else. You looked at me and saw — " Another pause. The words came with difficulty, as though he were excavating them from somewhere deep and long-sealed. "You saw the loneliness. And instead of recoiling from it, you offered to fill it. Even for a moment. Even knowing what I am."

He pulled back just enough to look at her face. His crimson eyes were still luminous, still carrying the particular brightness of recent feeding, but underneath that glow was something rawer. Something that looked almost like wonder.

"*Sei straordinaria,*" he said softly. *You are extraordinary.* "And I do not say that lightly. I have met a great many people over one hundred and eighty-five years. Very few of them have surprised me. Fewer still have —"

He stopped. His jaw tightened briefly, as though he were catching himself before he said too much.

"The venom will last another hour or two," he said instead, his voice steadying into something more controlled. "Warmth. Heightened sensation. A certain — looseness. You will remember everything, but the edges of the evening will feel softer than they might otherwise."

His thumb traced her cheekbone. Once. A gesture that was becoming familiar.

"I can walk you back to your suite now, if you wish. Or —" A fractional pause. "We can remain here a while longer. The roses are still at their best, and I find I am not yet ready to relinquish your company."

It took a few moments, but the initial, overwhelming spike of heat and desperate need slowly ebbed into something more manageable. She still ached with a heavy, throbbing pulse, acutely aware of how warm, wet, and incredibly open her body felt beneath the rigid lacing of her corset. But her lungs finally remembered how to draw a steady breath, and the trembling weakness in her legs began to subside. She tipped her head back slightly against his supporting arm, a sleepy, mischievous smirk curving her lips. "I bet you tell that to all the girls whose jugulars you drink from," she murmured, her voice thick and languid. Her mismatched eyes found his, the smirk softening to make sure he caught the teasing edge. "All zero of them."
She felt steady enough to stand on her own now, but she didn't pull away. Not yet. She lingered in the cool, safe harbor of his arms for just another second, allowing the venom to thoroughly dismantle the tight, protective guard she usually kept over her tongue. "In another life, Filippo," she whispered, the words slipping out with an absolute, unvarnished honesty she wouldn't have been capable of an hour ago. "I would have been honored to take your contract. There is some alternate reality out there in which I do. I am sure of it."
Her eyes grew glassy and half-lidded, her gaze drifting past the charcoal silk of his shirt as if she were physically peering through the veil of time and space to experience it. "In another life, I would let you feed from me," she breathed softly. "And I would watch the wisteria bloom from the window of your *loggia*. We would let Emanuele fuss over the both of us." Her voice dropped to a hazy, melancholic murmur. "And when I asked you to turn me... you would not refuse."
She stayed in that fleeting, beautiful reality for just a few seconds more, tasting the phantom shape of it. Then she blinked, her heavy lashes fluttering as the vision dissolved back into the dark garden of the Lavigne estate. She took a slow, careful step back, finally putting a sliver of cool night air between them. "I think I had better go back," she breathed, offering a small, rueful smile.

"Before I do something both of us would regret later."

Something moved across Filippo's face.

It was not quite pain. Not quite longing. Something older than both — the particular expression of a man who had just been shown a door he could not walk through, and who understood exactly why it had to remain closed.

He let her step back. His hands fell to his sides, though the movement seemed to cost him something. The cool night air rushed into the space between them, filling the absence where her warmth had been.

"*In un'altra vita,*" he repeated quietly. *In another life.* "Yes. I believe you are right."

He was silent for a moment. The fountain trickled behind them. The roses breathed their heavy perfume into the dark, indifferent to the weight of what had just passed between two people standing at the edge of something neither of them could name.

"You would have been —" He stopped. Started again. "I would not have refused you. In that life. I want you to know that."

The admission came out stripped of his usual careful precision. Raw. Unguarded. The venom had not touched him — could not touch him — but something else had. Something that left him standing in the dark garden looking at her with crimson eyes that held no hunger at all, only a quiet, aching recognition of what could never be.

"But this is the life we have," he said, his voice steadying. "And in this one, you have a ballroom to walk into tomorrow. A statement to make. A family to face." A pause. "And I will be watching from across the room, *cara*, when you do. I will see what you become when you step into that gown. And I will remember this night — this gift — for a very long time."

He offered her his arm. The gesture was formal, deliberate — a return to the careful architecture of courtesy that had governed their correspondence from the beginning. But underneath it, something had shifted. They both knew it.

"Come," he said quietly. "I will walk you back. The venom will carry you through the corridors, and you will sleep tonight without dreaming of basements or broken trust. That, at least, I can give you."

Underneath her perfume, underneath the lingering scent of roses and night air, there was something metallic. Something ancient. Blood.

"Jackie." His voice came out rough. Dangerous. "What did you do?"

Jackie didn't flinch. The dangerous, gravelly edge of his voice would normally have sent a spike of defensive adrenaline through her veins, but the venom running through her bloodstream buffered it entirely. It spun the threat into a heavy, intoxicating heat instead. She didn't answer right away. She simply slipped off her shoes, letting her bare feet sink into the plush carpet, and reached behind her back to begin unlacing the rigid, suffocating cage of her corset. "Whatever I wished, Theo," she said, her voice entirely devoid of its usual levity, replaced by a thick, languid purr. "I do not believe I am under any obligation to tell you. But since you are asking... I gave a gift. To a friend."
With a final, deliberate tug, the laces gave way. She slid the heavy corset off her body and tossed it carelessly onto the empty armchair. She took a deep, unrestricted breath, the navy blue dress hanging looser around her now, the fabric brushing against skin that felt overwhelmingly, electrically sensitive. "I have to say," she murmured, a wicked, hazy smile curving her lips, "I do not mind the side effects."
She looked up at him. She took in the rigid tension of his jaw, the white-knuckled fists at his sides, the barely leashed violence vibrating through his entire frame. And as she looked, something deep and feral stirred inside her chest. The venom was actively burning away the exhausting grief and the crushing betrayal of the day, leaving behind a terrifying, crystal-clear realization. Theodore Nott had lied to her. He had hidden things, withheld the truth, and manipulated the board to keep her safe and close. But there was a part of him that had *never* lied to her. The Malice. It was the darkest, most terrifying fraction of his soul. It viewed her as His absolute property. It wanted her submission, it needed her with a ferocity that bordered on unholy worship, and it had never once pretended to be noble or safe. It was pure, unadulterated, obsessive honesty. It was always exactly what it was.

And right now, humming with the heavy heat of the aphrodisiac and desperate for the one thing in her marriage she could actually trust, she wanted Him to come out and take over. Jackie took a slow, deliberate step closer to Theo. Then another. She closed the distance until she was standing just inches away, close enough to feel the furious heat radiating from his rigid body. "His lips were so soft on my neck," she whispered, tilting her head slightly to expose the pale, unblemished skin of her throat where the fangs had been. Her smile deepened into something feral and deliberately taunting. "I actually moaned when he licked the spot."

Something shifted behind Theo's eyes.

The pale blue of his irises darkened — not metaphorically, but *physically* — bleeding from ice to shadow until they were nearly black. The change was subtle, gradual, like watching ink spread through water. But Jackie knew what it meant. She'd seen it before, in the heat of their most violent encounters, in the moments when Theo stopped holding the leash and let the thing underneath take over.

The Malice was waking up.

"You let him *bite* you." The voice that came out of Theo's mouth was lower than usual. Deeper. A baritone rumble that seemed to originate from somewhere ancient and hungry. "You let that dead thing put his mouth on your throat and *drink* from you."

He didn't move. Didn't reach for her. But the air between them had changed — thickened into something electric and dangerous. The predator in him was fully alert now, every sense sharpened, every muscle coiled.

"And then you came back here." His head tilted — a fractional movement, almost serpentine. "Smelling like him. Flushed from his venom. And you tell me his lips were *soft*."

A sound escaped him — not quite a laugh, not quite a growl. Something in between.

"You're trying to make me angry, *menace*." The nickname landed differently in that voice. Darker. More possessive. "You're standing there with his poison in your blood, taunting me about the sounds you made for him, and you think I don't know exactly what you're doing."

He moved then. One step. Close enough that she could feel the heat radiating off him, close enough that his breath stirred the hair at her temple. His hand came up — not to her throat, not to her face, but to the loose fabric of her dress, his fingers curling into the neckline without pulling.

"You want the part of me that doesn't apologize." His voice had dropped to a whisper, but it carried more weight than shouting ever could. "The part that doesn't beg for forgiveness. The part that *takes*."

His other hand found her jaw, tilting her face up to meet those black, black eyes.

"You want the God."

The sound that came out of Him was not human.

It was a snarl — low, guttural, vibrating through His chest and into the narrow space between them. His hand moved from her jaw to her throat in one fluid motion, fingers wrapping around the column of her neck with a pressure that was just shy of painful. Not squeezing. Not yet. Just *holding*. Claiming.

"*Puppy.*"

The word came out serrated. His black eyes bore into hers, and something in them *burned* — not with anger, but with a dark, delighted recognition. She was baiting Him. She knew exactly what she was doing. And He *loved* it.

"You think you can provoke me into losing control," He said, His voice dropping into that ancient, hungry register. "You think if you push hard enough, taunt long enough, I'll snap and give you what you want without you having to ask for it."

His grip tightened fractionally. Her pulse fluttered against His palm like a trapped bird.

"But that's not how this works, *menace*. Not tonight."

He walked her backward — one step, two, three — until her spine hit the wall. The impact wasn't gentle. He pressed into her, pinning her there with the weight of His body, one thigh sliding between hers to hold her in place. His free hand found her hip, fingers digging into the fabric of her dress hard enough to bruise.

"You came to me for honesty," He breathed against her mouth, close enough that she could taste His words. "So here it is."

His lips brushed hers — not a kiss, not yet, just the ghost of contact.

"I don't care about the vampire. I don't care that he put his mouth on you, that he drank from you, that his venom is still burning through your blood." His thumb pressed against her pulse point, feeling the rapid flutter of her heartbeat. "You came *back*. You walked through that door and you came straight to *me*. Not Theo. Not Draco. *Me*."

His teeth grazed her lower lip — a warning, a promise.

"That means you're still mine. It means you know, somewhere underneath all that grief and rage, that you *belong* to me. That no matter how far you run, no matter how many dead things you let touch you, you will always end up right here."

The question hung in the dark between them.

For a moment, the Malice was silent. His black eyes searched her face, reading the genuine uncertainty beneath the defiance. She wasn't asking rhetorically. She was asking because she genuinely didn't know the answer — and because the answer mattered.

His grip on her hair loosened. Not releasing, but easing. The hand between her legs stilled, though it didn't withdraw.

"Let you leave," He repeated slowly, tasting the words. "You're asking if I would *permit* you to walk away from me."

Something shifted in His expression. Not softening — the Malice didn't soften — but something more complex than simple possession. He was considering the question seriously, which was perhaps more terrifying than an immediate *no* would have been.

"I would kill for you." His voice was quiet. Matter-of-fact. "I would burn this entire estate to the ground if someone tried to take you from me. I would snap the neck of anyone who touched you without your consent — including the vampire, if you asked me to."

His thumb traced the line of her throat, pressing against her pulse.

"But *let* you leave?" A pause. The black eyes held hers, unblinking. "If you truly wanted to go — if you looked at me and said *I don't want this anymore, I don't want you* — I would not stop you."

The admission seemed to cost Him something. His jaw tightened.

"Theo thinks I am incapable of that. He thinks I would chain you to this marriage by force if I had to. But he doesn't understand." His voice dropped lower. "I don't want a prisoner, Jackie. I want *you*. Willing. Choosing. Coming back to me even when you have every reason to run."

His hand slid from her hair to cup her jaw, tilting her face up to meet His gaze.

"That's why tonight matters. You could have stayed with the vampire. You could have slept in the secondary bedroom with the door locked. You could have left this Château entirely and never looked back." His thumb brushed her cheekbone. "But you didn't. You came back here, covered in his scent, and you asked for *me*. Not Theo. Not forgiveness. *Me*."

He leaned closer, His forehead nearly touching hers.

"*Let* you leave?" He repeated, as though she had asked if He would let the sun stop rising. "Oh, *menace*. You still don't understand, do you?"

His lips found the hollow of her throat, pressing a kiss there that was almost tender — almost — before His teeth scraped the same spot, a sharp contrast that made her gasp.

"Theo might let you go," He murmured against her pulse. "Theo might stand in a doorway and watch you walk away because he thinks that's what you deserve. Because he believes, somewhere in that pathetic, guilt-riddled heart of his, that loving you means giving you the freedom to destroy him."

His hand slid from between her legs, trailing up her body to rest over her sternum — directly above her heart. He pressed down, feeling the frantic rhythm beneath her ribs.

"But I am not Theo."

The words landed like a death knell.

"You are *mine*, Jacqueline Nott. You have been mine since the night I first took you. You will be mine until I decide otherwise — and I will *never* decide otherwise." His black eyes bore into hers, ancient and absolute. "You could run to the ends of the earth. You could hide behind wards, behind armies, behind that vampire who thinks his dead lips on your throat make you his. And I would find you. I would *always* find you."

His hand slid from her heart to her jaw, gripping hard enough that she couldn't look away.

He didn't flinch.

The spit landed on His cheek — a visceral, desperate act of defiance from a woman who had just surrendered. And instead of rage, instead of violence, something far more terrifying crossed His face.

*Satisfaction.*

His tongue darted out, catching the edge of it near His mouth. His black eyes never left hers.

"There she is," He breathed, and the words were almost *reverent*. "There's my menace. Fighting even when she's already lost. Spitting in my face while she promises to stay."

His grip on her jaw softened — not releasing, but shifting into something that was almost a caress. His thumb traced her lower lip, smearing the moisture there, pushing past her teeth to press against her tongue.

"You called me a monster," He murmured. "You're right. I am. And you *love* it. You love that I won't let you go. You love that I'll burn the world down before I let anyone else have you. You love that no matter how far you run, no matter how hard you fight, I will *always* drag you back."

He lowered her slowly — not dropping her, but letting her feet find the ground while His body kept her pinned to the wall. The torn remnants of her dress hung from her shoulders. The bite on her neck was still bleeding sluggishly, a dark mark against her pale skin.

"You didn't want Theo tonight," He said quietly. "You didn't want apologies or guilt or promises he can't keep. You wanted *me*. The part of him that doesn't pretend to be good. The part that takes what it wants and doesn't ask permission."

His hand slid from her jaw to her throat, resting over her pulse — not squeezing, just *holding*. Feeling her heartbeat flutter against His palm.

"And now you have me." His voice dropped to its lowest register. "You've chosen to stay. You've admitted you're mine. And somewhere in this skull, Theo is *weeping* — because he knows that everything I just said is true. He knows that if he'd been able to give you this, you wouldn't have needed to come to me."

He leaned in, His lips brushing the shell of her ear.

The Malice watched her go.

His black eyes tracked every step — the deliberate sway of her hips, the ruined dress pooling on the floor behind her, the blood still trailing down her collarbone like a dark ribbon. When she pressed her bloodied thumb to His lips, He tasted it. Let the copper and salt and *her* settle on His tongue.

*Mine.*

The bedroom door didn't close behind her. He could see her from where He stood — climbing into the bed, settling beside Draco's sleeping form, her pale skin luminous against the dark sheets. The bite on her neck was still weeping sluggishly. The bruises on her throat were already beginning to bloom.

*Good.*

He didn't follow immediately. He stood in the dim sitting room, breathing slowly, feeling the edges of His control start to fray in a different direction. The hunt was over. The prey had submitted. And now, with the immediate satisfaction of her surrender settling into His bones, something else was stirring.

Theo.

He could feel him — clawing at the walls of the cage, desperate to surface, to *see* her, to touch her with hands that weren't trying to hurt. The pathetic fool had been screaming the entire time, begging for mercy that the Malice had no interest in giving.

*You wanted to let her go,* He thought, not without contempt. *You would have stood in that doorway and watched her walk away. You would have called it love.*

The response came back wordless — a raw, anguished pulse of grief and fury and something that might have been gratitude, buried so deep Theo probably didn't even recognize it.

*She's staying. She chose to stay. And it took me to make her say it.*

He moved toward the bedroom. Slow. Deliberate. Each step bringing Him closer to the bed where Jackie lay beside Draco, her mismatched eyes open and watching the doorway.

Draco hadn't stirred. His breathing was deep and even, his pale hair silver in the moonlight, his face slack with exhausted sleep. He had no idea what had just happened in the sitting room. No idea that his position in this triad had just been threatened, bartered, weaponized.

# DAY EIGHT — AUGUST 11, 2001

## MORNING — The Suite

---

Draco woke to the smell of blood.

His eyes opened slowly, consciousness seeping back in fragments — the pale morning light filtering through the heavy curtains, the warmth of a body pressed against his chest, the familiar weight of an arm draped across his waist. For a single, disoriented moment, everything felt almost normal.

Then his vision cleared.

Jackie was curled between them, her dark hair fanned across the pillow, her breathing slow and even with sleep. Her back was pressed against someone else — Theo, whose arm was wrapped around her waist, whose face was buried in the curve of her neck.

But that wasn't what made Draco's breath catch.

It was the bruises.

Dark, mottled purple bloomed across Jackie's throat — the unmistakable pattern of fingers, of a hand that had squeezed hard enough to leave marks that would last for days. And on her neck, just below her jaw, a bite wound. Not the neat punctures she'd carried from whatever had happened last night before she returned — this was something else. Ragged. Possessive. The kind of mark that was meant to be seen.

Draco's hand moved before his mind caught up, his fingers hovering over the bruises without quite touching. His chest had gone tight, his breathing shallow.

*What happened?*

His eyes tracked to Theo — still sleeping, his face slack, his arm curled around Jackie with a possessiveness that looked almost protective. But something was wrong there too. Theo's knuckles were raw. His shirt was gone. And there was blood — dried, dark — smeared across his jaw and the corner of his mouth.

*Her blood.*

The realization landed like a physical blow. Draco's stomach turned. He pulled his hand back, his fingers curling into a fist against the sheets.

He'd been *asleep*. He'd been right here, in this bed, and something had happened — something violent, something that left Jackie looking like she'd been mauled — and he hadn't woken up. Hadn't heard it. Hadn't known.

His eyes moved back to Jackie's face. In sleep, she looked almost peaceful. The tension that had been living in her jaw for days was finally absent. Her lips were slightly parted, her breathing deep and even. Whatever had happened, she was *here*. She hadn't left. She hadn't run.

*She came back to this bed.*

The thought should have been comforting. It wasn't.

Draco lay very still, watching the slow rise and fall of her chest, watching Theo's arm tighten fractionally around her waist in sleep. The morning light crept across the sheets, illuminating the damage in stark, unforgiving detail.

He didn't know what had happened. He didn't know if he wanted to.

But he knew, with absolute certainty, that something had shifted in the night. Something had cracked open between Jackie and Theo — or perhaps between Jackie and the thing that lived inside Theo, the thing Draco had glimpsed but never fully witnessed. And whatever it was, it had left marks that would take a long time to fade.

---

Theo surfaced slowly.

The transition was not gentle. One moment He was there — the Malice, coiled around Jackie in the dark, satisfied and watchful — and the next, Theo was clawing his way back to consciousness through a fog of exhaustion and something that felt almost like grief.

His body registered information before his mind caught up. The warmth of Jackie's skin against his chest. The scent of her — blood and roses and something underneath that was just *her*. The weight of his arm around her waist, holding her close.

Then he opened his eyes.

The first thing he saw was the bite mark on her neck.

*His* bite mark. The Malice's bite mark. Dark and ragged and still faintly swollen, positioned directly over where the vampire's fangs had been. A territorial claim. An overwrite.

The second thing he saw was Draco.

Grey eyes, wide and horrified, staring at him across Jackie's sleeping form. Draco's face was pale, his jaw tight, his hand fisted in the sheets like he was physically restraining himself from reaching out.

*He sees it. He sees what I did.*

She did not pull her shields up. She let Theo flow into her, and let herself spill into him in a steady hum. She almost moaned at the *correctness* of the bond being open. He could feel the lack of anger in her, but also the lack of remorse.

The tether slammed open.

Theo gasped — a raw, involuntary sound — as Jackie flooded into him for the first time in days. The absence had been agony, a phantom limb that ached with every breath, and now suddenly she was *there*. Warm and present and so achingly *real* that his eyes burned with the force of it.

No anger. That was the first thing he registered. The white-hot fury that had been radiating from her since the Solar was simply... absent. Not suppressed, not walled off. *Gone*.

But there was no remorse either. No guilt over what had happened in the night, no shame about the choices she'd made. Just a steady, humming warmth — and underneath it, something that felt almost like *relief*.

She was staying. She had chosen to stay. And she was letting him feel that choice, letting him know it in his bones rather than just his ears.

*But she chose Him. Not me. Him.*

The thought cut through the relief like a blade. Theo could still feel the echo of the Malice's satisfaction, His dark pleasure at having won what Theo had been too weak to claim. The monster had given her what she needed — honesty, possession, the absolute certainty that she would never be let go — and Theo had watched from the cage, screaming, while it happened.

Draco was still staring at him. Grey eyes wide, horrified, demanding an answer to a question Theo didn't know how to answer.

*What did you do to her?*

"I —" Theo's voice came out wrecked. He swallowed, tried again. "She asked for Him."

The words landed in the quiet morning air. Draco's expression flickered — confusion first, then something darker as comprehension began to dawn.

"She came back last night," Theo continued, his voice barely above a whisper. "Smelling like vampire. His venom in her blood. And she —" His jaw tightened. "She didn't want me. She wanted the part of me that doesn't apologize. The part that doesn't lie. The part that would never let her go."

Theo felt like he'd been eviscerated.

She was *settled*. He could feel it through the bond — the ease in her body, the comfort of being claimed, the particular warmth of a woman who had found something she could trust. And it wasn't him. It was the thing that lived inside him. The monster he'd spent years trying to leash, to contain, to keep from destroying everything he loved.

And she *trusted* it more than she trusted him.

*"He would've used the Obliviate."*

The words landed like a blow to the sternum. Because it was true. The Malice had said as much last night — had told her, in that deep, ancient voice, that He would have carved the memory from her mind without a moment's hesitation. Because she was *His*. Because keeping her was the only thing that mattered.

Theo had refused. Theo had knelt on the carpet and *begged* her not to ask him to violate her again. He'd thought — stupidly, naively — that the refusal was the right thing. The noble thing. The thing that proved he was more than what his father had made him.

And she'd wanted the monster instead.

Draco hadn't moved. He was frozen on the other side of Jackie, his grey eyes tracking between them, his face a careful mask that didn't quite hide the horror underneath. He'd heard everything. He was hearing everything now. And Theo could see the questions forming behind those storm-colored eyes — questions about what the Malice was, about what Theo had done in the past, about the thing that lived inside the man Draco had said he loved.

"Jackie." Theo's voice came out rough, scraped raw. "You understand what you're saying. You're telling me that the part of me that *hurts* you — the part that doesn't care about your consent, your comfort, your *choices* — is the part you trust."

He sat up slowly, the sheets pooling at his waist. His hand found her jaw — gentle, so gentle, nothing like the grip the Malice had used — and tilted her face toward him.

"I'm glad you're staying." The words were quiet. Honest. "I would have — I don't know what I would have done if you'd left. But *menace* —"

His thumb traced the edge of the bruises on her throat. His bruises. *His* bruises.

Theo felt her question land in his mind like a stone dropped into still water.

*Do you think Malice would like it?*

The intimacy of it — the casual, almost playful tone, the first words she'd sent through the bond since Thursday morning — cracked something open in his chest. She was *talking* to him again. Not just aloud, not just through the careful architecture of words, but *inside*. In the place that belonged only to them.

And she was asking about *Him*.

Theo closed his eyes. He could feel the Malice stirring somewhere in the dark of his psyche — not surfacing, not taking control, but *listening*. Aware. Pleased.

*He would love it.*

The thought came unbidden, half his own and half something else. The Malice's satisfaction bleeding through the walls Theo usually kept between them.

*He would want everyone in that room to see what He did to you. To know that you belong to Him. To see the proof written on your skin.*

Theo opened his eyes. Jackie was standing in the bathroom doorway, her reflection visible in the mirror beyond — the dark bruises, the ragged bite, the pale expanse of skin marked and claimed. She looked like something out of a war zone. She looked like something that had been *owned*.

He sent the answer through the bond, letting her feel the truth of it alongside his own complicated tangle of emotions.

*He would be insufferable about it. He would spend the entire evening watching people notice and knowing exactly what they were thinking. He would consider it a declaration of war against everyone who ever thought they might have a claim on you.*

A pause. Then, quieter:

*But the Luminary is Geneviève's event. And your grandmother's opinion of this triad matters to you.*

He sat up fully, swinging his legs over the edge of the bed. Draco still hadn't moved — still frozen, still watching, still processing everything he'd heard and seen. Theo could feel the weight of Draco's gaze on his back.

*What do you want, menace?*

He sent it through the bond, but he also said it aloud — for Draco's benefit, so he wasn't entirely shut out of the conversation happening in their heads.

"What do you want, Jackie? The marks, or the performance?"

Draco's jaw tightened.

He reached for his wand — the movement mechanical, automatic — but his eyes stayed fixed on Jackie's face. On the bruises ringing her throat. On the ragged bite wound that looked like something out of a nightmare.

*Cassius would be proud.*

The words landed like acid. She'd said it deliberately — a needle slipped between Theo's ribs, a reminder that the violence he carried came from somewhere, from *someone*, and that the Malice's particular brand of possession had a lineage. Draco didn't miss the flinch that passed across Theo's expression, there and gone in an instant.

He didn't understand everything that had happened last night. He'd heard words — *the God of Malice*, *He would've used the Obliviate*, *I trust His obsession* — and he'd seen the aftermath written on Jackie's skin. But the full picture remained fractured, pieces of a mosaic he couldn't quite assemble.

What he did understand was this: Jackie had come back. She was sitting on his side of the bed, asking him to heal her, looking at him with those mismatched eyes that carried exhaustion and ease in equal measure. She was *here*.

And whatever had happened between her and the thing inside Theo, it had brought her back to this bed instead of driving her away from it.

"Hold still," he said quietly.

He lifted his wand, the tip hovering over the worst of the bruising on her throat. The healing charm came out steady — *Episkey*, then a more complex incantation for the deeper tissue damage. The purple faded to yellow, then to nothing. The bite wound knitted closed, the ragged edges smoothing into fresh pink skin that would be invisible within the hour.

He worked in silence, methodical and precise. Each spell erased another piece of evidence, another mark of whatever had transpired while he slept three feet away.

When he finished, he set the wand down. His hand hovered near her jaw — hesitant, uncertain — before settling against her cheek. His thumb traced the spot where the worst bruise had been.

"You're really staying," he said. Not a question. A confirmation. Something he needed to hear himself say aloud to believe it.

His grey eyes flickered to Theo, then back to Jackie.

"Both of you are going to explain this to me. All of it. The — the *Malice*, or whatever it is. What happened last night. What it means." His voice was carefully controlled, but something underneath it trembled. "But not now. Not before the Luminary. I can't —"

He stopped. Swallowed.

"I can't process this and perform at the same time. So we're going to get dressed. We're going to walk into that ballroom. And tonight, after it's over, you're going to tell me everything."

His hand dropped from her face.

"Can you do that? Can we do that?"

The silence that followed was deafening.

Theo felt the information land in his chest like a second blow — not because he hadn't known, but because hearing her say it so *casually*, as though it were simply another item on a list of things to be aware of, made it real in a different way. He'd smelled the vampire on her last night. He'd known what had happened. But hearing her *say* it, while biting into a croissant and pouring coffee, while the Malice's marks were still fresh beneath the healed skin —

*She gave him her vein. Willingly. As a gift.*

The Malice stirred, somewhere deep. A low rumble of territorial displeasure that Theo had to consciously push back down. *Not now. Not today.*

Draco had gone very still beside him. His grey eyes were fixed on the doorway where Jackie had disappeared, his expression carefully blank in a way that meant everything underneath was in freefall.

"She —" Draco's voice came out strangled. He stopped. Tried again. "She let the *vampire* feed from her."

"Yes." Theo's voice was flat. Controlled. The only alternative was letting the Malice's possessive fury bleed through, and they didn't have time for that. "Before she came back to the suite last night. That's why —"

He didn't finish the sentence. He didn't need to. *That's why she smelled like him. That's why the venom was in her blood. That's why she came to me flushed and wanting and asked for the part of me that doesn't apologize.*

Draco's jaw worked. His hands were fisted in the sheets, knuckles white.

"And we're just —" He gestured vaguely toward the sitting room, toward where Jackie was eating her croissant as though the world hadn't tilted on its axis. "We're just *accepting* this? She gave her blood to a vampire, came back here and let you — let *Him* —" He couldn't finish that sentence either. "And now we're going to get dressed and attend a ball?"

Theo rose from the bed. His body ached — the particular exhaustion that came after the Malice surfaced and then retreated, leaving Theo to deal with the aftermath. He crossed to where his trousers lay crumpled on the floor and pulled them on.

"Yes," he said quietly. "That's exactly what we're doing."

## AFTERNOON — The Receiving Line & Preparations

---

The Lavigne receiving line stretched through the grand entrance hall like a river of silk and old money.

Draco stood between Jackie and Theo, his spine a perfect line, his expression carved from marble. The white celestial suit fit him like armor — luminous ivory, gold embroidery radiating across his chest, the flowing cape of lavender and starlit blue trailing behind him. He looked untouchable. He looked exactly like a Malfoy.

It was, perhaps, the most exhausting performance of his life.

"Ah, *Monsieur Malfoy*." The French Ministry official's smile didn't reach his eyes. "Your father and I crossed paths once. At a conference in Geneva. Before the... unpleasantness."

"How fortunate for you," Draco replied, his voice smooth as glass. "I trust the memory serves you well."

The official's smile faltered. Draco inclined his head — a dismissal wrapped in courtesy — and the man moved on.

Three more guests. Five. A dozen. Each one carrying the weight of the Malfoy name in their eyes, calculating what it meant that Lucius's son was standing in the Lavigne receiving line, presented by the matriarch herself as the partner of her granddaughter. Some were curious. Some were contemptuous. A few looked almost sympathetic, which was somehow worse.

Draco let none of it touch him. He kept the mask perfect, impenetrable, answering each veiled slight with the particular cold courtesy that had been drilled into him since childhood. *A Malfoy does not flinch. A Malfoy does not explain. A Malfoy simply is.*

But through it all, he felt Theo's shoulder brush his — a grounding pressure — and Jackie's hand find his for a fraction of a second between guests. Small anchors. Enough to keep him upright.

---

Samaya appeared halfway through the afternoon, resplendent in emerald silk that matched her sharp, assessing eyes.

She kissed Jackie on both cheeks — lingering, deliberate, the particular warmth of a sister who had been worried. Her hand squeezed Jackie's arm, her voice dropping to a murmur that Theo couldn't quite catch.

Then she turned to the men.
